More certainly and more safely, by its rule, not the Lesbian one, we should both execute and judge the things that demand the ornament of thought, § 70.

> § 76. Neque vanus augur arbitror fore, si praedixerim, quod aliquibus exemplis iam expertus scribo, per eandem se viam non paucis ingeniis, non paruis, erectioribusque animis commendatura bona liberalium studia, vt [p. 34] non puerilia tantum, sed et viris, iisque sapientibus, digna, sicuti sint, videantur, eoque moueant, vt vel ipsi audeant aliquid noui et egregii in aestheticis exercitiis vel saltim de artibus eo ducentibus moderatius, aequius, honorificentius iudicent, de applicationibus earundem, vti iudices, bene satis instructi, magisque competentes. §. 70.

§ 76. Nor do I think I shall be a vain augur, if I foretell, what I write having already learned by experience from some examples, that by the same way the good liberal studies will commend themselves to not a few wits, and those not small, and to loftier minds, so that [p. 34] they appear, as they are, worthy not only of boys but also of men, and of wise ones, and move them to the point that either they themselves dare something new and outstanding in aesthetic exercises or at least judge more moderately, more fairly, more honourably of the arts that lead thither, and of their applications, as judges well enough instructed and more competent. § 70.

> § 77. Iterum moneo. Ille ego non sum qui aesthetica scientia, quasi numeris omnibus absolutum, mihi vel aliis fingam ingenium generatim venustum, vel omnino speciatim laudabilem oratorem, poëtam, musicum e. c. Jam postulaui, ante theoriam eiusmodi, naturam, ingenium, indolem, exercitia, culturam iugenii [sic: ingenii] nunc sine aliqua eruditione vix satis impetrandam, regularum pulcre cogitandi peritiam, quam vnice probaui vere praestare, si sit prima saltim et primaria sua ex parte scientia. Nunc denuo postulo correctiora ac certiora illa exercitia, de quibus §. 58. in quibus nulla dies sine linea, sine quibus mortuas ipse speculatiuasque, quas vocant, regulas, vtiles quidem, quibus tamen non vtaris, nunquam edico profuturas, eo, quo maxime debent. Nec ita multa post plura postulabo. Postulabit recte adhuc plura specialem felicis aesthetici characterem informaturus. §. 27.

§ 77. Again I warn. I am not the one who, by the aesthetic science, as if it were complete in every respect, would feign for myself or others a wit charming in general, or at all a specifically praiseworthy orator, poet, musician, etc. I have already demanded, before a theory of this kind, nature, wit, disposition, exercises, a culture of wit now scarcely to be obtained sufficiently without some erudition, a skill in the rules of thinking beautifully, which I have only proved to be truly excellent if it is a science at least in its first and principal part. Now I demand anew those more correct and more certain exercises, of which § 58, in which no day passes without a line, without which I declare that the dead and speculative rules, as they call them, useful indeed, but which you do not use, will never profit there where they most ought to. Nor shall I thereafter demand so many more. He who is to form the special character of the happy aesthetician will rightly demand still more. § 27.

[p. 35]

#### Sectio V. Impetus Aestheticus. — Section V. Aesthetic Impetus.

> § 78. Ad characterem felicis aesthetici generalem §. 27. requiritur IV. IMPETVS AESTHETICVS (pulcra mentis incitatio, inflammatioque, ὁρμή, ecstasis, furor, ἐνθουσιασμός, πνεῦμα θεοῦ), cuius haec est genesis: Excitatior natura, S. II. iam in ipsis αὐτοσχεδιάσμασι, S. III. magis adiuta doctrinis ingenium acuentibus et magnam animam nutrientibus, S. IIII. pro positu corporis, animaeque statu antecedente, M §. 512, 596. fauentibus circumstantiis, M. §. 323. iam ad ipsum pulcre cogitandi actum facultates suas inferiores, habitus, vires, huc vsque mortuas, M. §. 220, eo intendit, vt maiores consensu phaenomeno viuant, quam quas multi alii circa idem thema, vel ipse homo, non ita concitus alio tempore, possent exhibere, atque adeo dent effectus his suis viribus viuis aequales, viribus ordinariis maiores, et ad eas se circiter habentes, vti quadratum ad radicem. Status animae, cuius genesin descripsi, est ipsa illa ὁρμή, cuius antea dixi varias pro graduum diuersitate denominationes.

§ 78. For the general character of the happy aesthetician, § 27, there is required IV. AESTHETIC IMPETUS (the beautiful arousal and inflammation of the mind, ὁρμή [impulse], ecstasy, frenzy, ἐνθουσιασμός [enthusiasm], πνεῦμα θεοῦ [the spirit of God]), whose genesis is this: a more excitable nature, S. II, already in its very αὐτοσχεδιάσμασι [improvisations], S. III, further aided by doctrines sharpening the wit and nourishing a great soul, S. IIII, according to the posture of the body and the preceding state of the soul, M. § 512, 596, with favouring circumstances, M. § 323, now strains its lower faculties, habits and powers, until now dead, M. § 220, towards the very act of thinking beautifully, to such a degree that they live greater, in the consensus of the phenomenon, than those which many others could exhibit on the same theme, or the man himself, when not so aroused at another time, and so give effects equal to these living powers of his, greater than his ordinary powers, and standing to them roughly as the square to the root. The state of the soul whose genesis I have described is that very ὁρμή [impulse], of which I earlier gave the various denominations according to the diversity of its degrees.

> [p. 36] § 79. In minoribus huius feruoris gradibus, effectus vi mentis ordinaria maior, vt talis, non patet omnibus, si vere tamen adfuerit ὁρμή, eueniet tentanti, dum friget,

[p. 36] § 79. In the lesser degrees of this fervour, the effect greater than the ordinary force of the mind, as such, is not evident to all; yet if the ὁρμή [impulse] has truly been present, it will come about for one who tries, while he is cold,

> *Vt sibi quiuis* / *Speret idem, sudet multum frustraque laboret* / *Ausus idem.* Hor.

*that anyone may hope* / *the same for himself, may sweat much and labour in vain* / *having dared the same.* Hor.

> Character eius apud ipsum iustum sui aestimatorem, eo non nunquam corripiendum, erit, 1) si e. g. scripta sua, dum scribit, et immediate post conceptionem ipsi minus placeant, ac post aliquid temporis heterogeneis occupationibus insumti: 2) ipsa maior celeritas, character etiam virium viuarum in physicis.

Its character, for one who is a just estimator of himself, which one must sometimes be seized by, will be, 1) if e.g. his own writings, while he writes and immediately after their conception, please him less than after some time spent in heterogeneous occupations: 2) the greater speed itself, which is also the character of living forces in physics.

> § 80. Psychologis patet in tali impetu totam quidem animam vires suas intendere, maxime tamen facultates inferiores, ita, vt omnis quasi fundus animae, M. §. 511. surgat nonnihil altius, et maius aliquid spiret, pronusque suppeditet, quorum obliti, quae non experti, quae praeuidere non posse nobis ipsis, multo magis aliis, videbamur. Hic animae fundus quum a multis adhuc ignoretur, etiam philosophis, effectus eius extraordinarius, quem §. 78. descripsimus, diis adscriptus est auctoribus, secundum illud Lucretii:

§ 80. It is evident to psychologists that in such an impetus the whole soul indeed strains its powers, but most of all the lower faculties, so that the whole ground, as it were, of the soul, M. § 511, rises somewhat higher, and breathes something greater, and readily supplies things which we had forgotten, which we had not experienced, which we seemed unable to foresee for ourselves, much less for others. Since this ground of the soul is still unknown to many, even philosophers, its extraordinary effect, which we described in § 78, has been ascribed to the gods as its authors, according to that saying of Lucretius:

> *Ignorantia caussarum conferre deorum* / [p. 37] *Cogit ad imperium res, et concedere regnum, vt* / *Quorum operum caussas nulla ratione videre* / *Possunt, haec fieri diuino numine rentur.*

*Ignorance of causes compels them to assign things* / [p. 37] *to the sway of the gods and to concede them the kingdom, so that* / *the things whose causes they can in no way see* / *they think are brought about by divine power.*

> § 81. Lustremus aliquas incitationis eiusmodi opportunitates pro positu corporis aut aucupandas, aut saltim oblatas arripiendas, in quibus *aut nunc, aut nunquam.* Eo refero 1) motionem agitationemque corporis, praesertim non nihil melancholici, e. g. perequitationem celeriorem. §. 46. Hinc forte pegasus hippocrenen recludens, hinc tot in itineribus carmina scripta. *Mirum est, vt animus agitatione motuque corporis excitetur.* Plin. L. I. ep. 6.

§ 81. Let us survey some opportunities for arousal of this kind, according to the posture of the body, either to be sought out or at least seized when offered, in which it is *now or never.* I refer hither 1) the motion and agitation of the body, especially of a somewhat melancholic body, e.g. a rather swift ride on horseback. § 46. Hence perhaps Pegasus opening Hippocrene, hence so many poems written on journeys. *It is wonderful how the mind is aroused by the agitation and motion of the body.* Plin. L. I. ep. 6.

> § 82. 2) Occasio impetus ad venuste cogitandum est, status animae, in quo praeuisio praesagiumque naturaliter faciliores sunt, M. §. 602, ad eleganter cogitanda praesertim necessariae vires, ordinario maxime debiles, §. 39. M. §. 597, et mens sana in corpore sano, E. §. 254, per venustum alterius ingenium ad imitationem inclinatur, §. 56, 44. Hac ratione excitatus Φοιβόληπτος est. Ita, circa criticas huius vitae vicissitudines, instante magna mutatione, plurimum habitura momenti;

§ 82. 2) An occasion of the impetus to think charmingly is the state of the soul in which foresight and presentiment are naturally easier, M. § 602, powers especially necessary for the things to be thought elegantly, ordinarily most feeble, § 39, M. § 597, and a sound mind in a sound body, E. § 254, is inclined to imitation by the charming wit of another, § 56, 44. One aroused in this manner is Φοιβόληπτος [seized by Phoebus]. So, around the critical vicissitudes of this life, when a great change is at hand, that will have very great moment;

> *poscere fata* / *Tempus erit. Deus, ecce, deus!* §. 80.

*the time will come* / *to demand the fates. A god, behold, a god!* § 80.

> [p. 38] § 83. 3) Historiae (Clio), etiam fictae, praesertim heroicae, (Calliope), vel tristioris (Melpomene), vel laetioris euentus (Thalia), musicae, (Terpsichore) saltationes, (Erato) picturae, (Polyhymnia) et quaeuis liberalium artium specimina, dum ad aemulandum prouocant, ipsa natura extra nos positorum, dum vel amabiliter ludit, vel maioribus mundi e. g. solis, spectaculis in stuporem rapit. (Vranie), §. 82. Hac ratione concitatus μουσόληπτος καὶ μουσοπάτακτος est. Hinc Musae non minus, ac Gratiae, sociae sunt, neque bene diuelluntur. Vna florente e. g. circa tempora Alexandri M. Augusti, Ludouici XIIII. floruerunt etiam aliae.

[p. 38] § 83. 3) Histories (Clio), even fictitious ones, especially heroic (Calliope), whether of sadder (Melpomene) or of happier outcome (Thalia), music (Terpsichore), dances (Erato), pictures (Polyhymnia) and any specimens of the liberal arts, while they provoke to emulation, the very nature of the things placed outside us, while it either plays amiably or sweeps us into amazement with the greater spectacles of the world, e.g. of the sun (Urania), § 82. One aroused in this manner is μουσόληπτος καὶ μουσοπάτακτος [seized and struck by the Muses]. Hence the Muses, no less than the Graces, are companions, and are not well torn apart. When one flourished, e.g. around the times of Alexander the Great, of Augustus, of Louis XIIII, the others flourished too.

> § 84. 4) Otium comparatiuum, E. §. 267. M. §. 638. quando mens curis soluta laborum negotiorumque reponit onus et per amoena §. 83. ambulacra temere errans, §. 81. serena patet in secessu diuinis afflatibus, §. 80. Hoc forsan est in Helicone pascere, somniare in Parnasso. *O! dulce otium honestumque, ac paene omni negotio pulcrius! o! mare! o! littus! verum secretumque μουσεῖον! quam multa inuenitis! quam multa dictatis!* Plin. L. I. ep. 9.

§ 84. 4) Comparative leisure, E. § 267, M. § 638, when the mind, released from cares, lays down the burden of labours and business and, wandering at random through pleasant walks, § 83, § 81, lies serenely open in retirement to divine inspirations, § 80. This perhaps is to pasture on Helicon, to dream on Parnassus. *O sweet and honourable leisure, and more beautiful than almost any business! O sea! O shore! true and secret μουσεῖον [seat of the Muses]! how many things you discover! how many things you dictate!* Plin. L. I. ep. 9.

> § 85. 5) Si pulcre cogitaturo requiritur status, [p. 39] qualem §. 39. descripsi, praesertim in sensationibus themati satis heterogeneis constituto, aquae potori, pro positu corporis, §. 78. opportunus erit generosioris laticis modicus haustus, quo remittentibus nonnihil sensationibus e. g. molestis clarescere necessariae e. g. hilares imaginationes et praeuisiones eo magis possint. M. §. 554. Hunc autem satis multis esse fontibus historici naturae narrant. Pone talem vim in Aganippe fuisse.

§ 85. 5) If, for one who is about to think beautifully, there is required a state [p. 39] such as I described in § 39, especially one constituted amid sensations sufficiently heterogeneous to the theme, then for a drinker of water, according to the posture of the body, § 78, a moderate draught of a more generous liquor will be opportune, by which, as the sensations, e.g. troublesome ones, somewhat relent, the necessary ones, e.g. cheerful imaginations and foresights, may become the clearer. M. § 554. Natural historians relate that there are enough springs with this virtue. Suppose there was such a power in Aganippe.

> § 86. 6) Fontanae eiusmodi praeferent vinum §. 85. cum Horatio iudicantes

§ 86. 6) To such a spring they will prefer wine, § 85, judging with Horace

> *Nulla placere diu neque viuere carmina posse,* / *Quae scribuntur aquae potoribus.* / *Ille liquor docuit voces inflectere cantu,* §. 83. / *Mouit et ad certos nescia membra modos,* §. 81. / *Bacchus et agricolae magno confecta labore* / *Pectora tristitiae dissoluenda dedit.* §. 84, 52. / *Bacchus et afflictis requiem mortalibus affert,* / *Crura licet dura compede pulsa sonent.* § 85. Tib.

*that no poems can please for long or live* / *which are written by drinkers of water.* / *That liquor taught voices to bend in song,* § 83, / *and moved untutored limbs to fixed measures,* § 81. / *Bacchus too gave the farmer’s heart, worn out by great labour,* / *to be loosed from sadness.* § 84, 52. / *Bacchus also brings rest to afflicted mortals,* / *though their legs ring, struck with the hard fetter.* § 85. Tib.

> Hinc et Bacchus incitationis inflammationisque aestheticae auctor est. §. 80. licet illepide fallatur, qui fictam Horatii od. L. II. 19. III. 25. ebrietatem bona ac germana fide, ceu veram, imitaturus, tamdiu libat Apollini ac Musis, Bacchoque litat, donec iam iamque promturus oracula

Hence Bacchus too is an author of aesthetic arousal and inflammation, § 80, although he is unwittily deceived who, about to imitate in good and genuine faith, as if it were real, the feigned drunkenness of Horace, od. L. II. 19, III. 25, so long pours libations to Apollo and the Muses, and sacrifices to Bacchus, until, now at the very point of uttering oracles,

> [p. 40] *Sternitur, exanimisque tremens procumbit humi — — — — .* Virg.

[p. 40] *he is laid low, and lifeless, trembling, falls prostrate on the ground — — — — .* Virg.

> § 87. 7) Noua occasio est castis aestheticis, qui sedentes aduersus, identidem, nescio quam, spectant et audiunt dulce ridentem. Misere quod omnes eripit sensus ipsis. Nam simul suam Lesbiam adspiciunt, nihil est super illis,

§ 87. 7) A new occasion exists for chaste aestheticians, who, sitting opposite, again and again, look upon and hear I know not whom sweetly laughing. Which wretchedly snatches all their senses from them. For as soon as they behold their Lesbia, nothing is left to them,

> *Lingua sed torpet, tenuis sub artus* / *Flamma dimanat, sonitu suopte* / *Tintinant aures, gemina teguntur* / *Lumina nocte.* Cat.

*but the tongue grows numb, a thin flame* / *runs down beneath the limbs, with their own sound* / *the ears ring, the eyes are covered* / *with twofold night.* Cat.

> Quando autem absentis angiportum perambularunt, §. 81. clausam ianuam fenestrasque vacuas salutantes, subito se in montes et lucos ex vrbe remouent, §. 84. ibique suum naturae miraculum procul vident dulce ridens, dulce loquens audiunt, fingunt, scribunt, canunt, psallunt, pingunt, Silua interpres harum curarum et conscia sidera, §. 83. ne sperare quidem ausos esse, quae praeuident summa cum voluptate perinuiti, §. 82. Certe Venus ac Amor horum potius caussa habentur auctores incitationis, de qua loquimur, §. 78, quam ob prostibulorum praecones,

But when they have walked up and down the alley of the absent one, § 81, saluting the closed door and the empty windows, suddenly they remove themselves from the city to the mountains and groves, § 84, and there from afar they see their miracle of nature sweetly laughing, hear her sweetly speaking, imagine, write, sing, play, paint, the wood being the interpreter of these cares and the stars their confidants, § 83, things they would not even have dared to hope for, which they foresee with the highest pleasure, most unwillingly, § 82. Certainly Venus and Cupid are held to be the authors of the arousal of which we speak, § 78, rather on account of these than on account of the criers of brothels,

> *Quando immunda crepant ignominiosaque,* §. 54, 59.

*when they rattle off filthy and shameful things,* § 54, 59.

> [p. 41] § 88. Veriores forsan, ac dii sunt, §. 80, occasiones erunt, 8.) si quem

[p. 41] § 88. Occasions perhaps truer than the gods, § 80, will be, 8.) if

> *Decisis humilem pennis, inopemque paterni* / *Et laris et fundi paupertas impulit audax,* / *Vt versus faceret,*

*bold poverty, since he was humbled, his wings clipped, and destitute* / *of his father’s hearth and farm, has driven* / *someone to make verses,*

> sicut Horatium, qui de se pergit per iocum narrare, quod bene multi serio verissimum putant:

as it did Horace, who goes on to relate of himself in jest what very many quite seriously think most true:

> *Quod non desit, habentem,* / *Quae poterunt vnquam satis expurgare cicutae,* / *Ni melius dormire putem, quam scribere versus?*

*Having enough that nothing is lacking,* / *what hemlocks will ever suffice to purge me,* / *if I did not think it better to sleep than to write verses?*

> § 89. 9) Indignatio

§ 89. 9) Indignation

> *Archilochum proprio rabies armauit iambo.* Hor.

*Rage armed Archilochus with his own iambus.* Hor.

> Horatius eandem occasionem sibi praesagit, Serm. L. II. 1. v. 40-60. Juuenalis eam statim ab initio spirat:

Horace forebodes the same occasion for himself, Serm. L. II. 1. v. 40–60. Juvenal breathes it right from the start:

> *Semper ego auditor tantum nunquam ne reponam* / *Vexatus toties rauci Theseide Codri?* e. c. / *Difficile est saturam non scribere. Nam quis iniquae* / *Tam patiens vrbis, tam ferreus, vt teneat se?* e. c. / *Quid referam, quanta siccum iecur ardeat ira?* e. c. / *Haec ego non credam Venusina digna lucerna.* / [p. 42] *Haec ego non agitem?* / *Si natura negat, facit indignatio versum* / *Qualemcunque potest, quales ego.* Sat. I.

*Shall I always be a hearer only, and never retort,* / *vexed so often by the Theseid of hoarse Codrus?* etc. / *It is difficult not to write satire. For who is so patient* / *of the unjust city, so iron-hearted, as to hold himself in?* etc. / *Why should I tell with how great a wrath my dry liver burns?* etc. / *Shall I not believe these things worthy of the Venusine lamp?* / [p. 42] *Shall I not pursue these things?* / *If nature refuses, indignation makes the verse,* / *such as it can, such as I make.* Sat. I.

> Ita pergit in reliquis. Ex eodem fonte Demosthenis et Ciceronis Philippicae, huius Verrinae et Catilinariae, Ouidii Ibis, e. c.

So he goes on in the rest. From the same source the Philippics of Demosthenes and Cicero, the latter’s Verrines and Catilinarians, Ovid’s Ibis, etc.

> § 90. Satis cognata indignationi est 10) irrisio, M. §. 684. Horatio tamen magis amica, ac indignatio, minus amara, plusque salis, quam fellis habens. Hinc αὐτοσχεδιάσματα, de quibus §. 52, militumque currus triumphales stipantium. Hinc vetus

§ 90. Closely akin to indignation is 10) derision, M. § 684, yet friendlier to Horace than indignation, less bitter, and having more salt than gall. Hence the αὐτοσχεδιάσματα [improvisations] of which § 52, and of the soldiers crowding about the triumphal chariots. Hence the old

> *Comoedia non sine multa* / *Laude, sed in vitium libertas excidit, et vim* / *Dignam lege regi.* Hor.

*comedy, not without much* / *praise, but its liberty fell into vice and a violence* / *worthy to be governed by law.* Hor.

> Hinc Aristophanes, hinc Lucianus paene omnis, et plura Martialis epigrammata.

Hence Aristophanes, hence almost all of Lucian, and many of Martial’s epigrams.

> § 91. 11.) Omnes animi commotiones, quae tantae non sunt, vt omnem symbolicam paene cognitionem intuitus opprimat, quando de pulcre non cogitandis tantum, sed et efferendis loquimur, 12) omnes fortunae casus tristiores, nisi frangant, laetiores, nisi obtundant et distrahant omnino animum. §. 82. Plus tamen elegantiarum sinistris auctorum fatis debemus, quam admodum ridentibus.

§ 91. 11.) All commotions of the mind which are not so great that the intuition overwhelms almost all symbolic cognition, when we speak not only of things to be thought beautifully but also of things to be expressed, 12) all the sadder accidents of fortune, unless they break the mind, and the happier ones, unless they altogether blunt and distract it. § 82. Yet we owe more elegances to the adverse fates of authors than to the very smiling ones.

> [p. 43] § 92. 13. Agmen claudat in catalogo facile locupletando iuuentus, s. potius illa huius vitae periodus, qua nondum ἀκμὴν suam eo vsque transiit anima, vt imaginationes etiam insigniter decreuerint. Sicut enim facultates cognoscitiuae inferiores primae fiunt in eadem phaenomena, ita et eodem, quo creuerunt, ordine minuuntur naturaliter. Vnde duabus iam potiorem pulcre cogitandi materiem suppeditaturis, §. 30, 31. languescentibus transiisse iudicatur eleganter cogitandi princeps opportunitas. Vnde Horatius non praecipit solum,

[p. 43] § 92. 13. Let youth close the ranks in a catalogue easily enriched, or rather that period of this life in which the soul has not yet passed its ἀκμήν [prime] so far that even the imaginations have notably declined. For just as the lower cognitive faculties are the first to become phenomena in it, so too they naturally diminish in the same order in which they grew. Whence, when the two which are to supply the more important matter for thinking beautifully, § 30, 31, are already languishing, the chief opportunity for thinking elegantly is judged to have passed. Whence Horace not only teaches,

> *Solue senescentem mature sanus equum, ne* / *Peccet ad extremum ridendus, et ilia ducat,*

*Be wise and unharness in good time the ageing horse, lest* / *he stumble at the last, a laughing-stock, and strain his flanks,*

> sed etiam spectatus satis et donatus iam rude non vult antiquo ludo includi,

but also, having been sufficiently looked at and already presented with the wooden sword, does not want to be shut up in his old school,

> *Et versus et caetera ludicra ponens.*

*laying aside both verses and other playthings.*

> § 93. Per se patet 1) his occasionibus non vtendum esse contra fortiores vitae beatae leges, 2) occasiones eas esse tantum non caussas solitarias, quibus circumfluere possit laeuum aut tardum ingenium sine effectu, qui quaerebatur, §. 78.

§ 93. It is self-evident 1) that these occasions are not to be used against the stronger laws of the blessed life, 2) that they are occasions only, not solitary causes, with which a clumsy or slow wit might be surrounded on every side without the effect that was sought, § 78.

> § 94. In maiori pulcra meditatione quum difficilior [p. 44] sit pulcritudo totius, ac pulcritudo cuiusuis partis, pulcritudo rerum et ordinis, pulcritudine signorum, §. 18-20, ad priores potissimum informandas vtendum est impetu mentis aesthetico, dum feruet opus, et eius occasionibus, §. 78-92.

§ 94. Since in a greater beautiful meditation the beauty of the whole is more difficult [p. 44] than the beauty of any part, and the beauty of things and of order than the beauty of signs, § 18–20, the aesthetic impetus of the mind, while the work is glowing, and its occasions, § 78–92, are to be used above all for forming the former.

> § 95. Durante ἐνθουσιασμῷ dum pulcre ponere totum, partesque principes intenditur omnis anima, §. 78. laudabiliter a minoribus minorum partium elegantiis exasciandis abstrahit ingenium etiam satis felix, M. §. 529. ne fiat simile fabro, qui

§ 95. While the ἐνθουσιασμῷ [enthusiasm] lasts, while the whole soul is bent on setting out the whole and the principal parts beautifully, § 78, even a sufficiently happy wit laudably withdraws itself from hewing out the lesser elegances of the lesser parts, M. § 529, lest it become like the craftsman who

> *Et vngues* / *Exprimet et molles imitabitur aere capillos* / *Infelix operis summa, quia ponere totum* / *Nesciet. Hunc ego me, si quid componere curem,* / *Non magis esse velim, quam prauo viuere naso,* / *Spectandum nigris oculis nigroque capillo.* Hor.

*will both express the nails* / *and imitate the soft hair in bronze,* / *unhappy in the sum of his work, because he will not know* / *how to set out the whole. If I cared to compose anything, I should* / *no more wish to be this man than to live with a crooked nose,* / *to be gazed at for my black eyes and black hair.* Hor.

[p. 45]

#### Sectio VI. Correctio Aesthetica. — Section VI. Aesthetic Correction.

> § 96. Quaedam pulcre cogitanda efferenda sunt ita, vt non admittant curas posteriores, et esse debeant velut extemporalia, e. g. colloquia et epistolae vere familiaria. In his vbi summa nitet, resque principes vere pulcrae sunt, §. 94. quoniam castigationes non habuere locum, hoc iniquior iudex sim, si paucis

§ 96. Some things to be thought beautifully must be brought forth in such a way that they admit no later cares, and must be, as it were, extemporaneous, e.g. conversations and letters that are truly familiar. In these, where the chief thing shines and the principal matters are truly beautiful, § 94, since corrections have had no place, I should be the more unfair a judge if by a few

> *Offendar maculis, quas aut incuria fudit, / Aut humana parum cauit natura.* §. 95.

*I were offended by blemishes, which either carelessness let fall, / Or human nature too little guarded against.* § 95.

> § 97. Quaedam pulcre cogitata non obligamur efferre prius, quam omnes iis, quas potuimus, gratias conciliauimus, curas posteriores admittentia. In his, quoniam omnis partialis pulcritudo, caeteris paribus, auget pulcritudinem totius, M. §. 185. characterem felicis aesthetici coronat V.) CORRECTIONIS STVDIVM (limae labor et mora) s. habitus protensa attentione in pulcre informatum opus, quantum possis, minores, minutarum etiam [p. 46] eius partium, perfectiones augendi, tollendi imperfectiones, aliquantula phoenomena, citra detrimentum totius, §. 27. Pulcra cogitatio omnis erit, vt pictura.

§ 97. Some things beautifully thought we are not obliged to bring forth before we have won for them all the graces we could, since they admit later cares. In these, since every partial beauty, other things being equal, increases the beauty of the whole, M. § 185, the character of the happy aesthetician is crowned by V.) the STUDY OF CORRECTION (the labour and delay of the file), or the habit of increasing, by sustained attention to a work that has been beautifully formed, as far as one can, the lesser perfections, even those of its [p. 46] minute parts, and of removing imperfections, the smallish phenomena, without detriment to the whole, § 27. Every beautiful thought will be like a picture.

> *Haec* §. 96. *amat obscurum, volet haec* §. 97. *sub luce videri,* / *Iudicis argutum quae non formidat acumen,* / *Haec* §. 96. *placuit semel, haec* §. 97. *decies repetita placebit.* Hor.

*This one,* § 96, *loves the dark; that one,* § 97, *will wish to be seen in the light,* / *Which does not fear the keen acumen of the judge;* / *This one,* § 96, *pleased once; that one,* § 97, *will please ten times repeated.* Hor.

> § 98. Correctio quum facilior sit pulcra totius elaboratione, §. 94, 97. auctor

§ 98. Since correction is easier than the beautiful elaboration of the whole, § 94, 97, the author,

> *Ni turpem putat inscitus metuitque lituram,* Hor.

*Unless, unskilled, he thinks a blot shameful and fears the erasure,* Hor.

> aut offenditur limae labore ac mora, M. §. 527: vbi iam transiit mentis impetus maior, §. 78.

or is offended by the labour and delay of the file, M. § 527: when the greater impetus of the mind has now passed, § 78,

> *Vt primum cessit furor, et rabida ora quierunt,* Virg.

*As soon as the frenzy has ceased, and the raging lips have grown quiet,* Virg.

> poterit peragi, iam distinctius praelucente intellectu et ratione, iudicioque intellectuali, §. 38. ad aesthetices etiam artificialis regulas singula exigente, S. IV.

it will be possible to carry it through, now that the intellect and reason shine forth more distinctly, and the intellectual judgement, § 38, measures each single thing also by the rules of artificial aesthetics, S. IV.

> § 99. Aesthetica artificialis non solum diriget pulcre cogitatorum, vel turpiuscule, conscientiam, vt ita dicam antecedentem, S. IV. et concomitantem, S. V. sed etiam consequentem, §. 98. tunc nondum inutilem, quando adhuc

§ 99. Artificial aesthetics will direct not only the conscience, so to speak, antecedent, S. IV, and concomitant, S. V, of what has been thought beautifully, or somewhat uglily, but also the consequent one, § 98, which is still not useless as long as

> [p. 47] *Membranis intus positis delere licebit,* / *Quod non edideris,* §. 98.

[p. 47] *It will be permitted to delete, with the parchments kept at home,* / *What you have not published,* § 98.

> § 100. Si quis limam, quibus probe potuisset, §. 97. tamen adhibere neglexerit, hoc id iniquius ferre solent acutiores, quod vident, qui potuit maius, eum et suffecisse minori, §. 98, sed spectatores suos non duxisse tanti, quorum ius aestumant contemtum sui contemtu auctoris rependere, et sic, nugae quae viderentur,

§ 100. If someone has nevertheless neglected to apply the file where he could well have done so, § 97, the more acute take this the more unfairly, because they see that he who could do the greater thing also sufficed for the lesser, § 98, but did not reckon his spectators worth so much; and they deem it their right to repay contempt of themselves with contempt of the author, and thus, things that seemed trifles,

> *seria ducent* / *In mala derisum semel exceptumque sinistre.*

*will lead to serious* / *Ills, once laughed at and received with ill omen.*

> § 101. Neglectum correctionis, de qua loquimur, Horatius vnicam caussam iudicat esse, cur romani graecis in scribendo cedant. A. P. v. 291, reprehendens eum in Lucilio peculiariter Serm. I, 10. Quam necessaria sit vltima lima, doceat Apelles post tabulam, Virgilius Aeneida flammis per testamentum legans, Ouidius, qui malis exsilii solis excusat eius neglectum *de Ponto* I. *ep.* V. 17. Romae non semel lituras a se fieri meminit, II. *ep.* IV. et in ipso oratore laudat, si sua *limet tenui cura.* IV. *ep.* VI. consentiente Cicerone, cuius *oratori* ne *minuta* quidem *negligenter tractanda* sunt, *limatumque dicendi genus* exemplo ac praeceptis commendatur.

§ 101. Neglect of the correction of which we speak Horace judges to be the single cause why the Romans yield to the Greeks in writing, A. P. v. 291, reproving it in Lucilius in particular, Serm. I, 10. How necessary the final file is, let Apelles teach, behind his picture; Virgil, bequeathing the Aeneid to the flames by his testament; Ovid, who excuses his neglect of it only by the ills of exile, *de Ponto* I. *ep.* V. 17, remembers that at Rome he more than once made erasures, II. *ep.* IV, and praises it in the orator himself if he *polishes* his work *with fine care,* IV. *ep.* VI; Cicero concurring, whose *orator* must not handle even *small things carelessly,* and *the polished manner of speaking* is commended by his example and precepts.

> § 102. [p. 48] Si quis interim cum Nasone senserit:

§ 102. [p. 48] If someone meanwhile has felt with Naso:

> *Nec tamen emendo, labor hic, quam scribere, maior.* / *Mensque pati durum sustinet aegra nihil.* / *Scilicet incipiam lima mordacius vti,* / *Et sub iudicium singula verba vocem?*

*Yet I do not emend; this labour is greater than writing,* / *And the sick mind endures to suffer nothing hard.* / *Shall I, forsooth, begin to use the file more bitingly,* / *And call each single word before judgement?*

> confundit ille, plus taedii secum ferens, et plus virium postulans. Prius concedo quadrare in emendationem, non posterius. §. 98. Deuorandum autem est, quicquid sit taedii ob reuerentiam, quae tua probaturis

he confounds what brings more tedium with it and what demands more strength. The former, I grant, squares with emendation, not the latter, § 98. But whatever tedium there may be must be swallowed out of the reverence which is

> *Maxima debetur,* §. 100.

*Most due* to those who are to approve your work, § 100.

> § 103. Sunt, quibus adsueuimus pueri, volentes etiam viri, scilicet, vt alius sua corrigat, quem deesse sibi queruntur:

§ 103. There are things to which we grew accustomed as boys, and willingly also as men, namely that another, forsooth, should correct our work, and we complain that such a one is wanting to us:

> *Suus cuique attributus est error,* / *Sed non videmus, manticae quod in tergo est.*

*To each is assigned his own error,* / *But we do not see what is in the wallet on our back.*

> Concedo recitationem veterum, nisi corrumpatur et haec adulationibus, saluberrimum esse consilium, et iuste queri, cui desit vir bonus et prudens, qui rogatus in nostris diiudicandis, dum adhuc nonum forsan in annum premuntur,

I grant that the recitation of the ancients, unless this too be corrupted by flatteries, is a most salutary counsel, and that he rightly complains who lacks a good and prudent man who, asked to judge our work while it is perhaps still being kept back to the ninth year,

> *Fiat Aristarchus.*

*May become an Aristarchus.*

> Neque tamen ab eiusmodi censore plura postulanda sunt, quam vt vel dicat: *Corrige, sodes, hoc et hoc,* vel vt

Yet from a censor of that kind no more is to be demanded than that he either say: *Correct, pray, this and this,* or that

> [p. 49] *incomtis allinat atrum* / *Transuerso calamo signum.*

[p. 49] *he smear a black mark on the unpolished lines* / *With his pen laid crosswise.*

> Vt ipse meliora suggerat, non aequus est, qui rogat virum vir. Est cuilibet sua cogitandi ratio, in quibusdam propria. Si circiter aequales viribus sumimur ego, mihique recitans, facilius vtique mihi nonnunquam esset mea cogitandi ratione totum opus absoluere, §. 78, quam remissiori animo, §. 98. per cogitationes alienas ita meas interserere, vt meliores sint in auctoris impetu ab eodem fusis, conducant tamen et haereant apte reliquis, a me meaque cogitandi ratione non profectis.

That he himself should suggest better things is not a fair request for one man to make of another. Each has his own way of thinking, in some things peculiar to him. If we are taken as roughly equal in strength, I and the one who recites to me, it would certainly sometimes be easier for me to finish the whole work in my own way of thinking, § 78, than, with a more relaxed mind, § 98, so to interweave another’s thoughts with mine that they are better than those poured out by the author himself in his impetus, and yet conduce to and cohere aptly with the rest, which have not proceeded from me and my way of thinking.

> *Si defendere delictum, quam vertere malis,* / *Nullum vltra verbum aut operam insumamus inanem,* / *Quin sine riuali teque et tua solus ames.* Hor.

*If you prefer to defend a fault rather than to change it,* / *We shall spend no further word or vain effort,* / *But that without rival you alone may love yourself and your own.* Hor.

#### Sectio VII. Cautiones Quaedam. — Section VII. Certain Cautions.

> § 104. NATVRALE COGITANDI GENVS si dicatur naturalibus animae cogitaturae viribus, obiectorum, eorumque naturae proportionatum, quibus et quorum in vsus vel delectationem cogitatio suscepta praesumenda [p. 50] est, s. breuius has naturas imitatum, adeo necessarium est pulcre cogitaturo naturale cogitandi genus, §. 14. vt minus adhuc cognita animae pulcre cogitaturae, multorumque obiectorum natura, omne venustae cogitationis artificium hac vnica regula comprehendi videretur: *Naturam imitare*

§ 104. If the NATURAL MANNER OF THINKING be defined as one proportioned to the natural powers of the soul that is to think, and to the nature of the objects and of those for whose use or delight the thought undertaken is to be presumed [p. 50] to be, or more briefly as one that imitates these natures, then the natural manner of thinking is so necessary to one who is to think beautifully, § 14, that while the nature of the soul that is to think beautifully, and of many objects, is as yet too little known, the whole art of charming thought would seem to be comprehended in this single rule: *Imitate nature.*

> § 105. Hinc pulcre cogitaturus caueat, 1) ne laudem ingenii venusti affectet, nisi omnino, tamen insigniter, destitutus ea, quam S. II. descripsimus, natura, CONTRA NATVRAM, asinus ad lyram, 2) ne forsan habens naturae generatim, quantum satis est, specialem tamen characterem et naturae quandam inflexionem, vt ita dicam, peculiarem requirentia sibi cogitare sumat, ante, quam viderit, an speciali suo etiam characteri has naturae dotes indiderit, alias cogitaturus PRAETER NATVRAM, Suffenus,

§ 105. Hence let him who is to think beautifully beware, 1) lest he affect the praise of a charming wit when he is destitute, if not altogether, yet signally, of that nature which we described in S. II, CONTRARY TO NATURE, an ass at the lyre; 2) lest, perhaps possessing in general as much of nature as is enough, he nevertheless take upon himself to think things that require a special character and a certain peculiar bent, so to speak, of nature, before he has seen whether nature has bestowed these gifts upon his own special character too, since otherwise he will think BESIDE NATURE, a Suffenus,

> *Homo venustus, et dicax et vrbanus,*

*A charming man, both witty and urbane,*

> cuius si versus legas

whose verses, if you read them,

> *Tum bellus ille, et vrbanus* / *Suffenus vnus caprimulgus, aut fossor* / *Rursus videtur, tantum abhorret ac mutat.* Cat.

*Then that pretty fellow, that urbane* / *Suffenus seems one goatherd, or a ditch-digger* / *Once more; so much does he differ and change.* Cat.

> Vtrumque COGITANDI GENVS est INVITA MINERVA SVSCEPTVM

Each MANNER OF THINKING is UNDERTAKEN AGAINST THE WILL OF MINERVA:

> *Tu nihil inuita dices faciesue Minerua.* Hor. Cic. Off. L. I, 110.

*You will say or do nothing against the will of Minerva.* Hor. Cic. Off. L. I, 110.

> § 106. [p. 51] Genus cogitandi naturale rectissime sequutus, §. 104, ne, nubem pro Iunone, amplectatur *pinguem* et *crassam Mineruam*

§ 106. [p. 51] Let him who follows the natural manner of thinking most rightly, § 104, beware lest, embracing a cloud for Juno, he embrace a *fat* and *gross Minerva*,

> *Rusticus, abnormis sapiens,*

*A rustic, a sage against the rule,*

> non tam iuuenilia, quam puerilia sua, si quid non aspernandae naturae, S. II. pelluceat, iam omnibus numeris absoluta statuens, S. III., aut etiam rudi ingenio contentus per omnem vitam, pro naturali laudando, sequatur RVDE COGITANDI GENVS, cuius ad naturam saepe satis mediocrem, nihil doctrinae, nihil artis accesserit. S. IV.

setting down his own not so much juvenile as puerile productions, if any trace of a nature not to be despised, S. II, shines through in them, as already finished in every number, S. III, or even, content with a rude wit for his whole life, in place of the natural, which is to be praised, follow the RUDE MANNER OF THINKING, to whose nature, often middling enough, nothing of doctrine, nothing of art has been added. S. IV.

> § 107. Rude cogitandi genus duplici ratione fit satis deforme phaenomenon, §. 14. 1) INSCITO (indocto, inerudito) COGITANDI GENERE, quando vel in eum gradum eruditionis pulcrae, quem generatim in omni requirimus vltra plebem sapere auso, grauius impingitur, vel apparet speciatim de aliquibus efferre suas cogitationes aliquem, ceu venustas, voluisse, quorum naturam vel mediocri doctrina potuisset nosse penitius, §. 104. de quibus tamen ignoret, quicquid

§ 107. The rude manner of thinking becomes a sufficiently deformed phenomenon in two ways, § 14: 1) in the UNSKILLED (unlearned, unerudite) MANNER OF THINKING, when either there is a graver offence against that degree of beautiful erudition which we require in general of everyone who dares to know more than the common people, or it appears in particular that someone has wished to bring forth his thoughts, as if they were charming, about things whose nature he could have known more thoroughly even with middling learning, § 104, and yet is ignorant about them of whatever

> Non omnis *fricti ciceris* sciat *ac nucis emtor.* §. 66, 67.

Not every *buyer of roasted chickpea* and *nut* may know. § 66, 67.

> § 108. [p. 52] Rude cogitandi genus est, 2) INERS COGITANDI GENVS, denuo vel generatim probe fundatarum eleganter cogitandi regularum, vel speciatim eius artis peculiaris aut ignorantiam prodens, cuius tamen specimen profitearis, §. 106, 68. 69. aut neglectum exceptionibus, quibus nihil insit elegantiae, §. 25, 72.

§ 108. [p. 52] The rude manner of thinking is, 2) the INERT MANNER OF THINKING, betraying again either, in general, ignorance of the well-founded rules of thinking elegantly, or, in particular, of that peculiar art of which you nevertheless profess to give a specimen, § 106, 68, 69, or else neglect of them by exceptions in which there is nothing of elegance, § 25, 72.

> § 109. Duplicis huius, §. 107, 108. duplex

§ 109. Of this twofold fault, § 107, 108, the twofold

> *In vitium ducit culpae fuga, dum caret arte*

*Flight from blame leads into vice, when it lacks the art*

> vera naturam belle supplente, S. IV. Primum est VMBRATILE et scholasticum COGITANDI GENVS, quando in iis, quae pulcram cogitandi rationem requirunt, adeoque naturam, etiam alteram, consuetudinem elegantioris inter moratiores viuendi generis imitari sequique debent, §. 104. aut tantum constipatur eruditionis reconditioris, vt desinat esse pulcritudo, §. 15. aut omnino speciem eruditionis tantum apud pueros et grammaticorum aliquos mentientia congeruntur.

that truly and beautifully supplements nature, S. IV. The first is the SHADOWY and scholastic MANNER OF THINKING, when, in those things which require a beautiful way of thinking, and therefore must imitate and follow nature, and also a second nature, the custom of the more elegant kind of life among the better-mannered, § 104, either so much of the more recondite erudition is crammed in that beauty ceases to be, § 15, or things that altogether counterfeit the mere appearance of erudition, and that only among boys and some grammarians, are heaped together.

> § 110. Alterum est AFFECTATVM et coactum COGITANDI GENVS, naturam per artem male supplens, quando *artes*, nescio quae, [p. 53] *nimia subtilitatis affectatione frangunt atque concidunt*, quod Quintilianus docet, *quicquid est in* meditationum elegantiis *generosius*. Pestis haec naturale cogitandi genus, §. 105. enecans se exserit 1) quando naturalis vnice decor et non fucatus suffecisset, artis tamen cuiuscunque pigmenta vocantur in subsidium superfluum, hic nocens, 2) vbi satis infelix aliquis fuit, vt in malas deceptricis artis regulas incideret, 3) vbi bonae artis regulae applicantur, vbi locum habent, sed inepte, §. 105. E. §. 336.

§ 110. The second is the AFFECTED and forced MANNER OF THINKING, which badly supplements nature by art, when *arts*, I know not which, [p. 53] *by an excessive affectation of subtlety break and cut to pieces*, as Quintilian teaches, *whatever is* of a *nobler* kind in the elegances of meditations. This plague, which kills the natural manner of thinking, § 105, shows itself 1) when the natural and uncosmeticised comeliness alone would have sufficed, and yet the pigments of some art or other are called in as a superfluous, and here harmful, aid; 2) where someone has been unhappy enough to fall into the bad rules of a deceiving art; 3) where the rules of a good art are applied where they have a place, but ineptly, § 105. E. § 336.

> § 111. Alii naturale cogitandi genus recte sequuti, §. 104. cum natura confundunt ordinarium eius statum, et vires, aliqua licet doctrina promotas, S. IV. mortuas tamen et remissas, ex quibus nullum per impetum, nullam per inflammationem viuentibus LANGVIDVM (frigidum, somnolentum, oscitans) COGITANDI GENVS contra S. V.

§ 111. Others, rightly following the natural manner of thinking, § 104, confuse with nature its ordinary state and its powers, advanced indeed by some doctrine, S. IV, yet dead and slack, from which, since they are alive by no impetus and no inflammation, arises the LANGUID (cold, somnolent, yawning) MANNER OF THINKING, contrary to S. V.

> § 112. *Dum vitant stolidi vitia, in contraria currunt*, ieiunumque langnorem [sic: languorem] in cogitando cauturi incidunt in parenthyrsum et EFFRAENE COGITANDI GENVS, quod excusso non intellectus solum et rationis iugo, sed spicerioris [sic: sincerioris] etiam saporis negligens, citra vllam [p. 54] rationem phaenomenon, quae circiter sufficeret, tantum furorem prae se ferent, qui naturam, sed male sani sincipitis, vnice videatur imitari. §. 104. Tali vesano deridendo Horatius artis suae dedicauit epilogum:

§ 112. *While fools avoid vices, they run into their contraries*, and, wishing to guard against a jejune languor in thinking, they fall into parenthyrsus and the UNBRIDLED MANNER OF THINKING, which, having shaken off not only the yoke of intellect and reason but neglectful also of purer taste, without any [p. 54] reason for the phenomenon that would roughly suffice, displays so great a frenzy that it seems to imitate nature alone, but the nature of an unsound head, § 104. To the derision of such a madman Horace dedicated the epilogue of his art:

> *Certe furit, ac velut vrsus,* / *Obiectos caueae valuit si frangere clathros,* / *Indoctum doctumque fugat.*

*Surely he rages, and like a bear,* / *If he has been strong enough to break the bars set across his cage,* / *He puts to flight the unlearned and the learned alike.*

> § 113. Sicut pigri philosophi ac medici nonnunquam naturam, quasi deum ex machina, legunt asylum suae desidiae, sunt etiam, qui naturale COGITANDI GENVS appellant, nisi omnino rude, inscitum ac iners, §. 106-108 incomtum tamen et INCOMPOSITVM, quando non in ipso solum impetu animi, de quo S. V. non satis lente festinas, et quicquid occurrit primo, tanquam optimum, adoptas, sed etiam postea, quae satis cito fudisti, vel nunquam animo castigandi retractas, vel non sine blanda parentum indulgentia, qua quicquid eradicandum esset vitii, vix tangunt, ne naturam suorum perdant, veriti. Cauendum hoc malum genus cogitandi, secundum S. VI, LIMATO COGITANDI GENERE.

§ 113. Just as lazy philosophers and physicians sometimes choose nature, like a god from the machine, as the asylum of their idleness, there are also those who call natural the MANNER OF THINKING which, if not altogether rude, unskilled and inert, § 106–108, is yet unkempt and UNCOMPOSED, when not only in the very impetus of the mind, of which S. V, do you hasten not slowly enough, and adopt whatever occurs first as the best, but afterwards too you either never go back over what you poured out quickly enough with a mind to chastise it, or not without the fond indulgence of parents, by which they scarcely touch whatever vice ought to be rooted out, fearing lest they destroy the nature of their own. This bad manner of thinking is to be guarded against, according to S. VI, by the POLISHED MANNER OF THINKING.

> § 114. Neque tamen commendatur LIMA magis [p. 55] ATTERENS, quam poliens, excessus in corrigendo, vel in foetus ingenii, qui subiti et extemporales postulantur, tantum studii diligentiaeque impendens, vt lucernam olentes male non habeant pulcram subitaneorum verisimilitudinem, §. 96. vel impetus ad maiora dati prodigus, qui in minutulis eundem moratur aut distrahit, contra §. 95, vel ita sua retractans, quando *motus omnis animi*, *tanquam ventus*, cogitantem *deseruit*, *et omnis ardor consedit*, vt *flaccescant* non sine aliqua vi primum fusa, reiectisque quibusdam, aliis, velut ornatioribus, adiectis, omnis incitatio et quasi *flamma* pulcre cogitandorum simul *exstinguatur*, §. 111. Eiusmodi lima minorem maiori praefert elegantiam exceptione non eleganti, §. 25. quia

§ 114. Yet no more is the FILE commended that [p. 55] WEARS AWAY rather than polishes, an excess in correcting, which either, on the offspring of wit that are demanded sudden and extemporaneous, spends so much study and diligence that, smelling of the lamp, they do not have the beautiful verisimilitude of improvisations, § 96; or, prodigal of the impetus given for greater things, delays or dissipates it on trifles, contrary to § 95; or so goes back over one’s own work, when *every movement of the mind*, *like a wind*, *has deserted* the thinker, *and all the ardour has settled*, that the things first poured out not without some force *grow flaccid*, and, some being rejected and others, as more ornate, added, all the incitement and, as it were, *flame* of the things to be thought beautifully *is extinguished* at the same time, § 111. A file of this kind prefers a lesser elegance to a greater by an inelegant exception, § 25, because

> *sectantem leuia nerui* / *Deficiunt animique.* Hor.

*in one who pursues smooth things the sinews* / *And the spirit fail.* Hor.

#### Sectio VIII. Ubertas Aesthetica. — Section VIII. Aesthetic Richness.

> § 115. Si quis partim ab enumeratis S. II-VI. iam instructus, partim non abhorrens, satis felix futurus aestheticus, §. 27 consilium amplius rogauerit, de pulcre cogitando generatim, [p. 56] §. 17, praesertim de pulcritudine rerum, §. 18,

§ 115. If anyone who is partly already instructed by the things enumerated in S. II–VI, and partly not averse to them, a future aesthetician happy enough, § 27, should ask for further counsel about thinking beautifully in general, [p. 56] § 17, and especially about the beauty of things, § 18,

> *vtar vice cotis, acutum* / *Reddere quae ferrum valet, exsors ipsa secandi.* / *Munus et officium, nil scribens ipse, docebo:* / 1) *Vnde parentur opes.* Hor.

*I shall serve in the place of a whetstone, which can make* / *Iron sharp, though itself without a share in cutting.* / *The task and the duty, writing nothing myself, I shall teach:* / 1) *Whence resources are to be procured.* Hor.

> Prima nempe cura sit in rebus cogitandis VBERTAS (copia, abundantia, multitudo, diuitiae, opes) M. §. 575, sed AESTHETICA, qua datum subiectum, certus cogitaturus, de dato obiecto, certa cogitandi materia, plura pulcre cogitare possit. §. 22.

The first care, namely, in the things to be thought, should be for RICHNESS (abundance, plenty, multitude, riches, resources), M. § 575, but AESTHETIC richness, by which a given subject, a certain person about to think, can think many things beautifully about a given object, a certain matter for thought, § 22.

> § 116. Sic incipit laudes Isaei Plinius: *Summa est facultas, vbertas, copia.* L. II. *ep.* 3. Quam primo diuidamus in ABSOLVTAM, omni pulcre cogitando necessariam, § 115, 22, et RELATIVAM, illum absolutae gradum, qui quibusdam pulcre cogitandis forte necessarius est, e. g. minus notis, aut admodum vtilibus minus attento tamen inculcandis, quemque *latitudinem platonicam* dicamus, sequuti Plinium eundem, quando Euphratis quidem *sermonem* omnem *copiosum*, §. 115. dicit, eundem tamen affirmat *frequenter latitudinem illam platonicam effingere*, L. I. *ep.* X.

§ 116. Thus Pliny begins the praises of Isaeus: *Supreme is his facility, his richness, his abundance.* L. II. *ep.* 3. Let us divide it first into ABSOLUTE richness, necessary for all beautiful thinking, § 115, 22, and RELATIVE richness, that degree of the absolute which happens to be necessary for certain things to be thought beautifully, e.g. for things less known, or very useful, which must nevertheless be inculcated upon a less attentive person, and which we may call *Platonic breadth*, following the same Pliny, when he calls all of Euphrates’ *discourse copious*, § 115, and yet affirms of the same man that he *frequently reproduces that Platonic breadth*, L. I. *ep.* X.

> § 117. [p. 57] Etiamsi non velit pulcre meditaturus aliquando latitudinem comparatiuam sequi, §. 116, tamen copia rerum vere affluens satis eam eleganter, quasi per lancem saturam, ostentat, velut ex longinquo, ne spectator exhauriri putet materiam postea monstrandis propius. §. 115. Ita Virgilius:

§ 117. [p. 57] Even if he who is to meditate beautifully should sometimes not wish to pursue comparative breadth, § 116, nevertheless a truly overflowing abundance of matter displays it elegantly enough, as if on a heaped dish, as from afar, lest the spectator think that the matter has been exhausted by things afterwards to be shown more closely, § 115. Thus Virgil:

> *Non mihi si linguae centum sint, oraque centum,* / *Ferrea vox,* e. c.

*Not if I had a hundred tongues, and a hundred mouths,* / *A voice of iron,* etc.

> Ita Cicero: *Nullius tantum est flumen ingenii, nulla dicendi aut scribendi tanta vis, tantaque* copia, *quae, non dicam exornare, sed enarrare,* e. c.

Thus Cicero: *No one has so great a stream of genius, no one so great a force and so great an* abundance *of speaking or writing, that could, I will not say adorn, but recount,* etc.

> § 118. VBERTAS AESTHETICA, porro est vel OBIECTIVA, (rerum, materialis) quatenus in obiectis et cogitandis ipsis est praecipua ratio, cur per humani vires ingenii possint vbertim pingi, vel SVBIECTIVA, (ingenii et personae) possibilitas physica et potentia certi hominis, etiam secundum quid, et hypothetice talis certam rem vbertim repraesentandi. Sunt obiecta, velut vltro suas diuitias offerentia. Vix in mentem incidunt,

§ 118. AESTHETIC RICHNESS, further, is either OBJECTIVE (of things, material), insofar as in the objects and the things to be thought themselves lies the chief reason why they can be richly painted by the powers of human wit, or SUBJECTIVE (of wit and person), the physical possibility and the power of a certain man, even in a certain respect and hypothetically such, to represent a certain thing richly. There are objects that offer their riches, as it were, of their own accord. Scarcely do they come to mind, when

> *apparetque beata pleno* / Copia *cornu.* Hor.

*there appears blessed* Abundance *with her full* / *horn.* Hor.

> Tunc modo capacitatis habueris, quantum satis est, non aliis solum, sed et

Then, if only you have as much capacity as is enough, not to others only, but also

> [p. 58] *tibi copia* / *Manabit ad plenum benigno* / *Ruris honorum opulenta cornu.* Hor.

[p. 58] *to you abundance* / *Will flow to the full from her kindly* / *Horn, rich in the honours of the countryside.* Hor.

#### Sectio VIIII. Ubertas Materiae. — Section VIIII. Richness of Matter.

> § 119. HORIZON (sphaera) COGNITIONIS HVMANAE est finitus materiarum ex vniuersitate rerum infinita numerus, quae mediocri ingenio humano latius dicto possunt clarescere, harum quae possunt ab ingenio mediocriter philosophico perfectius concipi, HORIZONTEM LOGICVM (territorium et sphaeram) rationis et intellectus constituunt, quae possunt ingenio mediocriter aesthetico pulcre splendescere, HORIZONTEM AESTHETICVM (territorium et sphaeram pulcri rationis analogi) constituunt. Si qua

§ 119. The HORIZON (sphere) OF HUMAN COGNITION is the finite number of matters, out of the infinite universe of things, which can become clear to a middling human wit in the broader sense; those of these which can be conceived more perfectly by a middlingly philosophical wit constitute the LOGICAL HORIZON (territory and sphere) of reason and intellect; those which can shine beautifully for a middlingly aesthetic wit constitute the AESTHETIC HORIZON (territory and sphere of the beautiful of the analogue of reason). If there are things which

> *Desperas tractata nitescere posse, relinque.* §. 115.

*You despair can shine when handled, leave them.* § 115.

> § 120. INFRA HORIZONTEM AESTHETICVM POSITA sunt, quae ex obscuritate [p. 59] comparatiua et relatiua mediocriter aestheticum ingenium protrahere non potest in lucem pulcram. Qualia si themata sibi sumat pulcre cogitaturus, aut id serio fiet, et nascetur RERVM INOPIA et *meditationis exilitas*, contra §. 115, 119. aut delabetur in allotria, aut periculose iocabitur. Hinc esto eiusmodi

§ 120. PLACED BENEATH THE AESTHETIC HORIZON are those things which a middlingly aesthetic wit cannot draw forth from comparative and relative obscurity [p. 59] into beautiful light. If he who is to think beautifully take such things as his themes, either this will be done in earnest, and there will be born a POVERTY OF MATTER and a *thinness of meditation*, contrary to § 115, 119, or he will slip into irrelevancies, or he will jest dangerously. Hence let there be a theme of this kind,

> Thema *irrepertum, et sic melius situm,* / *Quum terra celat, spernere fortior.* Hor.

A theme *undiscovered, and better placed thus,* / *While the earth hides it, to be the stronger in scorning it.* Hor.

> Conferantur *admiranda rerum admirabilium encomia*.

Let the *wondrous encomia of wondrous things* be compared.

> § 121. *Carmina vel caelo possint deducere lunam*, nec ego tamen suaserim pulcre cogitaturo sibi materiem legere, SVPRA HORIZONTEM AESTHETICVM POSITA, nec ea tantum hic intelligo, vel maxime, quae horizontem cognitionis humanae transcendunt omnino, §. 119. sed ea potissimum, quae ex superiori scientiarum distincta adaequataque cognitione non potest ad pulcram illam lucem deducere mediocriter aestheticum ingenium, quae rosea placeat, non praestringat oculos analogi rationis et inferiorum cognoscendi facultatum. Si tentaueris nihilominus, aut incides in incommoda, §. 120. commemorata, aut iocis expones, quae grauissima putas, aut *illigaberis angustis illis et concisis disputationibus*, quas Antonius apud Ciceronem de Or. L. II, 61. *philosophis* generatim graecis exprobrat, [p. 60] non sine solenni formula: *Verbum prorsus nullum intelligo.* Quod contra §. 22.

§ 121. *Songs may even draw down the moon from heaven*, yet I would not advise him who is to think beautifully to choose for himself as matter THINGS PLACED ABOVE THE AESTHETIC HORIZON, nor do I here understand only, or chiefly, those which altogether transcend the horizon of human cognition, § 119, but above all those which a middlingly aesthetic wit cannot draw down from the superior, distinct and adequate cognition of the sciences into that beautiful light which, rosy, may please, and not dazzle the eyes of the analogue of reason and of the lower faculties of cognition. If you try nonetheless, you will either fall into the inconveniences mentioned in § 120, or expose to jests what you think most grave, or *be entangled in those narrow and concise disputations* which Antonius in Cicero, de Or. L. II, 61, casts in the teeth of the Greek *philosophers* in general, [p. 60] not without the solemn formula: *I understand no word at all.* Against which § 22.

> § 122. Egone vero reiiciam ac reprehendam concisum cogitandi genus, cui tot ambitiosa scriptionum mearum ornamenta philosophicarum immolaui, quod nunc ipse sequor, licet paulisper laxius? Vtinam Zenoni iam Stoico deprehensa veritas, quam repetit Ciceronis Orator, 113, 114. et Quinctilianus II, 21. nostris saltim temporibus fieret apertior, esse duo cogitandi genera, alterum *perpetuum, et latius, quod rhetorices sit,* alterum *concisum, et contractius, quod dialectices.* Illud horizonti aesthetico, hoc logico proprium autumo, §. 119. Comparationem *compressae in pugnum manus* et *explicitae* meam non facio. Sufficit concisum cogitandi genus in scientificis, praesertim acroamaticis, apprime necessarium, quod Aristoteles iam vidit, aestheticus sane, sicut practicus, ita theoreticus, alieno in loco et extra rationis circulos esse posse vitium, et si qua in iis, quae copiosam orationem requirunt, *crebris paruisque conatibus se attollunt* in horizontem logicum, *inaequalia tantum et velut confragosa, nec admirationem consequi eminentium, et planorum gratiam perdere.* VIII, 5. Virtute ac facultate *rationali non tam est minute atque concise in* aestheticis [p. 61] *vtendum, quam in disputationibus* scientiarum logicis, XII, 2.

§ 122. Shall I, then, reject and reprove the concise manner of thinking, to which I have sacrificed so many ambitious ornaments of my philosophical writings, and which I myself now follow, though a little more loosely? Would that the truth already discovered by Zeno the Stoic, which Cicero’s Orator repeats, 113, 114, and Quintilian II, 21, might at least in our times become more evident: that there are two manners of thinking, the one *continuous and broader, which is that of rhetoric*, the other *concise and more contracted, which is that of dialectic*. The former I hold proper to the aesthetic horizon, the latter to the logical, § 119. The comparison of *the hand pressed into a fist* and *opened out* I do not make my own. It is enough that the concise manner of thinking, which is especially necessary in scientific matters, above all acroamatic ones, as Aristotle, surely an aesthetician, theoretical as well as practical, already saw, can be a vice in an alien place and outside the circles of reason, and that if in those things which require copious discourse some *raise themselves by frequent and small efforts* into the logical horizon, they are *only uneven and, as it were, rugged, and neither attain the admiration of eminences, nor keep the grace of level places.* VIII, 5. *One must not use the rational* virtue and faculty *so minutely and concisely in* aesthetic matters [p. 61] *as in* the logical *disputations* of the sciences, XII, 2.

> § 123. Horizonti aesthetico logicoque possunt esse multae materiae communes, §. 119, hinc ideo, quia aliquid in scientiis pertractatur, non excluditur idem ex sphaera pulcritudinis omnino, sed quatenus punctim et minutim cum accuratione philosophica mathematicaque conciperetur, §. 121. Quatenus autem eadem materia vel intellectu pulcro ipsa M. §. 637. notae autem eius sensitiue ac viuide, vel ipsa etiam, nunc certe, viuida tantum ac venusta cogitari potest, intra horizontem aestheticum recipitur.

§ 123. Many matters can be common to the aesthetic and the logical horizon, § 119; hence, because something is treated in the sciences, the same is not therefore excluded altogether from the sphere of beauty, but only insofar as it would be conceived point by point and minutely, with philosophical and mathematical accuracy, § 121. But insofar as the same matter can be thought either itself by the beautiful intellect, M. § 637, while its marks are thought sensately and vividly, or itself too, now at least, only vividly and charmingly, it is received within the aesthetic horizon.

> § 124. *Quid sit bonum, praeter honestatem? Verine sensus? Quae sit solis magnitudo? Quaestiones* eiusmodi *procul ab oratoris persona esse facile omnes intelligere exsistimat* Cicero. *Nam quibus,* inquit, *in rebus summa ingenia philosophorum plurimo cum labore consumta intelligimus, eas, sicut aliquas paruas res, oratori attribuere magna amentia videtur.* Recte vidit esse quaedam in scientiis supra horizontem aestheticum, §. 121, quae sicut omnis pulcre meditaturus, ita orator, perperam sibi themata legeret, §. 122. Quaestiones autem [p. 62] exempli loco commemoratas, si non orator, aestheticus certe practicus satis eleganter, arbitror, enarrare posset, modo aliam cogitandi de iisdem rationem sequeretur, ac demonstrator ethicus, logicus, physicus atque mathematicus, §. 123.

§ 124. *What is good, apart from the honourable? Are the senses true? What is the magnitude of the sun? Questions* of this kind Cicero *thinks that all easily understand to be far removed from the person of the orator. For in those matters,* he says, *on which we understand the highest geniuses of the philosophers to have been spent with the greatest labour, to assign these, like some small things, to the orator seems great madness.* He rightly saw that there are certain things in the sciences above the aesthetic horizon, § 121, which the orator, like everyone who is to meditate beautifully, would be wrong to choose as his themes, § 122. But the questions [p. 62] mentioned by way of example, if not the orator, at least the practical aesthetician could, I think, recount elegantly enough, provided he followed a different way of thinking about them from the ethical, logical, physical and mathematical demonstrator, § 123.

> § 125. Non de omnibus quidem pulcre cogitandi datur copia, §. 119-121, *oratoremque plenum atque perfectum, qui de omnibus rebus possit varie copioseque dicere,* Cic. de Or. I, 59. cum sapiente Stoico,

§ 125. It is not, indeed, about all things that the abundance for thinking beautifully is given, § 119–121, and *the full and perfect orator, who can speak about all things variously and copiously,* Cic. de Or. I, 59, together with the Stoic sage,

> *Discipulorum inter iubeo plorare cathedras:*

*I bid go and weep among the chairs of the pupils:*

> neque tamen venuste cogitandi facultas tantum est in ciuilibus controuersiis aut aliis leuioris momenti quaestionibus: sed in ipsis disciplinarum etiam et scientiarum 1) dogmatibus, theologicis, physicis, practicis, historicis, e. c. materialiter spectatis, quando ita cogites illa, significesque, *vt videaris voluisse esse illis, qui non sunt eruditissimi, familiaris.* ib. II, 61. 2) illustrationibus scholiorum instar interspergendis. §. 123. cf. Cic. de Or. I, 61.

yet neither does the faculty of thinking charmingly lie only in civil controversies or other questions of lighter moment, but in the very 1) dogmas of the disciplines and sciences too, theological, physical, practical, historical, etc., regarded materially, when you so think them, and signify them, *that you seem to have wished to be familiar to those who are not the most erudite,* ib. II, 61; 2) in illustrations to be interspersed in the manner of scholia, § 123, cf. Cic. de Or. I, 61.

> § 126. Theologi primi fuerunt theogoniarum cantores, *referre* quibus

§ 126. The first theologians were singers of theogonies, to whom

> *Musa dedit fidibus diuos, puerosque deorum.* Hor.

*The Muse gave* to recount *on the strings the gods, and the sons of gods.* Hor.

> [p. 63] *Cythara crinitus Iopas* / *Personat aurata, docuit quae maximus Atlas.* / *Hic canit errantem lunam, solisque labores,* / *Vnde hominum genus et pecudes, vnde imber et ignes.* e. c. / *Ingeminant plausum Tyrii Troesque sequuntur.* Virg. Aen. I. 745.

[p. 63] *Long-haired Iopas* / *Sounds on his gilded lyre what mightiest Atlas taught.* / *He sings the wandering moon, and the labours of the sun,* / *Whence the race of men and the beasts, whence rain and fire,* etc. / *The Tyrians redouble their applause, and the Trojans follow.* Virg. Aen. I. 745.

> *Rem tibi Socraticae poterunt ostendere chartae.* / *Qui didicit, patriae quid debeat, et quid amicis,* / *Quo sit amore parens, quo frater amandus et hospes,* / *Quod sit conscripti, quod iudicis officium, quae* / *Partes in bellum missi ducis,*

*The Socratic pages will be able to show you the matter.* / *He who has learned what he owes his country, and what his friends,* / *With what love a parent, with what a brother and a guest is to be loved,* / *What is the duty of a senator, what of a judge, what* / *The part of a general sent to war,*

> habebit, vnde nomen et honorem venustae quondam sapientiae restituat, si nouerit res grauissimas ad vulgarem popularemque sensum accommodare, §. 123. atque ita

will have whence he may restore the name and honour of a once charming wisdom, if he knows how to accommodate the gravest matters to the common and popular sense, § 123, and thus

> *lenire tigres rabidosque leones* / *Saxa mouere sono testudinis, ac prece blanda,* / *Publica priuatis secernere, sacra profanis,* / *Concubitu prohibere vago, dare iura maritis,* / *Oppida moliri, leges incidere ligno.* Hor.

*to soothe tigers and raging lions,* / *To move stones by the sound of the lyre, and by gentle entreaty,* / *To separate public from private, sacred from profane,* / *To forbid promiscuous union, to give laws to the married,* / *To build towns, to carve laws on wood.* Hor.

> *Historia vero, testis temporum, lux veritatis, vita memoriae, magistra vitae, nuncia veritatis [sic: vetustatis],* [p. 64] quam eleganter possit *immortalitati commendari,* §. 125. vel vnum Liuii genus cogitandi doceat, *fusum atque tractum, et cum lenitate quadam aequabili profluens.* cf. Cic. de or. L. II, 36, 64.

*But history, the witness of the times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the mistress of life, the messenger of antiquity,* [p. 64] how elegantly it can be *commended to immortality,* § 125, let the single manner of thinking of Livy teach, *diffuse and drawn out, and flowing on with a certain even-tenored smoothness,* cf. Cic. de or. L. II, 36, 64.

> § 127. Intra horizontem aestheticum posita sunt, praeter communia ipsi cum horizonte logico, §. 121-126. de quibus plura cogitare pulcrius datur ingenio mediocriter aesthetico, quae tamen scientificis curis et exactioribus, §. 120. perspicere, vel vires hominum non patiuntur, vel operae pretium rerum suarum satagenti non videatur. §. 119. Exempli gratia liceat

§ 127. Placed within the aesthetic horizon are, besides the things it has in common with the logical horizon, § 121–126, those things about which a middlingly aesthetic wit is given to think more, and more beautifully, which nevertheless either the powers of men do not allow to be seen through with scientific and more exact cares, § 120, or which do not seem worth the effort to one busy with his own affairs, § 119. For example, let it be permitted

> *Huc pugilem victorem, et equum certamine primum,* / *Et iuuenum curas, et libera vina referre.*

*Hither to bring the victorious boxer, and the horse first in the race,* / *And the cares of young men, and wine that makes free.*

> § 128. Aestheticum dynamicum exploraturum, an materia quaedam satis locuples futura sit, vel aliena pericula docebunt, §. 60, 61. vel sua, dum vires quasi praetentat in themate, quando primo venit in mentem, aut sola natura, S. II. nonnihil in pulcre cogitando exercita, S. III. aut adiuta per artem, S. IV. Si maiore se sentiat impetu mentis latum in certum thema, nihilo tamen minus, nescio quam rerum inopiam et informandi iam ipsius [p. 65] operis exilitatem ieiunam experiatur, §. 120. aut, sicca quidem omnia ac sincera, minutim tamen et concisius animo obuersantia, nihil dubitet illud relinquere, siue sit in rebus, siue sit in ipso, iam certe, potior ratio, vnde de eius eleganter exsequendi facultate desperandum sit, S. V. et §. 119.

§ 128. The dynamic aesthetician who is to explore whether a certain matter will be rich enough will be taught either by the trials of others, § 60, 61, or by his own, while he tests his powers, as it were, on the theme when it first comes to mind, either by nature alone, S. II, exercised somewhat in thinking beautifully, S. III, or aided by art, S. IV. If he feels himself borne by a greater impetus of mind towards a certain theme, and nevertheless experiences I know not what poverty of matter and a jejune thinness in the very forming of the [p. 65] work, § 120, or if all things, dry indeed and genuine, present themselves to his mind minutely and rather concisely, let him not hesitate to abandon it, since, whether it lies in the things or in himself, there is now certainly a weightier reason why one must despair of his faculty of carrying it out elegantly, S. V and § 119.

> § 129. ARS his periculis commendanda duplex est 1) ANALOGICA qua ex vno pulcro cognito per principium reductionis idem (simile, aequale, congruens) partialiter aliud colligitur. Hinc omnis imitatio virilis pendet, et quicquid est vbique parodiarum. Per hanc Theocritum in eclogis, Homerum in Aeneide sequutus est Virgilius, Menandrum Terentius. e. c. Quam nec ego me diffiteor vtiliorem expertum esse. Ne nimis metuas censores plagii vitio creatos, en! edictum iudicis sane competentis:

§ 129. The ART to be commended in these trials is twofold: 1) the ANALOGICAL, by which from one thing beautifully known, through the principle of reduction, the same (the similar, the equal, the congruent) is partially gathered in another. On this depends all manly imitation, and whatever there is anywhere of parodies. By this Virgil followed Theocritus in the eclogues, Homer in the Aeneid, Terence Menander, etc. And I do not deny that I have found it most useful. Lest you fear too much the irregularly appointed censors of plagiarism, behold the edict of a judge surely competent:

> *Publica materies priuati iuris erit,* Hor.

*Public matter will become private property,* Hor.

> Neque tamen eiusdem definitiones negligas:

Yet do not neglect the same judge’s definitions:

> *Nec verbum verbo curabis reddere.* / *Nec desilies imitator in arctum* / *Vnde pedem proferre pudor vetet, aut operis lex.*

*You will not take care to render word for word.* / *Nor will you, as an imitator, leap down into a narrow place* / *Whence shame forbids you to draw back your foot, or the law of the work.*

[p. 66]

#### Sectio X. Topica. — Section X. Topics.

> § 130. 2) TOPICA s. TOPOLOGIA, quae definitur ars s. disciplina inueniendorum argumentorum, §. 26. Cic. top. 2. Eandem *inueniendi artem* Cicero salutans, l. c. 6. et Aristoteles etiam multis tradens, sua velut auctoritate stabiliuerunt. Interim si dicendum, quod res est, non est ea tam heuristica, quam ars praedicata certi subiecti secundum certum notionum subiecto sociarum ordinem in memoriam reuocandi.

§ 130. 2) TOPICS or TOPOLOGY, which is defined as the art or discipline of finding arguments, § 26, Cic. top. 2. Cicero, saluting it as the *art of finding*, l. c. 6, and Aristotle too, handing it down in many words, have established it, as it were, by their authority. Meanwhile, if the truth is to be told, it is not so much heuristic as the art of recalling to memory the predicates of a certain subject according to a certain order of the notions associated with the subject.

> § 131. Potest doctrina topicorum diuidi in LOGICAM cognitioni intellectuali potissimum argumenta suppeditaturam, §. 130. et AESTHETICAM, cognitionem sensitiuam quae promoueat, §. 17. Logica erit denuo vel ANALYTICA, subsidium incidendi in quaestiones, quas deinde demonstrare nitaris et ex complete certis complete certa reddere, vel DIALECTICA, subsidium hylen aliquam copiamque sibi comparandi notionum praeceptionumque de dato probabili, vnde colligere liceat rationum decidendi prae rationibus [p. 67] dubitandi superpondium. Hanc sibi colendam sumsit Aristoteles, ita tamen, vt multa eo facientia non analyticis solum, sed et aestheticis applicari commode possint topicis, §. 130.

§ 131. The doctrine of topics can be divided into the LOGICAL, which is to supply arguments chiefly to intellectual cognition, § 130, and the AESTHETIC, which is to promote sensate cognition, § 17. The logical will again be either ANALYTIC, an aid for lighting upon questions which you then strive to demonstrate and to render completely certain from the completely certain, or DIALECTIC, an aid for procuring for oneself some stuff and abundance of notions and preconceptions about a given probable matter, whence one may gather a preponderance of the reasons for deciding over the reasons [p. 67] for doubting. This Aristotle took upon himself to cultivate, yet in such a way that many things bearing on it can conveniently be applied not only to analytic but also to aesthetic topics, § 130.

> § 132. Notio subiecto, quod meditandum sumis, socianda, vt periculum facias, an fieri tibi possit argumentum, vel latius, locupletans aut nobilitans, aut illustrans, aut mouens, §. 26. vel strictius, probans, aut persuadens, §. 131. pars illius seriei, cuius ordinem memoriae mandasti, LOCVS est s. sedes argumenti. Tales loci commendantur vel VNIVERSALES, omnibus quaestionibus, thematibus omnibus, aptandi, successiue cum re quacunque, de qua meditari velis, combinandi: vel PARTICVLARES, certis tantum thematibus certi generis proprii ac peculiares, et pro ratione disciplinarum, e. g. ad quas datum thema referri posset, diuersi, §. 131.

§ 132. A notion to be joined to the subject you take up for meditation, in order to make trial whether it can become an argument for you—either in the wider sense, one that enriches, or ennobles, or illustrates, or moves, § 26, or in the stricter sense, one that proves, or persuades, § 131—a part of that series whose order you have committed to memory, is a TOPIC, or seat of an argument. Such topics are recommended either as UNIVERSAL, to be fitted to all questions, to all themes, to be combined successively with any matter whatever on which you wish to meditate; or as PARTICULAR, proper and peculiar only to certain themes of a certain kind, and differing according to the disciplines, e.g., to which a given theme might be referred, § 131.

> § 133. Vniversalium eiusmodi locorum formula paullisper ad naturalem cogitandi rationem inflexa, pueris etiam notus est versus:

§ 133. A formula of universal topics of this kind, bent a little towards the natural manner of thinking, is the verse known even to schoolboys:

> *Quis? quibus auxiliis? quid? quomodo? / cur? vbi, quando?*

*Who? with what aids? what? how? / why? where, when?*

> [p. 68] Aliam, olim pluris habitam, et logicis etiam pertractatam, §. 132. decem exhibent categoriae, siue primus eas coordinauerit, siue iam constructas ab aliis celebriores tantum reddiderit Aristoteles. Nouam, scientiis etiam profuturam, magno hiatu promisit Lullus, de qua vel ea legens, quae S. R. Bruckeri hist. philos. crit. T. IV. P. I. narrat p. 16-21. vix temperare tibi poteris, quin applices arti futili Martialis illud:

[p. 68] Another, once held in higher esteem and treated by the logicians too, § 132, is presented by the ten categories, whether Aristotle was the first to coordinate them or only made more celebrated what others had already constructed.
