I would rather have it considered here as a condition, without which not, of a truly beautiful work of wit; and where it is wholly lacking, a certain deformity shows through, disfiguring whatever other elegance there is, not to the spirit alone, not to reason alone, § 15, but to the very analogue of reason, when it is supported by a greatness of heart that is inborn, § 45, and confirmed by practice, § 50, and discipline, § 63; because one may not dwell on such things without loss to morals, except by an exception that is certainly not elegant, § 25, or at the discretion of one who would measure morals by taste alone, and that not a public and meretricious taste, § 35.

> § 184. [p. 102] Iam hinc enim constabit, turpissimas licet poenas aliter sentientibus minantem, falli tamen Catullum, et turpiter falli, quando: c. 16.

§ 184. [p. 102] For from this it will now be clear that Catullus, although he threatens the most shameful punishments on those who think otherwise, is nevertheless deceived, and shamefully deceived, when: c. 16.

> *Castum,* ait, *esse decet pium poetam / Ipsum, versiculos nihil necesse est. / Qui tum denique habent salem et leporem, / Si sunt molliculi et parum pudici, / Et, quod pruriat, excitare possint.*

*It is fitting,* he says, *that the pious poet himself be chaste, / but his little verses need not be so. / Only then do they have salt and charm, / if they are soft and not quite modest, / and can rouse what itches.*

> Quanquam non verius Martialis l. I. 35.

Although Martial, l. I. 35, is no more truthful:

> *Lex haec carminibus data est iocosis:* / Non *possunt, nisi pruriant, placere,*

*This law has been given to jesting poems:* / They *cannot please unless they itch,*

> dignum ille tamen patella reperit operculum ita turpem suam legem, vti decet, probans:

yet he found a lid worthy of the dish, approving his shameful law, as is fitting, thus:

> *quis stolatum / Permisit meretricibus pudorem?* §. 165.

*who has permitted a matron’s / modesty to harlots?* § 165.

> Rectius vtique Persius sat. 1. nisi peccat in forma:

More rightly in any case Persius, sat. 1, unless he sins in form:

> *Hic neque more probo videas, neque voce serena,* §. 183. / *Ingentes trepidare Titos, quum carmina lumbum / Intrant, ac tremulo scalpuntur vbi intima versu.*

*Here you may see, neither in seemly manner nor with serene voice,* § 183, / *the huge Tituses quiver, when the poems enter / the loins, and the inmost parts are tickled by the tremulous verse.*

> § 185. DIGNITAS AESTHETICA, §. 182. pars et [p. 103] species magnitudinis aestheticae, sicut haec, §. 177. 178. vel ABSOLVTA erit, omni pulcre cogitando necessaria, de qua iureconsultos romanos imitati, quicquid cogitare fusius contra bonos mores esset, illi nos ne cogitando quidem immorari posse censeamus, §. 183, 184. vel RELATIVA, quae quibusdam pulcre cogitandis peculiaris requiritur, non eodem in gradu in omnibus, §. 178. De hac loquitur Cornelius, quando *non dubitat fore plerosque,* qui suum *genus scribendi leue, et non satis dignum summorum virorum personis iudicent,* et Cicero de Fin. l. I. *suspicatus aliquos futuros, qui hoc genus scribendi (quae philosophi graeco sermone tractarunt, latinis litteris mandans,) etsi sit elegans, personae tamen et dignitatis esse negent.*

§ 185. AESTHETIC DIGNITY, § 182, a part and [p. 103] species of aesthetic magnitude, will, like the latter, § 177, 178, be either ABSOLUTE, necessary for all beautiful thinking, concerning which, imitating the Roman jurists, we may judge that we cannot even in thought dwell upon whatever it would be contrary to good morals to think at length, § 183, 184; or RELATIVE, which is required as peculiar to certain things to be thought beautifully, not in the same degree in all, § 178. Of this Cornelius speaks, when *he does not doubt that there will be many* who judge his *manner of writing slight, and not sufficiently worthy of the persons of the greatest men,* and Cicero, de Fin. l. I, *suspecting that there will be some who, though this manner of writing (committing to Latin letters what the philosophers treated in the Greek tongue) be elegant, deny that it befits his person and dignity.*

> § 186. De eadem relatiua §. 185. tantum intelligendus est Cicero, quando Off. l. I. 130. *pulcritudinis duo genera* constituit, *quorum in altero venustas sit, in altero dignitas, venustatem muliebrem ducens, dignitatem virilem.* Nam et ipse poscit in oratoris perfecti *vultu,* ne *dignitatem* solum sed etiam *venustatem afferat,* Or. 60. et *dignitati,* Fam. X. ep. 6. sane non venustatem, sed *deformitatem* opponit. Est et matronis sua dignitas et praecisius, vti ICtum decet, §. 15. Vlp. de senator: *Maior dignitas est in sexu virili.* Interim pace Ciceronis et auctoritate, [p. 104] licebit omnia, quibus omnino deest dignitas, etiam absoluta, deformia dicere, §. 185, 177. et in vera, mascula praesertim pulcritudine, e. g. actionis, ad venustatem in primis dignitatem poscere, de Or. l. I. 142. et statuere *deformari* rem personamque *detrahendo spoliandoque dignitatem.* Or. pro Caelio 3.

§ 186. Of the same relative dignity, § 185, alone is Cicero to be understood, when, Off. l. I. 130, he establishes *two kinds of beauty, in one of which there is charm, in the other dignity, taking charm as womanly, dignity as manly.* For he himself demands that the *countenance* of the perfect orator should bring not *dignity* alone but also *charm,* Or. 60, and to *dignity,* Fam. X. ep. 6, he opposes certainly not charm but *deformity.* Matrons too have their own dignity, and, more precisely, as befits a jurist, § 15, Ulp. de senator: *There is greater dignity in the male sex.* Meanwhile, with Cicero’s leave and authority, [p. 104] it will be permitted to call deformed all things in which dignity, even absolute dignity, is wholly lacking, § 185, 177, and in true, especially masculine, beauty, e.g. of delivery, to demand dignity above all for charm, de Or. l. I. 142, and to lay down that a thing and a person *are deformed by taking away and stripping off dignity,* Or. pro Caelio 3.

> § 187. Neque diffiteor hoc confidentius me germanum dignitatem in primis pulcre cogitandorum venustatibus legere, §. 186. germanis potissimum scribentem; quoniam expertus noui, in aliis, in quibus gens germanorum romanis est apprime similis, hanc etiam laudem vtrique populo communem esse, de qua Cic. pro Mur. 23. *Omnes artes, quae nobis populi romani* (nationis germanicae) *studia conciliant, et admirabilem dignitatem et pergratam vtilitatem debent habere.* Vel absolutam dignitatem vniuersim et strenue commendanti arti nostrae aestheticae, relatiuam etiam clarius ob oculos ponenti, forte non sua solum constabit absoluta dignitas, sed et relatiua quaedam tribuetur a grauibus, neque tamen tetricis, inter ciues iudicibus. §. 185.

§ 187. Nor do I deny that I, a German, writing above all for Germans, read dignity the more confidently among the first charms of things to be thought beautifully, § 186; since I know from experience that, among the other respects in which the German nation is especially like the Roman, this merit too is common to both peoples, of which Cic. pro Mur. 23: *All the arts that win for us the favour of the Roman people* (of the German nation) *must have both an admirable dignity and a most welcome utility.* Perhaps, for our aesthetic art, which commends absolute dignity universally and strenuously, and sets relative dignity too more clearly before the eyes, not only will its own absolute dignity stand firm, but a certain relative dignity too will be attributed to it by serious, though not grim, judges among our fellow citizens. § 185.

> § 188. Erunt interim, nisi fallor, et in germanis ciuibus, qui §. 182. n. 1. et 3. satis liberaliter concedant, tamen n. 2. et 4. postulari iudicent [p. 105] aliquid, quod vbique requirere, quando pulcre cogitatur, videatur iusto venustoque rigidius. Verum his excusabor facilius, quando 1) expresse et explicite paraenetica didicerint curatius distinguere ab iis, quae tacite et implicite et longa veluti manu, admodum mediate vel ad minorum morum praecepta non omnino nihil conferant, 2) vitam pulcrae cognitionis dotem primariam, §. 22. penitius inspexerint, quam variis illa se modis ac gradibus belle soleat exserere. Nunc §. 169. ita me defendam, vt negem mihi vitio verti posse, si vel eadem, vel omnino minora poposcerim, respectu disciplinae morum aut probitatis, ac ille, qui se ipse dicit,

§ 188. There will meanwhile be, unless I am mistaken, even among German citizens, those who grant § 182 n. 1 and 3 liberally enough, yet judge that in n. 2 and 4 [p. 105] something is demanded which it would seem, more rigidly than is just and charming, to require everywhere, whenever one thinks beautifully. But I shall be more easily excused by these, when 1) they have learned to distinguish more carefully what is expressly and explicitly paraenetic from those things which tacitly and implicitly and, as it were, at long range, quite mediately contribute not nothing at all even to the precepts of the lesser morals, 2) they have looked more deeply into life, the primary gift of beautiful cognition, § 22, and into the various ways and degrees in which it is wont to display itself finely. Now, § 169, I shall defend myself thus, by denying that it can be counted a fault in me if I have demanded either the same or altogether less, in respect of the discipline of morals or of probity, than what he who calls himself

> *Epicuri de grege porcum,*

*a pig from Epicurus’ herd,*

> Horatius de poetis generatim iterum asserit iterumque, e. g.

Horace, asserts again and again of poets in general, e.g.

> *Et prodesse volunt et delectare poëtae / Et simul et iucunda et idonea dicere vitae. / Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit vtile dulci / Lectorem delectando pariterque monendo.*

*Poets wish both to profit and to delight, / and to say at once what is pleasant and what is fit for life. / He has won every vote who has mixed the useful with the sweet, / delighting the reader and admonishing him alike.*

> § 189. MAGNITVDO tandem AESTHETICA §. 177. hinc et DIGNITAS §. 182. tam ABSOLVTAE, quam RELATIVAE, §. 178, 185. erunt vel OBIECTIVAE (rerum, materiae,) quatenus in obiectis et cogitandis ipsis est praecipua ratio, cur per pulcrum [p. 106] ingenium et pectus, S. II. proportionata in magnitudine ac dignitate possint pingi, vel SVBIECTIVAE, (personae) possibilitates physicae potentiaeque certi hominis, etiam secundum quid et hypothetice tales, cum appetitionibus et decreto datam materiem, qua pote, qua fas est, in magnitudine et dignitate venuste sistendi ob oculos. Has posteriores dicamus MAGNANIMITATEM ET GRAVITATEM AESTHETICAM. E. §. 489.

§ 189. Finally, AESTHETIC MAGNITUDE, § 177, and hence DIGNITY too, § 182, both ABSOLUTE and RELATIVE, § 178, 185, will be either OBJECTIVE (of things, of the material), insofar as the principal reason why they can be painted in proportionate magnitude and dignity by a beautiful [p. 106] wit and heart, S. II, lies in the objects and the things to be thought themselves, or SUBJECTIVE (of the person): the physical possibilities and powers of a certain man, even such as are so in a certain respect and hypothetically, together with his appetitions and his resolution to set the given material before the eyes charmingly in magnitude and dignity, as far as he can, as far as is right. Let us call these latter AESTHETIC MAGNANIMITY AND GRAVITY. E. § 489.

> § 190. Sunt res, et materiae, quarum adspectu primo describendarum cum aliqua pulcritudine statim exprimatur nobis, quod olim Virgilio:

§ 190. There are things and materials at the first sight of which, as they are to be described with some beauty, there is at once wrung from us what once was wrung from Virgil:

> *Maior rerum mihi nascitur ordo, / Maius opus moueo.* VII. 44. Aen.

*A greater order of things is born for me, / I set in motion a greater work.* VII. 44. Aen.

> Tunc felix ille, qui iustus aestimator sui vere tamen de themate tali a se pulcre exsequendo, possit praedicere, quod idem de saeculis aureis se viuo redituris:

Then happy is he who, a just judge of himself, can nonetheless truly predict, of such a theme to be beautifully executed by him, what the same poet predicted of the golden ages that would return in his lifetime:

> *Non me carminibus vincet nec Thracius Orpheus, / Nec Linus, huic mater quamuis, atque huic pater adsit, / Orphei Calliopea, Lino formosus Apollo. / Pan deus Arcadia mecum si iudice certet, / Pan etiam Arcadia dicet se iudice victum.* §. 189.

*Neither Thracian Orpheus shall surpass me in song, / nor Linus, though his mother stand by the one, and his father by the other, / Calliopea by Orpheus, fair Apollo by Linus. / Should Pan, with Arcadia as judge, contend with me, / Pan too, with Arcadia as judge, will own himself beaten.* § 189.

#### Sectio XVI. Magnitudo Materiae Absoluta. — Section XVI. Absolute Magnitude of Matter.

> § 191. [p. 107] Magnitudo materiae aesthetica absoluta, §. 189. poscit, ne cogitanda ac themata sumantur pulcre meditaturo obiecta ac materiae, quibus intra horizontem hominum aestheticum constitutis, §. 119, 127. omnino deest magnitudo, §. 177, NVGAE VERE TALES (res infimae et nugatoriae, quisquiliae, ineptiae) *Poetam non audio in nugis,* Cic. Par. 3. Vnde sat. V. 19. Persius optime:

§ 191. [p. 107] The absolute aesthetic magnitude of the material, § 189, demands that there be not taken, as things to be thought and as themes by one who would meditate beautifully, objects and materials which, set within the aesthetic horizon of mankind, § 119, 127, wholly lack magnitude, § 177—TRIFLES TRULY SUCH (the lowest and trifling things, rubbish, inanities). *I do not listen to the poet in trifles,* Cic. Par. 3. Whence, sat. V. 19, Persius excellently:

> *Non equidem hoc studeo bullatis vt mihi nugis / Pagina turgescat, dare pondus idonea fumo. / Excutienda damus praecordia,* §. 182.

*I do not indeed strive that my page should swell / with bubbled trifles, fit to give weight to smoke. / We give our hearts to be searched,* § 182.

> § 192. *Si quis rixatur de lana saepe caprina, et / Propugnat nugis armatus,*

§ 192. *If anyone wrangles, as often, over goat’s wool, and / fights armed with trifles,*

> huc §. 191. materia litis vere pertinet, nisi velit omnino suas tricas vltra horizontem aestheticum tollere, §. 121. Catullus atque Martialis in ea sua cogitata, quae scripserunt ex turpi lege, de qua §. 184. iusto leniores sunt, quando ea nugas vocant, alia tamen pulcrius a se concepta inuoluentes eodem [p. 108] titulo sunt interpretandi ex §. 179. Habentur etiam saepius in nugis, quae non sunt, qualia §. 100. et forsan huc opinio Democriti, probe intellecta, quam Cicero male refutatam de Diu. II. 20. non aequius in magnis nugis habet, ac *physicorum genere nihil* ait *arrogantius* esse.

here, § 191, the matter of the dispute truly belongs, unless he wishes to lift his quibbles altogether beyond the aesthetic horizon, § 121. Catullus and Martial, in those of their thoughts which they wrote according to the shameful law of which § 184, are more lenient than is just when they call them trifles; yet, since they wrap other things more beautifully conceived by them under the same [p. 108] title, they are to be interpreted according to § 179. Things are also often counted among trifles which are not, such as § 100, and perhaps here belongs the opinion of Democritus, properly understood, which Cicero, having badly refuted it, de Diu. II. 20, counts not more fairly among great trifles, when he says that *nothing is more arrogant than the tribe of physicists.*

> § 193. DIGNITATEM AESTHETICAM §. 182. et absolutam et relatiuam, §. 185. et obiectiuam et subiectiuam, quatenus in ea deprehenduntur n. 1. et 3. §. 182. liceat in sequentibus NEGATIVAM, quatenus autem simul n. 2. et 4. §. c. considerantur, POSITIVAM appellare. Et quoniam nobilem iam ΗΘΟΥΣ AESTHETICI partem aggredimur, definiam illud, psychologis saltim perspicue, generatim ante omnia per studium possibilitatis moralis, M. §. 723. aestheticum, vel in aestheticis obseruatum. *Ἤθους nomine, vt ego quidem sentio, caret sermo romanus. Mores appellantur — — — — Sed ipsam rei naturam spectanti mihi non tam mores significari videntur, quam morum quaedam proprietas.* Quint. VI. 3.

§ 193. AESTHETIC DIGNITY, § 182, both absolute and relative, § 185, both objective and subjective, insofar as n. 1 and 3 of § 182 are found in it, let it be permitted in what follows to call NEGATIVE, but insofar as n. 2 and 4 of the same § are at the same time considered, POSITIVE. And since we are now entering upon the noble part of the AESTHETIC ΗΘΟΥΣ [character], I shall define it, perspicuously at least for psychologists, in general before all else, by the study of moral possibility, M. § 723, that is aesthetic or observed in aesthetic matters. *For the name Ἤθους [character] the Roman tongue, as I at least think, has no word. They are called mores — — — — But to me, considering the nature of the thing itself, it seems that not so much mores are signified as a certain property of mores.* Quint. VI. 3.

> § 194. ΗΘΟΣ AESTHETICVM habet etiam speciem suam partemque, ex qua NEGATIVVM dicatur, §. 193, 182. cuius haec est formula: Res, ordo, significatio, e. g. dictio, §. 13. si [p. 109] pulcrae intenduntur, ita instituantur, ne quid moraliter absurdi in iisdem, vel ipsi rationis analogo pelluceat, §. 16, 22. et alteram speciem ac partem, ex qua POSITIVVM appelletur, et secundum quam eadem, quae modo dixi, vere etiam consentire moribus et cum iisdem congruere, pulcre conuenire cum illis, quae moraliter, ethice, oeconomice, ciuiliter ex vsibus, consuetudinibusque fieri possunt, fiat phaenomenon, vel ipsi rationis analogo obseruabile, §. 23.

§ 194. The AESTHETIC ΗΘΟΣ [character] also has its species and part by which it may be called NEGATIVE, § 193, 182, of which this is the formula: let the things, the order, the signification, e.g. the diction, § 13, if [p. 109] they are intended to be beautiful, be so arranged that nothing morally absurd shows through in them, even to the analogue of reason itself, § 16, 22; and another species and part by which it may be called POSITIVE, according to which the same things I have just mentioned, truly agreeing with morals too and consonant with them, beautifully harmonising with those things which can morally, ethically, economically, civilly come about from usages and customs, become a phenomenon observable even to the analogue of reason itself, § 23.

> § 195. Veniamus ad vnam ἤθους partem ex primis, §. 194. quam naturalis nunc meditandi ratio subministrabit. Dignitas aesthetica, si vel absolutam tantum intelligas, §. 182, 185. postulat, ne qua cogitanda, multo minus themata sumantur, quibus intra horizontem aestheticum constitutis, vbertimque ac viuide e. c. §. 22. percipiendis omnis omnino deesset dignitas, OBIECTA VILIA ET PLEBEIA, quae luto potius, quam myricis, §. 178. conferas, et has humiles nuncupans illa HVMILLIMA dicas ET ABIECTA.

§ 195. Let us come to one part of ἤθους [character] among the first, § 194, which the natural order of meditating will now supply. Aesthetic dignity, even if you understand only the absolute kind, § 182, 185, demands that no things to be thought, much less themes, be taken which, set within the aesthetic horizon and to be perceived richly and vividly etc., § 22, would wholly lack all dignity—VILE AND PLEBEIAN OBJECTS, which you may compare to mud rather than to tamarisks, § 178, and, calling the latter lowly, you may call the former THE LOWEST AND ABJECT.

> § 196. *Vt quisque optime natus institutusque est* (haec autem est aesthetici practici persona, §. 45, 54, 63.) *nihil abiectum, nihil humile,* §. 195. *cogitant.* Cic. de Fin. V. 57. Eorum nemo

§ 196. *As each man is best born and brought up* (and this is the person of the practical aesthetician, § 45, 54, 63) *so they think nothing abject, nothing lowly,* § 195. Cic. de Fin. V. 57. None of them

> [p. 110] *Migret in obscuras humili sermone tabernas, / Offenduntur enim, quibus est equus, et pater et res.* Hor.

[p. 110] *would stray with lowly speech into obscure taverns, / for those who have a horse, and a father, and property, take offence.* Hor.

> Neque huc tantum traho turpissimam obscenitatem, de qua §. 184, 192. sed et humi repentem adulationem,

Nor do I bring under this head only the most shameful obscenity, of which § 184, 192, but also adulation crawling on the ground,

> *laudare paratam / Si bene — — — —, aut si quid fecit amicus, / Quod proferre palam non possit lingua modeste,* Iuu.

*ready to praise / if he has done well — — — —, or if a friend has done anything / which a modest tongue could not bring out openly,* Iuu.

> et luxuriantem contumeliis conuiciisque lixas inter et calones maledicentiam, quam olim quidam critici, bona mens! qui Critici! documentum vbertatis suae copiaeque voluerunt. §. 195.

and the abusiveness, luxuriating in insults and taunts fit for sutlers and camp-followers, which once certain critics—good heavens! what Critics!—wanted as a proof of their richness and abundance. § 195.

> § 197. In diiudicanda magnitudine ac dignitate materiarum absoluta, ne magna pusillis,

§ 197. In judging the absolute magnitude and dignity of materials, lest great things with petty ones,

> *sine pondere habentia pondus,* §. 177.

*things having weight without weight,* § 177,

> digna indignis, §. 182. fanda nefandis, §. 196. temere misceantur, non excluduntur ex materiis pulcre cogitandis, 1) vere nonnullam habentia magnitudinem, aliquando summam, §. 178. in quibus tamen non nemo, gigantum fraterculus, qui se solum putat aliquid magni, ac omnia refert ad grandem, quam in se solus miratur, mensuram, nihil omnino, nisi nihili facienda, vili pendenda, nugas meras, potest deprehendere. Non opus est [p. 111] *musicam Epaminondae* citare, quamdiu ipsa religio multis,

worthy with unworthy, § 182, speakable with unspeakable, § 196, be rashly mixed, there are not excluded from the materials to be thought beautifully 1) things truly having some magnitude, sometimes the highest, § 178, in which, however, many a one, a little brother of the giants, who thinks that he alone is something great, and refers everything to the grand measure which he alone admires in himself, can find nothing at all except things to be made nothing of, to be held cheap, mere trifles. There is no need to [p. 111] cite *the music of Epaminondas,* so long as religion itself, to many,

> *nisi cum re, vilior alga est.*

*unless it comes with property, is cheaper than seaweed.*

> § 198. 2) Quibus deest vtique quaedam magnitudo relatiua ac comparatiua, neque tamen absoluta, §. 178. e. g. in colloquiis epistolisque familiaribus, in quibus vel duo nonnunquam *satis magnum alter alteri theatrum sumus.* Sen. Talem se sistit Corydon:

§ 198. 2) Those which indeed lack a certain relative and comparative magnitude, yet not an absolute one, § 178, e.g. in familiar conversations and letters, in which even two of us are sometimes *a theatre great enough, the one for the other.* Sen. Such does Corydon present himself:

> *Despectus tibi sum, nec quis sim quaeris, Alexi,* / *Quam diues pecoris niuei, quam lactis abundans.* / *Mille meae siculis errant in montibus agnae.* e. c. Virg. Ecl. II. 19.

*I am scorned by you, nor do you ask who I am, Alexis,* / *How rich in snowy flocks, how abounding in milk.* / *A thousand lambs of mine wander on the Sicilian hills.* etc. Virg. Ecl. II. 19.

> § 199. 3) Quae non ipsa solum, sed et cum suis variis consectariisque satis multis pura mente cogitari possunt, etiam copiose, viuide e. c. §. 22. licet impura mens possit in ipsis eorumque variis et consectariis simul non pauca virtuti inimica excogitare, e. g. si,

§ 199. 3) Those which can be thought with a pure mind not only in themselves, but also together with their various and sufficiently numerous consequences, even copiously, vividly, etc., § 22, although an impure mind might at the same time devise in them and in their various features and consequences not a few things hostile to virtue, e.g. if,

> *Tityre, lentus in vmbra* / *Formosam resonare doces Amaryllida siluas.*

*Tityrus, at ease in the shade,* / *You teach the woods to echo fair Amaryllis.*

> ⁠4) quae morosae virtuti, vel etiam fucatae taedium afferunt, quando ab aliis cogitantur, innocentia, non sine suspicione inuidiae: e. g. Mart. IX. 98:

⁠4) those which bring tedium to a morose virtue, or even to a counterfeit one, when they are thought by others in innocence, not without a suspicion of envy: e.g. Mart. IX. 98:

> *quod amamur, quodque probamur.*

*that we are loved, and that we are approved.*

> [p. 112] § 200. 5) Quae non omnibus personis ac aetatibus, temporibus ac locis conueniant, aliquibus autem vtique, salua tam magnitudine, quam dignitate absolutis, §. 197. e. g. quae solebant cum Lucilio,

[p. 112] § 200. 5) Those which are not suited to all persons and ages, times and places, but certainly to some, with absolute magnitude as well as absolute dignity remaining intact, § 197, e.g. those with which, in the company of Lucilius,

> *vbi se a vulgo et scena in secreta remorant* / *Virtus Scipiadae ac mitis sapientia Laeli* / *Nugari* §. 192. faciles, *discincti et ludere, donec* / *Decoqueretur olus.* Hor. Serm. II. 1. 75.

*when they had withdrawn from the crowd and the stage into privacy,* / *the virtue of Scipio and the mild wisdom of Laelius* / *used to trifle,* § 192, easy-going, *and, ungirt, to play, until* / *the greens were cooked.* Hor. Serm. II. 1. 75.

> ⁠6) non explicite, immediate, aut propius virtutes inculcantia. e. g. Lucretii l. 49:

⁠6) those not explicitly, immediately, or more closely inculcating the virtues, e.g. Lucretius I. 49:

> *De summa caeli ratione deumque* / *Disserere incipiam, et rerum primordia pandam,* / *Vnde omnes natura creet res, auctet, alatque,* / *Quoue eadem rursum natura peremta resoluat.* e. c.

*Of the supreme order of heaven and of the gods* / *I shall begin to discourse, and shall unfold the first beginnings of things,* / *From which nature creates all things, increases and nourishes them,* / *And into which the same nature again resolves them when they perish.* etc.

> § 201. 7) Quibus vtique deest quaedam dignitas relatiua ac comparatiua, neque tamen absoluta, § 188. e. g. *Epaminondam saltasse commode, scienterque tibiis cantasse.* Corn. Huc Anacreon et celebris Catulli passer, viuens, c. 2. ac mortuus, c. 3:

§ 201. 7) Those which indeed lack a certain relative and comparative dignity, yet not an absolute one, § 188, e.g. *that Epaminondas danced gracefully and played the pipes skilfully.* Corn. To this belong Anacreon and Catullus’s famous sparrow, alive, c. 2, and dead, c. 3:

> [p. 113] *Lugete, o veneres, cupidinesque,* / *Et quantum est hominum venustiorum!* / *Passer mortuus est meae puellae,* / *Passer, deliciae meae puellae.* e. c.

[p. 113] *Mourn, O Venuses and Cupids,* / *And all you men of finer feeling!* / *My girl’s sparrow is dead,* / *The sparrow, my girl’s delight.* etc.

#### Sectio XVII. Magnitudo Materiae Relatiua. — Section XVII. Relative Magnitude of Matter.

> § 202. Quibus et magnitudo conuenit et dignitas absoluta, §. 182, 185. MATERIAE, relatiuam et magnitudinem, §. 180. et dignitatem habebunt I.) myricae, minimam, cum aliqua latitudine, quae deceat aestheticum, §. 15, 16. honore vno ex minoribus dignae, TENVES. Huc et personas, obiecta personalia, pertinere ne dubites, referamus et nos, post Demetrium,

§ 202. The MATTERS to which both absolute magnitude and absolute dignity belong, § 182, 185, will have also a relative magnitude, § 180, and a relative dignity: I.) the tamarisks, the least, with some latitude, such as befits the aesthetician, § 15, 16, worthy of one of the lesser honours, the SLENDER. That persons too, personal objects, belong here, do not doubt; let us also, after Demetrius, refer here

> *Vulteium nomine Menam,* / *Praeconem, tenui censu, sine crimine natum,* / *Et properare loco et cessare, et quaerere, et vti,* / *Gaudentem paruisque sodalibus, et lare curto,* / *Et ludis, et post decisa negotia Campo.* e. c. Hor. I. ep. 7. 55.

*Vulteius, Mena by name,* / *An auctioneer, of slender means, born without reproach,* / *Who both hastened and rested in due season, both earned and spent,* / *Delighting in his humble companions and his own small hearth,* / *And in the games, and in the Campus when business was done.* etc. Hor. I. ep. 7. 55.

> § 203. II. Siluae, maximam, cum eadem aestheticum [p. 114] decente latitudine, §. 202. honore vno ex maximis dignae, excellenter MAGNAE, GRANDES ATQVE SVBLIMES. Non pugnabo contra Senecam, quando magnitudinem et dignitatem rerum intrinsecam spectans: *Omnia*, inquit, *vitia, non refert, in quantum procedant, extendantque se. Angusta sunt, misera, depressa.* §. 195. *Sola sublimis et excelsa* (moraliter etiam) *virtus est. Nec quicquam magnum est, nisi quod simul et placidum*, nisi forsan in effatum vltimum, de Ira. I. 16. Nobis autem hic sermo est de magnitudine et dignitate obiectiua, non quatenus ipsis obiectis inhaeret, sed quatenus obiectis inhaerens, quicquid illud sit, rationem propiorem continet, vt de obiectis magnae dignaeque cogitationes formari possint, §. 189, 18.

§ 203. II. The forests, the greatest, with the same latitude [p. 114] befitting the aesthetician, § 202, worthy of one of the greatest honours, eminently GREAT, GRAND AND SUBLIME. I shall not contend against Seneca when, considering the intrinsic magnitude and dignity of things, he says: *All vices, it matters not how far they advance and extend themselves, are narrow, wretched, low.* § 195. *Only virtue is sublime and lofty* (morally too). *Nor is anything great, unless it is at the same time also calm*, except perhaps as regards the last pronouncement, de Ira I. 16. But our discourse here is of objective magnitude and dignity, not insofar as it inheres in the objects themselves, but insofar as, inhering in the objects, whatever it may be, it contains the more proximate ground why great and worthy thoughts can be formed about the objects, § 189, 18.

> § 204. Sicut itaque recti quidam habitus, non abiecti quidem ac humiles, tenues tamen illi possunt esse, §. 202. partim in destitutis magnitudine quadam relatiue maiori naturali, partim expertes multis variis consectariisque, etiam moralibus, sed per analogon rationis obseruabilioribus, §. 181, 182: ita praui quidam habitus et facinora videantur esse posse magna pulcre cogitaturo materia, vel omnino grandis, quando 1) varia eorum, etiam ad materiale remotum et proximum realia pertinentia [p. 115] M. § 914. ipsumque formale simul habeant magnitudinem naturalem per plura etiam consectaria, denuo vel ex materiali, vel ex formali mali effluentia per ipsum analogon rationis detegenda, 2) non tam ipsorum formale dictorum, quam huius ingens deformitas thema pulcre sistendum ob oculos aesthetice meditaturo sumitur, quod vtique fieri potest dignissime, §. 18, 203. Ita Catilinae scelus et Ciceroni et Salustio thema grande fuisse videatur, §. 89. Nec facile, nisi in eiusmodi thematibus, aliquis, ex Petronii consilio,

§ 204. Just as, therefore, certain right habits, though not abject and lowly, can nevertheless be slender, § 202, partly in those destitute of a certain relatively greater natural magnitude, partly in those lacking many various consequences, even moral ones, yet more observable through the analogue of reason, § 181, 182: so certain depraved habits and deeds may seem able to be a great matter, or even an altogether grand one, for one who is to think beautifully, when 1) their various real features, pertaining [p. 115] both to the remote and to the proximate material, M. § 914, and their formal element too, have at the same time natural magnitude through a number of consequences as well, flowing anew either from the material or from the formal element of the evil and to be detected through the analogue of reason itself; 2) not so much the formal element of the said deeds themselves as the enormous deformity of this is taken as the theme to be beautifully set before the eyes by one who is to meditate aesthetically, which can indeed be done most worthily, § 18, 203. Thus the crime of Catiline may seem to have been a grand theme both for Cicero and for Sallust, § 89. Nor easily, except in themes of this kind, will anyone, on Petronius’s advice,

> *ingentis quatiat Demosthenis arma,* / *Grandiaque indomiti Ciceronis verba minetur.*

*shake the arms of mighty Demosthenes,* / *And brandish the grand words of untamed Cicero.*

> § 205. Nec excludam obiectis aesthetice grandibus, §. 203. ea, quibus est magnitudo naturalis tantum, §. 187. relatiue vna ex maximis, etiamsi moraliter videantur indifferentia, si sistantur in dignitate, negatiua quidem tantum, §. 193. quam tamen summa cum diligentia tuearis. §. 203. Ita Lucr. I. 720. grandia de Sicilia:

§ 205. Nor shall I exclude from the aesthetically grand objects, § 203, those which have natural magnitude only, § 187, relatively one of the greatest, even if morally they seem indifferent, provided they be set forth in dignity, though only a negative one, § 193, which nevertheless you must guard with the utmost diligence, § 203. Thus Lucr. I. 720, grand things about Sicily:

> *Hic est magna Charybdis et hic Aetnea minantur.* / *Murmura flammarum,*

*Here is great Charybdis, and here the Aetnean rumblings* / *Of the flames threaten,*

> An satis dignum, quando pergit:

Is it worthy enough, when he continues:

> *rursum se colligere iras?*

*to gather their wrath once more?*

> [p. 116] Equidem τῷ:

[p. 116] For my part, to the words:

> *Magna modis multis miranda videtur* / *Gentibus humanis regio,*

*A region which seems in many ways wondrous* / *To the races of men,*

> grandia cogitaturus non addidissem:

had I been about to think grand things, I would not have added:

> *visendaque fertur.* cf. Aen. III. 571. sqq.

*and is said to be worth seeing.* cf. Aen. III. 571. sqq.

> § 206. Interim in ipsis generice maximis, §. 203. eminent, quibus ad magnitudinem naturalem et dignitatem negatiuam, quas ex maximis dixeris, accedat etiam dignitas aliqua positiua, §. 193. Huc referrem, si Ciceronem ex animi sententia scripsisse putarem, de nat. deorum l. II. 166: *Nemo vir magnus sine aliquo afflatu diuino vnquam fuit.* 167: *Magnis viris prospere eueniunt semper omnes res, si quidem satis a nostris, et a principe philosophorum, Socrate, dictum est de vbertatibus virtutis et copiis.* 168: *mala et impia consuetudo est contra deos disputandi, siue animo id fit, siue simulate.*

§ 206. Meanwhile, among those which are generically the greatest, § 203, those stand out in which, to the natural magnitude and the negative dignity which you would call among the greatest, there is added also some positive dignity, § 193. Here I would refer, if I thought Cicero had written from the conviction of his heart, de nat. deorum l. II. 166: *No man was ever great without some divine inspiration.* 167: *To great men all things always turn out prosperously, if indeed enough has been said by our philosophers, and by the prince of philosophers, Socrates, on the richness and abundance of virtue.* 168: *it is an evil and impious habit to dispute against the gods, whether it be done in earnest or in pretence.*

> § 207. *Sunt* enim vtique, quod Quintilianus habet, VIII. 3. *alia aliis honestiora, sublimiora,* e. c. sicut et magis minusue tenuia, §. 202. Neque tenuitas, neque sublimitas heic consideranda est illa, quam intellectus forsan et ratio sola tandem in distincte, quantum fieri potest, repraesentatis detegat: §. 15, 16. sed a minimis [p. 117] ad maxima obseruabilium et pulcre sistendorum elegans per analogon rationis, non sine dignitate, paullatim exsurgens complexus materiarum omnis diuidatur in partes aequales tres. Infima erit aestetice [sic: aesthetice] tenuis, suprema aesthetice sublimis, quaeuis suos iterum gradus et magnitudinis et dignitatis comprehensa. §. 203.

§ 207. *There are* indeed, as Quintilian has it, VIII. 3, *some things more honourable, more sublime than others,* etc., just as there are also more or less slender ones, § 202. Neither the slenderness nor the sublimity to be considered here is that which perhaps the intellect and reason alone would at last detect in things represented as distinctly as can be, § 15, 16; but let the whole complex of matters, rising gradually and elegantly, not without dignity, from the least [p. 117] to the greatest of the things observable and beautifully to be set forth through the analogue of reason, be divided into three equal parts. The lowest will be the aesthetically slender, the highest the aesthetically sublime, each again comprising its own degrees both of magnitude and of dignity, § 203.

> § 208. III. Arbusta, mediam inter tenuia et sublimia §. 207. partem occupantia, MATERIAE MEDIOCRES, *interiectae, intermediae, et quasi temperatae, vicinae* tenui sublimique, *vtriusque participes, vel vtriusque, si verum quaerimus, potius expertes.* Cic. Huc e. g. Pamphili descriptio apud Ter. Andr. I. 1.:

§ 208. III. The shrubs, occupying the middle part between the slender and the sublime, § 207, the MIDDLING MATTERS, *interposed, intermediate, and as it were tempered, neighbouring on* the slender and the sublime, *sharing in both, or rather, if we seek the truth, destitute of both.* Cic. Here belongs e.g. the description of Pamphilus in Ter. Andr. I. 1.:

> *Quod plerique omnes faciunt adolescentuli,* / *Vt animum ad aliquod studium adiungant, aut equos* / *Alere, aut canes ad venandum, aut ad philosophos,* / *Horum ille nihil egregie praeter cetera* / *Studebat, et tamen omnia haec mediocriter.* e. c.

*What nearly all young men do,* / *To devote their mind to some pursuit, either to keep horses* / *Or hounds for hunting, or to the philosophers,* / *In none of these did he engage eminently beyond the rest,* / *And yet in all of these moderately.* etc.

> § 209. Longinus videtur magnum, §. 177. etiam relatiue tale, §. 203. et in magnis eiusmodi maximum confundere, quando: οὐδὲν, ait, ὑπάρχει [p. 118] μέγα, οὗ τὸ καταφρονεῖν ἐστι μέγα. S. VII. exemplaque adducit generatim honores et dignitates, et quae habent πολὺ τὸ ἔξωθεν προστραγῳδούμενον, caussam interserens, quia sapienti nequeant videri bona eximia, quorum contemtus sit aureae mediocritatis, quaeque contemnentes, quando ea habere possunt, magis admiramur, quam iisdem fruentes, §. 207. Quando porro characterem bonorum sublimium exhibet, si sint διὰ παντὸς ἀρέσκοντα καὶ πᾶσιν, quaeritur an huic maiori quicquam vnquam certo subsumi possit. Si possit, erit illud sane non magnum, sed maximum. e. g. quando S. VIII. poscit, τὸ σφοδρὸν καὶ ἐνθουσιαστικὸν πάθος, confer Senecam citatum, §. 203.

§ 209. Longinus seems to confound the great, § 177, even the relatively great, § 203, and the greatest among such great things, when he says: οὐδὲν ὑπάρχει [p. 118] μέγα, οὗ τὸ καταφρονεῖν ἐστι μέγα [nothing is great, the contempt of which is great], S. VII, and he adduces as examples, in general, honours and dignities, and the things which have πολὺ τὸ ἔξωθεν προστραγῳδούμενον [much outward pomp tacked on], interposing as the reason that they cannot seem eminent goods to the wise man, the contempt of which belongs to the golden mean, and that we admire those who despise them, when they can have them, more than those who enjoy them, § 207. When, further, he exhibits as the character of sublime goods that they are διὰ παντὸς ἀρέσκοντα καὶ πᾶσιν [pleasing always and to all], the question is whether anything can ever with certainty be subsumed under this major premise. If it can, that will surely be not great, but the greatest, e.g. when in S. VIII he demands τὸ σφοδρὸν καὶ ἐνθουσιαστικὸν πάθος [vehement and inspired passion]; compare Seneca as cited, § 203.

> § 210. Recte Longinus S. VIII. sublime, §. 203. distinguit a pathetico, quia quaedam

§ 210. Rightly does Longinus, S. VIII, distinguish the sublime, § 203, from the pathetic, since certain

> *Curae leues loquuntur, ingentes stupent.* Sen.

*Light cares speak, great ones are dumb.* Sen.

> et esse sublime potest sine perturbationibus animi, §. 205. fidenter tamen simul affirmans, nihil tam magnificum esse, quam affectum vehementem, vbi opus est. §. 206. In quaestione, quam multis expendit, S. XXXIII. sqq. an praestet magnitudo (relatiuam intellige sublimitatem §. 203.) inter quaedam, quae peccent, mediocribus, per omnia sanis et vitio carentibus §. 208. habebit omnino sibi affirmanti facilem in assentiendo philosophum [p. 119] aestheticum, si sublimitas et eam ambientia recte cogitanda sint adeo pulcra, vt subductis macularum adhaerentium summis, priorum tamen aggregatum pulcrius ac venustius sit residuum, ac mediocre quoddam aliud thema sic cogitatum, vt etiamsi non appareant eius gradui pulcritudinis subtrahendae maculae, tamen aggregatum pulcre cogitandorum de eodem infra priorem summam subsistat. Addamus ob sublimitatem sociam multa, quae in mediocribus, §. 208. non viderentur solum, sed et essent maculae, nec has quidem esse, sed tantum videri, vere exceptiones non inelegantes, §. 25.

and the sublime can exist without perturbations of the mind, § 205, while at the same time he confidently affirms that nothing is so magnificent as a vehement affect, where there is need of it, § 206. In the question which he weighs at length, S. XXXIII sqq., whether magnitude (understand relative sublimity, § 203) amid certain faults is preferable to middling things that are sound throughout and free from fault, § 208, he will have altogether an easy assent to his affirmation from the [p. 119] aesthetic philosopher, provided the sublimity and what surrounds it, when rightly thought, are so beautiful that, when the sum of the adhering blemishes has been subtracted, the aggregate of the former nevertheless remains more beautiful and more charming than some other middling theme thought in such a way that, even if no blemishes appear which must be subtracted from its degree of beauty, nevertheless the aggregate of the things to be beautifully thought about it remains below the former sum. Let us add that, on account of the companionship of sublimity, many things which in middling matters, § 208, would not only seem but also be blemishes, are not blemishes, but only seem so, being truly exceptions not inelegant, § 25.

> § 211. Virtutem bonosque mores heic tantum consideramus, quatenus phaenomena fiunt, aut per commercium hominum externamque viuendi rationem obseruantur, non exclusis ipsis virtutum vmbris, §. 45. quarum discrimen a vera virtute, non nisi per intellectum ac rationem detegeretur, §. 15, 16. Vnde patebit cultus externi diuini, morum, rituum, cerimoniarum ac consuetudinum, perspicaciae declaratae, disciplinae corporis comtioris, curae status externi, officiorum humanitatis generatim et praesertim decori, tam positiui, quam negatiui, nonnihil aliam esse rationem ad ethica grauiora, ac solet intelligi a meditante vitae praecepta beatae, quantum [p. 120] eius fieri potest, per puram rationem, E. §. 110, -- 383. e. c.

§ 211. We consider virtue and good morals here only insofar as they become phenomena, or are observed through the intercourse of men and the external manner of living, not excluding the very shades of the virtues, § 45, whose difference from true virtue would be detected only through the intellect and reason, § 15, 16. Whence it will be evident that the external worship of God, manners, rites, ceremonies and customs, declared perspicacity, the discipline of a more graceful body, the care of one’s external condition, the duties of humanity in general and especially of decorum, positive as well as negative, stand in a somewhat different relation to the weightier ethics than is usually understood by one who meditates on the precepts of the happy life, as far as [p. 120] that can be done, through pure reason, E. § 110, -- 383, etc.

> § 212. Nec aesthetico semper, immo perquam raro potius virtus bonique mores spectantur in statu hominis naturali generatim et velut in illimitato, sicut ethicis accuratioribus plerumque solum. E. §. 1, 9. Heic potius considerantur, vti exsistunt, non in specialibus solum status naturalis modificationibus, E. P. II. sed et simul in statibus hominum socialibus, in nexibus familiarum et consanguinitatum, diuersorum vitae generum, societatum inde varie discrepantium, ciuitatum et ex ciuili vinculo redundantium infinitorum paene respectuum, nec eorum vniuersalium tantum, quos abstrahit philosophus, sed particularium, immo singularium, quatenus a positu corporis in hoc illoue pendent, pro locis aetatibusque mutabiles. §. 22. Heic apprime sunt attendenda iam ea, quae *non eadem omnibus* sunt *honesta atque turpia, sed omnia maiorum institutis iudicantur.* Corn.

§ 212. Nor are virtue and good morals always, nay rather very rarely, regarded by the aesthetician in the natural state of man in general and, as it were, unlimited, as they mostly are by the more exact ethical writers alone, E. § 1, 9. Here they are rather considered as they exist, not only in the special modifications of the natural state, E. P. II, but also at the same time in the social states of men, in the ties of families and kinships, of the diverse kinds of life, of the societies variously differing therefrom, of civil states and of the almost infinite relations arising out of the civil bond, and not only the universal ones among these, which the philosopher abstracts, but the particular, nay the singular, insofar as they depend on the position of the body in this or that place, changeable according to places and ages, § 22. Here above all attention must now be paid to those things which *are not honourable and base alike for all, but are all judged by the institutions of one’s forefathers.* Corn.

> § 213. Ex his punctis visus, §. 211, 212. si contempleris virtutem moresque laudabiles, et pluribus vtique differre gradibus inter se, deprehendes et posse tamen cum aliqua rotunditate, §. 166. diuidi, sicut diligentia diuiditur [p. 121] gradus culpae doliue cognituris, et praedicanda tantum non omnia grammaticis, §. 180, 207. in SIMPLICITER HONESTAM VIVENDI RATIONEM, illum bene morati viuendi generis gradum, ad quem obtinendum cuiuscunque conditionis et educationis et consuetudinum necessitudinumque persona, si velit esse bona, vires sufficientes habere videatur, in MORES VIVENDIQVE RATIONEM NOBILEM, illum bene morati ex §. 211, 212. viuendi generis gradum, quem in melius natis feliciusque iam educatis ordinario non sine vsu, vel omnino aliqua disciplina, reperias tantum ordinario, adeoque quemcunque hominem eo pertingere vix posse, licet decreuerit, non sine verisimilitudine iudices, et in HEROICAM tandem VIRTVTEM VIVENDIQVE RATIONEM SINGVLARI CVM MAIESTATE CONIVNCTAM, illum optime viuendi modum ex §. 211, 212. conceptum, quem vel attingere, vel aequabilem et bono significatu semper eundem sibi conseruare, quod difficilius est,

§ 213. If from these points of view, § 211, 212, you contemplate virtue and praiseworthy morals, and that they certainly differ from one another by several degrees, you will find that they can nevertheless be divided with some roundness, § 166, just as diligence is divided [p. 121] into degrees for those who are to determine culpability or malice, and just about everything that is to be predicated, for grammarians, § 180, 207, into the SIMPLY HONOURABLE MANNER OF LIVING, that degree of the well-mannered kind of living, for the attainment of which a person of any condition, education, customs and connections whatever, if he wishes to be good, seems to have sufficient strength; into NOBLE MANNERS AND MANNER OF LIVING, that degree of the kind of living well-mannered according to § 211, 212, which you would find ordinarily only in those better born and already more happily educated, ordinarily not without practice, or indeed some discipline, so that you would judge, not without verisimilitude, that hardly any man whatever could reach it merely because he had resolved to; and finally into HEROIC VIRTUE AND A MANNER OF LIVING JOINED WITH SINGULAR MAJESTY, that best mode of living, conceived according to § 211, 212, which either to attain, or to preserve for oneself even-tenored and, in the good sense, always the same, which is harder,

> *pauci, quos aequus amauit* / *Juppiter, atque ardens euexit ad aethera virtus,* / *Diis geniti, potuere.*

*few, whom just Jupiter* / *has loved, or whom ardent virtue has raised to the heavens,* / *sons of gods, have been able.*

> § 214. Qui nouit viuere, E. §. 390. differentias, [p. 122] §. 213. breuiter notatas satis perspicue sibi ipse tradet vberius, nec haerebit in hac dignitatis aestheticae §. 182. relatiuae, §. 185. et obiectiuae §. 189. concipienda veluti scala; Simpliciter honestum viuendi genus: tenuia, §. 202. = nobile: mediocria, §. 208. = heroicum: sublimia, §. 203.

§ 214. He who knows how to live, E. § 390, will himself deliver to himself more fully the differences, [p. 122] § 213, briefly but clearly enough noted, nor will he stick at conceiving this as it were scale of aesthetic dignity, § 182, relative, § 185, and objective, § 189: the simply honourable kind of living: slender matters, § 202 = the noble: middling, § 208 = the heroic: sublime, § 203.

> § 215. Quae rerum humanarum est limitatio, nulla paene talis est, quae non duplicem, vt Epictetus ait, ansam habeat, tolerandam alteram, alteram minus. Non obiecta solum absolute digna, sed ipsa sublimia, si quadam ex parte sui considerantur, habent eadem simul aliam, ex qua si penitius inspiciantur, non sublimitas solum pereat, sed et omnis non raro dignitas. Par ratio magnitudinis naturalis, prout comparetur. S. XV. XVI. Hinc eo facilius est obseruatu quaedam obiecta, quasdam materias, prima fronte quae videantur semper eadem, pro diuersis tamen respectibus, variis ac momentis, quibus potissimum attendas, nunc humilia fore, saltim tenuia, nunc mediocria, alia nunc mediocria, nunc sublimia. Quaedam obiecta per omnes relatiuae magnitudinis dignitatisque gradus possunt transcurrere, prouti diuersis ex lateribus spectatorum oculis obiiciantur. §. 202. -- 214. *Quam multum interest, quid a quoque fiat? Eadem enim facta claritate vel obscuritate facientium* [p. 123] *aut tolluntur altissime, aut humillime deprimuntur.* e. c. Plin. VI. ep. 24.

§ 215. Such is the limitation of human affairs that there is hardly anything which does not have, as Epictetus says, a double handle, the one to be borne, the other less so. Not only objects that are absolutely worthy, but the sublime themselves, if they are considered from one side of themselves, have at the same time another side, from which, if they are inspected more deeply, not only sublimity perishes, but often all dignity as well. The same holds of natural magnitude, according as it is compared, S. XV, XVI. Hence it is all the easier to observe that certain objects, certain matters, which at first sight seem always the same, will nevertheless, according to the diverse respects, the various features and moments, to which you chiefly attend, be now lowly, or at least slender, now middling; others now middling, now sublime. Certain objects can run through all the degrees of relative magnitude and dignity, according as they are presented to the eyes of the spectators from diverse sides, § 202, -- 214. *How much does it matter by whom each thing is done? For the same deeds, according to the fame or the obscurity of the doers,* [p. 123] *are either exalted to the highest or sunk to the lowest.* etc. Plin. VI. ep. 24.

> § 216. In bucolicis, vbi plerumque tenuia sectatur Virgilius, Ecl. V. 35. ex MStis legit Vossius:

§ 216. In the Bucolics, where Virgil for the most part pursues slender things, Ecl. V. 35, Vossius reads from the manuscripts:

> *Infelix lolium et steriles nascuntur auenae,*

*The luckless darnel and the barren oats spring up,*

> quod ipsi, non sine ratione, minus videtur, ac idem §. 215. in Georgicis, vbi mediocria quaeruntur obiecta, l. I. 154. ita cogitatum:

which seems to him, not without reason, less than the same, § 215, thought thus in the Georgics, where middling objects are sought, l. I. 154:

> *Infelix lolium et steriles dominantur auenae.*

*The luckless darnel and the barren oats hold sway.*

> Si quis interim grandem, sicut Prudentius, Hamartigeniam meditaturus picturae lapsus inscriberet:

If meanwhile someone, like Prudentius, about to meditate a grand Hamartigenia, were to inscribe on the picture of the fall:

> *Infelix lolium et steriles nascuntur auenae,*

*The luckless darnel and the barren oats spring up,*

> picturae miseriarum corruptelarumque, quas post se nunc etiam trahit:

on the picture of the miseries and corruptions which it even now drags after it:

> *Infelix lolium et steriles dominantur auenae,*

*The luckless darnel and the barren oats hold sway,*

> et picturae demum euentus vltimi, naturalis quidem, at deplorandi:

and finally on the picture of the last outcome, natural indeed, but deplorable:

> *Infelix lolium et steriles* vruntur *auenae,*

*The luckless darnel and the barren oats* are burnt,

> inter alia, pro grauitate materiae, magnificentius concepta, non reor harum cogitationum vllam materias arduas depressuram. §. 215. Pacis fructus et tenues, et mediocres, et grandes, esse possunt materiae.

among other things conceived more magnificently in proportion to the gravity of the matter, I do not think any of these thoughts would lower arduous matters, § 215. The fruits of peace can be slender, and middling, and grand matters.

[p. 124]

#### Sectio XVIII. Ratio Cogitationum ad Materias Generatim. — Section XVIII. The Relation of Thoughts to Matters in General.

> § 217. Magnitudo aesthetica postulat, vt cogitationes proportionentur ac exaequentur suis obiectis, personalibus ac realibus, ipsique cogitanti subiecto, quatenus ipsum, aut status eius aliquis, sit suum simul obiectum, aut obiectum, cui congruenter cogitandum sit. §. 177. Genus cogitandi minus magnis vel absolute, vel relatiue talibus, obiectis ΒΑΘΟΣ est, (humile, humi repens cogitandi genus). Genus cogitandi maius suis obiectis TVMOR est (frigus, tumidum et inflatum, nimis altum, nimis exaggeratum cogitandi genus). Aequalitas cogitationum cum obiectis absolute magnis laus est, cuius oppositum peccans in defectu βάθος, in excessu tumor est.

§ 217. Aesthetic magnitude demands that thoughts be proportioned and made equal to their objects, personal and real, and to the thinking subject itself, insofar as it, or some state of it, is at the same time its own object, or an object to which thought must be congruent, § 177. A manner of thinking smaller than its great objects, whether absolutely or relatively such, is ΒΑΘΟΣ [bathos] (the lowly manner of thinking, creeping along the ground). A manner of thinking greater than its objects is TUMIDITY (the frigid, the swollen and inflated, the too lofty, the too exaggerated manner of thinking). The equality of thoughts with absolutely great objects is a merit, the opposite of which, erring by defect, is βάθος [bathos], by excess, tumidity.

> § 218. Ita Cicero, sequutus *Aristotelem, neque humilem nec abiectam orationem probat, nec nimis altam et exaggeratam, plenam tamen eam vult esse grauitatis,* §. 189. *vt eos, qui audiunt, ad maiorem possit admirationem traducere.* [p. 125] Or. 192. Quam primum humilitas dignitati generatim opponitur, vt Cic. pro Rosc. 156. illa pulcris ex meditationibus exsulet. §. 195. Sed exsulet simul tumor. §. 217. *Num manus affecta recta est, quum in tumore est? aut num aliud quodpiam membrum tumidum ac turgidum non vitiose se habet? Sic igitur inflatus animus et tumens in vitio est, sapientis autem animus semper vacat vitio, nunquam turgescit, nunquam tumet.* Cic. Tusc. quaest. III. 19.

§ 218. Thus Cicero, following *Aristotle, approves neither a lowly nor an abject speech, nor one too lofty and exaggerated, yet he wishes it to be full of gravity,* § 189, *so that it can carry those who hear it to greater admiration,* [p. 125] Or. 192. As soon as lowliness is opposed to dignity in general, as in Cic. pro Rosc. 156, let it be banished from beautiful meditations, § 195. But let tumidity be banished along with it, § 217. *Is a hand in a sound state when it is swollen? or is any other limb, swollen and turgid, not in a faulty condition? So then an inflated and swelling mind is in a fault, but the mind of the wise man is always free from fault, never grows turgid, never swells.* Cic. Tusc. quaest. III. 19.

> § 219. *Laudis amore tumes?* §. 217. *Sunt certa piacula, quae te* / *Ter pure lecto poterunt recreare libello.* Hor.

§ 219. *Do you swell with the love of praise?* § 217. *There are sure expiations which, with the little book* / *Thrice read in purity, can restore you.* Hor.

> Hic autem erit vel practice, per exempla, vel theoretice simul ostendens, tunc etiam, quando cogitationes res vocamus, §. 18. verum esse illud:

But here he will be showing, either practically, through examples, or theoretically at the same time, that even then, when we call thoughts things, § 18, this is true:

> *Est modus in rebus, sunt certi denique fines,* / *Quos vltra citraque nequit consistere rectum.*

*There is a measure in things, there are, in short, fixed limits,* / *Beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.*

> Huius enim sanctissimae legis probe memor, non humilia solum vitabis, sed ob eandem etiam tibi ipsi dices intra praecordia:

For, well mindful of this most sacred law, you will not only avoid lowly things, but on account of the same you will also say to yourself within your breast:

> *Intempestiuos igitur compesce tumores.* Ou. Trist.

*Restrain, then, your unseasonable swellings.* Ou. Trist.

> [p. 126] § 220. *Decipimur specie recti pars maxima.* / *Professus grandia turget.* / *Serpit humi tutus nimium timidusque procellae.* Hor.

[p. 126] § 220. *We are deceived by the appearance of right, the greatest part of us.* / *One who professes grand things swells.* / *One too safe and too fearful of the storm creeps along the ground.* Hor.

> *Rectius* cursum teneas *nec altum* / *Semper vrgendo, neque, dum procellas* / *Cautus horrescis, nimium premendo* / *Littus iniquum.* §. 217.

*More rightly* will you hold your course *neither by always* / *pressing the deep, nor, while, cautious, you shudder* / *at the storms, by pressing too close upon* / *the treacherous shore.* § 217.

> Sequeris enim tunc naturale cogitandi genus, §. 104. quoniam

For then you follow the natural manner of thinking, § 104, since

> *profecto, hoc sic est, vt puto,* / *Omnibus nobis vt res dant sese, ita magni atque humiles,* §. 195. *sumus.* Ter. Hec. III. 3.

*assuredly, this is how it is, I think:* / *as things present themselves to all of us, so great or lowly,* § 195, *are we.* Ter. Hec. III. 3.

> § 221. Vitandum est itaque I. NVGIGERVM (nugiuendulum) COGITANDI GENVS de nugis vere talibus, §. 191. nugantium, i. e. aequales obiectis cogitationes informantium exhibentiumque. Quoniam enim hoc cogitandi genus vel absolute magnis minus est §. 178. recte, §. 177. PRIMVM ΒΑΘΟΥΣ GENVS constituitur, §. 217.

§ 221. To be avoided, therefore, is I. the TRIFLE-PEDDLING (trifle-vending) MANNER OF THINKING of those who trifle about trifles truly such, § 191, i.e. of those who form and exhibit thoughts equal to their objects. For since this manner of thinking is smaller even than the absolutely great, § 178, it is rightly, § 177, constituted the FIRST KIND OF ΒΑΘΟΥΣ [bathos], § 217.

> *Nimirum sapere est abiectis vtile nugis,* / *Et tempestiuum pueris concedere ludum.*

*Assuredly, it is useful to be wise, having cast trifles aside,* / *And to leave to boys the play that suits their age.*

> [p. 127] Ex eiusmodi enim mustaceo laureolam non quaesiuerit, nisi Plauti forsan aliquis *nugipolyloquides.*

[p. 127] For from a cake of this kind no one will have sought a laurel-wreath, except perhaps some *nugipolyloquides* of Plautus.

> § 222. II. Genus cogitandi de nugis vere talibus §. 191. ac si essent aliquid, §. 177. 178. PRIMVM TVMORIS GENVS, §. 217. cuius species prima est, si malis auibus nugas loces in absolute magnis, licet tenuibus, §. 202. secunda, quoties easdem tentaueris mediocribus inserere, §. 208. maxima, si de iisdem veluti de grandibus ac sublimibus cogites, §. 203. Ridicule semper

§ 222. II. The manner of thinking about trifles truly such, § 191, as if they were something, § 177. 178, is the FIRST KIND OF TUMIDITY, § 217, of which the first species is, if under ill omens you place trifles among the absolutely great, albeit slender, § 202; the second, whenever you have tried to insert them among middling things, § 208; the greatest, if you think of them as of grand and sublime things, § 203. It is always ridiculous when

> *Maxima de nihilo nascitur historia.*

*The greatest story is born of nothing.*

> In primis tamen, quando

But above all when

> *Non de vi, neque caede, nec veneno,* / *Sed lis est mihi de tribus capellis,* / *Vicini queror has abesse furto,* / *Hoc iudex sibi postulat probari,* / *Tu Cannas Mithridaticumque bellum* / *Et periuria Punici furoris* / *Et Sullas, Mariosque, Muciosque,* / *Magna voce sonas, manuque tota.* / *Jam dic, Posthume, de tribus capellis.* Mart. VI. 19.

*Not about violence, nor slaughter, nor poison,* / *But my suit is about three she-goats;* / *I complain that they are missing through my neighbour’s theft,* / *This the judge demands to have proved to him;* / *You, of Cannae and the Mithridatic war* / *And the perjuries of Punic fury* / *And the Sullas, the Mariuses, the Muciuses,* / *Sound forth with a great voice and with full gesture.* / *Now, Postumus, speak of the three she-goats.* Mart. VI. 19.

> § 223. Ne tamen meras vetiti leges, prohibentesue [p. 128] scribere videamur, positiue suadetur materiis absolute saltim magnis aequale et proportionatum adhibere COGITANDI GENVS, quod absolute saltim, SATIS MAGNVM, et proposito conducens, apteque haerens ex veritate rei dicere liceat. §. 177, 217. Erit autem illud simul GENVS COGITANDI SATIS DIGNVM, saltim absolute, et negatiue, §. 182, 185, 193. simulque magnitudini dignitatique relatiuae suarum materiarum satis adaequatum, §. 162.

§ 223. Yet lest we seem to be writing mere laws of what is forbidden, or prohibitions, [p. 128] it is positively recommended to apply to matters, at least absolutely great, a MANNER OF THINKING equal and proportioned to them, which one may say, from the truth of the thing, is at least absolutely GREAT ENOUGH, conducive to the purpose, and aptly adhering to it, § 177, 217. That will at the same time be a MANNER OF THINKING WORTHY ENOUGH, at least absolutely and negatively, § 182, 185, 193, and at the same time sufficiently adequate to the relative magnitude and dignity of its matters, § 162.

> § 224. Hinc iam denuo dissuadetur MINVS DIGNVM COGITANDI GENVS, ob defectum improportionatum obiectis et materiis, vel absolute dignis, vel relatiue talibus, in suo βάθους genere species semper eminentior turpitudine, §. 217, 182. In diuersis per hoc cogitandi genus speciebus nunc animaduertendum est in VILE DE ABIECTIS COGITANDI GENVS humillimis suis obiectis §. 195. proportionatum et aequale, primi βάθους generis turpiorem speciem. §. 221. e. g. Hor. ep. 8. Serm. l. 8. Cat. 15, 16.

§ 224. Hence now again the LESS WORTHY MANNER OF THINKING is dissuaded, on account of a defect disproportioned to its objects and matters, whether absolutely worthy or relatively such, a species in its own kind of βάθους [bathos] always more eminent in baseness, § 217, 182. Among the diverse species of this manner of thinking, attention must now be paid to the VILE MANNER OF THINKING ABOUT ABJECT THINGS, proportioned and equal to its lowest objects, § 195, the baser species of the first kind of βάθους [bathos], § 221, e.g. Hor. ep. 8, Serm. l. 8, Cat. 15, 16.

> § 225. Neque minus heic est reiicienda species, tumoris in primo genere quae potest locum habere, si nugis vere talibus, immo abiectis et humillimis, sit tamen animus, nescio [p. 129] quid, dignitatis, non eius absolutae tantum, sed et relatiuae, forsan et maiestatis nonnihil, si diis placet, affricandi, §. 222. e. g. si quis parasitus minuti alicuius Trimalcionis ligurierit ius, et reduce die, cuius nomen hic habet,

§ 225. No less to be rejected here is the species of tumidity which can have a place in the first kind, if, in the case of trifles truly such, nay abject and lowest, there is nevertheless a mind to rub on to them some [p. 129] dignity or other, not only absolute, but also relative, and perhaps even something of majesty, if it please the gods, § 222, e.g. if some parasite has licked the sauce of some petty Trimalchio and, on the return of the day whose name he here bears,

> *Jam longum inualidi collum ceruicibus aequat* / *Herculis Antaeum procul a tellure tenentis.*

*Now he likens the long neck of a weakling to the neck* / *of Hercules holding Antaeus far from the earth.*

> § 226. MORATVM COGITANDI GENVS LATIVS dicitur omne ἦθος §. 193. strenue obseruans. Ita ad Horatii A. P. 319.

§ 226. The MORAL MANNER OF THINKING IN THE WIDER SENSE is the name given to every one that strenuously observes ἦθος [character], § 193. Thus on Horace’s A. P. 319,

> *Interdum speciosa locis, morataque recte* / *Fabula, nullius veneris, sine pondere et arte* / *Valdius oblectat populum meliusque moratur,* / *Quam versus inopes rerum nugaeque canorae.*

*Sometimes a play striking in its passages, and rightly drawn in character,* / *Though of no charm, without weight and art,* / *Delights the people more strongly and detains them better* / *Than verses empty of matter and melodious trifles,*

> iam Acron annotauit, *fabulam recte moratam* esse, *in qua singularum personarum mores optime exprimuntur.* Magna pars autem omnis ἤθους in pulcre cogitandis demum propter verisimilitudinem, deinde persuasionem, vitam denique, poscitur, adeoque nunc nondum euolui potest per naturalem methodum scientiae, nec adeo nunc hoc significatu moratum cogitandi genus licet exhaurire, vel, nisi per transennam et quasi praecipiendo sequentia, postulare, §. 22.

Acron already noted that *a play is rightly drawn in character* *in which the characters of the individual persons are best expressed.* But the greater part of all ἤθους [character] is demanded in things to be beautifully thought only on account of verisimilitude, then persuasion, and finally life, and so cannot yet now be unfolded by the natural method of the science, nor therefore may the moral manner of thinking in this signification now be exhausted, or demanded, except by a glimpse and as it were by anticipating what follows, § 22.

> [p. 130] § 227. MORATVM COGITANDI GENVS STRICTIVS, dicitur aequalem dignis, vel absolute saltim, vel etiam comparatiue, materiis ac obiectis, semper ad aequabilem proportionate cogitandi rationem seruans, et inde fauentem de cogitantis moribus praesumtionem spectatori velut extorquens. Quintilianus Ciceronem in his se sequi professus *expositionem* poscens *moratam: sed in oratione*, addit, *morata debent esse omnia cum dignitate, quae poterunt.* IIII. 2. Et hoc iam est moratum illud cogitandi genus, quod non solum heic per antecedentia licet, sed etiam necesse est postulare, si quis ad vere pulcra cogitata velit adspirare. §. 182, 185.

[p. 130] § 227. The MORAL MANNER OF THINKING IN THE STRICTER SENSE is the name given to one which always preserves a way of thinking proportionately equal to matters and objects that are worthy, either absolutely at least or also comparatively, and thereby as it were extorts from the spectator a favourable presumption about the morals of the thinker. Quintilian, professing to follow Cicero in these things, demands a *statement of facts* that is *moral: but in a speech*, he adds, *all things which can be should be moral, with dignity,* IIII. 2. And this is now that moral manner of thinking which it is not only permitted here, through what precedes, but even necessary to demand, if anyone wishes to aspire to truly beautiful thoughts, § 182, 185.

> § 228. GENVS COGITANDI BENE MORATVM STRICTIVS, erit denuo vel ABSOLVTE TALE, vel etiam comparatiue et RELATIVE, §. 227, 185. vel negatiue tantum, vel etiam positiue, §. 193, 194. Nunc sufficiat argumentis, vel ex ipsa pulcritudinis forma, §. 183. desumtis dissuadere GENVS COGITANDI MALE MORATVM STRICTIVS, sed ABSOLVTE, vel impium, vel inhonestum, vel indecorum, etiamsi vilibus humillimisque forsan materiis turpiter electis proportionatum sit. §. 224.

§ 228. THE MORALLY GOOD MANNER OF THINKING IN THE STRICTER SENSE will again be either ABSOLUTELY SUCH, or also comparatively and RELATIVELY, § 227, 185, either negatively only, or also positively, § 193, 194. For now let it suffice, by arguments drawn even from the very form of beauty, § 183, to dissuade the MORALLY BAD MANNER OF THINKING IN THE STRICTER SENSE, but ABSOLUTELY, whether impious, or dishonourable, or indecorous, even if it be proportioned to vile and lowest matters, perhaps basely chosen, § 224.

> [p. 131] *Si bene te noui, metues, liberrime Lolli,* / *Scurrantis speciem praebere professus amicum.* / *Vt matrona meretrici, dispar erit atque* / *Discolor, infido scurrae distabit amicus.* Hor. I. ep. 18.

[p. 131] *If I know you well, most free-spoken Lollius, you will fear,* / *having professed yourself a friend, to present the appearance of a buffoon.* / *As a matron will be unlike and of a different colour from a harlot,* / *so will a friend differ from a faithless buffoon.* Hor. I. ep. 18.

> § 229. Hoc lubentius genus bene moratum in cogitando, quod strictius tale dixi, §. 227. sedulo distinxi a morato latius cogitandi genere, quo saepius obseruaui venusta ingenia per ipsum verisimilitudinis et morum felicius exprimendorum ardorem, i. e. dum aliquam partem de morato cogitandi genere sectantur, eo delabi, vt alteram perdant ex oculis, quam dignitas poscit, §. 227. absoluta, §. 228. vel ipsa a verisimilitudine suadens exceptionem non inelegantem, si vitari non possit vtriusque perfectionis collisio. §. 25. Hinc Iuuenalis obscenitas et multorum satyricorum aliorum licentiae.

§ 229. This morally good manner of thinking, which I called such in the stricter sense, § 227, I have the more willingly taken pains to distinguish from the moral manner of thinking in the wider sense, because I have rather often observed charming wits, through the very ardour of verisimilitude and of expressing character more happily, i.e. while they pursue one part of the moral manner of thinking, slip so far as to lose sight of the other, which dignity demands, § 227, absolute dignity, § 228, or verisimilitude itself recommending an exception not inelegant, if the collision of the two perfections cannot be avoided, § 25. Hence the obscenity of Juvenal and the licences of many other satirists.

#### Sectio XVIIII. Tenue Cogitandi Genus. — Section XVIIII. The Slender Manner of Thinking.

> § 230. Interest magnitudinis aestheticae, vt cogitationes exaequentur etiam relatiuae suorum [p. 132] obiectorum S. XVII. magnitudini, §. 217. Hinc triplex nascitur cogitandi genus, cum duplici quodlibet sua παρεκβάσει; quod in oratione tantum deprehendentes olim vel triplicem eius characterem, vel ideam, vel formam, vel etiam figuram omnino dixerunt.

§ 230. It concerns aesthetic magnitude that thoughts be made equal also to the relative magnitude of their [p. 132] objects, S. XVII, § 217. Hence a threefold manner of thinking arises, each with its double παρεκβάσει [deviation]; which those who of old detected it only in speech called either its threefold character, or idea, or form, or even figure in general.

> *Trinum dicendi genus est, sublime, modestum,* / *Et tenui filo.* Aus.

*Threefold is the kind of speaking: the sublime, the modest,* / *And that of slender thread.* Aus.

> § 231. I. TENVE COGITANDI GENVS (subtile, attenuatum, deductum, gracile, atticum, ἰσχνόν) est tenuibus, §. 202. materiis ita proportionatum, §. 230. vt et absolutae dignitatis satis tenax, §. 223. et strictius, etiam relatiue, moratum, §. 228. simpliciter honesto viuendi generi non modo non contrarietur, §. 213. sed eius etiam moribus ex §. 211. 212. diiudicatis probe consentiat, §. 214. Huic iam dudum, Terentii tempore, *vetus poeta*, sed censor vitio creatus, obiecit, vt vitium:

§ 231. I. THE SLENDER MANNER OF THINKING (subtle, attenuated, drawn fine, thin, Attic, ἰσχνόν [lean]) is one so proportioned, § 230, to slender matters, § 202, that, being both sufficiently tenacious of absolute dignity, § 223, and moral in the stricter sense, even relatively, § 228, it is not only not contrary to the simply honourable kind of living, § 213, but even agrees well with its morals as judged according to § 211. 212, § 214. To this long ago, in Terence’s time, *an old poet*, but a censor irregularly appointed, objected, as a fault:

> *Tenui esse oratione et scriptura leui,* / *Quia nusquam insanum scripsit adolescentulum* / *Ceruam videre fugere et sectari canes,* / *Et eam plorare, orare, vt subueniat sibi.*

*That it was of slender speech and of light writing,* / *Because nowhere did he write of a young man in his madness* / *Seeing a hind flee and hounds pursue her,* / *And her weeping and begging him to come to her aid.*

> [p. 133] § 232. Cum hoc cogitandi genere laudabili, sed aesthetico tamen, multi, Cicerone duce, confundunt, de rebus grauissimis philosophice, quantumque fieri potest, scientifice disquirendi genus, quoniam in hoc conueniunt, vt vtrisque desit ille splendor, qui solet ambire grauiora phaenomena, vere bona, §. 211. et determinatissima quaeuis grandia, quae tantum non singularia, §. 212. e. g. *de diis immortalibus, de pietate, de concordia, de amicitia, de communi ciuium, de hominum, de gentium iure, de aequitate, de temperantia, de magnitudine, de omni virtutum genere* sit cogitandum. *Philosophis ego, vt de his rebus omnibus, in angulis, consumendi otii caussa, disserant, quum concessero: illud tamen oratori tribuam et dabo, vt, de quibus illi tenui quodam et exiguo sermone* (logico, §. 122. qua potiorem suam partem ad aesthetices regulas non exigendo, quas transcendit) *disputant, hic cum omni grauitate et iucunditate explicet.* (aesthetica) §. 124, 123. v. Cic. de Or. I. 56, 57. de Fin. III. 40. Or. 46.

[p. 133] § 232. With this manner of thinking, laudable yet still aesthetic, many, with Cicero as their leader, confuse the manner of inquiring into the weightiest matters philosophically and, so far as can be done, scientifically, because they agree in this, that both lack that splendour which is wont to surround the weightier phenomena, the truly good, § 211, and any most determinate grand things, which are all but singular, § 212, e.g. when one must think *of the immortal gods, of piety, of concord, of friendship, of the common right of citizens, of men, of nations, of equity, of temperance, of magnitude, of every kind of virtue.* *When I have granted to the philosophers that they may discourse of all these matters in corners, for the sake of using up their leisure: yet this I shall assign and grant to the orator, that what they dispute about in a certain thin and meagre speech* (logical, § 122, in that it does not measure its greater part by the rules of aesthetics, which it transcends), *he should set forth with all weight and pleasantness.* (aesthetic) § 124, 123. See Cic. de Or. I. 56, 57. de Fin. III. 40. Or. 46.

> § 233. Tenue cogitandi genus suos iterum gradus admittit, §. 231, quorum primum et infimum GENVS COGITANDI TENVICVLVM dixeris, §. 207. Exemplum esto *grammatica,* [p. 134] *partes alienas non occupans.* Nam *tenuis* (vel maxime) *a fonte*, quando

§ 233. The slender manner of thinking in its turn admits of degrees, § 231, the first and lowest of which you might call the RATHER SLENDER MANNER OF THINKING, § 207. Let the example be *grammar,* [p. 134] *not occupying parts that belong to others.* For it is *thin* (indeed most of all) *at its source*, when

> *pueris olim dant crustula blandi / Doctores, elementa velint vt discere prima.* Hor.

*the coaxing teachers once give little cakes to boys, / that they may be willing to learn their first elements.* Hor.

> *assumtis poetarum historiarumque viribus, pleno iam satis alueo fluit*, Quint. II. 1. neque tamen in omni disciplinarum ambitu surgit vltra tenuitatem, §. 202. Ad superiores tenuitatis gradus referamus orationem Ciceronis pro Caecina, quando eam ipse refert ad subtile cogitandi genus, temperato grauique contradistinctum.

*having taken on the strength of the poets and the historians, it now flows in a channel full enough*, Quint. II. 1, yet in the whole compass of the disciplines it does not rise above slenderness, § 202. To the higher degrees of slenderness let us refer Cicero’s oration for Caecina, since he himself refers it to the subtle manner of thinking, as contradistinguished from the tempered and the weighty.

> § 234. Si suum argumentum et materiem felicius exprimat, tenue cogitandi genus, non inepte de eo dixeris:

§ 234. If the slender manner of thinking expresses its argument and matter more happily, you might not unaptly say of it:

> *In tenui labor, at tenuis non gloria.* Virg. cf. Prop. III. 1.

*In a slender matter the labour, but not thin the glory.* Virg. cf. Prop. III. 1.

> *Habet enim certos sui studiosos, qui non tam habitus corporis opimos, quam gracilitates consectentur, quos, valetudo modo bona sit, tenuitas ipsa delectat, — — — — Habet suos laudatores, qui hac ipsa subtilitate admodum gaudeant.* Cic. de cl. Or. 64. Neque sine naso sunt hi laudatores, §. 230, 202,

*For it has its own sure devotees, who pursue not so much a plump habit of body as slendernesses, and whom, provided only the health be good, slenderness itself delights, — — — — It has its own praisers, who take great delight in this very subtlety.* Cic. de cl. Or. 64. Nor are these praisers without a nose, § 230, 202,

> *neque semper arcum / Tendit Apollo.*

*nor does Apollo always / keep his bow bent.*

> [p. 135] § 235. Neque generatim de triplici cogitationum charactere, quem nunc informamus, praeconcipienda est opinio, ac si per longiorem etiam meditationem aestheticam vnus ex his character in omnibus pulcre cogitandis ac singulis debeat aequabiliter transcurrere: neque de tenui cogitandi genere, §. 230. Opere in longo prout materiae necessario inaequales aliqualiter coniunguntur, ita habet illud et suam materiis proportionatam et apte haerentem cogitationum nunc ἄνεσιν et remissionem, nunc ἔπαρσιν et eleuationem, manente totius denominatione ab illo charactere, qui regnat et potior est. §. 217.

[p. 135] § 235. Nor, in general, is an opinion to be formed beforehand about the threefold character of thoughts which we are now setting out, as if even through a longer aesthetic meditation one of these characters ought to run evenly through all the things to be thought beautifully and through each one of them: nor about the slender manner of thinking, § 230. In a long work, as matters necessarily unequal are in some fashion joined together, so it has its own ἄνεσιν [relaxation] and remission of thoughts, proportioned to the matters and aptly cohering, now its ἔπαρσιν [raising] and elevation, while the denomination of the whole remains from that character which reigns and is predominant. § 217.

> § 236. In eadem oratione Cicero de Inu.
