SVBLIME COGITANDI GENVS, (magnificum, magnum, altum, summum, plenum, cf. §. 158. graue, copiosum, cf. §. 116. ornatum, validum, μεγαλοπρεπές, ἀξίωμα, ὕψος, ὑψηλόν.) est suis vere grandibus cogitandi materiis, §. 203 - 207. ita congruens, vt iisdem simul satis dignum §. 223. et optime moratum, §. 228. non modo non contrarietur heroicae virtuti, rationique cogitandi, quam haec comitem, nisi ducem, habere solet, sed et moribus singulari cum [p. 168] maiestate coniunctis probe consentiat. §. 213. 194.

§ 281. III. THE SUBLIME MANNER OF THINKING (the magnificent, great, lofty, highest, full, cf. § 158, grave, copious, cf. § 116, ornate, strong, μεγαλοπρεπές [magnificent], ἀξίωμα [dignity], ὕψος [height], ὑψηλόν [lofty]) is that which so conforms to its truly grand matters of thinking, § 203–207, that, being at the same time sufficiently worthy of them, § 223, and best in character, § 228, it not only is not contrary to heroic virtue and to the way of thinking which this is wont to have as companion, if not as leader, but also properly agrees with character joined with singular [p. 168] majesty, § 213, 194.

> § 282. Non per iocum solum Terentius iubet *Dauum sublimem intro rapi, quadrupedemque constringi*, sed et Horatius ridet.

§ 282. Not only in jest does Terence order *Davus to be snatched sublime indoors, and bound hand and foot*, but Horace too laughs at

> Hunc, *dum sublimis versus ructatur, et errat,* / Qui, *veluti merulis intentus, decidit, auceps* / *In puteum, foueamue.*

Him who, *while he belches sublime verses, and wanders,* / Who, *as if intent on blackbirds, has fallen, the fowler,* / *Into a well, or a pit.*

> Nobis heic serio, suoque loco locata sublimitas exploranda est. e. g. *Non fortibus solum, sed etiam fulgentibus armis praeliatus in caussa est Cicero Cornelii, quum assequutus esset dicendo, vt populus romanus admirationem suam, non acclamatione tantum, sed etiam plausu, confiteretur. Sublimitas, profecto, et magnificentia, et nitor, et auctoritas expressit istum fragorem. Nec tam insolita laus esset prosequuta dicentem, si vsitata et caeteris similis affuisset oratio.* Quint. VIII. 3. Huc comparatio Elegiae et Tragoediae, Ou. Am. III. 1. vbi illa fatetur:

For us here the sublimity that is placed seriously and in its proper place is to be explored. E.g. *Not only with brave, but also with shining arms did Cicero fight in the cause of Cornelius, when he had achieved by his speaking that the Roman people confessed their admiration not by acclamation only, but even by applause. Sublimity, assuredly, and magnificence, and brilliance, and authority wrung forth that thunder. Nor would so unwonted a praise have followed the speaker if his speech had been ordinary and like the rest.* Quint. VIII. 3. Here belongs the comparison of Elegy and Tragedy, Ov. Am. III. 1, where the former confesses:

> *Non ego contulerim sublimia carmina nostris,* / *Obruit exiguas regia vestra fores.*

*I would not compare sublime songs with mine,* / *Your palace overwhelms my little doors.*

> § 283. Magnificum adhuc saepius adhaerente conceptu superflui et ostentationis, quasi leuis notae macula quadam, adspergitur. Ita [p. 169] Clitipho apud Terentium, Heaut. I. 2. gratulatur Cliniae, qui

§ 283. The magnificent is still more often besprinkled, as with a certain stain of slight reproach, by the concept of the superfluous and of ostentation that clings to it. Thus [p. 169] Clitipho in Terence, Heaut. I. 2, congratulates Clinia, who

> *Habet bene et pudice eductam, ignaram artis meretriciae.* / *Mea,* addens, *est potens, procax, magnifica, sumtuosa, nobilis.*

*Has one well and chastely brought up, ignorant of the meretricious art.* / *Mine,* he adds, *is powerful, forward, magnificent, extravagant, noble.*

> Pari ratione Tibullus: II. 6.

In like manner Tibullus: II. 6.

> *Castra peto, valeatque Venus, valeantque puellae.* / *Et mihi sunt vires, et mihi facta tuba est.* / *Magna loquor. Sed magnifice mihi magna loquuto* / *Excutiunt clausae fortia verba fores.*

*I seek the camp; farewell Venus, and farewell girls.* / *I too have strength, and for me too the trumpet has been sounded.* / *Great things I speak. But when I have magnificently spoken great things* / *The closed doors shake the brave words out of me.*

> rediturus ad humilem suam querimoniam l. 5:

about to return to his humble complaint, l. 5:

> *Vre ferum et torque: libeat ne dicere quicquam* / *Magnificum posthac, horrida verba doma.*

*Burn the wild one and rack him: let him not wish to say anything* / *Magnificent hereafter; tame his rough words.*

> Clarius Cornelius, a quo laudatur *Atticus, elegans, non magnificus, splendidus, non sumtuosus, qui omni diligentia munditiam non affluentem, affectarit, supellex modica, non multa, vt in neutram partem conspici posset.* Ipse Cicero, magnifici patronus contra Atticos vel quasi, §. 248. non abstinet ab hac vocis sequiori significatione. Pro Rosc. Com. 5. *Vsque eone te diligis, et magnifice circumspicis?* eum alloquitur, quem mox accusabit amentiae.

More clearly Cornelius, by whom *Atticus* is praised as *elegant, not magnificent, splendid, not extravagant, one who with all diligence affected a neatness not affluent; his furniture moderate, not much, so that it could be remarked in neither direction.* Cicero himself, the patron of the magnificent against the Attics, or as it were, § 248, does not abstain from this poorer signification of the word. Pro Rosc. Com. 5, *Do you so far love yourself, and look about you so magnificently?* he addresses him whom he will soon accuse of madness.

> § 284. [p. 170] Nobis autem hic magnificentia cogitatur, §. 281. ex descriptione Ciceronis de Inu. II. 163. *rerum magnarum et excelsarum, cum animi ampla quadam et splendida propositione, agitatio atque administratio.* Secundum quam *magnificentiae publicae* amantem dicit, inimicum *priuatae luxuriae*, §. 281. 165. *populum Romanum*, Or. pro Mur. ex qua rectissime, Off. I. 72: *Capessentibus*, inquit, *rempublicam, nihilominus, quam philosophis, haud scio, an magis etiam, et magnificentia, et despicientia adhibenda sit rerum humanarum, quam saepe dico, et tranquillitas animi, atque securitas, siquidem nec anxii futuri sunt, et cum grauitate constantiaque victuri.* Secundum eandem notionem magnificentiae concedit eam et vitae priuatae cum simplicitate simul conuenire posse §. 213. philosophus, l. c. 92. *Haec praescripta* (vitae priuatae) *seruantem licet magnifice, grauiter, animoseque viuere, atque etiam simpliciter, fideliter, atque vitae hominum amice.* Ex eadem concipio verissimum Agamemnonis effatum apud Petronium, *sibi nihil esse magnificum, quod pueris placeret.*

§ 284. [p. 170] By us, however, magnificence is here thought, § 281, according to Cicero’s description, de Inv. II. 163, as *the agitation and administration of great and lofty things, with a certain ample and splendid resolve of mind.* According to which he calls the *Roman people* lovers of *public magnificence*, enemies of *private luxury*, § 281, 165, Or. pro Mur.; from which most rightly, Off. I. 72: *By those who take up the commonwealth*, he says, *no less than by philosophers, and I do not know whether even more, both magnificence and a contempt of human affairs, of which I often speak, must be employed, and tranquillity of mind, and security, if indeed they are not to be anxious, and are to live with gravity and constancy.* According to the same notion of magnificence the philosopher concedes that it can also agree with private life, together with simplicity, § 213, l. c. 92: *One who keeps these precepts* (of private life) *may live magnificently, gravely, and spiritedly, and also simply, faithfully, and in a manner friendly to the life of men.* From the same I conceive as most true the saying of Agamemnon in Petronius, *that nothing is magnificent to him which pleases boys.*

> § 285. Hinc igitur colligamus, quam animo sibi formauerit ideam de magnifico cogitandi genere orator, qui et ipse sciuit, et subinnuit [p. 171] l. II. de Or. 89. se eius quasi quoddam exemplar esse, dum narrat *Sulpicium*, qui loquentem et Crassum imitari promiserat, *omnino in illud genus Crassi magnificum natura ipsa ductum esse*, S. II. quae tamen addens, *non satis, proficere potuisset nisi eodem studio atque imitatione incidisset, atque ita dicere consuesset, vt tota mente Crassum atque omni animo intueretur.* Hinc eius primum praeceptum imitatio. §. 56.

§ 285. Hence then let us gather what idea of the magnificent manner of thinking the orator formed for himself in his mind, who himself knew, and hinted, [p. 171] l. II. de Or. 89, that he was as it were a certain model of it, when he relates that *Sulpicius*, who had promised to imitate the speaker and Crassus, *had altogether been led by nature herself into that magnificent manner of Crassus*, S. II; adding, however, that *he could not have made sufficient progress had he not fallen in with the same zeal and imitation, and so grown accustomed to speak as to behold Crassus with his whole mind and all his soul.* Hence his first precept is imitation, § 56.

> § 286. Nec caret ambiguitate sua *magni* denominatio, §. 291. Non huc traham magnum hominem aliquando pro stolido dictum videri, §. 179. Sane, in laudem non dici magnam linguam ab Horatio mythologia docet, vbi sic Apollinem alloquitur:

§ 286. Nor does the denomination of the *great* lack its own ambiguity, § 291. I shall not drag in here that a great man seems sometimes to have been said for a dolt, § 179. Assuredly, that a great tongue is not said in praise, mythology teaches from Horace, where he thus addresses Apollo:

> *Diue, quem proles Niobea magnae* / *Vindicem linguae, Tityosque raptor* / *Sensit.* IV. od. 6.

*God, whom the offspring of Niobe, as the avenger* / *Of a great tongue, and Tityos the ravisher,* / *Felt.* IV. od. 6.

> Nec *magnos* Iuuenalis *amicos*, nec *magnos* Horatii *pueros* sincere laudari hac appellatione puto. Interim bona fide magnum relatiue comparatiueque §. 178. cogitatum dicamus vere magnis apte congruens, §. 291. Ad huius penitiorem intellectionem notemus adhuc ad §. 203 - 207. de magnis materiis 1) *alia clariora esse, alia maiora.* Cui effato confirmando totam ep. XVI. l. III. destinauit [p. 172] Plinius, illustrans huc facientibus exemplis. 2) huc pertinentia magna vix verisimilia videri plurimis. Horatius cuidam

Nor do I think Juvenal’s *great friends*, nor Horace’s *great boys*, are sincerely praised by this appellation. Meanwhile let us in good faith call that which is thought great relatively and comparatively, § 178, aptly conformed to truly great things, § 291. For a deeper understanding of this let us note further, on § 203–207, concerning great matters, 1) that *some are clearer, others greater.* To confirm which saying Pliny devoted the whole ep. XVI of l. III, [p. 172] illustrating it with examples bearing on this. 2) that the great things pertaining here seem scarcely verisimilar to most. Horace relates to someone

> *noto sibi nomine tantum*

*known to him by name only*

> narrat apud Maecenatem sibi non opus esse submouere alios, vt in gratiam eius intimius penetret, nec *officere*,

that in Maecenas’s house he has no need to push others aside, so that he may penetrate more intimately into his favour, nor does it *stand in his way*

> *Ditior hic, aut est quia doctior. Est suus vnicuique* / *locus. Magnum narras, vix credibile.*

*That this one is richer, or because more learned. To each one* / *His own place. A great thing you tell, scarcely credible.*

> Ille, nescio quis, regerit.

the other, I know not who, retorts.

> § 287. Altum cogitandi genus, §. 291. et nimis altum §. 217. 218. ne confundantur. Illud pingit Horatius, IV. od. 9.

§ 287. Let the lofty manner of thinking, § 291, and the too lofty, § 217, 218, not be confounded. The former Horace paints, IV. od. 9.

> *Iudex honestum praetulit vtili, et* / *Reiecit alto dona nocentium* / *Vultu, et per obstantes cateruas* / *Explicuit sua victor arma.*

*As judge he preferred the honourable to the useful, and* / *Rejected the gifts of the guilty with lofty* / *Countenance, and through the opposing throngs* / *Victorious unfurled his arms.*

> Et Cicero Tusc. quaest. II. 11. *Fortes non modo fortuna adiuuat, vt est in veteri prouerbio, sed multo magis ratio, quae quibusdam quasi praeceptis confirmat vim fortitudinis. Te natura excelsum quendam videlicet, et altum, et humana despicientem genuit. Itaque facile in animo forti contra mortem habita oratio insedit.* e. c.

And Cicero, Tusc. quaest. II. 11: *The brave are aided not only by fortune, as the old proverb has it, but much more by reason, which by certain quasi-precepts confirms the force of fortitude. Nature begot you as one lofty, plainly, and high, and looking down upon human things. And so a discourse held against death easily settled in a brave mind,* etc.

> § 288. [p. 173] Copiosum ac plenum cogitandi genus si quos pro sublimi habere videas, §. 281. memor, §. 247, 187. quid assertis insit veri diiudicaturus oculos mentis ante omnia figo in virtutis huic cogitandi generi propriae et peculiaris summam veluti formulam: Tantum rotundae breuitatis, tantum verisimilitudinis, e. c. §. 22. neque plus, neque minus, in grande tuum thema cogitando confer, quantum quemuis ad heroicam virtutem et huius comitem, cogitandi rationem, ingeniique eleuationem euectum, vel ipsum thematibus eiusmodi adspersurum fuisse, vel saltim ab aliis allatum pulcre intellecturum esse possis confidere. §. 281.

§ 288. [p. 173] If you see some holding the copious and full manner of thinking for the sublime, § 281, then, mindful, § 247, 187, in order to judge what truth there is in their assertions, I fix the eyes of my mind before all things on the summary formula, as it were, of the virtue proper and peculiar to this manner of thinking: Bring into your grand theme in thinking so much rounded brevity, so much verisimilitude, etc., § 22, neither more nor less, as you can be confident that anyone raised to heroic virtue and to its companion, the way of thinking, and to elevation of wit, would either himself have sprinkled upon themes of this kind, or at least, when brought forward by others, would beautifully understand, § 281.

> § 289. Hinc sublime cogitandi genus multo adhuc minus, ac medium, §. 275. quemuis ex turba sibi spectatorem, obiectum personale, legit, et eum, cuius in gratiam potissimum cogitet. Minima nec ingenia, nec pectora, curans admodum, nec veritum oculos huiusmodi praestringere potius, quam reficere, duplex mortalium genus suum sibi templum quasi designat, in quo delectando grauiter laboret. 1) Summos homines non ingeniis solum superioribus excellentes, sed et indole praeclaros et maiestatem in moribus singularem consuetudine velut alteram quandam [p. 174] naturam, adeptos. His vbi cogitat de rebus grauissimis, in quibus illi tamen versari quotidie, quibus familiares esse, in quibus quasi habitare supponendi sunt. Eleganter et magnifice cogitat, et plene quidem atque perfecte, §. 158. tantum tamen abest, vt eximia quadam cum copia, meditationisque manifesta latitudine cum iisdem sua communicet, vt potius relatiuae etiam breuitatis, S. XIIII. studiosum sit et Laconismi vere grandis.

§ 289. Hence the sublime manner of thinking, much less still than the middle, § 275, chooses just anyone from the crowd as its spectator, its personal object, and as him for whose sake above all it thinks. Not caring much for the smallest wits or breasts, nor fearing to dazzle rather than refresh eyes of this sort, it designates for itself, as it were, a twofold race of mortals as its temple, in which it labours gravely in delighting. 1) The highest men, excelling not only in superior wits, but also distinguished in natural disposition, and having attained a singular majesty in character by habit, as a certain second [p. 174] nature. To these, when it thinks of the gravest things, in which however they are to be supposed to be engaged daily, with which to be familiar, in which as it were to dwell, it thinks elegantly and magnificently, and fully indeed and perfectly, § 158, yet so far is it from communicating its thoughts to them with a certain exceptional copiousness and a manifest breadth of meditation, that it is rather studious even of relative brevity, S. XIIII, and of a truly grand Laconism.

> § 290. Iupiter ad Mercurium post breuem expositionem eorum, quae displiceant in Aenea, Virg. Aen. IV. 236:

§ 290. Jupiter to Mercury after a brief exposition of the things that displease him in Aeneas, Virg. Aen. IV. 236:

> *Nauiget. Haec summa est, hic nostri nuncius esto.*

*Let him sail. This is the sum, let this be our message.*

> Mercurius fidus parentis interpres ad Aenean, caetera quum exprobrando retulisset, hoc ne ipsum quidem adeo breue mandatum expresse addit, v. 275. quoniam pius Aeneas illud ex expositis potuit colligere:

Mercury, the faithful interpreter of his parent, to Aeneas, when he had reported the rest by way of reproach, does not expressly add even this very mandate, brief as it is, v. 275, since pious Aeneas could gather it from what was set forth:

> *Ardet abire fuga, dulcesque relinquere terras* / *Attonitus tanto monitu imperioque deorum.* / *Mnesthea Sergestumque vocat fortemque Cloanthum* / *Classem aptent taciti, socios ad littora cogant,* / *Arma parent, et, quae sit rebus caussa nouandis* / *Dissimulent.* v. 290.

*He burns to go away in flight, and leave the sweet lands,* / *Thunderstruck by so great a warning and command of the gods.* / *He calls Mnestheus and Sergestus and brave Cloanthus:* / *Let them silently fit out the fleet, gather their companions to the shores,* / *Prepare arms, and what the cause may be of changing their plans* / *Dissemble.* v. 290.

> [p. 175] Satisne breuiter magnus Aeneas ad primos sociorum de rebus magnis, quarum hi dudum periti erant?

[p. 175] Is it not briefly enough that great Aeneas speaks to the chief of his companions of great matters, in which these had long been expert?

> § 291. 2) Alterum hominum genus, quibus sublime cogitandi genus seruire potissimum et placere studeat, §. 289. illi sunt, qui vel ad supra descriptos, aesthetico saltim, referri posse videantur, excelsam tamen aliquam et insigniter sublimem rem adhuc ignorare, aut omnino per errorem vilipendere supponendi sunt, vel igniculos quidem magni animi heroicaeque virtutis gerunt sub pectore, habentes, quod ad sublimia quaeuis erigi possit ac incitari, non tamen habent semper in promtu, quantum satis est maganimitatis [sic: magnanimitatis] praesentis ad grandia quaedam, sibi satis noua, vel breuissime sibi exposita, statim amplectenda, quo merentur, impetu. §. 288. Vtrisque sublime cogitandi genus iam salua grauitate, non vbertim solum, sed etiam copiosius, inauditam materiae suae magnitudinem, amplissimam dignitatem, incredibile pondus, et diuino quodam ardore dignissimam maiestatem, exquisitissimarum figurarum in ornatu pudico ac matronali, splendide declarabit. §. 116.

§ 291. 2) The other race of men, whom the sublime manner of thinking should strive above all to serve and to please, § 289, are those who either seem able to be referred, at least aesthetically, to those described above, yet are to be supposed still to be ignorant of some lofty and signally sublime thing, or altogether through error to hold it cheap; or who indeed bear beneath the breast the sparks of a great soul and of heroic virtue, having that which can be raised and incited to any sublime things whatever, yet do not always have ready to hand as much present magnanimity as suffices for immediately embracing, with the impetus they deserve, certain grand things which are quite new to them, or set forth to them very briefly, § 288. To both the sublime manner of thinking, now with gravity preserved, not only richly, but even more copiously, will splendidly declare the unheard-of magnitude of its matter, its most ample dignity, its incredible weight, and its majesty most worthy of a certain divine ardour, in the chaste and matronly ornament of the most exquisite figures, § 116.

> § 292. Iam fingamus nobis mente, vel [p. 176] Athenienses, quibus Demosthenes, vel romanos, quibus Cicero suis in orationibus de sublimibus aliquando vere pulcre cogitare laborarunt. Vel substituamus etiam illis, ex nostra viuendi ratione, concionem de grauissimis sacrorum momentis habendam. Quam hic pauci cogitari possunt ad primum obiectorum personalium genus §. 289. pertinentes? Ex iis autem ipsis, quotquot sint, esse tamen quidam possunt, qui, caeteroquin optimi, rigidique virtutis seuerioris, aut boni publici strenui defensores, id interim, de quo nunc agitur, praesertim admodum determinatum, vel omnino singulare si sit et indiuiduum, nunc forsan ignorantes, nunc omnino contra illud praeoccupati, parum illi pretii existimationisque tribuerent, nisi meliora doceremur. §. 291.

§ 292. Let us now imagine to ourselves in mind either the [p. 176] Athenians, for whom Demosthenes, or the Romans, for whom Cicero, laboured at times in their orations to think truly beautifully of sublime things. Or let us even substitute for them, from our own way of living, a sermon to be held on the gravest moments of sacred things. How few can here be thought of as belonging to the first kind of personal objects, § 289? But even among these themselves, however many they be, there can nonetheless be some who, otherwise the best, and rigid in a stricter virtue, or strenuous defenders of the public good, would meanwhile, now perhaps ignorant of that which is now being treated, especially if it be very determinate, or altogether singular and individual, now altogether prejudiced against it, attribute to it little value and esteem, unless we were taught better, § 291.

> § 293. Reliqui omnes, quorum in commodum orator sublime cogitandi genus possit suum facere, erunt, in quibus generosiores vtique latent instinctus, sunt, quae possint diuina luce collustrari sacrisque incitationibus inflammari, nunc autem bona pars minus attenta, alii satis remisso cum animo accedunt, vel ideo, quia sibi nota iam satis temere statuunt, quae sint audituri. His circumstantibus vtique sublime cogitandi genus oratoris, cuius ad haec voces bene multae possunt [p. 177] audientem transuolare, quas lector iterata forte lectione maturius perpendisset, §. 170. multum copiae, multum vbertatis et amplitudinis ad perfectam suam plenitudinem requiret, et latitudinem paene platonicam, §. 158, 116.

§ 293. All the rest, for whose benefit the orator can make the sublime manner of thinking his own, will be those in whom more generous instincts certainly lie hidden, in whom there are things which can be illuminated by divine light and inflamed by sacred incitements, but now a good part approach less attentive, others with a mind quite slack, or for this reason, that they rashly enough assume that what they are to hear is already known well enough to them. In these circumstances the sublime manner of thinking of the orator, a good many of whose words to these can [p. 177] fly past the hearer, which a reader would perhaps have weighed more maturely on a repeated reading, § 170, will certainly require much copiousness, much richness and amplitude for its perfect fullness, and an almost Platonic breadth, § 158, 116.

> § 294. Tragoediae adhuc magis necessariam cum sublimitate sua copiam et vbertatem etiam comparatiuam fecit

§ 294. For tragedy the copiousness and richness, even comparative, that are still more necessary along with its sublimity have been made so by the one who is

> *grata nouitate morandus, / Spectator, functusque sacris, et potus, et exlex,* §. 297-293. H. A. P.

*to be detained by grateful novelty, / the spectator, who has done with the sacred rites and is drunk and lawless,* § 297–293. H. A. P.

> *Quod numero plures, virtute et honore minores, / Indocti, stolidique et depugnare parati, / Si discordet eques, media inter carmina poscunt, / Aut vrsum, aut pugiles. His nam plebecula gaudet. / Verum equiti quoque iam migrauit ab aure voluptas / Omnis ad ingratos oculos et gaudia vana.* Hor. II. ep. 1. §. 275.

*Because those who are more in number, less in virtue and honour, / unlearned and stupid and ready to fight it out / if the knights disagree, call in the middle of the songs / for a bear or for boxers; for in these the rabble delights. / But even the knight’s pleasure has now all migrated from the ear / to the ungrateful eyes and to empty delights.* Hor. II. ep. 1. § 275.

> § 295. Quae quum ita se habeant, contrahamus in neruum controuersiam. §. 288. 1) Est quoddam sublime genus cogitandi, quod simul, [p. 178] non plenum solum, sed et copiosum est, illudque si semel relatiuae breuitatis fines transgressum est, gnauiter oportet esse locuples, apparatusque vere regios et magnificentiam publicam testatos exponere, §. 289-294. 2) non omne sublime cogitandi genus simul copiosum est, §. 289. in relatiue magnis potius maxima relatiue etiam breuia, §. 207. 209. 3) non omne copiosum dicendi genus sublime est. S. VIII. §. 281. Adeoque copiosum et sublime desinant in synonymis habere, qui nolunt Asianorum titulis condecorari. ὕψος ἀπότομον in Demosthene, ἐν χύσει Ciceroni plerumque tribuit Longinus. S. XII.

§ 295. Since these things are so, let us draw the controversy together to its sinew. § 288. 1) There is a certain sublime manner of thinking which is at once [p. 178] not only full but also copious, and this, if it has once crossed the bounds of relative brevity, must be strenuously opulent and display a truly regal apparatus and a magnificence that bears witness to public state, § 289–294. 2) Not every sublime manner of thinking is at the same time copious, § 289; in relatively great things rather the greatest things are relatively brief as well, § 207, 209. 3) Not every copious manner of speaking is sublime. S. VIII. § 281. So let those who do not wish to be adorned with the titles of the Asiatics cease to hold the copious and the sublime as synonyms. Longinus generally attributes to Demosthenes the ὕψος ἀπότομον [abrupt sublimity], to Cicero the sublime ἐν χύσει [in diffusion]. S. XII.

> § 296. Sublime cogitandi genus *graue* (δεινόν) si dicitur, §. 281. de relatiua quadam et comparatiua grauitate, graduque eius maximo denominationem accepit, quoniam omnis magnitudo aesthetica postulat etiam aliquam, absolutam certe, grauitatem, §. 189. Si dicitur ornatum, §. 281. ambiguitas tolli potest ad imitationem §. 295. et emendatur plerumque per adiectum, quasi synonymon, aliud vocabulum. e. g. *ornatum* et *graue*. *Ornatos in dicendo grauesque viros* Scaeuolae apud Ciceronem de Or. I. 42. si interpretemur, sublimitatem attingere qui cogitando dicendoque possint, videbimus eos recte mediis interpositos philosophis refutare *Crassum,* [p. 179] *qui oratorem in omnis sermonis disputatione copiosissime posse versari, quasi suo iure sumserat.* §. 125. Augeretur inconcinnitas a Crasso asserti, si copiosissimum et sublime confunderemus, §. 295. et ornatum, l. c. 50. §. 257.

§ 296. If the sublime manner of thinking is called *grave* (δεινόν [forceful]), § 281, it has received that name from a certain relative and comparative gravity and from its highest degree, since every aesthetic magnitude demands some gravity too, an absolute one at least, § 189. If it is called ornate, § 281, the ambiguity can be removed after the pattern of § 295, and it is generally corrected by the addition of another word as a kind of synonym, e.g. *ornate* and *grave*. If we interpret Scaevola’s *men ornate and grave in speaking*, in Cicero, de Or. I. 42, as those who can attain sublimity in thinking and speaking, we shall see that they, set between the philosophers, rightly refute *Crassus,* [p. 179] *who had assumed, as if by his own right, that the orator can range most copiously over the discussion of every subject.* § 125. The incongruity of what Crassus asserts would be increased if we confounded the most copious with the sublime, § 295, and with the ornate, l. c. 50. § 257.

> § 297. Sublime cogitandi genus qui tandem *validum* dicunt, §. 281. denuo videntur de relatiuo quodam et comparatiuo robore loqui velle, quod huic vtique cogitandi generi summum generice debet adscribi, §. 288. Iam tenue poscit aliquid neruorum ac sanguinis, §. 242-244. plus medium, §. 274. sublime plurimum. M. §. 515. Videamus insignem eius vim et efficaciam paullo distinctius, vt eandem a spurii sublimis larua sit hoc facilius distinguere.

§ 297. Those who at last call the sublime manner of thinking *strong*, § 281, seem once more to wish to speak of a certain relative and comparative strength, which generically must indeed be ascribed to this manner of thinking in the highest degree, § 288. Now the slender manner demands some sinew and blood, § 242–244, the middle more, § 274, the sublime the most. M. § 515. Let us look at its remarkable force and efficacy a little more distinctly, so that it may be the easier to distinguish it from the mask of a spurious sublime.

> § 298. 1) Habet sublime cogitandi genus summas generice diuitias, §. 158, 288. quas nonnunquam paene omnes relinquit, §. 160. vnico veluti, sed pretiosissimo, tantum adamante fulgens, §. 289. vnde tacitus tecum concludas ad opes reliquas, §. 177, 148. non nunquam magnificentius exponit, §. 293. Vnde tunc περιαγωγαὶ καὶ περιβολαί, circumducta quaedam et accumalata [sic: accumulata] meditandi ratio, non sine synathroismis, §. 148. Neque tamen omnis sublimis, nec in sublimibus [p. 180] summa, meditatio circumducta est et accumulata, multo minus omnis circumducta meditandi ratio, et adhuc minus longitudo quaedam et diffusio distorsioue signorum tantum e. g. dictionis et vocabulorum, grandis atque sublimis est. §. 295. Aristophanes habet vocabulum sex versuum, et repit Plauti

§ 298. 1) The sublime manner of thinking has generically the greatest riches, § 158, 288, which it sometimes almost wholly leaves aside, § 160, shining with only a single, but most precious, diamond, as it were, § 289, from which you may silently infer for yourself the remaining wealth, § 177, 148; and sometimes it displays them more magnificently, § 293. Hence then the περιαγωγαὶ καὶ περιβολαί [circuits and amplifications], a certain circuitous and accumulated manner of meditating, not without synathroisms, § 148. Yet not every sublime meditation, nor the highest among the sublime [p. 180] ones, is circuitous and accumulated, much less is every circuitous manner of meditating, and still less a certain length and diffusion or distortion of the signs alone, e.g. of the diction and the words, grand and sublime. § 295. Aristophanes has a word of six verses, and there creeps along Plautus’s

> *Quodsemelarripidesnunquamposteaeripides,* §. 237.

*Whatyouhaveoncesnatchedyouwillneverafterwardsbesnatchedof,* § 237.

> § 299. 2) Magnitudinem cogitandorum, etiam naturalem, §. 181. eam seruat, quae nec comparata primario themati, personisue vel loquentibus, vel obiectis personalibus, in nihilum comparatiuum abeat, euanescens, e. g. §. 198. nec e contrario sub eadem comparatione illa, quae iam dixi, primarium thema, e. c. quando semper in magnis maxima legitur magnitudo cogitandorum quorumuis, si grandia quidem illa, thema, e. c. fuerint, neque tamen in magnis maxima, §. 207. eleuet potius, obscuret, et minuat, quam amplificet, ornet et extollat. Par est sublimi cogitationum generi cura dignitatis generice maximae, sed in maxime dignis gradus simul, vt ita dicam, specifici, §. 207. ne tollatur altius, aut deprimatur, ac et hic requirit, earum etiam partium laterumue, ex quibus eximia contemplanda sunt, vt talia, sedulo cautis vergentibus ad mediocritatem, vel omnino tenuitatem variis lateribusque [p. 181] cogitandi non male electi, §. 215. nisi opere in longo habeat aliquando locum et hic. §. 235.

§ 299. 2) It preserves the magnitude of the things to be thought, even the natural magnitude, § 181, such that it neither, compared with the principal theme or with the persons, whether speaking or personal objects, passes away into a comparative nothing, vanishing, e.g. § 198, nor, on the contrary, under that same comparison which I have just mentioned, does the principal theme, for instance, when the greatest magnitude in great things is always expected of any thoughts whatever, if those things, the theme for instance, have indeed been grand, yet not the greatest among great things, § 207, rather lower, obscure and diminish than amplify, adorn and exalt. The sublime manner of thoughts has a care for a dignity that is generically the greatest, but at the same time, in the most dignified things, for a degree that is, so to speak, specific, § 207, so that it is neither raised too high nor lowered, and here too it requires that even of those parts or sides from which the eminent things are to be contemplated as such, those that tend to mediocrity, or to slenderness altogether, be carefully guarded against among the various sides and manners [p. 181] of thinking that have been not badly chosen, § 215, unless in a long work this too has its place at some time. § 235.

> § 300. Exemplum huius cogitandi generis Cicero ipse suam orationem pro Rabirio citat, eodemque iure suo referuntur oratio pro Milone paullatim surgens, Catilinaria II. Philippica II. et in Pisonem. In Aeneide imum ex grandibus cogitandi generibus Scaliger in descriptione ludorum L. V. medium L. I. summum L. II. et VI. deprehendit. Liceat ex sacris exemplum addere. Sit magnum in maximis, quod Longino S. IX. vehementer placuit: *Sit lux et fuit.* Maius est: Τετέλεσται. Maximum: *Sit deus omnia in omnibus.*

§ 300. As an example of this manner of thinking Cicero himself cites his own oration for Rabirius, and by the same right his oration for Milo, rising little by little, the second Catilinarian, the second Philippic and the speech against Piso are referred to it. In the Aeneid Scaliger finds the lowest of the grand manners of thinking in the description of the games, Book V, the middle in Book I, the highest in Books II and VI. Let me add an example from Scripture. Let the great among the greatest be that which strongly pleased Longinus, S. IX: *Let there be light, and there was.* Greater is: Τετέλεσται [It is finished]. The greatest: *Let God be all in all.*

> § 301. 3) Sublime cogitandi genus verisimilitudinem, §. 22. sed eam proprie tantum sectatur, quae ingeniis superioribus et animis erectioribus comprehendi probarique possit, §. 288. licet eadem plebeculae sit vix credibilis, §. 286. nec apud nobiles sic satis animos facilem inueniat fidem. §. 213. Quam suam verisimilitudinem aut tacitae spectatoris ἀναθεωρήσει, §. 177. relinquit, §. 289. aut eam adeo luculenter probat, §. 291-294. vt abhorrens primo, vel maxime a sensibus nostris, nunc tandem, non solum, non odium, [p. 182] sed etiam admirationem et desiderium sui pariat veritas. §. 293.

§ 301. 3) The sublime manner of thinking pursues verisimilitude, § 22, but properly only that which can be comprehended and approved by superior wits and more elevated minds, § 288, though the same may be scarcely credible to the rabble, § 286, and may not find easy credence even among sufficiently noble minds. § 213. This verisimilitude of its own it either leaves to the silent ἀναθεωρήσει [reconsideration] of the spectator, § 177, 289, or proves so luminously, § 291–294, that the truth which at first was abhorrent, or most abhorrent, to our senses now at last produces not only no hatred, [p. 182] but even admiration and longing for itself. § 293.

> § 302. Sublime Pompeii dictum, quum dissuadente nauta per tempestatem nauem conscenderet: Proficisci me necessarium est, viuere non est necesse, contradictionis apertae damnat Gallorum nonnemo. Neque defendat, Pompeio aequalis animus, nec accuset Caesar aliquis, vel hostis. Ambo enim pulcre intelligent. §. 288, 301. *Magnum est efficere, vt quis intelligat, quid sit illud verum et simplex bonum, quod non possit ab honestate seiungi.* Cic. qu. ac. l. 7. Quod bonum quale sit, sane, non solus *Epicurus* verbis *negat sine voluptatibus sensum mouentibus se suspicari posse*, sed plures ad hunc vsque diem factis, inter eos etiam, in quibus summos mores et virtutem excellentem suspicetur aestheticus. Neque tamen illius nuda veritas *acute, argute, obscure*, vti videatur analogo rationis, §. 121. *studio philosophiae* seueriori *disseritur* tantum, *quo nullum* Varroni Platonique videtur *maius aut melius a diis datum munus homini:* sed iam etiam aestheticis et vere sublimibus tot meditationibus est exposita, et exponitur paene quotidie, eiusdem verisimilitudo, vt ex hac parte rerum humanarum parum aut nihil superesse desiderandum videatur. §. 301.

§ 302. Pompey’s sublime saying, when he was embarking in a storm against the sailor’s dissuasion, It is necessary that I sail, it is not necessary that I live, is condemned by a certain Frenchman as an open contradiction. Let no mind equal to Pompey’s defend it, and let no Caesar, or enemy, accuse it. For both will understand it beautifully. § 288, 301. *It is a great thing to bring it about that someone understands what that true and simple good is which cannot be separated from honour.* Cic. qu. ac. l. 7. What sort of thing that good is, surely, not only *Epicurus denies* in words *that he can conceive it without pleasures that move the senses*, but many more down to this day deny it by their deeds, among them even those in whom the aesthetician would suspect the highest morals and an excellent virtue. And yet the naked truth of that good is not only argued *acutely, subtly, obscurely*, as it seems to the analogue of reason, § 121, *in the* more severe *study of philosophy*, *than which* no *greater or better gift given to man by the gods* seems to Varro and Plato to exist: its verisimilitude has already been set forth in so many aesthetic and truly sublime meditations too, and is set forth almost daily, so that on this side of human affairs little or nothing seems left to be desired. § 301.

> [p. 183] § 303. 4) Summa in luce magnum hoc exsplendescit cogitationum genus, §. 22. sed in ea, cui ferendae, cui capiendae, cui fruendae potissimum aquilarum oculi requirantur §. 288. Quos aliquando iam supponit, §. 289. et eo splendore satiat, ad quem ipsa caecutiat Mineruae noctua, aliquando mira arte naturaliter bonos nondum tot radiis imbibendis adsuetos, vel etiam desuetos iterum, ita sensim allicit, et blande pascendo simul acuit atque confirmat, vt tandem ibi solem meridianum, plana ac perspicua omnia mirentur, vbi caecitatem et tenebras et obscuritatem non ita multo ante sibi deprehendere visi erant. §. 291.

[p. 183] § 303. 4) This great manner of thoughts shines forth in the highest light, § 22, but in a light for the bearing, the grasping and the enjoying of which the eyes of eagles are chiefly required § 288. These it sometimes already presupposes, § 289, and sates with that splendour at which Minerva’s own owl would be dazzled; sometimes, by a wonderful art, it so gradually entices those who are naturally good but not yet accustomed to drinking in so many rays, or who have grown unaccustomed to them again, and, by gently feeding them, at once sharpens and strengthens them, that at last they marvel at the midday sun and at everything plain and perspicuous there where not so long before they had seemed to themselves to find blindness and darkness and obscurity. § 291.

> § 304. Vt hanc verissimam sublimium lucem, obscuritatem apparentem, possis in exemplo dignoscere a tenebris, lege, sis, vaticinium Sibyllae Aen. VI. 83-97. vbi priuilegium quasi poeta habuisset obliuiscendi verae perspicuitatis ob verisimilem oraculorum caliginem. Quamuis et ipse dicat

§ 304. That you may be able in an example to distinguish this truest light of sublime things, an apparent obscurity, from darkness, read, if you will, the Sibyl’s prophecy, Aen. VI. 83-97, where the poet would have had, as it were, the privilege of forgetting true perspicuity on account of the verisimilar mist of oracles. Although he himself says

> *Talibus ex adyto dictis Cumaea Sibylla, / Horrendas canit ambages, antroque remugit / Obscuris vera inuoluens,*

*With such words from the shrine the Cumaean Sibyl / sings her dreadful riddles and bellows in her cave, / wrapping true things in obscurities,*

> tamen deprehendes vere sublimia, quae nec nunc, quid sibi velint, quantumque habeant [p. 184] ponderis, quiuis ex plebe litteratorum intelligat, interim nihil obscuritatis in verbis et ratione cogitandi, praeter id, quod in futuris ordinarium est, et ob deficientem omnimodae determinationis eorundem notitiam in homine, vel maximo, mero tamen homine, vehementer necessarium, adeoque post euentum et impletionem historiae fabulaeue perito satis peruium.

yet you will find things truly sublime, whose meaning and whose weight [p. 184] anyone from the common crowd of the lettered may now understand, with meanwhile nothing of obscurity in the words and in the manner of thinking, except what is ordinary in things to come and, because man, even the greatest, but still a mere man, lacks the knowledge of their complete determination, strongly necessary, and so, after the event and the fulfilment, sufficiently passable for one versed in the history or the story.

> § 305. 5) Sublime cogitandi genus persuadet, §. 22. sed iis persuadendis tantum, certe potissimum, laborat, quorum iam intimis praecordiis inseuit virtutis rectorumque morum semina, cum certitudine, magnitudo pectoris, §. 45. insignior. Quibus non cognita solum, sed et ipsorum caussa non indigentia probationibus quum insint principia: his nunc tribus, quod aiunt verbis, aut omnino vel vnico, instruit, quasi immotis fundamentis suam persuasionem breuissimis, nunc pro diuersa obiectorum suorum personalium conditione, §. 289-294. tot pondera, tot sententias, tot firmamenta congerit in certius reddendum suum thema, non illa trita, sed magni quid semper spirantia, vt maiores animi plenissime persuadeantur, minores obruantur, et ad prudentissimum, quod ab ipsis sperari potest, ad silentium compellantur.

§ 305. 5) The sublime manner of thinking persuades, § 22, but it labours to persuade only, or at any rate chiefly, those in whose inmost hearts a more remarkable magnitude of heart, § 45, has already sown, with certainty, the seeds of virtue and of right morals. Since these men have within them principles not only known but also, for their own sake, not in need of proofs, it now builds up its persuasion in three words, as they say, or even in a single one, in the briefest terms, as upon unmoved foundations, and now, according to the different condition of its personal objects, § 289–294, it heaps up so many weights, so many maxims, so many supports, to make its theme more certain, not those trite ones, but ones always breathing something great, so that the greater minds are most fully persuaded, the lesser are overwhelmed and are driven to the most prudent thing that can be hoped of them, to silence.

> [p. 185] § 306. Exemplum persuasionis, et eius quidem efficacissimae, per vnam vocem habet Suetonius in Caesare. 70. *Decumanos Romae cum ingentibus minis, summoque etiam vrbis periculo, missionem et praemia flagitantes, ardente tunc in Africa bello, nec adire cunctatus est quanquam deterrentibus amicis, neque dimittere. Sed vna voce, qua Quirites eos pro militibus appellarat, tam facile circumegit et flexit, vt et milites esse confestim responderint, et quamuis recusantem vltro in Africam sint sequuti.* Paullo fusius persuasit idem Caesar, verae sublimitatis aestheticae peritus, metum imminentis hostis suos deponere *amplificando ementiendoque* copiarum eius numerum, 66.

[p. 185] § 306. An example of persuasion, and indeed of the most efficacious kind, by a single word Suetonius has in his Caesar, 70. *When the men of the tenth legion at Rome, with enormous threats and even the greatest danger to the city, were demanding their discharge and their rewards, while the war was then blazing in Africa, he did not hesitate to go to them, though his friends tried to deter him, and to dismiss them. But with a single word, in that he addressed them as Quirites instead of soldiers, he so easily turned them about and bent them that they at once answered that they were soldiers, and of their own accord followed him to Africa, though he refused them.* A little more diffusely the same Caesar, versed in true aesthetic sublimity, persuaded his men to lay aside their fear of the approaching enemy *by amplifying and falsifying* the number of his forces, 66.

> § 307. *Pollio Asinius parum integra veritate compositos putat commentarios Caesaris*, 56. quantum tamen inest plerisque, quae scribit, persuasionis? Putares eos legens rectissime fecisse, qui, Catullo si fides est, nihil potuit,

§ 307. *Asinius Pollio thinks that Caesar’s commentaries were composed with too little regard for the truth*, 56; yet how much persuasion there is in most of what he writes! Reading them you would think that those had acted most rightly who, if Catullus is to be believed, could do nothing

> *Nisi vncta deuorare patrimonia.*

*Except devour greasy patrimonies.*

> Non deterreor eorum opinione, qui hos commentarios humiles iudicant, quo minus eorum heic mentionem faciam. Quoniam eorum verba satis et pueri capiunt et aliquem sensum, quantum possunt pro aetate, non sunt ideo humiles, non tenue cogitandi [p. 186] genus demonstrant, et, nisi omnem tibi historiam placeat medium cogitandi genus amplecti debere, §. 267. nullus dubito, quin ipsis aequabile quidem cogitandi genus, §. 267, 268. et temperatum §. 270. adscribam, et, cum Cicerone, *nudum, rectum, ac omni ornatu orationis, tanquam veste detracta, venustum*, ita tamen, qua res, sublime, vt, *dum voluit* (aut velle simulauit) *alios habere parata, vnde sumerent, qui vellent scribere historiam, ineptis gratum fortasse fecerit, qui illa volunt calamistris inurere, sanos quidem homines a scribendo deterruerit.*

I am not deterred by the opinion of those who judge these commentaries humble from making mention of them here. Because even boys grasp their words well enough and some sense, as far as they can for their age, they are not on that account humble, they do not display the slender manner [p. 186] of thinking, and, unless you think that all history must embrace the middle manner of thinking, § 267, I have no doubt in ascribing to them an even-tenored manner of thinking indeed, § 267, 268, and a tempered one, § 270, and, with Cicero, one *naked, straight and, with every ornament of speech stripped off as it were a garment, charming*, yet, as the matter requires, sublime, so that, *while he wished* (or pretended to wish) *that others should have materials ready from which those who wanted to write history might draw, he has perhaps gratified the fools who want to curl those materials with the curling-iron, but he has deterred sensible men from writing.*

> § 308. 6) Sublime genus cogitationum in eo regnat, vt animos, sed generosioris impetus capaciores, §. 289-294. nunc in summam inflammationem et diuinum paene furorem incitare, nunc a turbulentissimis animi commotionibus ex re quapiam minutula ortis retrahere decoram ad serenitatem et altioris spiritus tranquillitatem valeat, §. 288. pro vti, vel hic, vel ille status animorum heroibus est conuenientior. §. 213.

§ 308. 6) The sublime manner of thoughts reigns in this, that it is able, § 288, now to incite minds, but minds more capable of a nobler impulse, § 289–294, to the highest inflammation and an almost divine frenzy, now to draw them back from the most turbulent commotions of the mind, arisen from some trifling matter, to a becoming serenity and the tranquillity of a loftier spirit, according as this or that state of minds is more suitable for heroes. § 213.

> § 309. Aeneas, l. II. frustra dissuadente Hectore in somnis, v. 295. *arma amens capit,*

§ 309. Aeneas, Book II, though Hector in a dream dissuades him in vain, v. 295, *madly takes up arms,*

> *furor iraque mentem / [p. 187] Praecipitant, pulcrumque mori succurrit in armis,* v. 315.

*fury and anger drive / [p. 187] his mind headlong, and it comes to him how beautiful it is to die in arms,* v. 315.

> *Otriadae [sic: Othryadae] dictis in flammas et in arma fertur, quo tristis Erynnis, / Quo fremitus vocat, et sublatus ad aethera clamor.* v. 338.

*At the words of Othryades he is borne into the flames and into arms, whither the grim Erinys, / whither the roar and the shouting raised to heaven call.* v. 338.

> *Addentes se socios, per lunam oblatos, alloquitur.*

*He addresses his companions, who join him, met by moonlight.*

> *Sic animis iuuenum furor additus,* v. 355.

*Thus fury is added to the spirits of the young men,* v. 355.

> Adhuc *furiata mente fertur* Aeneas v. 588. et est

Still *with maddened mind* Aeneas *is borne along* v. 588, and there is

> *dignus vindice nodus,*

*a knot worthy of a deliverer,*

> pium heroa a defensione patriae retrahere. En! adest deus, mater, dextra prehendens, et orationem suam, animum pectusque filii mulcentem, ecstatica visione corroborans. v. 589-625.

to draw the pious hero back from the defence of his country. Lo! the god is at hand, his mother, taking him by the right hand and strengthening her speech, which soothes her son’s mind and heart, with an ecstatic vision. v. 589-625.

#### Sectio XXII. Vitia Sublimi Opposita. — Section XXII. Vices Opposed to the Sublime.

> § 310. In cogitanda grandi materia cauendum est I. QVARTVM ΒΑΘΟΥΣ (manifesti) GENVS, in quo statim appareat magnitudine obiectorum comparatiua et generice maxima, §. 207. minores et inferiores esse mente [p. 188] formatas cogitationes. §. 217. In quo 4 denuo species facili negotio detegas: 1) si in maximis generice denuo excellentia cogitentur quidem maximis generatim satis apta dignaque ratione, sed non adeo excellente, ac ipsa themata mereri videantur, 2) si siluae arbustis, 3) si siluae myricis exaequentur 4) si summa deprimantur omnino humum vsque et in meras nugas intra animum venuste, si diis placet, cogitaturi redigantur. Vltima species tertiam classem nugatorum in re seria constituet, et eam quidem turpissimam, §. 245.

§ 310. In thinking about grand matter one must beware of I. A FOURTH KIND OF (MANIFEST) ΒΑΘΟΥΣ [bathos], in which it at once appears that the thoughts formed by the mind [p. 188] are smaller and lower than the magnitude of the objects, which is comparative and generically the greatest, § 207. § 217. In this you may again easily detect four species: 1) if, within what is generically the greatest, excellent things are indeed thought again in a manner suitable and worthy enough of the greatest things in general, but not so excellent as the themes themselves seem to deserve, 2) if forests are made equal to shrubs, 3) if forests are made equal to tamarisks, 4) if the highest things are pressed down altogether to the ground and reduced to mere trifles by one who means, if the gods please, to think charmingly within his mind. The last species will constitute the third class of triflers in a serious matter, and indeed the most shameful, § 245.

> § 311. Ad primam βάθους huc pertinentis speciem referamus cogitandi rationem, quam in Homero iam reprehendit Longinus, S. VIIII. qua ille *ex hominibus*, qui *rebus Iliacis* interfuerunt, *quantum potest, deos* dum *facit, ex diis* facit *homines, quorum vulnera, dissidia, vltiones, lacrumas, vincula, et infelicem immortalitatem* canat. Contra hoc vitium dirigi videtur Horatii praeceptum:

§ 311. To the first species of the βάθους [bathos] belonging here let us refer the manner of thinking which Longinus already censures in Homer, S. VIIII, by which he, *out of the men* who took part in *the affairs of Troy*, *as far as he can*, while he *makes gods*, makes *men out of gods, whose wounds, quarrels, revenges, tears, bonds and unhappy immortality* he sings. Against this vice Horace’s precept seems to be directed:

> *Intererit multum Diuusne loquatur, an heros.* A. P. 114.

*It will make much difference whether a god speaks or a hero.* A. P. 114.

> Ex hoc enim versu cum Bentleio *Dauum* exsulare iubeo. Ad eandem speciem deprimentis se nonnihil infra suam maiestatem sublimis, §. 310. pertinet Homeri ab eodem Longino S. VIIII. obseruata *declinatio ab Iliade in Odysseae* [p. 189] *amorem fabularum.* Ob quem Homerum in odyssea comparat *occidenti soli, cuius sine intensione* caloris et virium *maneat* §. 298 --- 309. *magnitudo.* Non esse, ait, ἴσον τόνον Homeri in odyssea, ac in Iliade, οὐδ' ἐξωμαλισμένα τὰ ὕψη καὶ ἱζήματα μηδαμοῦ λαμβάνοντα, breuiter, *senectutem, sed senectutem Homeri.*

For from this verse, with Bentley, I order *Davus* into exile. To the same species of the sublime lowering itself somewhat beneath its own majesty, § 310, belongs Homer’s *decline from the Iliad into the love of stories in the Odyssey,* [p. 189] observed by the same Longinus, S. VIIII. On account of which he compares Homer in the Odyssey to *the setting sun, whose magnitude remains without the intensity* of its heat and strength § 298–309. There is not, he says, the ἴσον τόνον [same tension] of Homer in the Odyssey as in the Iliad, οὐδ' ἐξωμαλισμένα τὰ ὕψη καὶ ἱζήματα μηδαμοῦ λαμβάνοντα [nor are the heights kept level, nowhere admitting a sinking]; in short, *old age, but the old age of Homer.*

> § 312. Secundae speciei §. 310. exemplum sit Timaeus apud Longinum S. IIII. qui *Alexandrum magnum* ait *intra pauciores annos totam Asiam subegisse, quam* intra quos *panegyricam orationem de bello contra persas Isocrates conscripserit. Egregia scilicet Macedonis illius cum Sophista comparatio. Vincit strenuitate Lacedomios* [sic: Lacedaemonios] *Isocrates. Illi triginta annos in expugnanda Messene terunt, hic in conscribenda oratione panegyrica tantum decem.* Huc et, praeter comparationes, traherem sublimium, nisi tenues, medias certe partes et varia, circumstantias dicunt, externa, praesertim si minus necessaria earundem commemoratio, nec breuissima videatur. An magnus interdum et Maro dormitat? e. g. Aen. l. 177.

§ 312. Of the second species, § 310, let the example be Timaeus in Longinus, S. IIII, who says that *Alexander the Great subdued all Asia in fewer years than* those within which *Isocrates composed his panegyric oration on the war against the Persians. An excellent comparison, forsooth, of that Macedonian with the Sophist. Isocrates surpasses the Lacedaemonians in energy. They spend thirty years in the conquest of Messene, he only ten in composing his panegyric oration.* Here too, besides comparisons, I would bring the thin, or at any rate middle, parts of sublime things and the various matters they call circumstances, externals, especially if the mention of them, being less necessary, does not seem very brief either. Does even great Maro nod sometimes? e.g. Aen. l. 177.

> *Ac primum silicis scintillam excudit Achates, / Suscepitque ignem foliis, atque arida circum / Nutrimenta dedit, rapuitque in fomite flammam.*

*And first Achates struck a spark from flint, / caught the fire in leaves, and gave dry / nourishment round about, and quickly took the flame in the tinder.*

> [p. 190] § 313. Ad tertiam iusto submissioris de sublimibus cogitandi generis speciem §. 310. nondum audeo referre omnes heroum cum bestiis, animantibusque comparationes. Interim tamen nostro, quod viuimus, saeculo solos reor leones et aquilas adhuc in maiori theatro suum locum tueri, praesertim auxilia ferente arte, quam heraldicam blasonicamque dicunt. Reliqua tantum non omnia loco graduque mota disparuerunt in heroicis, quando laus intenditur, animantia, dum philosophi, sintne machinae, sintne spiritus, euidentius inter se constituerint. Homeri adhuc heroes, vt canes, nisi latrant, tamen pugnant. Virgilii heroes, Aen. II. 355.

[p. 190] § 313. To the third species of a manner of thinking about sublime things that is lower than is right, § 310, I do not yet dare to refer all comparisons of heroes with beasts and living creatures. Meanwhile, however, in this age in which we live I think that only lions and eagles still hold their place in the greater theatre, especially with the aid of the art which they call heraldry or blazonry. Almost all the remaining animals, moved from their place and rank, have vanished from heroic works when praise is intended, until the philosophers have settled more clearly among themselves whether they are machines or spirits. Homer’s heroes still, like dogs, if they do not bark, at least fight. Virgil’s heroes, Aen. II. 355,

> *lupi ceu / Raptores, atra in nebula, quos improba ventris / Exegit caecos rabies, catulique relicti / Faucibus exspectant siccis: per tela, per hostes / Vadunt.*

*like ravening / wolves in a black mist, whom the wicked madness of the belly / has driven out blind, and whose whelps, left behind, / wait with dry throats: through weapons, through enemies / they go.*

> Agnoscas inter arma virosque Tityrum, expertum quam sit

You may recognise among arms and men Tityrus, who had learned how

> *Triste lupus stabulis.*

*grievous the wolf is to the folds.*

> § 314. Horatii iam Drusus, IV. od. 4. comparatur lautius 1) aquilae, quam non *improba ventris rabies*, §. 313. sed

§ 314. Horace’s Drusus, now, IV. od. 4, is compared more handsomely 1) to the eagle, whom not *the wicked madness of the belly*, § 313, but

> [p. 191] *Olim iuuentus et patrius vigor, / Nido laborum propulit inscium.*

[p. 191] *once youth and inherited vigour / drove from the nest, ignorant of toils.*

> Sed an satis dignum est, illi

But is it sufficiently worthy of him

> *Quod rex deorum regnum in aues vagas, / Permisit, expertus fidelem / Iuppiter in Ganymede flauo?*

*that the king of the gods has entrusted to it the kingdom over the roaming birds, / Jupiter, having found it faithful / in the matter of fair-haired Ganymede?*

> ⁠2) Leoni. Transeat. Sed an sunt etiam *Rhaetis sub Alpibus Vindelicorum obarmatae Amazoniis securibus dextrae,*

⁠2) To the lion. Let it pass. But are there also, *beneath the Rhaetian Alps, right hands of the Vindelici armed with Amazonian axes,*

> *diuque / Lateque victrices cateruae*

*and troops long / and widely victorious,*

> *laetis caprea pascuis / Intenta?*

*a roe intent / on the glad pastures?*

> Si sunt, an eorum *in poena nomen* est Drusi *memorabile?*

If there are, is the name of Drusus *memorable in the punishment* of them?

> *habet victoria laudem?*

*Has the victory its praise?*

> § 315. *Ohe! iam satis est, ohe!* poeta! / *Tu procedis adhuc, et ire quaeris.* / Maiores aquilis leonibusque / Nosti, maxime, comparationes?

§ 315. *Ho there! that is enough now, ho there!* poet! / *You still go on, and seek to go further.* / Greater comparisons than with eagles and lions / do you know, greatest of poets?

> Comparat principes iuuentutis romanae, quos Augustus, filiorum instar, habuit, 3) iuuencis:

He compares the princes of the Roman youth, whom Augustus held in the place of sons, 3) to bullocks:

> *Est in iuuencis, est in equis patrum / Virtus.*

*There is in bullocks, there is in horses the virtue / of their sires.*

> [p. 192] Hoc et in se deprehendetur exemplum et simile,

[p. 192] In this too will be found an example and a likeness of itself,

> *Magna modis tenuare paruis,*

*To thin great things by small measures,*

> et, quanquam non ignoro boues olim maiori in reuerentia habitos, ac nunc, tamen, non Horatii carpendi gratia, sed amore veri, βάθος iudico, in quod si quis nunc simili in occasione prolabetur, nisi *Romani*, §. 212. certe

and, although I am not unaware that oxen were once held in greater reverence than now, nevertheless, not for the sake of carping at Horace, but for love of the truth, I judge it βάθος [bathos], and if anyone now slips into it on a similar occasion, if not the *Romans*, § 212, at least

> Germani *tollent equites peditesque cachinnum,*

the Germans *will raise a laugh, horse and foot,*

> et *patres*, quos Bentleius *peditibus* substituit.

and *the fathers*, whom Bentley substituted for *the foot*.

> § 316. Quartam speciem §. 310. memorati vitii ornet vetus illud:

§ 316. The fourth species, § 310, of the vice mentioned may be graced by that old line:

> *Iuppiter interea cana niue conspuit Alpes.*

*Jupiter meanwhile bespat the Alps with white snow.*

> et recentius: *emunctioris naris mortales*, quando placet facetos et elegantes

and by the more recent one: *mortals of a cleaner nose*, when it pleases them to parade the witty and the elegant

> *Grandisonis pompare modis, tragicoque boatu.*

*in grand-sounding measures and with tragic bellowing.*

> Transmittatur enim *emunctae naris homo* Horatii,

For let Horace’s *man of a well-wiped nose* be allowed to pass,

> *madidique infantia nasi*

*and the childhood of a dripping nose*

> apud Iuuenalem, cum *ructantibus* eorundem personis, quoniam tunc sublimia scribere non cogitarunt. §. 310. Huc potius Hesiodi, vel quisquis poematis *scutum* dicti sit auctor, quam Longinus S. VIIII. reprehendit, *Tristitia, cuius ex naribus humores fluebant.*

in Juvenal, together with the *belching* persons of the same, since they did not then intend to write sublime things. § 310. Here rather belongs the *Sorrow, from whose nostrils the humours flowed,* of Hesiod, or whoever is the author of the poem called the *Shield*, which Longinus censures, S. VIIII.

> *Tu grauis es nobis, et saepe emungeris, exi / Ocius et propera. Sicco venit altera naso.* Iuu.

*You are a burden to us, and you often wipe your nose; go out / quickly and make haste. Another comes with a dry nose.* Iuu.

> [p. 193] Longinus eiusdem vitii accusat *Platonem et Xenephontem* [sic: Xenophontem] *nonnunquam* διὰ τὰ οὕτως μικροχαρῆ *sui metipsorum obliuiscentes, quanquam ex Socratica sint palaestra*, e. g. tunc, vbi *Xenophon de republ. Laced. scribens pupillas, quae sunt in oculis, verecundas virgines dicat.*

[p. 193] Longinus accuses *Plato and Xenophon* of the same vice, *as sometimes forgetting themselves* διὰ τὰ οὕτως μικροχαρῆ [through such petty conceits], *although they come from the Socratic wrestling-school*, e.g. there where *Xenophon, writing on the Lacedaemonian republic, calls the pupils that are in the eyes modest maidens.*

> § 317. Omnium harum depressius iusto de grandibus cogitandi rationum gradus semper turpiores sunt, in quibus non magnitudo solum forte naturalis, sed etiam simul dignitas et in magnis necessarius rigidae honestatis et seuerioris virtutis amor laeditur per VILE DE SVBLIMIBVS COGITANDI GENVS e. g. Ioui adscriptum praemium nefandi lenocinii, §. 314. et magna pars metamorphoseon Ouidii, eo procedens aliquando dedecorum, vt ipse sane non castus poëta putarit consultum, praefari, X, 300.

§ 317. Of all these degrees of manners of thinking about grand things more lowly than is right, those are always the more shameful in which not only the magnitude, perhaps the natural magnitude, but also at the same time the dignity and the love of rigid honour and of severer virtue that is necessary in great things are wounded by THE VILE MANNER OF THINKING ABOUT SUBLIME THINGS, e.g. the reward for abominable pandering ascribed to Jupiter, § 314, and a great part of Ovid’s Metamorphoses, which sometimes proceeds to such shameful things that the poet himself, who was certainly not chaste, thought it advisable to preface them, X, 300.

> *Dira canam. Procul hinc, natae, procul este, parentes. / Aut mea si vestras mulcebunt pectora mentes, / Desit in hac mihi parte fides, nec credite factum, / Vel, si credetis, facti quoque credite poenam.*

*I shall sing dreadful things. Far from here, daughters, far from here be, parents. / Or if my songs shall soothe your minds, / let me in this part be denied belief, and do not believe the deed, / or, if you will believe it, believe also the punishment of the deed.*

> Rectissime grauissimeque cauet Horatius, A. P. 227.

Most rightly and most gravely Horace warns, A. P. 227,

> *Ne, quicunque deus, quicunque adhibebitur heros / [p. 194] Regali conspectus in auro nuper et ostro, / Migret in obscuras humili sermone tabernas.*

*lest whatever god, whatever hero shall be brought on, / [p. 194] lately seen in royal gold and purple, / should migrate with humble speech into dark taverns.*

> Huc heroum mutua conuicia, quorum exempla non opus est in Homero quaerere, quum ante pauca saecula publicis adhuc in scriptis illustrium principum vel ipsos iam titulos macularent.

Here belong the mutual insults of heroes, examples of which there is no need to seek in Homer, since a few centuries ago they still stained the public writings of illustrious princes, or even their very titles.

> § 318. Pergens l. c. Horatius;

§ 318. Horace, continuing, l. c.,

> *Ne, dum vitat humum, nubes et inania captet,*

*lest, while he avoids the ground, he catch at clouds and empty things,*

> hos deducit ad vitium maiora cogitaturis fugiendum II. QVARTVM TVMORIS GENVS, res excellenter magnas inani sublimitatis in cogitando specie nequicquam inuoluens. Cuius meteoris quoniam vere materia et obiectum illustre non exaequetur, omnis tumor huius generis erit βάθος κρυπτικόν, §. 217, 310. Potiores eius species, velut in ipso suo fonte videbimus, si praecipuarum de sublimi veritatum memores falsam earum conuersionem, hinc detorsionem, hinc laruam et vmbram sublimitatis attendemus in amplectentibus tumidam et sufflatam nubem pro Iunone.

leads these men to the vice that those who would think greater things must avoid, II. A FOURTH KIND OF TUMIDITY, which in vain wraps excellently great things in the empty appearance of sublimity in thinking. Since its meteors are not truly matched by an illustrious matter and object, every tumidity of this kind will be a βάθος κρυπτικόν [hidden bathos], § 217, 310. We shall see its chief species, as it were in their very source, if, mindful of the principal truths about the sublime, we attend to their false conversion, hence to the distortion, hence to the mask and the shade of sublimity in those who embrace a tumid and puffed-up cloud in place of Juno.

> § 319. I. Sublime cogitandi genus est admodum pulcrum. Hoc verissimum, §. 210. Hinc [p. 195] inferuntur male conuersae: 1) Quicquid pulcrius reddendum, illud sublimandum est. Vnde tumorum genera, huc usque considerata, 2) pulcella et comtula ac venustula erunt sublimia. Hic primus fons, primam tumoris nunc considerandi speciem dabit, §. 318, si affectato pulcritudinis studio, fucos omnes et flosculos, et quicquid est vbique pigmentorum ac ornatus, periodos quouis globo rotundiores, argutas antitheses, et ipsas dictionis figuras ad nauseam vsque congerentes, sublimiter se scripsisse somniant, §. 165-307.

§ 319. I. The sublime manner of thinking is very beautiful. This is most true, § 210. Hence [p. 195] badly converted propositions are inferred: 1) Whatever is to be rendered more beautiful must be made sublime. Hence the kinds of tumidity considered up to now; 2) pretty, neat and dainty things will be sublime. This first source will yield the first species of the tumidity now to be considered, § 318, if, through an affected pursuit of beauty, heaping up all cosmetics and flowers, and whatever there is anywhere of pigments and ornament, periods rounder than any ball, subtle antitheses and the very figures of diction to the point of nausea, men dream that they have written sublimely, § 165–307.

> § 320. II. Sublimia nonnunquam admodum breuia, nonnunquam excellenter copiosa sunt et affluentia, §. 298. Hinc conuertendo pessime torquentur; 1) quo breuior, 2) quo diffusior eris, hoc eris sublimior. Vnde duplex tumoris species, 2) qua admodum sibi sublimis videtur, cuius

§ 320. II. Sublime things are sometimes very brief, sometimes excellently copious and overflowing, § 298. Hence by conversion they are most wretchedly twisted: 1) the briefer, 2) the more diffuse you are, the more sublime you will be. Hence a twofold species of tumidity, 2) that by which a man seems to himself very sublime whose

> *Sortilegis non discrepuit sententia Delphis,*

*sentence did not differ from the oracular Delphi,*

> modo breuis sit, etiamsi in longissimam quasi breuitatem incidat. §. 171. Huc Trimalcionis sublimis *vrbanitas*, vbi *lentissima voce Carpe* saepius *ingerens, Carpum, qui obsonium carpebat, eodem verbo vocabat, et imperabat.* Petr. Huc autem propius pertinet, si quis e. g. de eo vere grandi, de quo praesertim exponenda mens esset, si quid sublimis [p. 196] cogitare vellet, adhibet tritum illud: *De hoc praestat nihil, quam pauca dicere*, adeoque nec nihil, nec pauca, nec multa, nec magna. Interim sibi plaudit, ac si maxima. Quid enim? Nonne breuissime peracta sunt omnia?

provided only it be brief, even if it falls into what may be called a very long brevity. § 171. Here belongs the sublime *urbanity* of Trimalchio, where, *forcing out Carpe* repeatedly *in the slowest voice, he called Carpus, who was carving the dish, and gave him his order with the same word.* Petr. But here belongs more closely the case when someone, e.g. concerning something truly grand, about which above all his mind would have to be set forth if he wished to think anything sublime, [p. 196] applies that trite saying: *About this it is better to say nothing than little*, and so says neither nothing, nor little, nor much, nor anything great. Meanwhile he applauds himself as if he had said the greatest things. For why not? Has not everything been dispatched most briefly?

> § 321. 3) Qua alius tunc sibi sublimis videtur, quando omnia ita circumscribit, vt nec gallum quidem gallinaceum, satis longam vocem putet, sed praeferat illud Iuuenalis:

§ 321. 3) That by which another man seems to himself sublime when he so circumscribes everything that he does not think even “farmyard cock” a long enough expression, but prefers that phrase of Juvenal’s:

> *Quo mordetur gallina marito*

*that by which the hen is bitten by her husband.*

> Huc magis pertinet exemplum frigoris a Vossio allatum, Sex. Rufus habet: *per D. Brutum Hispanias obtinuimus, et vsque ad Gades et Oceanum peruenimus.* Idem ita tumens Florus narrat: *D. Brutus aliquanto latius Gallaecos, atque omnes Gallaeciae populos, formidatumque militibus flumen obliuionis, peragratoque victor Oceani littore, non prius signa conuertit, quam cadentem in maria solem, obrutumque aquis ignem, non sine quodam sacrilegii metu et horrore deprehendit.*

Here belongs rather the example of frigidity adduced by Vossius. Sextus Rufus has: *through D. Brutus we obtained the Spains, and reached as far as Gades and the Ocean.* The same thing Florus relates thus tumidly: *D. Brutus, somewhat more widely, having traversed as victor the Gallaeci and all the peoples of Gallaecia, and the river of oblivion dreaded by the soldiers, and the shore of the Ocean, did not turn his standards back before he had beheld, not without a certain fear and horror of sacrilege, the sun falling into the seas and its fire overwhelmed by the waters.*

> § 322. III. Sublime cogitandi genus ita maxima (generice,) cogitat, vt ad minuta, (omni magnitudine aesthetica destituta,) nunquam delabatur, §. 299. Hinc conuertitur principium; Qui ergo de re quapiam, tanquam de [p. 197] optima maxima, quae vnquam est, fuit, erit, ita cogitat, vt et omnia eam ambientia, circumstantia, et vlla ratione concernentia, eo vsque eleuet, vnde non datur vel imaginationi plus vltra, sublimiter ille, profecto, cogitabit. Habes quartam tumoris huc pertinentis, §. 318, speciem. Hic est ille *tumor*, qui secundum Longinum. S. III. *altius insurgere vult, quam sublimia, puerilis autem omnino sublimibus opponitur*, §. 318. Exemplum dabit tempestatis descriptio in Aen. l. I. comparata ea, quam Lucanus fluctibus suis aeque tumentem habet, l. V. in qua

§ 322. III. The sublime manner of thinking thinks the greatest things (generically) in such a way that it never slips down to minute things (destitute of all aesthetic magnitude), § 299. Hence the principle is converted: Whoever, then, thinks about some matter as about [p. 197] the best and greatest thing that ever is, was or will be, in such a way that he raises everything that surrounds it, stands about it and in any way concerns it to the point beyond which there is no further even for the imagination, he, assuredly, will think sublimely. Here you have the fourth species of the tumidity belonging here, § 318. This is that *tumidity* which, according to Longinus, S. III, *wishes to rise higher than the sublime, but, being puerile, is altogether opposed to the sublime*, § 318. An example will be given by the description of the storm in Aen. l. I, compared with the one which Lucan has, swelling as much as his own waves, l. V, in which

> (Neptuni) *regno accessit terra secundo, / Quum mare conuoluit gentes, quum littora Tethys / Noluit vlla pati, caelo contenta teneri. / Tunc quoque tanta maris moles creuisset in astra, / Ni superum rector pressisset nubibus vndas. / fluctus in nubibus accipit imbrem.* e. c.

*the earth was added to* (Neptune’s) *second kingdom, / when the sea rolled the nations together, when Tethys / would not endure any shores, content to be held by the sky. / Then too so great a mass of sea would have grown up to the stars, / had not the ruler of the gods pressed down the waves with clouds. / The wave receives the rain in the clouds,* etc.

> § 323. IV. Sublimia quorundam fidem superant, §. 301, 286. Hinc, qua consequentia? tamen infertur: Omnem fidem superantia quo largius congeres, hoc sublimius cogitabis. Haec quinta tumoris, de quo nunc, §. 318. species in incredibilitate qualicunque sublimitatem quaerentium. His semetipsum [p. 198] transcendere videbitur Ouidius, quando ait Met. VII. 104:

§ 323. IV. Sublime things exceed the belief of some people, § 301, 286. Hence, by what consequence? it is nevertheless inferred: the more lavishly you heap up things that exceed all belief, the more sublimely you will think. This is the fifth species of the tumidity now in question, § 318, that of those who seek sublimity in incredibility of whatever sort. In these Ovid will seem to have transcended himself [p. 198] when he says, Met. VII. 104:

> *Ecce! adamanteis Vulcanum naribus efflant / Aeripedes tauri: tactaeque vaporibus herbae / Ardent, vtque solent pleni resonare camini, / Pectora sic intus clausas voluentia flammas, / Gutturaque vsta sonant.*

*Behold! the bronze-footed bulls breathe out Vulcan from adamantine nostrils, / and the grass touched by the vapours / burns, and as full furnaces are wont to resound, / so their breasts, rolling the flames shut up within, / and their scorched throats resound.*

> Hos sublimes Petronius ridet, *qui nihil ex iis, quae in vsu habemus audiunt, et vident, sed tyrannos edicta scribentes, quibus imperent filiis, vt patrum suorum capita praecidant*, e. c.

Petronius laughs at these sublime men, *who hear and see nothing of the things we have in common use, but tyrants writing edicts in which they command sons to cut off the heads of their own fathers*, etc.

> § 324. V. Sublimia non omnibus omnia lucent, §. 303. Hinc inepte concluditur: Quo obscurius: hoc sublimius. Habes sextam tumoris et ineptae sublimitatis, §. 318, speciem. Huius amicis Tacitus Liuio, Lucanus et Statius Virgilio praestant, qua sublimitatem, quoniam intellectu saepe difficiliores sunt. Videamus exemplum. Virgilius Augusto:

§ 324. V. Sublime things do not shine with everything to everyone, § 303. Hence it is foolishly concluded: the more obscure, the more sublime. Here you have the sixth species of tumidity and of foolish sublimity, § 318. To its friends Tacitus surpasses Livy, Lucan and Statius surpass Virgil, as regards sublimity, because they are often harder to understand. Let us look at an example. Virgil to Augustus:

> *Iam pridem nobis caeli te regia, Caesar, / Inuidet, atque hominum queritur curare triumphos,* Georg. I. 503.

*Long since the palace of heaven has grudged you to us, Caesar, / and complains that you care for the triumphs of men,* Georg. I. 503.

> Statius, inuentionis gloriam habere quia non potest, ob obscuritatem tamen fautoribus huius palmam sublimitatis eripuisse videbitur Virgilio, sic Titum alloquens:

Statius, because he cannot have the glory of invention, will nevertheless, on account of his obscurity, seem to its partisans to have snatched the palm of sublimity from Virgil, addressing Titus thus:

> [p. 199] *O! Latiae decus addite famae!* / *Quem noua maturi subeuntem exorsa parentis* / *Aeternum sibi Roma cupit: licet arctior omnes* / *Limes agat stellas, et te plaga lucida caeli* / *Pleiadum, Boreaeque et hiulci fulminis expers* / *Sollicitet: licet ignipedum fraenator equorum* / *Ipse tuis alte radiantem crinibus arcum* / *Imprimat, aut magni cedat tibi Iuppiter aequa* / *Parte poli, maneas hominum contentus habenis* / *Vndarum terraeque potens, et sidera dones.*

[p. 199] *O glory added to the fame of Latium!* / *Whom, as you take up the new undertakings of a father ripe in years,* / *Rome desires for herself for ever: though a narrower* / *bound drive all the stars, and the shining tract of heaven* / *free of the Pleiades, of Boreas and of the gaping thunderbolt* / *call upon you; though the curber of the fire-footed horses* / *himself press upon your locks his arch that gleams on high,* / *or great Jupiter yield to you an equal* / *share of the sky: may you remain content with the reins of men,* / *lord of waves and land, and bestow the stars.*

> § 325. Haec Statiana Virgilii periphrasis in hac tumoris specie nouam mihi modificationem reuocat in mentem, quando tumidum cogitandi genus quasi obscurum, §. 303. explicat per vere obscurum et simul asiatico, nescio quo, apparatu omnem sublimitatem opprimit. Si nauta, cui timenti procellam Caesar: *Bono*, ait, *animo esto. Caesarem vehis*, non intellexit Caesarem, de quo non pugnabo, quaeritur, an Lucani Caesarem intellexisse credibile sit, quando ille sane verbosus ad rectorem nauis: l. V.

§ 325. This Statian periphrasis of Virgil recalls to my mind a new modification in this species of tumidity, since it explicates the tumid manner of thinking, which is quasi-obscure, § 303, through what is truly obscure, and at the same time, with some Asiatic apparatus or other, crushes all sublimity. If the sailor to whom, as he feared the storm, Caesar said, *Be of good cheer; you carry Caesar*, did not understand Caesar—a point I shall not contest—the question is whether it is credible that he understood Lucan’s Caesar, when the latter, verbose indeed, addresses the ship’s helmsman, book V:

> *Sperne minas*, inquit, *pelagi, ventoque furenti* / [p. 200] *Trade sinum. Italiam si caelo auctore recusas,* / *Me pete. Sola tibi caussa haec est iusta timoris* / *Vectorem non nosse tuum, quem numina nunquam* / *Destituunt, de quo male tunc fortuna meretur,* / *Quum post vota venit.*

*Scorn the threats*, he says, *of the sea, and to the raging wind* / [p. 200] *give your sail. If, with heaven for your warrant, you refuse Italy,* / *seek me. The only just cause of fear for you is this,* / *not to know your passenger, whom the powers never* / *desert, of whom fortune then deserves ill,* / *when she comes after prayers.*

> Ita Lucani Caesar verum in Caesarem adhuc per decem versus subobscure commentatur, et tamen succenset suo paene Caesari poeta

Thus Lucan’s Caesar goes on commenting somewhat obscurely on the true Caesar for ten more verses, and yet the poet is almost angry with his own Caesar

> *non plura loquuto:*

*for having said no more:*

> § 326. VI. Sublimia adeo persuadent, §. 308. vt potius *extra se rapere*, et *vim ac impetum inexpugnabilem afferentia se supra omnem auditorem erigere*, quam persuadere dicantur Longino, S. I.
