> *I. Amphion Dircaeus in Actaeo Aracyntho,*

*I. Amphion of Dirce on Actaean Aracynthus,*

> Actaeumque Atticum interpretantur, non ac si Aracynthus fuerit in Attica, sed quasi simularit Virgilius pastoris ignorantiam geographicam:

and they interpret *Actaean* as Attic, not as if Aracynthus were in Attica, but as if Virgil had feigned the shepherd’s geographical ignorance:

> *II. Pars Scythiam et rapidum Cretae veniemus Oaxen,*

*II. Some of us will go to Scythia and the swift Oaxes of Crete,*

> nec constructiones de populis, terris, fluuiis, ad quos veniamus, consuetas adhibet, nec Cretae flumen adscribit, quod habeat, quoniam Oaxen hi quaerunt in Scythia, illi in Mesopotamia. Quos penes verum sit, nosse pastori licet cum ignarissimis.

nor does he employ the customary constructions concerning peoples, lands and rivers to which we come, nor is the river he assigns to Crete one that it possesses, since some seek the Oaxes in Scythia, others in Mesopotamia. With whom the truth lies, a shepherd may know as well as the most ignorant.

> [p. 234] § 373. Quam Longinus S. XXXXIIII. forsan animi sui sententiam philosophi, nescio cuius, quem loquentem ab initio fingit, ex persona prodens principem caussam indicat, cur suis temporibus sit vniuersalis adeo sublimium et magnificorum ingeniorum penuria, seruitutem, die dimidium virtutis auferentem: ea, si vel plenaria fuerit, praecordiis in libertate maiora ausuris tantum saltim relinquit magnitudinis relatiuae, quantum ad tenuia pulcre cogitanda satis est.

[p. 234] § 373. The servitude which Longinus, S. XXXXIIII, bringing forth, in the person of some philosopher, I know not whom, whom he feigns as speaking from the beginning, perhaps the opinion of his own mind, indicates as the principal cause why in his times there was so universal a dearth of sublime and magnificent wits, servitude that in a single day takes away half of virtue: this, even if it be complete, leaves to hearts that would dare greater things in liberty at least as much relative magnitude as suffices for thinking slender things beautifully.

> *Seruitus obnoxia, / Quia, quae volebat, non audebat dicere, / Affectus proprios in fabellas transtulit, / Calumniamque fictis elusit iocis.* Phaedr. l. III.

*Servitude, exposed to harm, / because it did not dare to say what it wished, / transferred its own affects into little fables, / and eluded calumny with feigned jests.* Phaedr. l. III.

> Quam apologorum genesin egregie confirmat, prima superstitum, Iothami fabula de arboribus regem quaerentibus, licet adhuc maius aliquid et sublimius applicando spirans, ac seriores mancipiorum ac libertorum fabellae aesopicae.

This genesis of apologues is excellently confirmed by the first of those that survive, Jotham’s fable of the trees seeking a king, though it still breathes something greater and more sublime in its application than the later Aesopic fables of slaves and freedmen.

> § 374. Magnitudo animi relatiue minima, vel potentialis etiam tantum, vel saltim actualis in elaborandis tenuibus nunc occupatorum est ingenium ac propensio simpliciter honestam viuendi rationem modumque cogitandi huic congruentem, et negatiue, et positiue, [p. 235] sequi aptum et cupida, §. 213, 214. obiecta non mediae solum, sed et maximae mensurae capacia simul, ex lateribus suis, absolute quidem magnis et dignis, horum tamen minoribus, contuenda sistere, §. 215. βάθους, §. 217. et primum, §. 221. et secundum genus, §. 245. tumoris, §. 217. et primum, §. 222. et secundum genus, §. 263. effugere potest, tendit et fouet.

§ 374. The relatively least magnitude of mind, whether only potential, or at least actual in those now occupied in elaborating slender things, is a wit and propensity apt and eager, both negatively and positively, [p. 235] to follow a simply honourable manner of living and a mode of thinking congruent with it, § 213, 214; it can, tends, and cherishes to present objects capable not only of a middle but also of the greatest measure, for contemplation at the same time from those of their sides which, though absolutely great and dignified, are nevertheless the lesser of these, § 215, and to escape βάθους [bathos], § 217, both its first, § 221, and its second kind, § 245, and tumidity, § 217, both its first, § 222, and its second kind, § 263.

> § 375. Eadem adeo genus cogitandi satis absolute magnum, praesertim absolute dignum, §. 223, exhibere, vile de abiectis, §. 224. vel etiam de tenuibus cogitandi genus, §. 262. cauere, quaerere genus cogitandi absolute moratum, vt latius, §. 226, ita strictius, §. 228, male moratum vtrumque vitare, §. 228, gradus etiam et intercapedines in ipsis tenuibus belle metiri, §. 233. data occasione inter βωμολοχίαν, scurrilitatem omni modo risui inhiantem, et ἀγροικίαν, feritatem omnibus naturaliter asperi, medium tenere, quod εὐτραπελίας aliquando nomine significatur, *in ludo iocisque concinne se et decenter gerentium*, et amat, et potest, §. 237.

§ 375. The same magnitude accordingly both loves and is able to exhibit a manner of thinking absolutely great enough, especially absolutely dignified, § 223; to beware of a cheap manner of thinking about abject things, § 224, or even about slender things, § 262; to seek a manner of thinking absolutely moral, in the broader sense, § 226, as in the stricter, § 228; to avoid the manner ill-moral in either sense, § 228; to measure prettily the degrees and intervals even within slender things, § 233; and, when occasion is given, to keep the mean between βωμολοχία [buffoonery], the scurrility that gapes after laughter in every way, and ἀγροικία [boorishness], the wildness of one naturally rough to all, which is sometimes signified by the name of εὐτραπελία [wittiness], *of those who bear themselves neatly and decently in play and jests*, § 237.

> § 376. Εὐτραπελίας mentionem iniicere non possum, quin veniat forsan aliquibus eius in mentem, quod Eph. V, 4. illa omnino Christianis [p. 236] prohibita censeatur. Non inquiram heic in id, an omnia per fidem sanctissimam illicita possint etiam, vt vetita, considerari per solas aesthetices regulas philosophicas: dabo modo obiter interpretationem loci, quam ego verissimam habeo: *Ne audiatur quidem inter vos turpitudo et obscenitas, nec morologia.* Si autem quaeratis, quid morologias amplectar titulo, est illa εὐτραπελία (κατὰ) τὰ οὐκ ἀνήκοντα, *omnis illa cogitandi, agendique ratio, quam vrbanitatis festiuitatisque titulis tegunt, quae vere tamen decoro, eoque Christiano, contraria est*, §. 212.

§ 376. I cannot throw in a mention of εὐτραπελία [wittiness] without its perhaps coming into some people’s minds that, by Eph. V, 4, it is judged altogether [p. 236] forbidden to Christians. I shall not inquire here into whether all things that are illicit by the most holy faith can also be considered as forbidden by the philosophical rules of aesthetics alone; I shall only give in passing an interpretation of the passage which I hold to be most true: *Let not even turpitude and obscenity be heard among you, nor morology.* But if you ask what I embrace under the title of morology, it is that εὐτραπελία (κατὰ) τὰ οὐκ ἀνήκοντα [wittiness (in) things not fitting], *all that manner of thinking and acting which they cover with the titles of urbanity and festivity, but which is truly contrary to decorum, and to Christian decorum at that*, § 212.

> § 377. Difficillimum vtique vel psychologice tantum rem considerantibus haberi debet, ita ingenium deliberato consilio versatile reddere, moresque toties amabiliter variare, semper tamen rectos et vere bellos, vt

§ 377. It must surely be held most difficult, even by those considering the matter only psychologically, so to render the wit versatile by deliberate design, and to vary one’s manners so often and so amiably, yet always right and truly fine, that

> *omnis te deceat color, et status, et res,*

*every colour, and condition, and circumstance may become you,*

> neque naufragium facias vnquam in scopulos dicacium, obscenitatem, maledicentiam, vel omnino rerum caelestium profanationem, nec dictum tuum vllum, vllum ridiculum, suasore Cicerone, vel sit nimis frequens, quia scurrae hoc est, vel subobscenum, quia est mimi, vel petulans, quia improbi hominis, nec in calamitosos, quia iuhumanum [sic: inhumanum], nec in facinorosos, quia leue id supplicium, neque quaesitum et domo allatum, quia frigidum, nec [p. 237] fere ad lacessendum, quia respondetur et ingeniosius et humanius, nec in caros vel nostros, vel multorum, quia odiosum, nec in potentes et dignitate praeditos, quia praeter debitam venerationem et obseruantiam, nec atrox et contumeliosius in quenquam, quia insanabile.

and that you never suffer shipwreck on the rocks of the sharp-tongued, obscenity, slander, or any profanation of heavenly things, and that, with Cicero as adviser, no saying of yours, no jest, be either too frequent, for that is the buffoon’s, or somewhat obscene, for that is the mime’s, or petulant, for that is the wicked man’s, nor against the unfortunate, for that is inhuman, nor against criminals, for that is too light a punishment, nor sought out and brought from home, for that is cold, nor, [p. 237] generally, made to provoke, since the reply is both wittier and more humane, nor against those dear to us or to many, for that is odious, nor against the powerful and those endowed with dignity, for that is beyond the veneration and respect that are due, nor atrocious and too insulting against anyone, for that is incurable.

> § 378. Eidem Ciceroni off. I. *facilis est distinctio ingenui (elegantis, vrbani, ingeniosi, faceti) et illiberalis ioci.* Prior *tempore fit ac remisso animo libero dignus*, eique *sicut incipiendi ratio est, ita desinendi modus.* Verum sit facilis in theoria et in abstracto, quod aiunt, facilis sit in multis, ex vna parte liberalioribus, ex altera ad infimam humilitatem et faecem vergentibus, instar plumbi, sit facilis animo sereno, quieto, lente festinanti, extraque teli iactum immo extra ipsas partes posito, velut iudex litem suam non faciens. Disparebit tamen facilitas, si iam iamque dictum dicturus, quod subito occurrens iam in primo ore habeas, citissime transitura opportunitate, concipiaris, quod honesti maleque morati

§ 378. For the same Cicero, off. I, *the distinction between a gentlemanly (elegant, urbane, witty, facetious) and an illiberal jest is easy.* The former *is made at the right time and with a relaxed mind, worthy of a free man*, and for it, *as there is a rule for beginning, so there is a measure for leaving off.* But let it be easy in theory and in the abstract, as they say; let it be easy in many cases, on the one side the more liberal, on the other those verging toward the lowest baseness and dregs, like lead; let it be easy for a mind serene, quiet, hastening slowly, placed beyond the cast of the weapon, nay outside the parties themselves, like a judge who does not make the suit his own. The ease will nevertheless vanish if, on the very point of saying a saying which, suddenly occurring, you already have on the tip of your tongue, with the opportunity about to pass most swiftly, you are seized with something which, of the honourable and the ill-moraled,

> *circa confinia ludat,*

*plays about the borders,*

> nonnihil animo commotior, et in quendam iocandi velut ἐνθουσιασμὸν delatus, S. V. vel si dictum examines alterius te vel ipsum, vel tuos petentis, vel a quo certe timeas. e. c.

your mind somewhat more agitated, and carried away into a certain ἐνθουσιασμός [enthusiasm], as it were, of jesting, S. V; or if you examine a saying of another who is attacking either you yourself, or yours, or one whom you surely fear, etc.

> [p. 238] § 379. Secundum nos iudicaturum reor, qui porro perpenderit, an exempla iocorum elegantium ab ipso Cicerone generatim dicta l. c. sint ea vere omnia. 1) *Plautus noster*, §. 262. de quo tamen denuo generatim et indefinite Horatius A. P. 270:

[p. 238] § 379. I think that he will judge in agreement with us who further weighs whether the examples of elegant jests given in general by Cicero himself, l. c., are truly all such. 1) *Our Plautus*, § 262, of whom, however, Horace again speaks generally and indefinitely, A. P. 270:

> *At vestri proaui Plautinos et numeros, et / Laudauere sales, nimium patienter vtrumque / Ne dicam stulte, mirati, si modo ego et vos / Scimus inurbanum lepido seiungere dicto.*

*But your forefathers praised both the numbers and / the witticisms of Plautus, too patiently admiring both, / not to say foolishly, if only you and I / know how to separate the boorish from a graceful saying.*

> ⁠2) *Atticorum antiqua comoedia*, cuius tamen, auctore Horatio l. c. 282. dicacitatis vitio reprimendo lege opus fuit.

⁠2) *The old comedy of the Athenians*, which however, on Horace’s authority, l. c. 282, needed a law to restrain the vice of its sharp tongue.

> *Lex est accepta, chorusque / Turpiter obticuit, sublato iure nocendi.*

*The law was accepted, and the chorus / fell shamefully silent, the right of harming being removed.*

> ⁠2) [sic: 3)] *philosophi Socratici*, quorum tamen ipse dux, ab oraculo sapientissimus mortalium declaratus effugere non potuit, quin, referente ipso Cicerone, a Zenone Stoico *scurra atticus* nominaretur. Addamus, velut argumentum ad hominem, et eorum dictum, qui Ciceronem hunc ipsum *scurram consularem* salutarunt iniuria, praeeuntem sequuti Catonem, quando ille subridens aliquando: *Quam ridiculum*, inquit de Cicerone loquens, *habemus consulem.*

⁠3) *The Socratic philosophers*, whose leader himself, declared by the oracle the wisest of mortals, could not escape being named, as Cicero himself reports, *the Attic buffoon* by Zeno the Stoic. Let us add, as an argumentum ad hominem, the saying of those too who, with injustice, saluted this same Cicero as *the consular buffoon*, following Cato, who led the way, when he once said with a smile, speaking of Cicero: *What a ridiculous consul we have.*

> [p. 239] § 380. Quorsum autem ista? §. 377-379. Vt non assentiamur solum Ciceroni, quando ille l. c. *Turpe est*, ait, *valdeque vitiosum in re seuera conuiuii dicta, aut delicatum inferre sermonem*: sed et in ipsis tenuibus et remissius suo quodam merito cogitandis εὐχαριστίαν malimus, ex sanctissimo consilio, comitatem et gratiam affabilem, non sine sale, sectari, quam aut μωρολογίας valde suspectam, aut periculis vndiqne [sic: vndique] septam εὐτραπελίαν, eo cautiores, quo certius

[p. 239] § 380. But to what end all this, § 377–379? That we may not only assent to Cicero when he says, l. c., *It is shameful, and very faulty, to bring sayings of the dinner-table, or a dainty conversation, into a serious matter*: but also that, even in slender things, and things to be thought more loosely by a certain merit of their own, we prefer, by the most holy counsel, to pursue εὐχαριστία [graciousness], affability and amiable grace, not without salt, rather than either a εὐτραπελία [wittiness] strongly suspected of μωρολογία [morology], or one hedged about on every side with dangers; the more cautious, the more certain it is that

> *Risu est inepto res ineptior nulla,* §. 376. 191.

*Nothing is more inept than an inept laugh,* § 376, 191.

> § 381. Eo promtius natio solatium inueniet, cuius forte genius aptus quidem et tenuibus cum dignitate quadam excogitandis et ipsis iocis ac dictis cum lepore iaciendis est, gracilitate tamen et subtilitate nescio qua, per quam amabili, vinci dicitur a vicinis aliquibus, quoniam ingenia pulcra soli huic characteri forsan nata plura si numeret gens quaedam in ciuibus suis, mirum non est, ea si artem, quam solam possunt assequi, colunt felicius, ac vicini, quorum et altius surgere plura grauioresque simul personas induere valent et desiderant ingenia ac praecordiorum ingentes impetus, §. 249. His enim

§ 381. The more readily will a nation find consolation whose genius perchance is indeed apt both for devising slender things with a certain dignity and for throwing out jests and sayings with grace, but is said to be surpassed by some of its neighbours in a certain slenderness and subtlety, I know not what, though a very amiable one; since, if some people counts among its citizens more beautiful wits born perhaps for this character alone, it is no wonder if they cultivate more happily the art which alone they can attain than do their neighbours, whose wits and the huge impulses of their hearts both can and desire to rise higher and to put on at once more numerous and graver persons, § 249. For these

> *facilis iactura iocorum est.*

*the loss of jests is easy.*

> [p. 240] § 382. Magnum satis ad tenuia proportionate cogitanda pectus ac ingenium, et potest, et ardet hoc magis pura a sordibus et rerum et significationis eloquutionisue sua et intaminata seruare, quo se meminit plebi vicinius, quo hinc facilius posset turbae inuolui, quam tamen non minus abhorret, ac illud sublime:

[p. 240] § 382. A heart and wit great enough for thinking slender things proportionately both can, and burns the more, to keep itself pure and unstained from the filth both of things and of signification or of elocution, the nearer it remembers itself to be to the common people, and the more easily, hence, it could be wrapped up in the crowd, from which it nevertheless shrinks no less than does that sublime one:

> *Odi profanum vulgus et arceo,* §. 243.

*I hate the profane crowd and keep it off,* § 243.

> Idem in absolute magnis vel minimus, vel nunc saltim, ac vnum ex minimis, se gerens animus, non sectatur paradoxa honestis tantum non omnibus ex simpliciori viuendi formula, sed satagit rerum suarum, si iisdem probare sua, si iisdem sine salebris ac spinis mentem euidenter declarare, si potest eosdem eius certiores reddere, quod persuadere volebat bonis, idque sine ambagibus, quas pauci capiant aequalium, §. 244.

The same mind, bearing itself in absolutely great things as either the least, or at least now as one of the least, does not pursue what is paradoxical to almost all honourable people by the simpler formula of living, but is busy with its own affairs, to prove its own to them, to declare its mind evidently to them without roughness or thorns, to make them, if it can, more certain of what it wished to persuade the good of, and that without circumlocutions which few of its contemporaries would grasp, § 244.

> § 383. Magnus in tenuibus laborans eleganter animus mauult aliquam siccitatem, quam tumidis vel inanibus emboliis lasciuire, gnarus odiosam esse circensibus pompam, §. 301, 284. exilitatem quandam, §. 249. praeferet lutulento cuiuis flumini, quale Lucilii, si

§ 383. A great mind labouring elegantly in slender things prefers some dryness to wantoning in tumid or empty insertions, knowing that pomp is odious at the circus games, § 301, 284; it will prefer a certain thinness, § 249, to any muddy river, such as Lucilius’s, if

> *in hora saepe ducentos, / Vt magnum, versus dictabat stans pede in vno.*

*often in an hour, as a great feat, / he dictated two hundred verses standing on one foot.*

> aridum autem, §. 255, exsangue, §. 258, et [p. 241] ieiunum cogitandi genus, §. 259. aeque abhorrebit, ac friuolum, §. 261. omnia denique cogitabit, volet, aget, ex veteri prudentum formula: *Vti bene inter bonos agier conuenit.*

but the arid, § 255, the bloodless, § 258, and [p. 241] the jejune manner of thinking, § 259, it will shun equally with the frivolous, § 261; finally it will think, will, and do all things by the old formula of the prudent: *As it is fitting to deal well among good men.*

> § 384. Magnitudinem animi aestheticam huc vsque saepius descriptam relatiuam ad tenuia si placeret breuius SIMPLICEM AESTHETICORVM HONESTATEM appellare: mediis rebus medioque cogitandi generi vel tantum sufficientem, vel ad hoc tamen vnice iam requisitam NOBILITATEM ANIMI AESTHETICAM dicere liceret, grauitatem et magnanimitatem materiem aliquam mediam in exaequante cogitationum et digna magnitudine venuste sistendi ob oculos, §. 189.

§ 384. If one wished to call more briefly the aesthetic magnitude of mind relative to slender things, which has hitherto been so often described, THE SIMPLE HONOURABLENESS OF AESTHETIC MATTERS, it would be permitted to call that which is either only sufficient for middle things and the middle manner of thinking, or is at least now uniquely required for them, AESTHETIC NOBILITY OF MIND, the gravity and magnanimity of setting charmingly before the eyes some middle material in an equalising and worthy magnitude of thoughts, § 189.

> § 385. In hac concipienda neutiquam excludo *nobilitatem* generis, quam alicubi *blandam* Cicero *conciliatriculam* dicit *opinioni hominum* non parum *commendantem*, eum tamen ingenii pectorisque tum naturalem habitum, tum vero statum praesentem et exsistentem cogitari volo, quem nobili loco natus amplectitur,

§ 385. In conceiving this I by no means exclude *nobility* of birth, which Cicero somewhere calls a *bland little conciliator*, not a little *commending* one *to the opinion of men*; yet I wish there to be thought that habit of wit and heart, both natural and in its present and existing state, which one born in a noble place embraces,

> *Ni coram Lepidis male viuitur, alea pernox / Ante Numantinos nisi luditur.* Iuu. Sat. VIII.

*Unless one lives badly before the Lepidi, unless the all-night dice / are played before the Numantini.* Iuu. Sat. VIII.

> [p. 242] si potius animus dignus illustri maiorum serie, *altae*

[p. 242] or if rather a mind worthy of the illustrious line of its ancestors, whose morals

> *Indicium, mores, nobilitatis habet.* Ou. Fast. III, 2.

*bear the mark of lofty nobility.* Ou. Fast. III, 2.

> aut omnino, quod adhuc maius est,

or altogether, what is yet greater,

> *nominibus quum sit generosus auitis, / Exsuperat morum nobilitate genus*, Trist. IV, 4.

*though he be well-born by ancestral names, / he surpasses his race by the nobility of his morals*, Trist. IV, 4.

> § 386. *Qui increpitus a quodam, quod in aciem claudus descenderet, pugnare non fugere,* volo, *respondens Spartanus* respondisse dicitur Valerio Maximo *nobiliter*, III. 7. ex nostra nunc notione, nec in eiusdem responso simplicem modo honestatem deprehendes, neque maiestatem e contrario singularem, sed medium quid inter vtramque, quod illud ipsum est accurate, quod nunc volumus, quod vtique iam in se magis arduum, ac magnus satis tenuibus animus, facilius a bene natis obtinetur, quando ad erectiorem cogitandi rationem politioresque viuendi mores a teneris, quod aiunt, vnguiculis, veluti manu, ducuntur, plus iam difficultatis habet, vt eo serius demum eleuentur animi, neque tamen omnino fieri nequit, si gnauiter exercearis in laudabili vere nobilium consuetudine, disciplinis ac vsu, vehementerque despicias, quicquid [p. 243] est infra locum, quo tendis, vbique nugarum, §. 191.

§ 386. *The Spartan who, being reproached by someone because he went down lame into the battle-line, answered: to fight,* I wish, *not to flee,* is said by Valerius Maximus to have answered *nobly*, III. 7; by our present notion you will find in his answer neither merely simple honourableness, nor, on the contrary, singular majesty, but something midway between the two, which is precisely that which we now wish; which, at any rate, being already in itself more arduous than a mind great enough for slender things, is more easily obtained by the well-born, when from their tender nails, as they say, they are led as if by the hand to a more upright manner of thinking and more polished manners of living, and has more difficulty for others, so that their minds are raised to it only the later, though it still cannot altogether fail to happen, if you exercise yourself diligently in the praiseworthy society of the truly noble, in disciplines and practice, and vehemently despise whatever [p. 243] is below the place to which you tend, and trifles everywhere, § 191.

> § 387. Animus ad medium in pulcre cogitandis genus satis habiturus nobilitatis, §. 383. non absolutae solum dignitatis memor est et tenacior, §. 193. quoniam amicam luto suem nobilem nemo dixerit, sed eius etiam comparatiuae, quam studia moresque verae nobilitatis postulant, §. 213, 1) negatiuam. Hinc poterit et volet omnem, etiam longa manu, mouere lapidem, ne quid ignorantiae, ne quid erroris, ne quid prauae consuetudinis et aegritudinis animorum deprehendatur in cogitandis a se venustius, quod, etiamsi bene conuenire cum simplici satis honestate possit, maiorem tamen personarum ac rerum dedeceat ordinem non sine turpitudine.

§ 387. A mind that is to have nobility enough for the middle manner in thinking beautifully, § 383, is mindful and rather tenacious not only of absolute dignity, § 193, since no one would call a sow that is a friend of the mud noble, but also of the comparative dignity which the pursuits and the manners of true nobility demand, § 213, 1) the negative. Hence it will be able and willing to move every stone, even with a long arm, lest anything of ignorance, anything of error, anything of the depraved habit and sickness of minds be detected in the things it thinks more charmingly, which, even if it could agree well enough with simple honour, would nevertheless disgrace the higher order of persons and things, not without baseness.

> § 388. *Turpe* fuit olim *nobili ius ignorare, in quo versetur*, forsan et erit iterum aliquando. Hinc Iuuenalis sibi videtur absurdi quid retulisse, dum: *Facundus*, ait *aliquis ima de plebe solet defendere caussas*

§ 388. It was once *base for a nobleman to be ignorant of the law in which he moves*, and perhaps it will be so again some day. Hence Juvenal seems to himself to have reported something absurd when he says: *some eloquent fellow from the lowest of the plebs is wont to defend the causes*

> *Nobilis indocti, veniet de plebe togata,* / *Qui iuris nodos et legum aenigmata soluat.*

*Of the unlearned nobleman; one from the gowned plebs will come* / *To untie the knots of the law and solve the riddles of the statutes.*

> Turpe fuit alicubi nobilem non militasse. [p. 244] Hinc idem Iuuenalis arbitratur, se rem absurdam acu tetigisse, quando pergit:

It was base in some places for a nobleman not to have served in war. [p. 244] Hence the same Juvenal thinks he has hit the absurd thing on the head when he continues:

> *Hic petit Euphraten iuuenis, domitique Bataui* / *Custodes aquilas, armis industrius, at tu* / *Nil, nisi Cecropides, truncoque simillimus Hermae.*

*This youth makes for the Euphrates and the eagles that guard* / *The conquered Batavians, industrious in arms; but you* / *Are nothing but a Cecropid, most like a Herm’s trunk.*

> In his turpitudinibus, et vere tales, et eae veniunt in censum, quae maiorum institutis iudicantur, §. 212.

Among these base things, and truly such, those also come into the reckoning which are judged so by the institutions of our ancestors, § 212.

> § 389. Animus ad res medias pulcre cogitandas satis nobilis dignitatem porro comparatiuam et studiis vitaeque nobilium conuenientem circumspiciet 2) positiuam, vt ea didicerit, et id quidem satis exacte, vt ea et nouerit ad finem perducere, et animo constanti decernat, quae nosse, velle, velle constanter, et agere, simplex forsan honestas non potest, aut imbecillitate sua facilius excusatur, si peccauerit, quae vero si cum decore possint exhiberi, perfectaque sistantur antea dubitantium oculis, tum vero non amplius incertum relinquunt, esse, qui talis sit, non vnum ex multis, sed eximiis ingenii, virtutis, ac animi dotibus conspicuum.

§ 389. A mind noble enough to think middling things beautifully will further look round for the comparative dignity that befits the pursuits and the life of the nobility, 2) the positive, so that it has learned those things, and that indeed exactly enough, so that it both knows how to carry them through to their end, and with a constant mind decides upon them, things which simple honour perhaps cannot know, will, will constantly and do, or is the more easily excused by its own weakness if it has gone wrong, but which, if they can be displayed with decorum and set perfected before the eyes of those who doubted before, then indeed no longer leave it uncertain that he who is of such a kind is not one of the many, but conspicuous for the exceptional gifts of his wit, his virtue and his mind.

> § 390. [p. 245] Breuitas non patitur ad hanc dignitatem pertinentia congerere, vel omnia, vel pleraque, id est omnem paene philosophiam practicam excutere, eamque mathematicam, et simul in late patentem morum in gentibus aetatibusque diuersorum prouehi oceanum, §. 212. Inadaequatam nostris finibus, aliquam tamen eius imaginem exhibent Iuuenalis consilia:

§ 390. [p. 245] Brevity does not allow us to gather together what belongs to this dignity, either all of it or most of it, that is, to go through almost the whole of practical philosophy, and of mathematics as well, and at the same time to be carried out upon the wide-spreading ocean of the manners of men differing in nations and ages, § 212. Some image of it, though inadequate to our limits, is offered by Juvenal’s counsels:

> *Esto bonus miles, tutor bonus, arbiter idem* / *Integer, ambiguae si quando citabere testis* / *Incertaeque rei, Phalaris licet imperet, vt sis* / *Falsus, et admoto dictet periuria tauro,* / *Summum crede nefas animam praeferre pudori,* / *Et propter vitam viuendi perdere caussas.* / *Prouincia quum te* / *Rectorem accipiet, pone irae fraena modumque,* / *Pone et auaritiae, miserere inopum sociorum,* / *Respice, quid moneant leges, quid curia mandet,* / *Praemia quanta bonos maneant, quam fulmine iusto* / *Et Capito et Numitor ruerint, damnante senatu.*

*Be a good soldier, a good guardian, likewise an arbiter* / *Of integrity; if ever you are called as witness in a doubtful* / *And uncertain matter, though Phalaris command you to be* / *False and, with the bull brought near, dictate perjuries,* / *Count it the highest wickedness to prefer life to honour,* / *And for the sake of living to lose the reasons for living.* / *When the province* / *Receives you as its governor, set rein and measure to anger,* / *Set them also to avarice, pity the destitute allies,* / *Look to what the laws advise, what the senate-house commands,* / *What rewards await the good, with how just a thunderbolt* / *Both Capito and Numitor fell, when the senate condemned them.*

> § 391. [p. 246] Nobilitas, de qua nunc loquimur, §. 388. aspernatur humillima quaeuis et abiecta, §. 195.

§ 391. [p. 246] The nobility of which we are now speaking, § 388, scorns whatever is lowest and abject, § 195.

> *An, quae* / *Turpia cerdoni, Volesos Brutumque decebunt?*

*Or will what* / *Is base in a cobbler become the Volesi and Brutus?*

> Sed et illa, quae simplici forsan honestati non repugnant, ex abstracta philosophorum formula, detrahunt tamen ex opinione moribusque hominum, quorum iudiciis stare, vel nobilis, existimatio debeat, aliquid illius dignitatis, dum media est, non minimae, §. 212. quam ferre in oculis, et a qua ne latum quidem vnguem recedere, secum constituit cogitando decernendoque, quem nunc animo formamus, aestheticus medias res venuste picturus. Quam durus censor est poeta?

But even those things which perhaps do not conflict with simple honour, on the abstract formula of the philosophers, nevertheless take away, in the opinion and manners of men, by whose judgements even a nobleman’s reputation must stand, something of that dignity which, while it is middling, is not the least, § 212; and the aesthetician whom we are now forming in our mind, who is to paint middling things charmingly, resolves with himself, in thinking and deciding, to keep that dignity before his eyes and not to depart from it by the breadth of a nail. How harsh a censor is the poet?

> *Laureolum velox, etiam bene, Lentulus egit,* / *Iudice me, dignus vera cruce.*

*Lentulus played Laureolus nimbly, even well,* / *And deserves, in my judgement, a real cross.*

> § 392. Animus eleganter nobilis in talibus etiam materiis, quae tenuiter possent, possent sublimius cogitari, singulare quaeret artificium declarare, non meditatus solum, quae proferat, sed et quae omittat, quando catus et harum rerum peritus spectator ipse sibi tradet multa, nunc ob tenuitatem, nunc ob sublimitatem, quae non exhibita deprehendet, deprehendet nihilominus auctori venisse in mentem, [p. 247] sed eum non remisisse vires, et simul iisdem belle pepercisse, §. 215.

§ 392. A mind elegantly noble will, even in such materials as could be thought slenderly or could be thought more sublimely, seek a singular artifice in order to declare that it has meditated not only what it brings forward, but also what it leaves out, since the shrewd spectator, experienced in these things, will himself supply to himself many things, now on account of their thinness, now on account of their sublimity, which he will find not exhibited, but will nonetheless find to have come into the author’s mind, [p. 247] and that he did not slacken his powers, and at the same time nicely spared them, § 215.

> § 393. Nobilitas animi, quam nunc volumus, βάθους, §. 317. praesertim genus tertium, §. 276. tertium tumoris §. 217. genus sibi cauendum putat, §. 279. sequitur potius bene moratam cogitandi rationem, quatenus et relatiue non omne solum decorum, sed et eius gradum in nobiliore hominum consuetudine paene sola regnantem obseruat, §. 228. praestabit aliquam quidem remissionem cogitationum eleuationemque, praesertim in opere longiori, §. 273, sed vti latius aequabilem semper, §. 268, ita et plerumque simul strictius talem, §. 267, praeferet aliquam mediocritatem, §. 269. mediis etiam strictius attemperatam, §. 270, 271. et pro thematibus electaque semel ea significandi formula, nunc altiorem, nunc minns [sic: minus], §. 272. spectatori nobilitatem cogitantis animis aequalem circiter afferenti facilem ac suauem, §. 274. non abiectis solum de media re cogitandi rationibus, §. 278, sed etiam fluctuantibus et incertis, §. 280.

§ 393. The nobility of mind which we now want thinks that it must guard against βάθους [bathos], § 317, especially its third kind, § 276, and against the third kind of tumidity, § 217, § 279; it rather follows the moral manner of thinking, inasmuch as it observes, even relatively, not only every kind of decorum, but also that degree of it which reigns almost alone in the society of the nobler sort of men, § 228; it will indeed afford some relaxation and elevation of its thoughts, especially in a longer work, § 273, but as it is always even-tenored in the broader sense, § 268, so for the most part it is at the same time such in the stricter sense, § 267; it will prefer a certain mediocrity, § 269, tempered to middling things even in the stricter sense, § 270, 271, and, according to the themes and the formula of signifying once chosen, now higher, now lower, § 272, bringing to a spectator of a nobility roughly equal to that of the mind that thinks something easy and sweet, § 274, not only with abject ways of thinking about a middling matter, § 278, but also with fluctuating and uncertain ones, § 280.

[p. 248]

#### Sectio XXVI. Magnanimitas in Aestheticis Genere Maxima. — Section XXVI. Magnanimity in Aesthetic Matters, the Greatest in Kind

> § 394. Restat MAGNANIMITAS AESTHETICA PER EMINENTIAM SIC DICTA, superius ingenium optimis genere maximisque cultum, et immortalitati natum, viuensque mortali iam in corpore pectus generice maximis sua pro maiestate cogitandis et par, et inuigilans, omni opera, quod

§ 394. There remains AESTHETIC MAGNANIMITY SO CALLED PAR EXCELLENCE, a superior wit cultivated by the best things and the greatest in kind, born for immortality, and a breast, while it still lives in a mortal body, both equal to thinking the things greatest in kind in accordance with their majesty, and watchful, with every effort, that

> Hinc saepe *insuetum miratur limen Olympi,* / *Sub pedibusque videt nubes* §. 318. *et sidera.* / Saepe *deum vitam,* S. V. §. 206. *accipiet, diuisque videbit* / *Permistos heroas,* idemque *videbitur illis.*

Hence it often *marvels at the unaccustomed threshold of Olympus,* / *And sees beneath its feet the clouds*, § 318, *and the stars.* / Often *the life of the gods*, S. V. § 206, *it will receive, and will see* / *Heroes mingled with the gods*, and likewise *will be seen by them.*

> § 395. *Vrit* idem *fulgore suo, quas praegrauat, artes* / *Infra se positas*

§ 395. The same *burns with its own brilliance the arts which it outweighs,* / *Set beneath itself,*

> non eas nugatorias solum, §. 191.

not those trifling ones only, § 191,

> Fastidioso *quas pede proruit,*

*which* it fastidiously *overthrows with its foot,*

> sed etiam magnos satis tenuibus, immo mediis, animorum habitus, qui comparati cum [p. 249] hac magnanimitate suis non raro titulis excidere videntur, quos optimo tamen iure habent extra metum comparationis constituti. Cum dignitate quadam aesthetica, §. 193. quae cogitaueris, sunt illa quidem omnia σεμνῶς cogitata, comparate vero Plinius II. ep. 11. *Respondit*, inquit, *Corn. Tacitus eloquentissimus, et, quod eximium eius orationi inest,* σεμνῶς, quasi sublimem Taciti grauitatem non attingentes σεμνῶς respondere non potuissent.

but also those habits of mind great enough for slender, nay for middling things, which, compared with [p. 249] this magnanimity, not rarely seem to fall from their titles, which they nevertheless hold by the best right when set outside fear of comparison. The things you have thought with a certain aesthetic dignity, § 193, are all of them indeed thought σεμνῶς [gravely]; but comparatively, Pliny II, ep. 11: *Cornelius Tacitus*, he says, *replied most eloquently, and, what is exceptional in his oratory,* σεμνῶς, as if those who do not attain the sublime gravity of Tacitus could not have replied σεμνῶς.

> § 396. A vilibus et abiectis non auocat §. 195. haec modo

§ 396. It does not call away from the vile and the abject, § 195, only this

> *Virtus, recludens immeritis mori* / *Caelum, negata tentat iter via,* / *Coetusque vulgares et vdam* / *Spernit humum fugiente penna:*

*Virtue, opening heaven to those who deserve* / *Not to die, essays its way by a path denied,* / *And the vulgar throngs and the damp* / *Ground it spurns on fleeing wing:*

> sed nec contenta quidem est absoluta magnitudine ac dignitate rerum et cogitationum, §. 198, 201. altius *pauperum* aliquando *parentum sanguinem*

but it is not even content with the absolute magnitude and dignity of things and thoughts, § 198, 201; higher, sometimes, it *snatches the blood of poor parents*

> *Non vsitata nec tenui* rapit / *Penna,*

*On a wing not customary nor slender,*

> vt *nec in terris* quidem *longius moretur*, et ipsas *vrbes relinquat, inuidiaque maior per liquidum aethera* sursum *feratur.*

so that *it does not linger longer on earth*, and *leaves the very cities, and, greater than envy, is borne upward through the liquid ether.*

> § 397. [p. 250] Magnanimitas haec aestheticarum generice maxima virtutem directo sibi sumit in omni sua maiestate pingendam.

§ 397. [p. 250] This magnanimity, the greatest in kind among aesthetic magnanimities, directly takes upon itself the painting of virtue in all its majesty.

> *Virtus, repulsae nescia sordidae,* / *Intaminatis fulget honoribus.* / *Nec sumit aut ponit secures* / *Arbitrio popularis aurae.* Hor. III. od. 2.

*Virtue, knowing nothing of sordid rebuff,* / *Shines with unstained honours.* / *Nor does it take up or lay down the axes* / *At the whim of the popular breeze.* Hor. III. od. 2.

> cf. od. 3. Per indirectum eiusdem est animorum magnitudinis vitia publica, velut epidemicas aliquas pestes, abominari, §. 203.

cf. od. 3. It belongs indirectly to the same magnitude of mind to abominate public vices, like so many epidemic plagues, § 203.

> *Foecunda culpae saecula nuptias* / *Primum inquinauere, et genus, et domos.* / *Hoc fonte deriuata clades* / *Inque patres populumque fluxit.* e. c. od. 6.

*Ages fruitful in guilt first defiled* / *Marriage, and the race, and the homes.* / *From this source the disaster flowed* / *Into the fathers and the people.* etc. od. 6.

> cf. II. od. 15, 18. III. 1, 24. Epod. 7. §. 204.

cf. II. od. 15, 18. III. 1, 24. Epod. 7. § 204.

> § 398. Animorum excellenter magnorum ingenium superius non admittit, vt practici pragmaticique sint cum neglectu theoriae, quam tunc etiam amant et amplectuntur, quando in maximarum naturaliter rerum contemplatione sic haerere fixa videtur, vt subito non appareat, quid eiusmodi consideratio faciat ad [p. 251] mores et vitam beatam. §. 205. Ita in homine verioribus sacris non imbuto non, nisi magnus eminenter, animus haec effatur:

§ 398. The superior wit of minds that are excellently great does not permit them to be practical and pragmatic with neglect of theory, which they love and embrace even then, when in the contemplation of things naturally greatest it seems to cling so fixedly that it does not at once appear what such a consideration contributes to [p. 251] morals and the blessed life. § 205. Thus in a man not imbued with the truer sacred rites none but an eminently great mind utters these words:

> *Nil maius generatur ipso (Parente)* / *Nec viget quicquam simile aut secundum,* / *Proximos illi tamen occupauit* / *Pallas honores,* e. c. Hor. I. od. 12.

*Nothing greater is begotten than he himself (the Father)* / *Nor does anything flourish like him or second to him;* / *Yet the honours next to him* / *Pallas has taken,* etc. Hor. I. od. 12.

> § 399. In rebus magnitudine naturali conspicuis, generice maximis, specifice etiam maximorum mentionem in exemplis inieci, diuinorum, ne forsan animos generice maximos sibi formaturus animo Polyphemos aliquos Enceladosue vel contemtores deorum Mezentios secum fabricetur, non eos vere magnos animorum, sed tumide superbos. Prima potius dignitatis positiuae per sublimia lex est: humana quaecunque, vel specifice maxima, diuinis subiicito, §. 206.

§ 399. In matters conspicuous for natural magnitude, the greatest in kind, I have also thrown into the examples mention of the things specifically greatest, divine things, lest perhaps one who is to form for himself minds greatest in kind should fabricate in his mind some Polyphemuses or Enceladuses, or Mezentiuses, despisers of the gods, who are not truly great of mind, but tumidly proud. The first law of positive dignity through sublime things is rather this: subject all human things, even the specifically greatest, to the divine, § 206.

> *Regum timendorum in proprios greges,* / *Reges in ipsos imperium est Iouis,* / *Clari giganteo triumpho,* / *Cuncta supercilio mouentis.*

*Over kings to be feared by their own flocks,* / *Over the kings themselves is the empire of Jove,* / *Famed for his triumph over the giants,* / *Moving all things with his brow.*

> § 400. Ex qua formula σεμνῶς Horatius I. od. 12.

§ 400. From which formula Horace, σεμνῶς [gravely], I. od. 12:

> *Gentis humanae pater atque custos,* / *tu secundo* / *Caesare regnes* / [p. 252] *Te minor latum reget aequus orbem,* / *Tu graui curru quaties olympum,* / *Tu parum castis inimica mittes* / *Fulmina lucis.*

*Father and guardian of the human race,* / *may you reign with Caesar* / *second to you;* / [p. 252] *Less than you, he will rule the wide world justly,* / *You with heavy chariot will shake Olympus,* / *You will send upon the groves that are not pure* / *Your hostile thunderbolts.*

> Idem de Romano populo, quo maius aliquid in humanis Romanus ignorabat. III. od. 6.

The same of the Roman people, than which the Roman knew nothing greater among human things. III. od. 6.

> *Diis te minorem quod geris, imperas.* / *Hinc omne principium, huc refer exitum.* / *Dii multa neglecti dedere* / *Hesperiae mala luctuosae.*

*Because you bear yourself as less than the gods, you rule.* / *From here take every beginning, to here refer the end.* / *The gods neglected have given many* / *Woes to mournful Hesperia.*

> Dum autem oda 5.

But when in ode 5

> *Caelo*, ait, *tonantem credidimus Iouem* / *Regnare: praesens Diuus habebitur* / *Augustus.*

*We have believed*, he says, *that Jove thundering in heaven* / *Reigns: Augustus will be held* / *A present god,*

> iam seruitutis, vel iustissimae, saltim acceptissimae, videtur expertus effectum, de quo §. 373, quoque secundum philosophum, quem Longinus citat, nihil euadimus, nisi adulatores μεγαλοφυεῖς.

he seems already to have felt the effect of servitude, be it the most just or at least the most acceptable, of which § 373; and also, according to the philosopher whom Longinus cites, we turn out nothing but flatterers μεγαλοφυεῖς [of great nature].

> § 401. Magnanimitas, cuius sublimia Longinus Echo dicit, et de qua nunc loquimur, non omnino quidem transcendit horizontem aestheticum, neque res ita sibi tantum concipit, vti pura philosophiae scientia, maximis tamen generice inter obseruabilia quia potissimum et paene solis inhaeret, versatur in iis [p. 253] materiis, quae sunt horizonti rationis logico aestheticoque communes, et hinc, ac simul aliis ex caussis, plus rationis admixtum habet eiusdem analogo, plus distinctionis etiam mathematicae, proptereaque gradus in ipsis generice maximis, vt ita dicam, specificos metitur obseruatque curatius, ac magni, de quibus S. XXV. animi. §. 207. Principum est et regum vere magnorum, ingenti cum facilitate, suum tamen in omni consuetudine cuique tribuere, vel in iis, quae minora videantur, et gradus honorum dignitatumque potiorum, vel infra, vel iuxta se positarum apprime tenere, et secundum hanc veluti scalam cuiuis reddere personae conuenientia.

§ 401. Magnanimity, whose sublime things Longinus calls its Echo, and of which we are now speaking, does not indeed wholly transcend the aesthetic horizon, nor does it conceive things only for itself in the way the pure science of philosophy does; yet because it cleaves chiefly and almost solely to the things greatest in kind among observables, it is occupied with those [p. 253] materials which are common to the logical and the aesthetic horizon of reason, and hence, and at the same time for other reasons, it has more of reason mixed with its analogue, more also of mathematical distinctness, and therefore measures and observes more carefully the degrees, so to speak specific, within the things themselves greatest in kind, than the great minds of which S. XXV. § 207. It belongs to princes and kings who are truly great to give, with immense ease, yet to each his own in all their intercourse, even in things that seem smaller, and to hold firmly the degrees of the higher honours and dignities, whether placed below or beside themselves, and according to this ladder, as it were, to render to every person what befits him.

> § 402. Hinc ne nobili quidem cogitandi viuendique generi sufficiens animus non solum ad hanc concipiendam magnanimitatem inhabilis est, sed etiam illi falluntur, qui in his generice maximis specifice sibi maxima semper legentes transuolant in his minora ac media, quibus fatentur se pulcre cogitandis impares esse, grandium interim maxima belle se posse describere secum oppido certi sunt, §. 209. Vires sunt potius praetentandae in grandibus, quorum alia in occasione neglectus ipse adhuc sublimior erit, in grandibus, quibus adhuc satis multum pompae, cerimoniarum, aurique et ostri regalis extrinsecus accedit, [p. 254] vt tandem vel nudam maiestatem, maiestatem, inquam, herois vnam ex maximis, vel puriora sacra, dum intra mentem peraguntur vnice, sublimius effingere sufficias. *Illa vero deridenda arrogantia est in minoribus nauigiis rudem esse se confiteri, quinqueremes vero, aut etiam maiores, gubernare didicisse.* Cic. de Or. I.

§ 402. Hence a mind not even sufficient for the noble manner of thinking and living is not only unfit for conceiving this magnanimity, but those also are deceived who, always choosing for themselves the specifically greatest among these things greatest in kind, fly over the smaller and middling things among them, which they confess themselves unequal to thinking beautifully, while they are quite certain with themselves that they can nicely describe the greatest of grand things, § 209. One’s powers are rather to be tried first in grand things of which on another occasion the very neglect will be still more sublime, in grand things to which a good deal of pomp, of ceremonies, of gold and of royal purple still accrues from without, [p. 254] so that at length you may suffice to fashion more sublimely either naked majesty, majesty, I say, of a hero, one of the greatest things, or the purer sacred rites, while they are performed solely within the mind. *That, however, is a laughable arrogance, to confess oneself unskilled in smaller vessels, but to have learned to steer quinqueremes or even larger ships.* Cic. de Or. I.

> § 403. Quanquam satis magnus sublimibus animus non est sapiens ille stoicus, quem,

§ 403. Although a mind great enough for sublime things is not that Stoic sage whom,

> *Si fractus illabatur orbis,* / *Impauidum feriant ruinae,* §. 353.

*If the world were shattered and fell in,* / *The ruins would strike undismayed,* § 353,

> non leuioribus tamen ille curis afficitur, nec ex tranquilla superum vitam imitante serenitate deturbatur. Minima non curat admodum, neque mouetur vehementius, si qua Parnassi reptilia, censores vitio creati, leuiculam in eius amictu maculam, non quod pueri in faba, reperisse se gloriantur, audaci potius impetu suum putat, in vera regularum collisione, dum fortissimas et Pygmeis ne cognitas quidem leges eleuatiori strenue sequitur orbita, ita rationes suas subducere, vt leuioribus animulis artis suae pusillae, quam vnice norunt, sanctissimas, si diis placet, regulas; vere minores et debiliores, spernere, pessundare, proculcare videatur, non sine [p. 255] pulcellorum ardelionum lacrimula, vere tamen exceptione non ineleganti. §. 210.

yet it is not affected by lighter cares, nor is it thrown out of a tranquil serenity that imitates the life of the gods above. It does not much care about the smallest things, nor is it moved more vehemently if some reptiles of Parnassus, censors irregularly elected, boast of having found a trifling stain on its garment, not what boys find in a bean; rather it thinks, in a true collision of rules, with a bold impulse, while it strenuously follows in a loftier orbit the strongest laws, not even known to the Pygmies, so to settle its accounts that to the lighter little souls of their own petty art, which alone they know, it may seem to spurn, to overthrow, to trample underfoot the most sacred rules, if it please the gods, really the lesser and weaker ones, not without [p. 255] a little tear from the pretty busybodies, yet truly with a not inelegant exception. § 210.

> § 404. Grauitatem absolutam aestheticam in animis nobilibus collocauimus §. 363., vti Cicero ipsum *moderatorem* ingeniorum ad magna nitentium describit, *non vt quendam magistrum atque artificem, sed quasi vnum e togatorum numero atque ex forensi vsu, hominem mediocrem, nec omnino rudem.* Quod si vero nobilis eiusmodi animus actu velit ad grandia cogitanda accedere, quasi suimet ipsius et ordinarii sui status oblitus, excitandus est, et velut extra se rapiendus in maius theatrum, quam in quo quotidie personam agit, et ita diuis heroibusque miscendus, vt excelsam aliquam cum iisdem familiaritatem contraxisse, nec tanquam in alienum orbem delatus, sed in eiusmodi consortio dudum habitans appareat, §. 213, 396.

§ 404. We have placed absolute aesthetic gravity in noble minds, § 363, as Cicero himself describes the *moderator* of wits that strive for great things, *not as some master and craftsman, but as one of the number of the gowned, and out of forensic practice, a man of middling kind and not wholly unskilled.* But if a noble mind of this kind wishes in act to approach the thinking of grand things, it must, as if forgetful of itself and of its ordinary state, be roused and as it were snatched out of itself into a greater theatre than that in which it daily plays its part, and so mingled with gods and heroes that it appears to have contracted some lofty familiarity with them, and not as if carried off into an alien world, but as long dwelling in such company, § 213, 396.

> *Auditis? an me ludit amabilis* / *Insania? audire et videor pios* / *Errare per lucos, amoenae* / *Quos et aquae subeunt et aurae.* Hor. III. od. 4.

*Do you hear? or does an amiable* / *Madness mock me? I seem to hear and to wander* / *Through holy groves, which pleasant* / *Waters and breezes enter.* Hor. III. od. 4.

> § 405. Quam nunc quaerimus, magnanimitas non magna solum themata, sed ex ea etiam [p. 256] parte considerare gestit, qua maiora et grandia apparent. §. 215. Memento Didonis 1) in eleganti illo epigrammate Ausonii:

§ 405. The magnanimity we are now seeking longs to consider not only great themes, but also from that [p. 256] side from which they appear greater and grand. § 215. Remember Dido 1) in that elegant epigram of Ausonius:

> *Infelix Dido, nulli bene iuncta marito!* / *Hoc pereunte fugit, hoc fugiente perit.*

*Unhappy Dido, to no husband well joined!* / *When this one perishes she flees, when that one flees she perishes.*

> ⁠2) quam Ouidius her. ep. VII. pingit hoc epitaphio:

⁠2) whom Ovid, her. ep. VII, paints with this epitaph:

> *Praebuit Aeneas et caussam mortis et ensem,* / *Ipsa sua Dido conciuit vsa manu.*

*Aeneas furnished both the cause of death and the sword;* / *Dido herself fell by the use of her own hand.*

> ⁠3) illam Virgilii sic ipsam sibi parentantem ad rogum Iliacis vestibus et noto cubili exstructum: IV. Aen. 651.

⁠3) that Dido of Virgil, thus performing her own funeral rites at a pyre built of Trojan garments and the familiar bed: IV. Aen. 651.

> *Dulces exuuiae, dum fata deusque sinebant,* / *Accipite hanc animam, meque his exsoluite curis.* / *Vixi, et, quem dederat cursum fortuna, peregi,* / *Et nunc magna mei sub terras ibit imago,* / *Vrbem praeclaram statui, mea moenia vidi.* / *Vlta virum poenas inimico a fratre recepi,* / *Felix, heu! nimium felix, si littora tantum* / *Nunquam Dardaniae tetigissent nostra carinae.*

*Sweet relics, while the fates and the god allowed,* / *Receive this soul, and release me from these cares.* / *I have lived, and the course which fortune gave I have finished,* / *And now a great image of me will go beneath the earth.* / *I founded a famous city, I saw my own walls,* / *Avenging my husband I exacted punishment from a hostile brother,* / *Happy, alas! too happy, if only the Dardanian* / *Keels had never touched our shores.*

> § 406. Quam Didonem malit magnanimitas heroica fictam a se? Equidem nihil haesitans [p. 257] Didonem Virgilii nomino. Rationem quaeris? Metire praedicata. Primum et in Cigarorum aliquam quadrare potest mulierculam, quae primo marito ob crimen in furcam acto fuga sibi consuluit, quum autem cum altero marito furfuris eiusdem atrox denuo crimen patrasset, hoc manibus lictorum elapso, communis sceleris poenas morte dedit. Secundum conueniet et vxori cuiusuis militis gregarii, qui fustibus eam in talem fortunae coniugalis desperationem compulerit, vt, hoc absente, eius gladio sibi iugulum soluerit. Apud Virgilium autem non solum excellenter magna est, de qua sermo est, sed ea etiam, quae de eadem praedicantur. §. 405.

§ 406. Which Dido would heroic magnanimity prefer to have feigned by itself? For my part, without any hesitation, [p. 257] I name Virgil’s Dido. You ask the reason? Measure the predicates. The first can fit even some little woman of the Gypsies, who, when her first husband had been sent to the gallows for a crime, saved herself by flight, but when with her second husband, of the same bran, she had again committed an atrocious crime, and he had slipped out of the hands of the lictors, paid with her death the penalty of their common crime. The second will suit also the wife of any common soldier, who with cudgels has driven her into such despair of her conjugal fortune that, in his absence, she cut her throat with his sword. In Virgil, however, not only is she of whom we speak excellently great, but so also are the things that are predicated of her. § 405.

> § 407. Nostra nunc magnanimitas omni opera cauebit et βάθους genus quartum et omnes eius species pro gradu turpitudinis, §. 310. Dii Virgilii iam θεοπρεπωτέρως loquuntur, agunt, patiuntur, ac Dii Homeri. §. 311. Virago Virgilii de rebus ad se pertinentibus commentatur augustius, §. 408. quam Dido Ouidii:

§ 407. Our magnanimity will now with every effort guard against both the fourth kind of βάθους [bathos] and all its species, according to the degree of their baseness, § 310. The gods of Virgil already speak, act and suffer θεοπρεπωτέρως [more befittingly for gods] than the gods of Homer. § 311. Virgil’s heroine comments more augustly on the things that concern her, § 408, than Ovid’s Dido:

> *Durat in extremum, vitaeque nouissima nostrae,* / *Prosequitur fati, qui fuit ante, tenor.*

*It endures to the last, and the tenor of my fate which was before* / *Follows the final moments of our life.*

> En! querulam de perpetua calamitate mulierem ordinariam! Virgilii Dido se felicem, [p. 258] excepta nouissima calamitate, fortior praedicat.

Behold! an ordinary woman complaining of perpetual calamity! Virgil’s Dido, stronger, proclaims herself happy, [p. 258] except for the last calamity.

> *Occidit internas coniux mactatus ad aras,* / *Et sceleris tanti praemia frater habet.*

*My husband fell, slaughtered at the household altars,* / *And my brother holds the rewards of so great a crime.*

> Haec queritur multis virum inultum et sicarium impunem immo praemia habentem; illa breuibus sibi viri vltionem fratrisque poenas gratulatur. Prius est cuiusuis foeminae.

The one complains at length of her husband unavenged and his assassin unpunished, indeed holding rewards; the other in a few words congratulates herself on the avenging of her husband and the punishment of her brother. The first is any woman’s.

> *Exsul agor, cineresque viri patriamque relinquo,* / *Et feror in duras hoste sequente vias.* / *Applicor ignotis, fratrique elapsa fretoque,* / *Quod tibi donaui, perfide, littus emo.*

*An exile I am driven, I leave my husband’s ashes and my fatherland,* / *And am carried over hard roads with the enemy following.* / *I land among strangers, escaped from my brother and the sea,* / *And buy the shore which, faithless one, I gave to you.*

> Quid hactenus legimus in Ouidio, quod non cuiuis praefecti cuiuscunque militaris euenire possit coniugi? §. 312.

What have we read so far in Ovid that could not happen to the wife of any military prefect whatever? § 312.

> § 408. Habeat grauitas nationis germanicae per omnes gradus magnorum cum decore decurrens, quae regerat suam gracilitatem vltra modum efferentibus vicinis. Fuit inter eos, quo dicam homuncionem nomine? qui cruciatus hominis optimi maximi genus humanum infinitis malis eximentes ludicris illis nouorum gelasimorum versiculis proscinderet, et Christianus tamen in regno Christianismi videri vellet. Centum ciuibus ipsa Iustitia veniam potius daret in tenuibus peccandi [p. 259] grauiter, quam huic vni in vna re, profecto, grauissima vile cogitandi genus leuissime adhibenti. §. 317.

§ 408. Let the gravity of the German nation, running with decorum through all the degrees of great things, have something with which to rebut its neighbours who exalt their own slenderness beyond measure. There was among them one — by what name shall I call the manikin? — who would lacerate with those playful little verses of the new jesters the torments of the best and greatest of men, which deliver the human race from infinite evils, and yet wished to be seen as a Christian in the kingdom of Christendom. Justice herself would sooner grant pardon to a hundred citizens for sinning grievously [p. 259] in slender matters than to this one man for applying, in one matter, indeed the gravest, a vile manner of thinking most lightly. § 317.

> § 409. Grandis illa magnanimitas, vnde sublimia vere sperari possunt, ita auersa est ab omni tumore, quarto eius genere, et huius speciebus, §. 318. vti, si esset alterutrum necessarium, in manifestum prius βάθος delabi, quam crypticis puerilium humilitatibus intricari mallet. Hinc illius in optimis auctoribus adhuc minus rara sunt exempla, ac harum ineptiarum, quibus Martianus Capella, Tertullianus, Sedulius, et his aequales, affatim turgent. Procul hinc magnidica mendacia, et quicquid est insulsae magniloquentiae!

§ 409. That grand magnanimity, from which sublime things can truly be hoped for, is so averse to all tumidity, its fourth kind, and the species of this, § 318, that, if either were necessary, it would rather fall into manifest βάθος [bathos] than be entangled in the cryptic lowlinesses of childish things. Hence examples of the former are still less rare in the best authors than of these ineptitudes, with which Martianus Capella, Tertullian, Sedulius, and their equals, abundantly swell. Far from here be big-talking lies, and whatever there is of insipid magniloquence!

> § 410. Animus in aestheticis generice maximus imitationem grandium ab Horatio, Cicerone, Longino, ab ipsa ratione per doctrinam de exspectatione casuum similium psychologicam, ita habet sibi commendatam, vt non *exemplaria* solum sublimium scriptorum, pictorum e. c.

§ 410. A mind greatest in kind in aesthetic matters has the imitation of grand things so commended to it by Horace, Cicero, Longinus, by reason itself through the psychological doctrine of the expectation of similar cases, that it rejoices not only to turn the *exemplars* of sublime writers, painters, etc.

> *Nocturna versare manu, versare diurna,*

*With nightly hand, to turn them with daily hand,*

> sed et illustrium per omnes aetates virorum facta dictaque, velut in speculum, intueri, moresque tum suos ipse, quantum licet, tum a se cogitando exprimendos ad horum similitudinem [p. 260] componere gaudeat. §. 285. Nec haerebit in solis clarioribus, eruere maiora quaeuis e tenebris, ab obliuionis iniuria vindicare, et, in ipso hoste si sint, laudare, pro caussae meritis, non erubescit. §. 286.

but also to look upon the deeds and sayings of illustrious men through all ages as into a mirror, and to compose both its own manners, as far as it may, and those which it is to express in its thinking, after the likeness of [p. 260] these. § 285. Nor will it stick only to the more famous: it does not blush to dig out any greater things from the darkness, to vindicate them from the injury of oblivion, and, even if they are found in the enemy himself, to praise them according to the merits of the cause. § 286.

> § 411. Animus in dicto saepe gradu magnus, non suspicax est et incredulus, si quid egregii et eminentis audire sibi, vel omnino videre videtur, et, quanquam aera lupinis distinguere dudum didicit, suo tamen experimento nouit, non ardua quaeuis et singulari ex virtute tantum fluentia, iam eo ipso numeranda esse, propter dedecus nostri generis, in absolute incredibilibus, §. 286. 301. Sicut eundem paruae quaedam occasiones parum mouent dignum cedris ad impetum, S. V. ita peculiarem aliis fortius incitationem aliquando sentit, quoniam, et ipsius iudicio,

§ 411. A mind great in the degree often mentioned is not suspicious and incredulous if it seems to itself to hear, or indeed to see, something outstanding and eminent, and, although it has long since learned to distinguish bronze from lupins, it nevertheless knows from its own experiment that not every arduous thing flowing only from singular virtue is by that very fact to be counted, on account of the disgrace of our race, among absolutely incredible things, § 286, 301. Just as certain small occasions move it, worthy of cedars, little to an impetus, S. V, so it sometimes feels, more strongly than others, a peculiar incitement, since, even in its own judgement,

> *Paullum sepultae distat inertiae* / *Celata virtus,*

*Hidden virtue differs little* / *From buried inertia,*

> si quando *dicenda Musis praelia*, si heroicum amorem patriae, si praeclaram detegit in multis vitae morumque sanctimoniam, ac illi tamen

if ever it detects *battles that should be told by the Muses*, if a heroic love of country, if an outstanding sanctity of life and manners in many, and yet those

> *omnes illacrimabiles* / *Vrgentur ignotique longa* / *Nocte, carent quia vate sacro.*

*all unwept* / *And unknown are pressed down by a long* / *Night, because they lack a sacred bard,*

> aut *liuidis obliuionibus* non ita multo post [p. 261] *carpendi* videntur, si et ipse *sileat eosdem inornatos.* Hor. IV. od. 9.

or seem not long afterwards to be *plucked* at [p. 261] by *envious oblivions*, if it too should *be silent about them, leaving them unadorned.* Hor. IV. od. 9.

> § 412. Magnanimitatis huius vtique natura bene natorum πρῶτον καὶ ἀρχέτυπον στοιχεῖον ἐπὶ πάντων ἐστί, vti Longinus S. II. liberaliter concedit, non ea solum, quae in ingeniis diuinis et praecordiis ad heroica sola paene natis, sed oppido paucis, est αὐτόνομος, sed et illa natura, nobilium animorum, §. 404. quae non ordinariis suis quidem viribus, viuis iis tamen et bona per consilia directis in altius quid atque sublimius, per exempla grandia validius incitatis, eo potest et decernit assurgere. S. II.

§ 412. The nature of the well-born is assuredly πρῶτον καὶ ἀρχέτυπον στοιχεῖον ἐπὶ πάντων ἐστί [the first and archetypal element over all things] of this magnanimity, as Longinus, S. II, liberally concedes; not that nature only which in divine wits and in hearts born almost solely for heroic things, but in very few, is αὐτόνομος [a law unto itself], but also that nature of noble minds, § 404, which, not indeed by its ordinary powers, but by those powers living and directed by good counsels toward something higher and more sublime, and more strongly incited by grand examples, can and resolves to rise to that height. S. II.

> § 413. Neque vero solam naturam, quatenus connascitur, heic certe, paginam vtramque facere, vel hinc efficere mihi posse videor, quod experientia confirmat, optimas maximas, aut saltim bonas excellenter naturas, §. 412. barbarie saeculorum ac aetatis suae, prauis exemplis, praeconceptis magnatum opinionibus, seruitute, vti apud Longinum est. S. XLIV. quasi *quadam animi arcula et publico carcere* posse deprimi, constringi, imminui, §. 359, *quemadmodum arculae, (si vera sit fama) in quibus nani, vocati Pygmaei, nutriuntur, non solum impediunt incrementa* [p. 262] *inclusorum, sed etiam contrahunt eos circumposito corporis vinculo.* §. 359.

§ 413. Nor indeed do I think that nature alone, so far as it is inborn, here at least, makes up both sides of the page, or that I can from this bring about what experience confirms: that the best and greatest natures, or at least excellently good ones, § 412, can be depressed, constricted and diminished by the barbarism of the ages and of their own time, by depraved examples, by the preconceived opinions of the great, by servitude, as it is in Longinus, S. XLIV, as if by *a certain little casket for the mind and a public prison*, § 359, *just as the little caskets (if the report be true) in which dwarfs, called Pygmies, are reared, not only hinder the growth* [p. 262] *of those shut in, but also contract them by the bond of the body set round them.* § 359.

> § 414. Si qua libertatis externae fraena, si qua seruitus externa deprimendis animis retundendisque maximis quibusuis et studiis et incitationibus apprime facta sunt, quod nullus nego: nec extra oleas vagari mihi videar, si, propter oppositorum oppositas rationes, in primis auxiliis animorum ad vere excelsa leuandorum numerem intimam persuasionem de copioso maximorum euentuum systemate, non praeteritorum solum et praesentium, sed etiam maxima ex parte adhuc exspectandorum, non optima solum et maxima sublimitatis ac venerandae virtutis exempla simpliciter ad imitandum proponente, sed etiam saluberrima proferendi in semet ipsum imperii, fugiendae seruitutis moralis omnis internae, victoriaeque in semet ipsum obtinendae remedia consiliis euidentissimis subministrante, persuasionem, inquam, de veris eiusmodi rebus et gestis et gerendis, quae simul eam animabus vim largiatur ac potentiam diuinitus, vt ne mortis quidem metu possint eo compelli, quo tyrannus improba poscens destinauerit, supernaturale libertatis internae psychologicaeque complementum ac supplementum.

§ 414. If any reins of external liberty, if any external servitude, are especially made for depressing minds and blunting all their greatest pursuits and incitements, which I by no means deny, nor would I seem to myself to wander beyond the olives if, on account of the opposite reasons of opposites, I were to count among the first aids for raising minds to the truly lofty an intimate persuasion concerning the copious system of the greatest events, not of those past and present only, but also, for the greatest part, of those still to be expected; a persuasion which not only sets forth simply for imitation the best and greatest examples of sublimity and venerable virtue, but also supplies, with the most evident counsels, the most salutary remedies for bringing forth command over oneself, for fleeing all internal moral servitude, and for obtaining victory over oneself; a persuasion, I say, about true things of this kind, both done and to be done, which at the same time bestows divinely on souls such force and power that not even by the fear of death can they be driven to that which a tyrant demanding wicked things has designed, the supernatural complement and supplement of internal and psychological liberty.

> § 415. [p. 263] Pergit Longinus, l. c. caussas penuriae sublimium suis temporibus ingeniorum enarrare 2) pacem vniuersi orbis, cui tamen caussae et ipse parum fidit, et satis prospexit Discordia fratrum, ne diu possit egestas heroum imputari, et imputaretur eadem falso, si quando sperare liceret pacem orbis habitabilis vniuersalem diuturnam, hominesque simul discerent excelsas pacis artes, quibus pater patriae summos etiam regnorum gentiumque domitores transcendit. 3) *Infinitum detinens cupiditates nostras bellum*, de quo, quale sit, interpretes disputant.

§ 415. [p. 263] Longinus, l. c., goes on to recount the causes of the dearth of sublime wits in his times: 2) the peace of the whole world, a cause in which, however, he himself puts little trust, and the Discord of brothers has sufficiently provided that the want of heroes cannot long be imputed to it, and it would be imputed to it falsely, if ever it were permitted to hope for a universal and lasting peace of the habitable world, and men at the same time were to learn the lofty arts of peace, by which the father of his country transcends even the supreme subduers of kingdoms and nations. 3) *The infinite war that holds our desires in its grip*, about which the interpreters dispute what sort of thing it is.

> § 416. Magnanimitatis excellentis status ordinarius est statns [sic: status] tranquillitatis, E. §. 445. supra perturbationes animi vulgares et tumultus mentis internos positae. Per altam rationis et inferiorum cognoscendi facultatum, voluntatis et inferiorum appetendi facultatum, harmoniam, quae saepe apud eminenter magnos viros restat, etiamsi vehementius, nec sine affectionibus, quoniam homines sunt, commoveantur. Abripiuntur in πάθος ἐνθουσιαστικόν, si ferat occasio, sed probante ratione, rationalique conscientia, tum antecedente, tum concomitante, et consequente. Hactenus nihil est interni dissidii. Si qua tamen [p. 264] aliquando lucta caelestibus in animis locum habet, non est ea sensitiuarum tantum cupiditatum in alias non nisi sensitiuas, παθῶν εἰς πάθη, sed decretorum, quibus admixtum sit aliquid sensitiui, pugnantium in meras appetitiones sensitiuas, nec diu, nec in infinitum, sed plerumque vincente parte meliori, cuius victoria profundam iterum pacem et antiquam tranquillis animis serenitatem reducit: M. §. 693.

§ 416. The ordinary state of excellent magnanimity is a state of tranquillity, E. § 445, set above the common perturbations of the mind and the internal tumults of the mind. Through a deep harmony of reason and the lower faculties of knowing, of the will and the lower faculties of desiring, which often remains in eminently great men, even if they are moved rather vehemently, and not without affections, since they are men. They are carried away into πάθος ἐνθουσιαστικόν [enthusiastic passion], if the occasion brings it, but with reason approving, and with a rational conscience, antecedent, concomitant and consequent. So far there is no internal discord. If, however, [p. 264] some struggle sometimes has a place in heavenly minds, it is not one of merely sensate desires against others no less sensate, παθῶν εἰς πάθη [of passions against passions], but of decrees, with which something sensate is mixed, fighting against mere sensate appetitions, and neither for long nor without end, but for the most part with the better part winning, whose victory brings back again deep peace and the old serenity to tranquil minds: M. § 693.

> § 417. Cum hoc statu confer statum bestialitatis, E. §. 434. Nulla quies huic, nulla tranquillitas, nulla sopitae rationis et affectuum, et instinctuum, nec horum inter se, concinens harmonia. Crederes nunc

§ 417. With this state compare the state of bestiality, E. § 434. No rest has this, no tranquillity, no concordant harmony of lulled reason and of the affects and the instincts, nor of these among themselves. You would now believe it

> *Nimborum patriam loca foeta furentibus Austris,*

*The homeland of the storm-clouds, places teeming with raging South winds,*

> qui totum hominem

which the whole man

> *Quippe ferant rapidi secum verrantque per auras.*

*Indeed the rapid winds would carry off with them and sweep through the air.*

> Falleris tamen. Non ita multo post

Yet you are deceived. Not long afterwards

> *Vna Eurusque Notusque ruunt, creberque procellis* / *Africus,*

*Together East wind and South wind rush forth, and the South-wester* / *Thick with squalls,*

> et suum cuique facinus. Ponat seruitus externa non nihil iisdem repaguli,

and to each its own crime. Let external servitude set some bar to them,

> *Illi indignantes magno cum murmure circum* / *Claustra fremunt,*

*They, indignant, with a great murmur roar around* / *The barriers,*

> [p. 265] *luctantes* intus continuo, et ad primam iterum opportunitatem,

[p. 265] *struggling* within continually, and at the first opportunity again,

> *velut agmine facto,* / *Qua data porta, ruunt.*

*as if in a formed column,* / *Where a gate is given, they rush out.*

> Ita misere talis animus nunc auri sacra fame, nunc ambitione et fastu, nunc voluptatum turbine, nunc desidia, nunc aliquibus, nunc omnibus, inter se dissentientibus, agitatur. Hoc est illud infinitum bellum, §. 415. magnanimitati sublimium foetae inimicissimum, §. 416.

Thus wretchedly is such a mind driven now by the accursed hunger for gold, now by ambition and pride, now by the whirlwind of pleasures, now by sloth, now by some of these, now by all, disagreeing among themselves. This is that infinite war, § 415, most hostile to the magnanimity pregnant with sublime things, § 416.

> § 418. Iam vna dictarum tempestatum infringit satis animum. Recte Longinus in caussis deficientis egregii ac sublimis narrat 4. φιλοχρηματίαν, appellans venuste φιλαργυρίαν νόσημα μικροποιόν, §. 45. eiusque cum magno sumtu (Sumtuositate) liberos fingit Fastum et Luxuriam, ex quibus sane non degeneres generentur denuo Contumelia, Iniustitia et Impudentia, quam inter progeniem contabescant et emarcescant animorum magnitudines.

§ 418. Already one of the storms mentioned breaks the mind sufficiently. Rightly Longinus, among the causes of the failure of the excellent and the sublime, recounts 4. φιλοχρηματίαν [the love of money], charmingly calling φιλαργυρίαν νόσημα μικροποιόν [avarice a disease that makes small], § 45, and feigns as its children, together with great expense (Sumptuousness), Pride and Luxury, from which indeed, no degenerate offspring, are begotten in turn Insolence, Injustice and Shamelessness, amid which progeny the magnitudes of minds waste away and wither.

> § 419. *An, haec animos aerugo et cura peculii / Quum semel imbuerit, speramus carmina fingi / Posse linenda cedro et leui seruanda cupresso?* A. P. 330.

§ 419. *Or, when once this rust and care for property has imbued our minds, do we hope that songs can be fashioned worthy to be smeared with cedar oil and kept in smooth cypress?* A. P. 330.

> [p. 266] Negat ipse Phaedrus de fabellis, quales scripsit, aut scripsisse dicitur. III. prol. *Nouem artium, quamuis curam*

[p. 266] Phaedrus himself denies it of the fables, such as he wrote, or is said to have written. III. prol. *Of the nine arts, although the care*

> *habendi penitus corde eraserim, / Et laude inuita in hanc vitam incubuerim, / Fastidiose tamen in coetum recipior. / Quid credis illi accidere, qui magnas opes / Exaggerare quaerit omni vigilia, / Docto labori dulce praeponens lucrum?* cf. Hor. od. II. 15, 18. III. 2, 24.

*of possessing I have utterly erased from my heart, / And have thrown myself upon this life with praise unwilling, / Yet I am received fastidiously into their company. / What do you think befalls him who seeks to heap up great wealth / with every vigil, / Preferring sweet gain to learned labour?* cf. Hor. od. II. 15, 18. III. 2, 24.

> § 420. 5) φιληδονία καταβυθίζει, §. 417, 418. Intemperans deliciarum externarum desiderium eo vsque mores emollit, vt tandem nihil omnino masculi roboris animo supersit, et minime tantum, quantum valoris grandia requirunt.

§ 420. 5) φιληδονία καταβυθίζει [the love of pleasure sinks it], § 417, 418. An intemperate desire for external delights softens morals to such a point that at last no masculine strength at all remains in the mind, and least of all as much worth as grand things require.

> *Vides, vt pallidus omnis / Coena desurgat dubia? Quin corpus onustum / Hesternis vitiis animum quoque praegrauat vna, / Atque adfligit humo diuinae particulam aurae.*

*Do you see how pale every man rises / from a doubtful dinner? Nay, the body, burdened / with yesterday’s vices, weighs down the mind too together with it, / And dashes to the ground that particle of the divine breath.*

> Hor. Serm. II. 2. quae tota paene huc pertinet satura. Numera modo dispendia temporis, quod insumendum est acquirendae theoriae, eiusque empiricae, crebrius repetitis experimentis ad eam certitudinem euectae, quae decet arbitrum elegantiarum eiusmodi, [p. 267] et miraberis superfuisse nonnihil otii, grauioribus concedendi.

Hor. Serm. II. 2, a satire which almost entirely pertains here. Only count the expenditures of time that must be spent in acquiring the theory, and an empirical one at that, raised by rather frequently repeated experiments to that certainty which befits an arbiter of elegances of this kind, [p. 267] and you will wonder that any leisure at all was left over to be granted to weightier matters.

> § 421. 6) Desidiam tandem Longinus in caussis animorum parum aut nihil in sublime surgentium numerat, Qua dum intermittuntur exercitia, non crescit habitus, ac eo ipso crescit desuetudo habitui opposita, id est difficultas, in veram denique degenerans impotentiam.

§ 421. 6) Finally Longinus numbers sloth among the causes of minds rising little or not at all to the sublime. For while exercises are interrupted, the habit does not grow, and by that very fact there grows the disuse opposed to the habit, that is, difficulty, degenerating at last into true impotence.
