Strictissime veris opposita quomodocunque, vel etiam ea solum, quae videntur iisdem opposita, dicuntur LATISSIME FALSA, et simpliciter in populari sermone. Hinc quicquid in hoc vniuerso nec fuit, nec est, nec erit, falsum illud omne vulgo perhibetur, et, quam primum irascatur, falsissimum. Sit pulcrius cogitandum finitum, in se possibile, sit naturaliter, sit moraliter, latius, strictius, et rationis et analogi rationis ex exactissimo iudicio, neque tamen sit huius vniuersi possibile, erit illud latissime falsum et ex vulgari loquendi formula falsum simpliciter.

§ 471. [p. 301] But what is this ambiguity? Now falsehoods are conceded, now again the aesthetician is dissuaded from them? State your opinion explicitly. As I have said hitherto, not without the necessary determinations, so I shall proceed. Things opposed in whatever way to what is most strictly true, or even those alone which seem opposed to them, are called FALSE IN THE WIDEST SENSE, and simply false in popular speech. Hence whatever in this universe neither was, nor is, nor will be, is all commonly declared false, and, as soon as one grows angry, most false. Let something to be thought rather beautifully be finite, possible in itself, possible naturally and morally, in the wider and in the stricter sense, by the most exact judgement both of reason and of the analogue of reason, and yet not possible in this universe: it will be false in the widest sense, and by the common formula of speech simply false.

> § 472. Tantum est bene studium veritatis, §. 423. pulcre cogitaturo, vt ne in strictissimam quidem veritatem impingere velit, sine pulcra necessitate, nec sine eadem vel latissime falsa meditari, §. 471. Hinc elegantes sibi praesertim dictum putant historici: *Ne quid falsi* (i. e. quod non sit strictissime verum). Tacitus strictissime veram sibi visam historiam de Drusi morte quum narrasset, addit rumorem [p. 302] de eadem suae narrationi contrarium, Ann. IV. 11. *Mihi,* pergens, *tradendi arguendique rumoris caussa fuit, vt claro exemplo falsas auditiones depellerem, peteremque ab iis, quorum in manus cura nostra venerit, ne diuulgata et incredibilia, auide accepta, veris, neque in miraculum corruptis, ante habeant.*

§ 472. So great is the pursuit of truth, § 423, in one who would think beautifully, that he will not offend even against the most strict truth without a beautiful necessity, nor without the same meditate things false even in the widest sense, § 471. Hence elegant historians think it said to themselves especially: *Nothing false* (i.e. nothing that is not most strictly true). Tacitus, when he had narrated the history of Drusus’ death as it seemed to him most strictly true, adds a rumour [p. 302] about the same contrary to his own narrative, Ann. IV. 11. *My reason,* he goes on, *for relating and refuting the rumour was that by a clear example I might dispel false hearsay, and might ask those into whose hands our work shall come not to prefer things divulged and incredible, greedily received, to the true and to what has not been corrupted into the marvellous.*

> § 473. Hanc ob caussam sane non refertur a bonis elegantiarum arbitris inter Veneres cogitationum, eaedem si nequicquam et nulla obseruabili ex necessitate contradicunt rigidae ac seuerae historiae, genealogiae, geographiae, chronologiae, reliquisque disciplinis, quae versantur in strictissime veris. Quoties ipse culpatus est Virgilius castam forsan Didonem cum duce Troiano in eandem speluncam deducens, reclamante chronologia, ab iis, qui necessitatem falsi non obseruare sibi visi sunt? In declamatione Pythagorae apud Ouidium hi versus:

§ 473. For this reason indeed it is not counted by good arbiters of the elegances among the Graces of thoughts, if these thoughts, to no purpose and from no observable necessity, contradict rigid and severe history, genealogy, geography, chronology, and the other disciplines which deal in the most strictly true. How often has Virgil himself been blamed for leading the perhaps chaste Dido with the Trojan leader into the same cave, chronology protesting, by those who seemed to themselves to observe no necessity for the falsehood? In Pythagoras’ declamation in Ovid these verses:

> *Clara fuit Sparte, magnae viguere Mycenae / Nec non Cecropiae, nec non Amphionis arces. / Vile solum Sparta est, altae cecidere Mycenae. / Oedipodioniae quid sunt, nisi nomina, Thebae? / Quid Pandioniae restant, nisi nomen, Athenae?*

*Sparta was famous, great Mycenae flourished, / and the citadel of Cecrops too, and that of Amphion. / Sparta is cheap ground, lofty Mycenae has fallen. / What is Oedipus’ Thebes but a name? / What remains of Pandion’s Athens but a name?*

> quoniam sine necessitate venusta pugnant in chronologiam, multis habiti sunt in glossematibus.

since without necessity they charmingly clash with chronology, have been held by many to be glosses.

> § 474. [p. 303] Quicquid est anachronismorum et ἀνιστορησίας citra necessitatem in pulcre cogitandum illatorum, pertinet illud omne ad falsitates etiam aestheticas, quam primum analogo rationis vitium appareat. §. 473, 445. Huc *triremes* Virgilii, nisi subtiliter facetus data opera *Chimaeram* dicit, L. V. 118.

§ 474. [p. 303] Whatever anachronisms and ἀνιστορησία [ignorance of history] are introduced without necessity into what is to be thought beautifully, all of it belongs to the falsities that are also aesthetic, as soon as the vice appears to the analogue of reason. § 473, 445. Here belong Virgil’s *triremes*, unless, subtly facetious, he purposely calls the ship *Chimaera*, L. V. 118.

> *Vrbis opus, triplici pubes quam Dardana versu / Impellunt, terno consurgunt ordine remi.*

*A city’s bulk, which the Dardan youth in triple tier / drive on; the oars rise up in threefold rank.*

> *Aeratas* saltim eius *puppes* ideo non possumus in exsilium ex hoc vniuerso relegare, quia rostra sunt inuenta, post heroica tempora. Plautum castiget, qui volet, quando eius non Sosias, sed et Mercurius ipse crebrum *hercule* iurant in Amphitryone, qui futurus erat demum Herculis *pater, quem iustae nuptiae declarant.*

Its *bronze-clad sterns*, at least, we cannot for that reason banish from this universe into exile, because beaks were invented after the heroic times. Let whoever will chastise Plautus, since not only his Sosia but Mercury himself swear frequently *by Hercules* in the Amphitryo — he who was only later to be Hercules’ *father, whom lawful wedlock declares.*

> § 475. Sed sit aliquando pulcre cogitaturo quaedam necessitas, secundum quam salua pulcritudine totius non possit in hoc vniuerso morari longius, exspatiandum potius eius ingenio sit per alios mundos possibiles, quam primum in eiusmodi itinere commoratur circa regiones mundi fabulosi, §. 456. descriptas, est in eius cogitatis falsitas heterocosmica aesthetica etiam, sin vltra limites, §. [p. 304] 455. descriptos non prosiliat, iure non accusatur falsitatis in heterocosmicis aestheticae, M. §. 445. Epaphus forte strictissime verum Phaetonti dixerat, Ou. Met. l. 752:

§ 475. But let there sometimes be, for one who would think beautifully, a certain necessity according to which, with the beauty of the whole preserved, he cannot tarry longer in this universe, but his wit must rather range abroad through other possible worlds; as soon as on such a journey he lingers about the regions of the fabulous world described in § 456, there is in his thoughts a heterocosmic falsity that is also aesthetic; but if he does not leap beyond the limits [p. 304] described in § 455, he is rightly not accused of aesthetic falsity in heterocosmic matters, M. § 445. Epaphus had perhaps said what is most strictly true to Phaethon, Ou. Met. l. 752:

> *Matri omnia demens / Credis et es tumidus genitoris imagine falsi.*

*Madman, you believe your mother in everything, / and are puffed up with the image of a false father.*

> § 476. In mundo tamen metamorphoseon ouidianarum est, per preces Phaëtontis, l. II. 35.

§ 476. In the world of the Ovidian metamorphoses, however, through the prayers of Phaëthon, l. II. 35,

> *O! lux immensi publica mundi,*

*O common light of the immense world,*

> strictissime verum, et simul heterocosmice, §. 441.

is most strictly true, and at the same time heterocosmically, § 441.

> *Phoebe, pater, si das huius mihi nominis vsum,*

*Phoebus, father, if you grant me the use of this name,*

> heterocosmice verum, §. 441. licet ex mundo fabuloso somnium, tamen iis, quibus vixit, Ouidius locis et temporibus, quibusque praesertim scripsit personis, non falsum aesthetice §. 455.

is heterocosmically true, § 441; though a dream from a fabulous world, nevertheless for the places and times in which Ovid lived, and for the persons for whom especially he wrote, it is not aesthetically false, § 455.

> *Nec falsa Clymene culpam sub imagine celat,*

*Nor does a false Clymene hide a fault beneath a pretence,*

> hoc in dicto Ouidii mundo falsum fuisset, supposita Phaëtontis fabula, etiam aestheticum.

this would have been false in the said world of Ovid, the fable of Phaëthon being supposed, and aesthetically false too.

> *Pignora da, genitor, per quae tua vera propago / Credar, et hunc animis errorem detrahe nostris.*

*Give pledges, father, by which I may be believed your true offspring, / and remove this error from our minds.*

> Verum habes heterocosmicum, quod nec aesthetice tunc falsum erat et iis, quum et quibus Ouidius potissimum scribebat.

You have a heterocosmic truth, which was not aesthetically false either, then, and for those when and for whom Ovid chiefly wrote.

> § 477. [p. 305] Iamque reor aliqua ex parte manifestum esse pulcre cogitaturum veritatis amicum esse quidem semper, S. XXVI. neque tamen vel illius abstractissimae de vniuersalibus, §. 440. vel illius strictissimae seruum esse, §. 441.

§ 477. [p. 305] And now I think it manifest in some measure that one who would think beautifully is indeed always a friend of truth, S. XXVI, and yet is not the slave either of that most abstract truth about universals, § 440, or of that most strict truth, § 441.

> *Exit in immensum foecunda licentia vatum, / Obligat historica nec sua verba fide.* Ou. Am. III. 12.

*The fertile licence of the bards goes out into the immense, / nor binds its words by historical faith.* Ou. Am. III. 12.

> vbi multa exempla congeruntur confirmatura sententiam huc facientem:

where many examples are heaped up to confirm the maxim that bears upon this:

> *Non, vt testes, mos est audire poetas.*

*It is not the custom to hear poets as witnesses.*

> Vt enim tandem omnibus videar perspicue scribere, §. 471. venustius ingenium,

For, that I may at last seem to everyone to write perspicuously, § 471: the more charming wit,

> *Quando ita mentitur, sic veris falsa remiscet, / Primo ne medium, medio ne discrepet imum,*

*When it lies thus, so mingles false with true / that the middle may not clash with the beginning, nor the end with the middle,*

> illius Musa memor §. 467, censoribus aestheticis est

its Muse mindful of § 467, is, to the aesthetic censors,

> *Splendide mendax, et in omne virgo / Nobilis aeuum.*

*Splendidly mendacious, and a maiden noble / for all time.*

[p. 306]

#### Sectio XXVIIII. Verisimilitudo Aesthetica. — Section XXVIIII. Aesthetic Verisimilitude

> § 478. *Quousque tandem abutere patientia nostra? quamdiu nos etiam furor iste tuus eludat? Quem ad finem sese effraenata iactabit audacia?* Tune vero magister veritatis logicae ac ethicae publice constitutus mendacia commendes, velut aliquando splendida, et falsa veris miscere, tanquam operam maximopere nobilem? Hac ego circiter ratione videor audire mihi quosdam obloquentes ex schola, quam pinxi, §. 279. Sed sedatis animis, boni viri, reuertamur ad nostrum, quod vos nonnunquam male habet, phlegma philosophicum. De salute Graeciae res non agitur. Interim tamen

§ 478. *How long, pray, will you abuse our patience? How long will that frenzy of yours mock us too? To what end will your unbridled audacity flaunt itself?* Do you, then, publicly appointed a teacher of logical and ethical truth, commend lies, as sometimes splendid, and the mixing of false with true, as a work in the highest degree noble? In roughly this fashion I seem to hear certain persons railing at me from the school which I have painted, § 279. But with calmed spirits, good men, let us return to our philosophical phlegm, which sometimes sits ill with you. The safety of Greece is not at stake. Meanwhile, however,

> *longa est iniuria, longae / Ambages, sed summa sequar fastigia rerum.*

*long is the wrong, long / the windings; but I shall follow the chief heads of the matter.*

> § 479. Adeone facile putatis, ac Claudiani panegyris Honorio, rationis etiam analogo,

§ 479. Do you think it so easy, as Claudian’s panegyric to Honorius does, even for the analogue of reason,

> *Mersum latebris educere verum?* v. 513.

*to draw forth the truth sunk in hiding-places?* v. 513.

> Vt et ego vobiscum magnis auctoritatibus agam, nonne meministis veritatem esse Democrito [p. 307] sitam in fundo, vnde difficulter protrahatur? Audietis certe Ciceronem, qui, dum plura dicit, ac ego probauerim, illud tamen illustrabit, de quo nunc quaeritur in fine l. de Or: *Nec in hac modo re* (de oratore, hinc et aesthetico) *quae ad vulgi assensum spectat, et ad aurium voluptatem* (et analogi rationis, qua res) *quae duo sunt ad iudicandum leuissima: sed ne in maximis quidem rebus quicquam inueni firmius, quod tenerem, aut quo iudicium meum dirigerem, quam id, quodcunque mihi quam simillimum veri videretur, quum illud ipsum verum in occulto lateret.*

That I too may deal with you by great authorities: do you not remember that truth, according to Democritus, [p. 307] lies at the bottom, whence it is drawn out with difficulty? You will surely listen to Cicero, who, while he says more than I would approve, will nonetheless illustrate the point now in question, at the end of book I de Or.: *Not only in this matter* (concerning the orator, hence the aesthetician too) *which looks to the assent of the crowd and to the pleasure of the ears* (and of the analogue of reason, as regards the matter), *which two are the slightest things for judging; but not even in the greatest matters have I found anything firmer to hold to, or by which to direct my judgement, than whatever seemed to me most like the truth, while the truth itself lay hidden in obscurity.*

> § 480. Non solum aduersus Ciceronem, §. 479. et scepticos academicosque, vel veteres, vel recentes, lubenter admitto dari rationi et intellectui puriori ac distinctiori per scientias assurgere nonnunquam vltra verisimilitudinem, non ad plenam quidem et omnibus numeris absolutissimam, completam tamen et eam, quae omnem oppositi formidinem excludat, veri notitiam et perspicientiam: sed id etiam addo, quod pauci recentiorum dogmaticorum forte concedant, inesse iam ipsis sensitiuis et confusis animae perceptionibus nonnihil completae tamen certitudinis, et conscientiae vera quaedam ab omnibus falsis distinguendi sufficientiam.

§ 480. Not only against Cicero, § 479, and the sceptics and academics, whether ancient or recent, do I gladly admit that it is granted to the purer and more distinct reason and intellect sometimes to rise through the sciences above verisimilitude, to a knowledge and insight of the true which is not indeed full and most absolute in every respect, yet complete, and such as excludes all fear of the opposite; but I add this too, which few of the more recent dogmatists would perhaps concede, that there is already in the sensate and confused perceptions of the soul themselves some certainty, which is nonetheless complete, and a sufficiency of consciousness for distinguishing certain true things from all false ones.

> § 481. [p. 308] Veritas quaedam, etiam aesthetica, §. 423. tamen complete cognoscatur ab analogo rationis, vt talis, §. 480. id est completa cum certitudine et persuasione, M. §. 531. Sed quaenam haec erit? 1) prima et maxime vniuersalia quaedam cognitionis humanae principia, quae sic inseuit iam ingeniis tantum non omnibus natura, metaphysicis naturalibus, M. §. 3. vt ea sensus communis aliquando titulo condecorata satis superque sint euidentia, M. §. 531. Sed ob hanc ipsam suam euidentiam, quae per se patere cuilibet videntur, eadem vberius, non sine ponderibus, in omni veritatis suae luce, multis cum argumentis et solicitationibus ad assensum ea cogitare expresse et manifesto, vel raro licet, vel nunquam. Plerumque supponuntur, quod aiunt, et omissa per venustum enthymema relinquuntur spectatori inter ea, quae ipse sibi tradat.

§ 481. [p. 308] Let a certain truth, even an aesthetic one, § 423, nevertheless be completely cognised by the analogue of reason, as such, § 480, that is, completely, with certainty and persuasion, M. § 531. But which will this be? 1) Certain first and most universal principles of human cognition, which nature has so implanted already in almost all wits, as natural metaphysicians, M. § 3, that, at times adorned with the title of common sense, they are evident enough and more than enough, M. § 531. But on account of this very evidence of theirs, by which they seem of themselves to be plain to anyone, it is only rarely, or never, permissible to think them expressly and manifestly in fuller form, not without weighty considerations, in all the light of their truth, with many arguments and solicitations to assent. For the most part they are, as they say, supposed, and, omitted by a charming enthymeme, are left to the spectator among the things he supplies to himself.

> § 482. 2) Paucissima illa intuitiua vere talia, quae immediate sentimus nullis subreptionum vitiis temerata. Stricte dictam experientiam huc vnam voco, non illam late dictam, complexum omnis cognitionis, cui aliquid inest sensationum, quamque parum habere certitudinis vel ii probant, qui sibi vere repugnantes ad eandem tamen vterque [p. 309] confidenter prouocant. Experientia stricte dicta multis reliquarum animae facultatum inferiorum perceptionibus praeter sensationes aliis est interstinguenda, si pulcrius aliquid excogitare sit animus, §. 140. Haec ipsa, quae concessi esse posse complete certa rationis etiam analogo, non sunt illa semper et omnibus, sed fides eorum saepe prorsus non attenditur, aliquando sophismatibus et argutationibus, licet inanibus, labefactatur tamen et paene conuellitur, nisi rationis et intellectus notionibus confirmetur.

§ 482. 2) Those very few intuitive perceptions truly such, which we sense immediately, unviolated by any vices of subreption. Experience in the strict sense alone I count here, not that in the wide sense, the complex of all cognition in which there is something of sensations, and which even those prove to have little certainty who, while truly contradicting one another, nonetheless both [p. 309] confidently appeal to it. Experience in the strict sense is to be set apart from the many other perceptions of the remaining lower faculties of the soul besides sensations, if one has a mind to think out something rather beautiful, § 140. These very things, which I have conceded can be completely certain even to the analogue of reason, are not so always and for everyone; but their credit is often not attended to at all, and sometimes, by sophisms and quibbles, empty though they be, it is nonetheless shaken and almost overthrown, unless it is confirmed by the notions of reason and intellect.

> § 483. Iam apertissimo putauerim calculo constare plurima inter venuste cogitandum appercipienda, non esse complete certa, neque luce completa veritatem eorum conspici, §. 481, 482. Nec in vllo tamen falsitatis aliquid sensitiuae deprehendi potest sine turpitudine, S. XXVIII. Talia autem, de quibus non complete quidem certi sumus, neque tamen falsitatem aliquam in iisdem appercipimus, sunt VERISIMILIA. Est ergo veritas aesthetica S. XXVII. a potiori dicta VERISIMILITVDO, ille veritatis gradus, qui, etiamsi non euectus sit ad completam certitudinem, tamen nihil contineat falsitatis obseruabilis.

§ 483. Now I should think it established by the plainest reckoning that very many of the things to be apperceived in the course of charming thought are not completely certain, nor is their truth beheld in complete light, § 481, 482. Yet in none of them can anything of sensate falsity be detected without disgrace, S. XXVIII. But such things, of which we are indeed not completely certain, and yet in which we apperceive no falsity, are VERISIMILAR. Aesthetic truth, S. XXVII, named from the predominant feature, is therefore VERISIMILITUDE, that degree of truth which, even if it has not been raised to complete certainty, nevertheless contains nothing of observable falsity.

> § 484. [p. 310] *Cuius habent* spectatores *auditoresue intra animum*, quum vident audiuntue, *quasdam anticipationes, quod plerumque fit, quod fieri solet, quod in opinione positum est, quod habet ad haec in se quandam similitudinem, siue id falsum* (logice, et latissime,) *siue verum sit.* (logice et strictissime) *quod non sit facile a nostris sensibus abhorrens:* hoc illud est εἰκός et verisimile, quod, Aristotele et Cicerone assentiente, sectetur aestheticus, §. 483. In rebus enim eiusmodi non solet analogon rationis quicquam falsitatis obseruare, licet non omnino de veritate eorundem conuictum sit. Hinc Ciceroni describitur *inuentio excogitatio rerum verarum aut verisimilium, quae caussam probabilem* (aesthetice) *reddant.*

§ 484. [p. 310] *Of which* spectators *or hearers have within the mind*, when they see or hear, *certain anticipations: what mostly happens, what is wont to happen, what is placed in opinion, what has in itself a certain likeness to these, whether it be false* (logically, and in the broadest sense) *or true* (logically and in the strictest sense), *what is not readily abhorrent to our senses:* this is that εἰκός [the likely] and verisimilar which, with Aristotle and Cicero assenting, the aesthetician should pursue, § 483. For in things of this kind the analogue of reason is not wont to observe anything of falsity, although it is not altogether convinced of their truth. Hence for Cicero invention is described as *the thinking out of things true or verisimilar, which render the cause probable* (aesthetically).

> § 485. Erunt itaque aesthetice vera, id est, verisimilia, §. 484. 1) sensitiue et intellectualiter complete certa, qua sunt prius, §. 480-482. 2) sensitiue tantum complete certa, §. 482. in quibus adhuc intellectus suam non exercuit operam, 3) logice et aesthetice probabilia, qua sunt posterius. PROBABILIA quoniam sunt, quibus ad dandum assensum plus rationis est, quam ad denegandum; et IMPROBABILIA, quibus ad denegandum assensum plus rationis est, quam ad dandum: [p. 311] quando rationes dubitandi et decidendi, pro assensu et contra eundem distincte cognoscuntur, oritur PROBABILITAS LOGICA, si sensitiue, AESTHETICA. A potiori desumitur denominatio, quoties est quaedam probabilitas aestheticologica. Par est ratio improbabilitatis. Patent ergo verisimilitudinum campi latius, quam probabilitatis territorium, etiamsi sit omne probabile simul verisimile. §. 483.

§ 485. Aesthetically true, that is, verisimilar, § 484, will therefore be 1) things completely certain both sensately and intellectually, which come first, § 480–482; 2) things completely certain sensately only, § 482, in which the intellect has not yet exercised its work; 3) things logically and aesthetically probable, which come later. Since PROBABLE things are those for which there is more reason to grant assent than to withhold it, and IMPROBABLE things those for which there is more reason to withhold assent than to grant it: [p. 311] when the reasons for doubting and for deciding, for assent and against it, are distinctly cognised, LOGICAL PROBABILITY arises; if sensately, AESTHETIC. The denomination is taken from the predominant feature whenever there is a certain aesthetico-logical probability. The same reasoning holds for improbability. The fields of verisimilitudes therefore extend more widely than the territory of probability, even if everything probable is at the same time verisimilar, § 483.

> § 486. Verisimilia aesthetica erunt 4) logice forte dubia, immo improbabilia, modo sint aesthetice probabilia §. 485. 5) aesthetice etiam dubia et improbabilia, non aliis solum, quam quibus potissimum venuste cogites, sed etiam his ipsis forsan alias, quando rationes contra assensum largius imbiberint, modo nunc et inter meditationis tuae seriem vel habeant, de iis, quae propinas, aut probabilitatem aestheticam, aut saltim in oppositum superponderantes rationes non habeant animo satis praesentes, vt obscurent id omne, quod tuis superest elegantis verisimilitudinis. §. 484.

§ 486. Aesthetically verisimilar things will be 4) things perhaps logically doubtful, indeed improbable, provided they are aesthetically probable, § 485; 5) things even aesthetically doubtful and improbable, not only to others than those for whom above all you think charmingly, but perhaps even to these very persons at another time, when they have imbibed more fully the reasons against assent, provided that now, and within the series of your meditation, they either have, concerning the things you set before them, an aesthetic probability, or at least do not have present enough to the mind the reasons preponderating on the opposite side, so as to obscure all that of elegant verisimilitude which remains to your thoughts, § 484.

> § 487. Conferamus consilium Ciceronis accusatoribus datum or. pro Rosc. Am. 57. *Maxime debetis in eos impetum facere, qui merentur* [p. 312] (quorum crimen est complete certum, logice et strictissime verum, aut etiam logice probabile et aesthetice). *Hoc populo gratissimum est. Deinde, si voletis, etiam tum, quum verisimile erit aliquem commisisse, in suspicione latratote.* (Etiamsi non complete certum nec logice probabile sit crimen, nec omnibus aesthetice, neque tamen iis improbabile aesthetice, quibus grati esse praesertim vultis). *Id quoque concedi potest. Sin autem sic agatis, vt aliquem arguatis patrem occidisse, neque dicere possitis, aut quare, aut quomodo, ac tantummodo sine suspicione* (verisimilitudine qualicunque aesthetica) *latrabitis: crura quidem nemo vobis suffringet, sed si ego hos bene noui, litteram illam, cui vos vsque eo inimici estis, vt etiam eas omnes oderitis, ita vehementer ad caput affigent, vt postea neminem alium, nisi fortunas vestras, accusare possitis.*

§ 487. Let us compare the advice given by Cicero to accusers, or. pro Rosc. Am. 57: *You ought above all to make your attack upon those who deserve it* [p. 312] (whose crime is completely certain, logically and most strictly true, or even logically and aesthetically probable). *This is most welcome to the people. Then, if you will, even when it is verisimilar that someone has committed a crime, bark away in suspicion* (even if the crime is not completely certain or logically probable, nor aesthetically so to everyone, yet not aesthetically improbable to those whom you especially wish to please). *That too may be allowed. But if you proceed in such a way that you accuse someone of having killed his father, and cannot say either why or how, and merely bark without suspicion* (without any aesthetic verisimilitude whatsoever), *no one indeed will break your legs; but if I know these men well, that letter to which you are so hostile that you hate even all the Kalends they will fasten so violently to your head that afterwards you will be able to accuse no one else but your own fortunes.*

> § 488. Aliud exemplum dabit Cicero philosophus de nat. Deorum l. I. 65: *Haec,* inquiens, *ego nunc physicorum oracula (nullum esse inane) fundo, vera, an falsa nescio.* (Complete certa logice, neque tamen analogo rationis, §. 482.) 66. *Sed veri tamen similiora, quam vestra. Ista enim flagitia Democriti, siue etiam ante Leucippi, esse quaedam corpuscula, quaedam laeuia, alia aspera, rotunda alia, partim angulata, curuata quaedam, et quasi adunca,* [p. 313] *ex his effectum esse caelum atque terras, nulla cogente natura, sed concursu quodam fortuito.* (Haec flagitia illustrabunt §. 486.)

§ 488. Another example will be given by Cicero the philosopher, de nat. Deorum l. I. 65: *These*, he says, *oracles of the natural philosophers (that there is no void) I now pour forth, whether true or false I do not know.* (Completely certain logically, yet not to the analogue of reason, § 482.) 66. *But still more like the truth than yours. For those scandalous doctrines of Democritus, or even before him of Leucippus, that there are certain corpuscles, some smooth, others rough, others round, some angular, some curved and as it were hooked,* [p. 313] *and that from these the heaven and the earth were made, with no nature compelling, but by some fortuitous concourse.* (These scandals will illustrate § 486.)

> § 489. Iam simul per rationem oppositorum oppositam reor patere falsum aestheticum, S. XXVIII. a potiori denominandum esse falsi simile, §. 483. de cuius falsitate quidem non complete certi simus, ex quo tamen nihil omnino veritatis insigniter elucescat. Sit aliquid complete certum intellectui, sit eidem probabile aliud: vtraque tamen aesthetice sint dubia, vel improbabilia, vel omnino nihil argumentorum pro veritate sui suggerant analogo rationis eorum, quibus praecipue placere velis, licet nec eidem eorum liqueat falsitas, tamen aesthetica verisimilitudine destituta, destituta anticipationibus intra mentem obiectorum tuorum personalium, quoniam insolita videntur his saltim, §. 484. abstrahendum est ab iisdem, falsi similibus. §. 485, 486.

§ 489. At the same time I think it evident, by the reasoning of opposites, that the aesthetically false, S. XXVIII, is to be named from the predominant feature the false-seeming, § 483, of whose falsity we are indeed not completely certain, yet from which nothing of truth at all shines forth notably. Let something be completely certain to the intellect, let something else be probable to it: if both are nevertheless aesthetically doubtful, or improbable, or suggest no arguments at all for their truth to the analogue of reason of those whom you chiefly wish to please, then although their falsity is not clear to it either, still, being destitute of aesthetic verisimilitude, destitute of anticipations within the mind of your personal objects, since they seem unusual at least to these, § 484, one must abstain from them, as false-seeming, § 485, 486.

> § 490. *Nocturnos lemures, portentaque Thessala rident*

§ 490. *Nocturnal spirits and Thessalian portents are laughed at*

> aliqui. An sciant, quare, an nesciant, non curabit aestheticus. Sufficiet ipsi spectatoribus eiusmodi, quicquid est vtique spectrorum artiumque, quas male magicas dicunt, adeo ridiculum videri per analogon rationis, vt in [p. 314] visionibus eiusmodi nihil apud eosdem restet elegantis verisimilitudinis, hinc ob hoc solum remouebit ex oculis talia omnia falsi similia iis, quorum maxime caussa scribit. Si tales fuissent Virgilio, astrologiam iudiciariam, vti nunc plures, susque deque habentes, non ille, profecto, scripsisset.

by some. Whether they know why, or do not know, the aesthetician will not care. It will suffice him that to spectators of this kind whatever there is of spectres and of the arts they wrongly call magical seems so ridiculous to the analogue of reason that in [p. 314] visions of this kind nothing of elegant verisimilitude remains for them; hence for this reason alone he will remove from the eyes all such false-seeming things, for those for whose sake he chiefly writes. If Virgil’s readers had been such, holding judicial astrology, as many now do, in contempt, he assuredly would not have written

> *Solem quis dicere falsum / Audeat? Ille etiam caecos instare tumultus / Saepe monet, fraudemque et operta tumescere bella.*

*Who would dare to call the sun false? / He too often warns that blind tumults are at hand, / and that fraud and hidden wars are swelling.*

> Georg. l. I. 463. veritus, ne quis eorum regereret, non solem falsum dicimus, sed te falsum ex eiusdem colore veraculum. §. 489.

Georg. l. I. 463, fearing lest one of them should retort: we do not call the sun false, but you false, a petty truth-teller from its colour, § 489.

> § 491. Aliquam necessitatem aestheticam iam aliquando subinnuimus non ea solum exhibendi, quae completa certitudine vera sint et strictissime. Nunc locus est quasdam harum necessitatum commemorare. 1) Sit cogitandum aesthetico, qui pansophus esse non obligatur, multo minus omniscius, de rebus, quarum veritatem metaphysicam complete non nouit, §. 423. 2) Obueniant ipsi cogitanda, quorum veritatem strictius logicam demonstrare rigide nequeat. §. 424. 3) Occurrant, de quibus ne aesthetice quidem sit complete certus, §. 427. 4) Incidat in cogitanda talia, quorum exacta veritas horizontem [p. 315] distinctionis non egrediatur, quo melius ipsi cognita est, hoc certior, eam non esse captui eorum commodam, quibus potissimum cogitat. §. 429: in his casibus omnibus confugiendum erit ad aliquam verisimilitudinem. §. 479.

§ 491. We have already at some point hinted at a certain aesthetic necessity of exhibiting not only those things which are true with complete certainty and most strictly. Now is the place to recall some of these necessities. 1) Let the aesthetician, who is not obliged to be a pansophist, much less omniscient, have to think about things whose metaphysical truth he does not completely know, § 423. 2) Let there come before him things to be thought whose more strictly logical truth he cannot rigidly demonstrate, § 424. 3) Let there occur things of which he is not completely certain even aesthetically, § 427. 4) Let him fall upon such things to be thought whose exact truth does not go beyond the horizon [p. 315] of distinctness, so that the better it is known to him, the more certain he is that it is not suited to the grasp of those for whom above all he thinks, § 429: in all these cases refuge will have to be taken in some verisimilitude, § 479.

> § 492. In casu primo erant romani paene omnes, si ad illos dirigebatur quaestio:

§ 492. In the first case were almost all the Romans, if the question were directed to them:

> *Paruum est, quod scire laboro. / De Ioue quid sentis?*

*It is a small thing that I labour to know. / What do you think of Jove?*

> In secundo putauerim Iopam fuisse canentem; Aen. I. 748.

In the second I should think Iopas was, as he sang, Aen. I. 748:

> *Quid tantum Oceano properent se tingere soles / Hiberni, vel quae tardis mora noctibus obstet.*

*Why the winter suns hasten so to dip themselves in Ocean, / or what delay stands in the way of the slow nights.*

> In tertio fuit illa Virgilii, quae ecl. VIII. 106.

In the third was that woman of Virgil’s, who, ecl. VIII. 106,

> *Adspice,* ait, *corripuit tremulis altaria flammis / Sponte sua, dum ferre moror, cinis ipse, bonum sit, / Nescio quid, certe est, et Hylax in limine latrat. / Credimus? an, qui amant, ipsi sibi somnia fingunt?*

*Look,* she says, *the ash itself, while I delay to carry it, has seized the altar with trembling flames / of its own accord; may it be a good sign. / Something it is, surely, and Hylax is barking on the threshold. / Do we believe? or do those who love make up dreams for themselves?*

> In casu quarto erit philosophus accuratior saepius ea themata moralia tractans aesthetice, quae ex Horatio adduxi §. 126.

In the fourth case will be the more accurate philosopher, who rather often treats aesthetically those moral themes which I adduced from Horace, § 126.

> § 493. [p. 316] Necessitas a veritate complete certa et strictissima recedendi erit aesthetica pulcre cogitaturo, 5) quando tanti non est, vt examinetur, quod ponendum est, an accurate verum, an tantum sit verisimile §. 430. 454. 6) Quando venit in mentem rei, quae num in se sit possibilis, nec ne, parum liqueat, §. 431. illud tamen liqueat, pulcre rem eam meditanti rationis analogo nihil absurditatis afferri, §. 431, 455. 7) Cogitando incidas in euentum, de quo dynamometria tua non exacte decidat, an viribus caussarum viuis plenus accurate sit aequalis, neque tamen dynamometriae naturali videatur cognitis sensitiue viribus vlla ratione, vel turpiter minor, vel maior, §. 432. 457.

§ 493. [p. 316] The aesthetic necessity of withdrawing from completely certain and most strict truth will arise for one who is to think beautifully, 5) when it is not worth so much to examine whether what must be set down is accurately true or only verisimilar, § 430. 454. 6) When there comes into his mind a thing of which it is little clear whether it is possible in itself or not, § 431, yet this much is clear, that to one meditating the thing beautifully nothing of absurdity is brought before the analogue of reason, § 431, 455. 7) When in thinking you fall upon an event about which your dynamometry does not decide exactly whether the full effect is accurately equal to the living forces of the causes, and yet to natural dynamometry, with the forces sensately cognised, it does not seem in any respect either disgracefully less or greater, § 432. 457.

> § 494. In casu quinto Virgilius Aen. I. 706. canit:

§ 494. In the fifth case Virgil, Aen. I. 706, sings:

> *Quinquaginta intus famulae, quibus ordine longo / Cura penum struere et flammis adolere penates. / Centum aliae, totidemque pares aetate ministri, / Qui dapibus mensas onerent, et pocula ponant.*

*Fifty maidservants within, whose charge it is in long order / to lay out the provisions and to make the hearth-gods glow with flames; / a hundred others, and as many attendants matched in age, / to load the tables with dishes and set out the cups.*

> [p. 317] numeris rotundis contentus errore calculi saluo. In casu sexto fuit Aeneas, quando:

[p. 317] content with round numbers, allowing for an error of reckoning. In the sixth case was Aeneas, when:

> *O! quam,* ait, *te memorem, virgo? namque haud tibi vultus / Mortales, nec vox huminem [sic: hominem] sonat. O! dea certe, / Aut Phoebi soror, aut nympharum sanguinis vna!*

*O! how,* he says, *shall I name you, maiden? for your countenance is not / mortal, nor does your voice sound human. O! a goddess surely, / either Phoebus’ sister, or one of the blood of the nymphs!*

> In casu septimo Virgilium lege, quando ipsi Nisus et Euryalus l. IX. 176-450. describuntur, vt huius verisimilitudo, iuxta Statii falsitatem posita, §. 460, 461. magis elucescat.

In the seventh case read Virgil, when Nisus and Euryalus are described by him, l. IX. 176–450, so that the verisimilitude of this, set beside the falsity of Statius, § 460, 461, may shine forth the more.

> § 495. Necessitas aesthetica a veritate, complete certa, et strictissima, saepius deueniendi ad verisimilitudinem erit, 8) quando morato latius cogitandi genere §. 226. iam nouam ἤθους speciem, §. 193. obseruaturus, §. 433. incidat in pingendum euentum cum moralibus personarum semel constitutarum characteribus, moribus maiorum, et consuetudinibus, aetate, patria e. c. apprime conspirare visum, §. 434. nec vlla ratione male qui habeat moralem analogi rationis dynamometrian, §. 462. cuius tamen euentus non complete certa sit strictissima veritas. In hoc casu Virgilius fuit Aenean armis induens pro patria Troia. l. II. §. 309.

§ 495. The aesthetic necessity of descending rather often from completely certain and most strict truth to verisimilitude will arise, 8) when one who, in the moral manner of thinking in the broader sense, § 226, is about to observe a new species of ἦθος [character], § 193, § 433, falls upon an event to be painted which seems to agree exceedingly with the moral characters of persons once established, with the customs of their ancestors, and with usages, age, country, etc., § 434, and in no respect ill-treats the moral dynamometry of the analogue of reason, § 462, yet whose most strict truth is not completely certain. In this case was Virgil, arming Aeneas for his country Troy, l. II. § 309.

> § 496. [p. 318] Necessitas verisimilitudinis pro exacte cognita veritate amplectendae aesthetica erit 9) quando, quid in certis virum bonum circumstantibus recte agendi occasionibus, ille, vel simpliciter honestus, vel nobilis, vel omnino heros vere egerit, tacet historia, tacet experientia, sed ἦθος docet et moratum strictius cogitandi genus, quid agere debuerit, tunc enim ad hanc veritatem moralem, licet veri tantum similem, §. 435. caute confugiendum est, §. 463-467. In hoc casu Virgilius erat descripturus, quid Aeneas in Pallantis funere dixerit egeritue, l. XI. 25.--100. et omnes paene veteres historici, quando suis inserunt habitas orationes.

§ 496. [p. 318] The aesthetic necessity of embracing verisimilitude in place of exactly cognised truth will arise 9) when, as to what a good man, whether simply honourable, or noble, or altogether a hero, truly did in certain circumstances surrounding him, on occasions for acting rightly, history is silent, experience is silent, but ἦθος [character] and the moral manner of thinking in the stricter sense teach what he ought to have done; for then refuge must cautiously be taken, § 463–467, in this moral truth, though only verisimilar, § 435. In this case was Virgil, about to describe what Aeneas said or did at the funeral of Pallas, l. XI. 25–100, and almost all the ancient historians, when they insert into their works the speeches that were delivered.

> § 497. 10.) Quando verae strictissime et completa cum certitudine rationes pulcre cogitandi, et vera eiusmodi consectaria, vel ignorantur, vel supra horizontem aestheticum posita sunt, vel ob alias caussas e. g. dignitatem et decorum, afferri non possunt, neque tamen hiatus turpis, aut aliquid omnino frustra factum sensibus analogoque rationis obiicienda sunt. §. 436. 468. In hoc casu Virgilius fuit, videns exercendae fortitudinis heroi suo se multas et magnas rationes suppeditare debere, multos et magnos hostes, L. VII. 641.

§ 497. 10.) When the most strictly true reasons, with complete certainty, for thinking beautifully, and true consequences of this kind, are either unknown, or placed above the aesthetic horizon, or for other causes, e.g. dignity and decorum, cannot be adduced, and yet neither a disgraceful gap nor anything at all done in vain is to be set before the senses and the analogue of reason, § 436. 468. In this case was Virgil, seeing that he had to supply his hero with many and great reasons for exercising fortitude, many and great enemies, L. VII. 641.

> [p. 319] *Pandite nunc Helicona, deae, cantusque mouete, / Qui bello exciti reges, quae quemque sequutae / Complerint campos acies, quibus Itala iam tum, / Floruerit terra alma viris, quibus arserit armis, / Et meministis enim, Diuae, et memorare potestis, / Ad nos vix tenuis famae perlabitur aura.*

[p. 319] *Open Helicon now, goddesses, and stir your songs: / what kings were roused to war, what battle-lines, following each, / filled the plains, with what men the Italian land, / the nourishing land, even then flourished, with what arms it blazed; / for you remember, divine ones, and you can recount, / to us scarcely a thin breath of fame glides down.*

> § 498. 11) Quando, quaedam ob ipsam forsan veritatem strictissimam, vel ob famam saltim, et quoniam eorum iam est nonnulla in spectatorum animis anticipatio, pulcre cogitanda sunt, quae tamen in vnitatem aestheticam grauius offendere videri possent, §. 439. 469. Tunc enim multa opus est verisimilitudine, ne iunxisse turpiter censearis insociabilia. Accedens ad implementum paradoxi, et inexspectati oraculi:

§ 498. 11) When certain things, perhaps on account of the most strict truth itself, or at least on account of their fame, and because there is already some anticipation of them in the minds of the spectators, are to be thought beautifully, which nevertheless might seem to offend more gravely against aesthetic unity, § 439. 469. For then there is need of much verisimilitude, lest you be judged to have disgracefully joined things that cannot be associated. Coming to the fulfilment of the paradoxical and unexpected oracle,

> *via prima salutis, / Quod minime reris, Graia pandetur ab vrbe,* VI. 96.

*the first way of safety, / which you least expect, shall be opened from a Greek city,* VI. 96,

> describendum Virgilius, ne male coacta sub vnum ducem arma graeca et troiana, vel analogo rationis, iudicentur, quanta opera mitescere [p. 320] curat inopinatum euentum. l. VIII. Deus interest, quoniam nodus eo vindice dignus adest, Tiberinus pater, qui consilium det Arcades adeundi,

which had to be described, Virgil, lest Greek and Trojan arms badly forced together under one leader be judged so, even by the analogue of reason, takes how great pains to soften [p. 320] the unlooked-for event, l. VIII. A god intervenes, since a knot worthy of such a deliverer is at hand, father Tiberinus, who gives the counsel of approaching the Arcadians,

> *Qui bellum assidue ducunt cum gente latina.* 55.

*who wage war continually with the Latin people,* 55.

> Aeneas ipse proficiscitur, non oratores mittit, nec se modo *Troiugenas* memorat, sed et statim

Aeneas himself sets out, he does not send envoys, nor does he merely call himself and his men *Trojan-born*, but also at once

> *tela inimica latinis,* 117. e. c.

*weapons hostile to the Latins,* 117, etc.

> § 499. 12) Quando de generalibus et per abstractam notionum regionem, veritas logica, vel ita latet in fundo, vt ne per intellectum quidem et rationem pulcre cogitaturi, inde erui possit, aut altius longiusque petita saltim tuis praecipuis obiectis personalibus videbitur, nisi omnino falsa, quoniam ea non continet, quae fieri solent, et quorum habent intra mentem anticipationes; altera autem opinio de iisdem generalibus, quae cum priori sententia simul esse vera non potest, innocuis tamen rationibus, et absque dolo malo, sine fraude nefanda, commendari potest, §. 470. popularior et veri maioris aliquid spirans, §. 440. e. g. Quanquam logice verum est aliquam salutem publicam non sine bello et per arma vere parari: tamen

§ 499. 12) When concerning general matters, and through the abstract region of notions, logical truth either lies so hidden at the bottom that it cannot be dug out from there even through the intellect and reason of one who is to think beautifully, or will seem, at least to your principal personal objects, to be fetched from too deep and too far, if not altogether false, since it does not contain those things which are wont to happen and of which they have anticipations within the mind; while another opinion about the same general matters, which cannot be true together with the former judgement, can nevertheless be commended by innocent reasons, and without evil deceit, without nefarious fraud, § 470, being more popular and breathing something of a greater truth, § 440. E.g. Although it is logically true that some public safety is truly procured not without war and through arms: nevertheless

> *Nulla salus bello.*

*There is no safety in war.*

> [p. 321] Quanquam sunt, qui omnia horrent, praeter ignauum otium, et omnia, quae supra se deprehendunt, nihil ad se pertinere iudicant, ex animi sententia, tamen

[p. 321] Although there are those who shudder at everything except idle leisure, and judge that everything they find to be above them is no concern of theirs, in the sincere opinion of their mind, nevertheless

> *Nil mortalibus arduum est, / Caelum ipsum petimus stultitia.*

*Nothing is too arduous for mortals, / we seek heaven itself in our folly.*

> § 500. 13) Ipsum veritatis studium, quod esse potest, maximum mentiri nonnunquam, i.e. latissime falsa, aut ea cogitare cogit, quae num logice strictissimeque sint omnino vera, ipse nescit, aestheticum. Pone eum exacte cognitum verum cogitare posse admodum abstractum, generale, et vniuersale, = circiter 20°. Pone ipsi venire in mentem determinatioris, minus generalis, minus abstracti; quod salua reliqua pulcritudine posset priori substituere. Sint in hoc 40 varia. De decem ex iis aut dubitet, an omni modo vera sint, aut omnino videat ea non esse purioris ad rationis examen defendenda, licet non dent falsitatem aestheticam, S. XXVIII. Reliqua 30 probe conspirent ad principia veri catholica, praesertim quatenus analogo rationis patent, et simul maiorem, ac prius, vbertatem, dignitatem, lucem e. c. dent themati, ac prius logice verum et complete certum, = 10°. In hoc casu prius eligens dabis verum = 20°. Posterius praeferens exhibes verum [p. 322] ad minimum = 40° — 10° = 30°. Hinc ipsum veritatis studium ad posterius falsum priori vero praeponendum impellere potest, §. 441.

§ 500. 13) The very pursuit of truth, which can be very great, sometimes compels the aesthetician to lie, i.e. to think things false in the broadest sense, or things of which he himself does not know whether they are altogether true logically and most strictly. Suppose he can think an exactly cognised truth, very abstract, general and universal, = about 20°. Suppose there comes into his mind something more determinate, less general, less abstract, which, the rest of the beauty being preserved, he could substitute for the former. Let there be in this 40 various things. Of ten of them let him either doubt whether they are true in every way, or see altogether that they are not to be defended before the examination of purer reason, although they do not yield aesthetic falsity, S. XXVIII. Let the remaining 30 agree properly with the catholic principles of truth, especially in so far as they lie open to the analogue of reason, and at the same time give the theme greater richness, dignity, light, etc. than the former, the logically true and completely certain, = 10°. In this case, choosing the former, you will give truth = 20°. Preferring the latter, you exhibit truth [p. 322] at least = 40° − 10° = 30°. Hence the very pursuit of truth can impel one to set the latter falsehood before the former truth, § 441.

> § 501. Est veritas generalis: Vir bonus iniquis etiam suspicionibus eorum, quos amat, aliquando cedit. Nonne autem illa maior apparet analogo rationis apud legentes Liu. II. 6. *in Valerium Consulem, non inuidiam solum, sed suspicionem etiam, cum atroci crimine, ortam, eum regnum affectare, quia aedificabat in summa Velia? Ibi alto et munito loco arcem inexpugnabilem fore.* Conuocato autem *in concilium populo* tunc Valerium in aliis dixisse: *Non obstabunt P. Valerii aedes libertati vestrae, Quirites. Tuta vobis erit Velia. Deferam non in planum modo aedes, sed colli etiam subiiciam, vt vos supra suspectum me ciuem habitetis. In Velia aedificent, quibus melius, quam Valerio, libertas creditur. Delatam* postea *confestim* esse *materiam omnem infra Veliam, et in infimo cliuo domum aedificatam.* Hinc opiniones ita *in contrarium versas* esse, vt *popularis* abhinc sit habitus, *vnde cognomen Publicolae.* Si maior haec Liuiana veritas recte iudicatur aliquo respectu, ac generalis illa; meminerimus orationem ementitum esse Liuium, §. 496.

§ 501. It is a general truth: a good man sometimes yields even to the unjust suspicions of those whom he loves. But does not that truth appear greater to the analogue of reason in those who read Liv. II. 6, that *against Valerius the consul there arose not only envy, but even suspicion, with an atrocious charge, that he was aiming at kingship, because he was building on the top of the Velia; that there, on a high and fortified spot, there would be an impregnable citadel?* And that, having summoned *the people to an assembly*, Valerius then said among other things: *The house of P. Valerius will not stand in the way of your liberty, Quirites. The Velia will be safe for you. I shall not only bring my house down to the plain, but shall set it beneath the hill, so that you may dwell above me, a suspected citizen. Let those build on the Velia to whom liberty is better entrusted than to Valerius.* That *brought down* afterwards *straightway* were *all the materials below the Velia, and the house built at the lowest part of the slope.* That hence opinions were so *turned to the contrary* that from then on he was held *a friend of the people, whence the surname Publicola.* If this Livian truth is rightly judged greater in some respect than that general one, let us remember that Livy invented the speech, § 496.

> § 502. [p. 323] 14) Sit strictissime verum aliquando, quod non ita raro contingit, hac ratione comparatum, vt non ex opinione vulgi tantum, sed etiam bonis factorum criticis falsi singulariter simile videatur, neque tamen vires locusue sint venuste cogitaturo multis eius vindicare verisimilitudinem, aut destituatur, quantum illud cognoscitur, requisita pulcritudini cogitatorum, vbertate, dignitate, luce, e. c. §. 22, solum si sit, et nullis exornatum latissime falsis. Habes in vnum contractos multos casus, in quibus veris heterocosmicis, quae strictissime vero vel substituantur, vel immisceantur, opus esse videatur. §. 444, 475.

§ 502. [p. 323] 14) Let something be most strictly true at some time, which happens not so rarely, so constituted that not only in the opinion of the crowd, but even to good critics of facts, it seems singularly like falsehood, nor yet does one who is to think charmingly have the strength or the room to vindicate its verisimilitude to many; or let it be destitute, so far as it is cognised, of the things required for the beauty of thoughts, richness, dignity, light, etc., § 22, if it stands alone and is adorned with nothing false in the broadest sense. You have gathered into one the many cases in which there seems to be need of heterocosmic truths, which are either substituted for the most strictly true or mingled with it, § 444, 475.

> § 503. Quoniam itaque tot necessitatibus vrgetur pulcre cogitaturus a veritate, quam dicunt, transeundi ad solam aliquam verisimilitudinem, §. 491-502: non raro *poeta fiet.*

§ 503. Since therefore one who is to think beautifully is pressed by so many necessities of passing from truth, as they call it, to some mere verisimilitude, § 491–502: not rarely *he will become a poet.*

> *Poeta, tabulas quum cepit sibi, / Quaerit, quod nusquam est gentium, reperit tamen, / Facit illud veri simile, quod mendacium est.* Plaut. Pseud. l. 4. v. 8.

*The poet, when he has taken his tablets to himself, / seeks what is nowhere in the world, and yet finds it, / he makes that like the truth which is a lie.* Plaut. Pseud. l. 4. v. 8.

> Aestheticus autem veritatem metaphysicam et aestheticologicam distinguens, vt obiectum et perceptionem eiusdem, vti rem, [p. 324] et conceptum de re; hanc aestheticologicam notat esse vel complete claram, vel minus. Priorem veritatem dicunt, posteriorem verisimilitudinem. Philosophus priorem completam certitudinem dicit; alteram veritatem in incertis, probabilibus, dubiis, improbabilibus. Hinc aestheticus suadet non in solis complete certis pulcre verum quaerere, sed idem rimari simul per incerta, probabilium, dubiorum, improbabilium, quamdiu semet ipsum non subducit amatoris oculis in turpem falsi similitudinem, vel ipsam falsi turpitudinem desinens. S. XXVIII.

But the aesthetician, distinguishing metaphysical and aesthetico-logical truth, as the object and the perception of it, as the thing [p. 324] and the concept of the thing, notes that this aesthetico-logical truth is either completely clear or less so. The former they call truth, the latter verisimilitude. The philosopher calls the former complete certainty; the other, truth in uncertain, probable, doubtful, improbable things. Hence the aesthetician advises that the beautifully true be sought not only among things completely certain, but that the same be searched out at the same time through the uncertain, through probable, doubtful, improbable things, so long as he does not withdraw himself from the lover’s eyes, ending in a disgraceful likeness of the false, or in the very disgrace of the false, S. XXVIII.

> § 504. Pulcre cogitaturus consilium, §. 503. prosequitur, circumstrepentibus falsi rumoribus, vnam veritatem, plerumque per incerta, sectatus,

§ 504. One who is to think beautifully follows the counsel, § 503, and, amid the surrounding din of rumours of falsehood, pursuing the one truth, mostly through uncertainties,

> *populumque falsis / Dedocet vti*

*and unteaches the people / to use false*

> *vocibus* falsi mendaciorumque, aut in verbis facilis de rerum et vitae veritate sibi gratulatur in sinu, quando nonnunquam per mediam, quam Falsitatis et Mendaciorum aiunt, siluam in plena sese refulgens offert luce

*words* of falsehood and of lies, or, easy in words, congratulates himself in his bosom on the truth of things and of life, when sometimes, through the midst of what they call the forest of Falsity and Lies, there offers herself, shining back in full light,

> *Pudor, et Iustitiae soror / Incorrupta Fides, nudaque Veritas.*

*Modesty, and Justice’s sister, / uncorrupted Faith, and naked Truth.*

[p. 325]

#### Sectio XXX. Fictiones. — Section XXX. Fictions

> § 505. Quae non totidem ideis sensimus, quot denuo cogitamus, quaeque tamen sensitiue cognoscenda sunt, sunt fingenda, M. §. 589. Hinc FICTIONES LATIVS DICTAE, M. §. 590. perceptiones combinando praescindendoque phantasmata formatae, longe maximam pulcre cogitandorum partem constituunt.

§ 505. Those things which we have not sensed in as many ideas as we think anew, and which nevertheless are to be sensately cognised, must be feigned, M. § 589. Hence FICTIONS IN THE BROADER SENSE, M. § 590, perceptions formed by combining and abstracting phantasms, make up by far the greatest part of the things to be thought beautifully.

> *Ficta voluptatis caussa sint proxima veris,* §. 504.

*Things feigned for the sake of pleasure should be very near the true,* § 504.

> § 506. Non proxima solum veris, sed et ipsa strictissime vera plurima, non nisi fictionibus latius dictis pulcre cogitari sensitiueque possunt. Quot ea sunt obiectorum pulcre cogitaturi, de quibus ille possit dicere: *quae ipse vidi,*

§ 506. Not only things very near the true, but even very many things themselves most strictly true, cannot be thought beautifully and sensately except by fictions in the broader sense. How many are those objects of one who is to think beautifully of which he could say: *which I myself saw,*

> *Et quorum pars magna fui?*

*And of which I was a great part?*

> Nec in his fictionibus carent, nisi experientiae stricte dictae, si narrentur omnino pure nudeque. Reliqua huius vniuersi vel praeterita, si narrem secundum fidem historicam, neque tamen stricte expertus, vel praesentia [p. 326] tempore, si percipiam absentia loco sensitiue, vel futura, etiamsi tandem ex mea praeconceptione fiant in hoc vniuerso, vt turris ex anticipatione architecti, tamen sunt FICTIONES (latius dictae, §. 505.) quas dicere liceat STRICTISSIME VERAS.

Nor are these without fictions, save only experiences strictly so called, if they are narrated altogether purely and nakedly. The remaining things of this universe, whether past, if I narrate them according to historical faith, yet without having strictly experienced them, or present [p. 326] in time, if I sensately perceive them absent in place, or future, even if at last they come to pass in this universe from my preconception, as a tower from the anticipation of the architect, are nevertheless FICTIONS (in the broader sense, § 505) which it is permissible to call MOST STRICTLY TRUE.

> § 507. Erunt itaque fictiones, sicuti veritates, falsitates et verisimilitudines, vel generales, vel singulares, et hae vel huius vniuersi cognitionem ingredientur, vel erunt heterocosmicae, §. 445, 441. Generales habent suas regulas S. XXVIIII. Singulares, pars cognitionis de hoc vniuerso venustae, aut erunt strictissime verae, §. 506, res facti, vel euentus praesentes, vel vere futura sistentes, quae tamen ipse cogitans non stricte expertus est, aut minus. Quae cognitione huius vniuersi percipiuntur, neque tamen accurate intuitiua, hinc fictiones latius dictae, §. 505. sunt FICTIONES HISTORICAE LATE DICTAE.

§ 507. Fictions, therefore, like truths, falsities and verisimilitudes, will be either general or singular, and the latter will either enter into the cognition of this universe or be heterocosmic, § 445, 441. The general ones have their rules, S. XXVIIII. The singular ones, a part of the charming cognition of this universe, will either be most strictly true, § 506, presenting matters of fact, or present events, or things truly future, which however the thinker himself has not strictly experienced, or less so. Those which are perceived in the cognition of this universe, yet not with accurate intuition, hence fictions in the broader sense, § 505, are HISTORICAL FICTIONS IN THE BROAD SENSE.

> § 508. Troianas romanorum origines narrant Virgilius et Liuius l. I. vterque non expertus, hinc vterque per fictionem historicam late dictam, §. 507. Ille Aenean narrat insciis Graiis et hostibus per fugam elapsum, hic in *Aeneam,* et ob *vetustum hospitii ius,* et [p. 327] quia *pacis reddendaeque Helenae semper auctor fuerat,* nullum *ius belli Achiuos* exercuisse. Ille Aenean primo ducit in Thraciam, hic in Macedoniam. Aduentum Aeneae in Italiam proxime sequuta vterque diuersim mente concipiunt. Illi Ascanius, ac Iulus idem Creusae filius. Huic *Ascanius ex Lauinia natus,* addenti tamen; *Haud nihil ambigam (quis enim rem tam veterem pro certo affirmet?) Hiccine fuerit Ascanius, an maior, quam hic, Creusa natus matre, Ilio incolumi, comesque inde paternae fugae, quem Iulum eundem Iulia gens auctorem nominis sui nuncupat. Vbicunque et quacunque matre genitus, certe natum Aenea constat.* Vbicunque et quocunque patre genita sit fictio strictissime vera, §. 506. amborum hae, praeter alias, sunt fictiones historicae late dictae, §. 507. Ascanius in Aeneide est persona verisimilis, S. XXVIIII.

§ 508. The Trojan origins of the Romans are narrated by Virgil and by Livy, l. I, neither having experienced them, hence each through a historical fiction in the broad sense, § 507. The former narrates that Aeneas escaped by flight unbeknown to the Greeks and the enemy; the latter, that against *Aeneas*, both on account of *the ancient right of hospitality* and [p. 327] because *he had always been an advocate of peace and of the restoration of Helen*, *the Achaeans* exercised no *right of war*. The former first leads Aeneas into Thrace, the latter into Macedonia. The events that next followed the arrival of Aeneas in Italy the two conceive in their minds differently. For the former, Ascanius and Iulus are the same, the son of Creusa. For the latter, *Ascanius* is *born of Lavinia*, though he adds: *I shall not deny some doubt (for who could affirm a matter so ancient as certain?) whether this was Ascanius, or an elder one than he, born of his mother Creusa while Ilium was still unharmed, and thereafter the companion of his father’s flight, the same whom the Julian clan, calling him Iulus, names as the author of their name. Wherever and of whatever mother born, it is agreed at any rate that he was the son of Aeneas.* Wherever and of whatever father the most strictly true fiction be born, § 506, these, besides others, are historical fictions in the broad sense of both authors, § 507. Ascanius in the Aeneid is a verisimilar person, S. XXVIIII.

> § 509. Fictiones historicae late dictae omnem cognitionem huius vniuersi apud pulcre cogitantem complexae, quam ipse non expertus est, aut sistunt saltim inexperto strictissime veros euentus huius vniuersi fictiones strictissime verae, §. 506, aut talia, quae suppositis omnibus in hoc vniuerso nobis sensitiue notis euentibus et momentis euentum circumstantibus, tamen fieri potuissent aut possent, et erunt FICTIONES, etiamsi a [p. 328] poëtis cogitentur, STRICTIVS HISTORICAE.

§ 509. Historical fictions in the broad sense, embracing all the cognition of this universe in one who thinks beautifully which he has not himself experienced, either present, at least to one who has not experienced them, most strictly true events of this universe, being most strictly true fictions, § 506, or such things as, all the events sensately known to us in this universe and the moments surrounding the event being supposed, nevertheless could have happened or could happen; and these will be FICTIONS, even if they are thought by [p. 328] poets, HISTORICAL IN THE STRICTER SENSE.

> § 510. Turnus Virgilii Aeneae tantum, *Turnus* Liuii *Aeneae Latinoque simul bellum infert,* et hic eo euentu, vt *Aborigines Troianique ducem Latinum victores amittant.* Mezentius Virgilii ab Aenea occiditur. Mezentius Liuii ab Aenea vincitur quidem, sed *operum mortalium* hoc *vltimo* patrato Aeneas sepelitur, Mezentio superstite. Vnum horum auctorem solum legenti tantum abest, vt fictionum vel strictius historicarum ipsius narrationes suspectae esse possent, vt eas potius in fictionibus strictissime veris haberet, §. 506. Conferenti tamen vtrumque non licet per auctoritatem Liuii Virgilianas fabulas numerare in fictionibus strictius historicis, §. 509.

§ 510. Virgil’s Turnus makes war on Aeneas only; Livy’s *Turnus makes war on Aeneas and Latinus together*, and this with the outcome that *the Aborigines and the Trojans, victorious, lose their leader Latinus*. Virgil’s Mezentius is killed by Aeneas. Livy’s Mezentius is indeed conquered by Aeneas, but, this *last of mortal works* accomplished, Aeneas is buried, Mezentius surviving. To one who reads only one of these authors, so far is it from being the case that his narratives could be suspected of being fictions, even historical in the stricter sense, that he would rather hold them among the most strictly true fictions, § 506. Yet to one who compares the two it is not permissible, on the authority of Livy, to count the Virgilian fables among the historical fictions in the stricter sense, § 509.

#### Sectio XXXI. Fictiones Poeticae. — Section XXXI. Poetic Fictions

> § 511. Si fingantur talia, quae ob notam et cogitanti et cogitaturis ipso duce, sicuti praesumi debet, circumstantiam, et hypothesin euentumque huius mundi certum, in eodem hoc vniverso locum non habeant, vt eiusdem [p. 329] possibilia, supposita tamen alia quadam hypothesi, quae non est possibile huius vniuersi, fieri pulcre potuissent aut possent, vel turpiter, per cognitionem mediam: tales FICTIONES heterocosmicae, §. 441, quia inuentor earum, quasi nouum creat orbem fingendo, si vel maxime ab historico proferantur, dicuntur POETICAE.

§ 511. If such things are feigned as, on account of a circumstance known both to the thinker and to those who are to think under his guidance, as must be presumed, and on account of a certain hypothesis and event of this world, have no place in this same universe, so that, as [p. 329] possibilities of it, on the supposition however of some other hypothesis which is not a possibility of this universe, they could have happened or could happen beautifully, or disgracefully, through middle cognition: such heterocosmic FICTIONS, § 441, since their inventor as it were creates a new world by feigning, even if they are most of all put forward by a historian, are called POETIC.

> § 512. Ira Iunonis Aen. I. 19-85. est fictio poetica, tempestas -- 127. historica. Neptunus aequorum pacator poetica -- 160. Troianorum descensus in Africam historica -- 227, nisi cerui dubium moueant. Colloquium Iouis et Veneris, legatioque Mercurii est fictio poetica, v. 308.

§ 512. The wrath of Juno, Aen. I. 19–85, is a poetic fiction; the storm, – 127, historical. Neptune, the pacifier of the seas, poetic, – 160. The landing of the Trojans in Africa historical, – 227, unless the stags raise a doubt. The conversation of Jupiter and Venus and the embassy of Mercury are a poetic fiction, v. 308.

> *At pius Aeneas per noctem plurima voluens, / Vt primum lux alma data est, exire, locosque / Explorare nouos, quas vento accesserit oras, / Qui teneant, (nam inculta videt) hominesne feraene, / Quaerere constituit, sociisque exacta referre* -- 317.

*But pious Aeneas, turning over many things through the night, / as soon as the kindly light was given, resolved to go out and to explore / the new places, what shores he had reached by the wind, / who hold them (for he sees them uncultivated), whether men or beasts, / and to report his findings to his companions* – 317,

> est fictio historica. Hinc incipit poetica de Didone fictio vltra l. I-V. protensa, §. 509, 511.

is a historical fiction. Here begins the poetic fiction of Dido, extended beyond l. I–V, § 509, 511.

> § 513. [p. 330] Complexum et satis male cohaerens systema fictionum omnis generis iam a pluribus elegantioribus ingeniis adoptatarum et suppositarum synecdochice dicamus MVNDVM POETARVM. Hic enim cosmogoniae philosophorum pleraeque, ne excepta quidem Cartesiana, non minus locum inueniunt, ac theogoniae veterum theologorum, et quicquid est mythologiae, non notioris illius solum, graecae ac romanae, sed et per alias gentes ab Indis ad Eddam πατροπαράδοτα. Huc acta sanctorum ex omni sua parte, quae vel historice, vel poetice ficta sit, ipsa signa illorum, ductus, positusque, quibus pingi sculpique solent. Huius terra quaedam noua est mundus cabbalisticus cum suis quatuor elementorum incolis, olim admodum in obscuro qui habitauerant. e. c.

§ 513. [p. 330] The complex and rather badly coherent system of fictions of every kind, already adopted and supposed by many of the more elegant wits, let us call synecdochically the WORLD OF THE POETS. For here most of the cosmogonies of the philosophers, not even the Cartesian excepted, find a place no less than the theogonies of the ancient theologians, and whatever there is of mythology, not only of that better-known one, Greek and Roman, but also of what is πατροπαράδοτα [handed down from the fathers] among other nations from the Indians to the Edda. Here belong the acts of the saints in every part of them that is feigned either historically or poetically, their very signs, the lineaments and postures with which they are wont to be painted and sculpted. A certain new land of this world is the cabbalistic world with its inhabitants of the four elements, who had once dwelt very much in obscurity, etc.

> § 514. In mundo poetarum est quaedam admodum late patens regio chimaerarum, fictionum omni veritate metaphysica, quae suis obiectis inesset, destitutarum, quam mundi poetarum dicamus VTOPIAM. Magna pars mundi fabulosi postquam est ingressa mundum poetarum, illum non tanget vltra limites, §. 456. pulcre cogitaturus. Contra hanc regulam impingunt, 1) qui nunc aeque sibi [p. 331] licitum putant ex mythologia veterum multa nugari, ac illud licitum olim graecis romanisque fuit, quorum spectatores praecipui per analogon rationis eiusdem absurda non eo vsque penetrauerant, ac nunc omnes, qui vix aere lauantur.

§ 514. In the world of the poets there is a certain very widely extended region of chimeras, fictions destitute of all the metaphysical truth that might be in their objects, which let us call the UTOPIA of the world of the poets. A great part of the fabulous world, after it has entered the world of the poets, will not be touched beyond its limits, § 456, by one who is to think beautifully. Against this rule offend 1) those who now think it equally [p. 331] permissible to themselves to trifle much out of the mythology of the ancients as that was once permissible to the Greeks and Romans, whose principal spectators had not, through the analogue of reason, penetrated so far into its absurdities as now all do who scarcely bathe for a copper.

> § 515. 2) Qui omnino nugas eiusmodi systemati optimo maximo verissimae religionis immiscent, aut iis auditoribus occinunt, quibus serpentes non auibus, sed angelis, aut certe columbis, geminare videantur, si vel ex solo suo sensitiuo iudicio ac sapore, non publico quidem, probe tamen maturo, pessime cohaerentem eiusmodi lucis et tenebrarum coagmentationem examinent, §. 415. Ipse Virgilius aduocans in auxilium, quicquid est vbique numinum rusticorum Georg. I.

§ 515. 2) Those who altogether mingle trifles of this kind into the best and greatest system of the truest religion, or chant them to those hearers to whom serpents would seem to be paired not with birds, but with angels, or at any rate with doves, if they examine, even by their own sensate judgement and taste alone, not public indeed, yet properly mature, so wretchedly incoherent a cementing-together of light and darkness of this kind, § 415. Virgil himself, calling to his aid whatever rustic divinities there are anywhere, Georg. I,

> *Diique deaeque omnes, studium quibus arua tueri, / Quique nouas alitis nonnullo semine fruges,* v. 21.

*All ye gods and goddesses, whose care it is to guard the fields, / And who nourish the new crops by no seed of man,* v. 21.

> probe cauet, ne quem deorum suis immisceat, quos venerantur tantum *sanctae gentes,*

carefully takes care not to mingle with his own any of the gods whom only *holy nations* venerate,

> *quibus haec nascuntur in hortis / Numina.* Iuu. XV.

*among whom these divinities grow in gardens.* Iuu. XV.

> [p. 332] § 516. Quaedam fictio poetica, §. 511. mundi poetici, §. 513, non tangens turpiter vtopiam, §. 514, 515. cuidam ex eodem parti conformiter, etiam positiue, i. e. ita concipiet suum orbem, quem creat heterocosmice fingendo, vt hic bene cohaereat, quantum aesthetice suos praecipuos auditores rem scrutaturos debet praesumere, probe cognitae parti mundi poetarum, ex eius anticipationibus mente formari possit, ita euentus suos sistat, vti solitum est, in regione mundi poetici data, habeat cum eadem vnitatem aestheticam, et ex eadem suam mutuo verisimilitudinem accipiat. Eiusmodi FIGMENTVM POETICVM dicamus ANALOGICVM.

[p. 332] § 516. A certain poetic fiction, § 511, of the poetic world, § 513, not shamefully touching upon utopia, § 514, 515, in conformity with a certain part of that same world, even positively, i.e. it will so conceive its own orb, which it creates by heterocosmic feigning, that this coheres well, so far as it ought aesthetically to presume that its principal hearers will scrutinise the matter, with the properly known part of the poets’ world, could be formed in the mind from the anticipations of that part, so presents its events, as is customary, in a given region of the poetic world, has aesthetic unity with the same, and receives from the same in turn its own verisimilitude. Let us call a POETIC FIGMENT of this kind ANALOGICAL.

> § 517. Harum fictionum praeceptum est Horatii, secundum S. XXVIIII.

§ 517. The precept for these fictions is Horace’s, according to S. XXVIIII.

> *Scriptor, honoratum si forte reponis Achillem, / Impiger, iracundus, inexorabilis, acer, / Iura neget sibi nata, nihil non arroget armis, / Sit Medea ferox inuictaque, flebilis Ino, / Perfidus Ixion, Io vaga, tristis Orestes.* A. P. 120.

*Writer, if perchance you put honoured Achilles back upon the stage, / Let him be tireless, wrathful, inexorable, keen, / Let him deny that laws were born for him, let him claim everything by arms, / Let Medea be fierce and unconquered, Ino tearful, / Ixion treacherous, Io a wanderer, Orestes mournful.* A. P. 120.

> Non leuiter moueor hic pro: *honoratum Homereum* [p. 333] cum Bentleio legere, licet rationem videam, cur honoratus Achilles dictus sit, cui summus et Alexandro etiam Magno inuidendus honor contigerit, ab optimo poetarum aeternitati consecrari. In his paene solis fictionibus poeticis acquieuit Virgilius.

I am not lightly moved here to read with Bentley *Homereum* for *honoratum*, [p. 333] though I see a reason why Achilles may have been called honoured, to whom fell the highest honour, to be envied even by Alexander the Great, of being consecrated to eternity by the best of poets. In these poetic fictions almost alone did Virgil rest content.

> § 518. FICTIO POETICA nouum ita creans orbem, vt eum nec cuidam ex mundo poetico regioni faciat admodum similem, aut conducentem et aptius haerentem, est PRORSVS IGNOTA. Huic quoniam non succurrit iam supponenda in spectatoribus verisimilitudo mundi poetici, §. 512. quoniam desunt anticipationes in iisdem bene multae, quas iam reperisset analogica fictio, §. 516. quoniam per ipsum mundum poeticum insolita est, nec in hoc vniuerso fieri potuit, §. 511. adeoqne [sic: adeoque] multis omnino falsi similis videbitur, §. 489. insignem habeat, oportet, verisimilitudinem internam, singularem venustius coniunctorum ordinem, successiuorum harmoniam et conuenientiam oculos multa cum luce ferientem, notabiliorem vnitatem, et generatim venustatem omnino singularem, si recto nihilominus talo stare debeat, satisque punctorum ferre, S. XXVII. §. 22.

§ 518. A POETIC FICTION so creating a new orb that it makes it neither very similar to any region of the poetic world, nor conducive to it and more aptly cohering with it, is WHOLLY UNKNOWN. Since the verisimilitude of the poetic world, now to be presupposed in the spectators, does not come to its aid, § 512, since there are lacking in the same a good many anticipations, which an analogical fiction would already have found, § 516, since by the poetic world itself it is unaccustomed, and could not have happened in this universe, § 511, and so will seem to many altogether like the false, § 489, it must have a remarkable internal verisimilitude, a singular order of things more charmingly conjoined, a harmony and agreement of successive things striking the eyes with much light, a more notable unity, and in general an altogether singular charm, if it is nonetheless to stand upon a straight ankle and win enough votes, S. XXVII. § 22.

> [p. 334] § 519. Hinc Horatius ex poemate tantae famae, ac Ilias est, rectius putat particulam aliquam diducere, A. P. 130.

[p. 334] § 519. Hence Horace thinks it more right to draw off some small part from a poem of such fame as the Iliad is, A. P. 130,

> *Quam si proferres ignota indictaque primus.*

*Than if you were the first to bring forth things unknown and unsaid.*

> Hinc denominationem sumsi fictionum, de quibus §. 518. Quales si quis tamen audeat, illum monet:

Hence I have taken the name of the fictions of which § 518. If anyone nevertheless dares such things, he warns him:

> *Si quid inexpertum scenae committis, et audes, / Personam formare nouam, seruetur ad imum, / Qualis ab incepto processerit et sibi constet. / Difficile est proprie communia dicere;*

*If you commit to the stage something untried, and dare / To form a new character, let it be kept to the end / Such as it went forth from the beginning, and be consistent with itself. / It is hard to say common things in one’s own way;*

> quod mihi sic videor recte interpretari: Veritates generales, quas nemo sibi videtur ignorare, primum in exemplo aliquo singulari sistere satis pulcras, quod nemo adhuc ante nos ex parte venustius pinxerit, prorsus adhuc ignotum: illud vero maioris est difficultatis, ac multis videatur.

which I think I interpret rightly thus: to present general truths, which no one thinks himself ignorant of, for the first time in some singular example, beautiful enough, which no one before us has yet in part painted more charmingly, is a thing still wholly unknown; but that is of greater difficulty than it seems to many.

> § 520. Fictio poetica, quae prae se quidem fert analogiam, nescio quam, cum mundo poetico, neque tamen multo post contra eandem, quam suam fecerat, mundi illius regionem grauiter impingit, eidem contradicentia affirmans, contra eius ἤθος pugnantia, quae fierent in eodem per casum purum, quae frustra [p. 335] fierent, quae seiungunt per eundem inseparabilia, spectatoribus obiiciens, erit talis fictio FIGMENTVM ANOMALON.

§ 520.
