Ex confusione duplicium dogmatica cogitandi generum, logici et aesthetici, duplex dominatur praeiudicata opinio 1) eorum, qui tunc etiam, quando de rigidiori primorum cognitionis alicuius vniuersalis principiorum intellectuali ac rationali theoria agitur, quam fieri potest exactissime, distinctissime, solidissimeque [p. 369] pertractanda, subsistunt in diluta, nec omnino leui, verisimili, satis perspicua, quantulumcunque certa, veritatis expositione, modo placeat illa satis auribus, oculisue, rationisque videatur ferre, vere ferat analogi potius rationis calculum. 2) Eorum, qui dogma quoddam ad captum minus exercitatorum in scientiis, vel omnino popularem intelligentiam, et viua quidem voce, proponendum cogitant, idque tamen breuissimis definitionibus, exactissimis axiomatibus, distinctissimis notionum resolutionibus, demonstrationibusque complete certis exornare nequicquam laborant. §. 567.

§ 568. From the confusion of the two dogmatic manners of thinking, the logical and the aesthetic, a twofold prejudiced opinion holds sway: 1) that of those who, even when it is a question of the more rigid intellectual and rational theory of the first principles of some universal cognition, to be treated as exactly, distinctly and solidly [p. 369] as can be done, stop short at a diluted, though not altogether light, verisimilar, sufficiently perspicuous, howsoever little certain exposition of truth, provided it pleases the ears or the eyes enough, and seems to bear the reckoning of reason, while in truth it bears rather that of the analogue of reason. 2) That of those who think that some dogma is to be propounded to the grasp of people less exercised in the sciences, or to altogether popular understanding, and that by the living voice, and yet labour in vain to adorn it with the briefest definitions, the most exact axioms, the most distinct resolutions of notions, and completely certain demonstrations. § 567.

> § 569. Genus cogitandi logicodogmaticum et aestheticodogmaticum, a potiori desumtis denominationibus, non forma solum inter se differunt, sed etiam materiis, quibus conuenire vel maxime prima fronte videbantur. Prius vti thematis sui principia potissimum sequitur, ita posterius principiata et consectaria. Prius vti potissimum eruit vniuersalia, sub quibus thema suum continetur, ita posterius eiusdem thematis inferiores conceptus attendit potissimum, quos sub se continet. Etiamsi materiae a tota disciplina nomen acceperint, sunt tamen in quauis disciplina prima quaedam ordine, quaedam in methodo synthetica velut vltima. Illa potissimum [p. 370] logicum, haec aestheticum ita sectatur per disciplinas cogitandi genus, vt dici circiter in qualibet possit, vbi desinit logicum, aestheticum cogitandi genus incipere. §. 566.

§ 569. The logico-dogmatic and the aesthetico-dogmatic manner of thinking, their names taken from the predominant feature, differ from one another not only in form, but also in the matters in which at first sight they seemed most of all to agree. As the former follows chiefly the principles of its theme, so the latter follows what is derived from the principles and the consequences. As the former chiefly draws out the universals under which its theme is contained, so the latter chiefly attends to the lower concepts of the same theme, which it contains under itself. Even if the matters have received their name from a whole discipline, there are nevertheless in any discipline certain things first in order, and certain things as it were last in the synthetic method. The former the logical, [p. 370] the latter the aesthetic manner of thinking so pursues through the disciplines that it can roughly be said, in any one of them, that where the logical manner of thinking leaves off, the aesthetic manner of thinking begins. § 566.

> § 570. Qui res interius perspexerunt, probe vident inter ea rerum genera, de quibus scientiae huc vsque stricte dictae cultae sunt, et indiuidua, interiacere adhuc magnam inferiorum generum, et specierum intercapedinem, in cuius raro territorium demonstratores descendant, in quod experimentatores et obseruatores accurati raro feliciter adscendant. Hoc est illud maxime stadium in quo cogitandi genus aestheticodogmaticum decurrat. Hinc vel ipsum sibi thema legit optime, vel thema etiam altius petitum eo tamen vsque detrahit, ad maiorem veritatem materialem, §. 440. etiamsi fiat eo ipso formaliter paullo minus exacta, secundum logicorum trutinam scientificam, i. e. elegantem ad verisimilitudinem. §. 565.

§ 570. Those who have looked more deeply into things see well that between those genera of things with which the sciences strictly so called have hitherto been concerned, and individuals, there still lies a great interval of lower genera and species, into whose territory demonstrators rarely descend, into which exact experimenters and observers rarely ascend with success. This is above all the course on which the aesthetico-dogmatic manner of thinking should run. Hence either it chooses its theme itself best of all, or it draws a theme sought from even higher down to that point, towards greater material truth, § 440, even if it thereby becomes formally a little less exact according to the scientific balance of the logicians, i.e. elegant to the point of verisimilitude. § 565.

> § 571. Studium veritatis in genere cogitandi aestheticodogmatico comparatiuum, §. 566. 1) veritatem etiam strictius logicam de ipsa materia, si fuerit horizontis aesthetico-logici, vel de eius generibus notionibusque superioribus [p. 371] sollicite quaeret, etiamsi non exprimendam acroamatice, tamen vt directricem explicite cogitandae verisimilitudinis in generalibus et adoptandis notionibus. §. 429, 424. 2) Notiones, in quibus aliquid contradictionis ad absurditatem vsque, vel paene eo vsque, iam detexit intellectus et ratio, cauebit hoc curatius, quo probabilius est, tales etiam spectatores e. c. fore meditationi eiusmodi aestheticodogmaticae, qui latentem inconuenientiam et ipsi ratione certissime perspicere possint, et aliis in spectando, legendo e. c. sociis aesthetice satis ostendere. §. 431-435.

§ 571. The comparative pursuit of truth in the aesthetico-dogmatic manner of thinking, § 566, 1) will solicitously seek even the more strictly logical truth about the matter itself, if it belongs to the aesthetico-logical horizon, or about its genera and superior notions, [p. 371] even if it is not to be expressed acroamatically, yet as the directrix of the verisimilitude to be thought explicitly in the general notions and in those to be adopted, § 429, 424. 2) Notions in which the intellect and reason have already detected something of contradiction reaching to absurdity, or almost reaching it, it will guard against the more carefully, the more probable it is that there will also be such spectators, etc., of an aesthetico-dogmatic meditation of this kind as can themselves perceive the latent incongruity most certainly by reason, and show it sufficiently aesthetically to other companions in watching, reading, etc. § 431–435.

> § 572. Studium veritatis in aestheticodogmaticis 3) in id praesertim incumbet, vt nexum materiae suae, breuius cum principiis, vberius cum grauissimis consectariis, verosimillimum viuidissime pingat, non sine desiderabili, vel taediorum ex auersando hauriendorum feraci persuasione, §. 437. 4) Si quid etiam progredi tentet in inferiora, ac ratio immediate praeluceat, supplementa tamen sua ad certitudine completa cognoscendum cum hoc inseparabiliter coniuncta sistere mouebit omnem lapidem, §. 439.

§ 572. The pursuit of truth in aesthetico-dogmatic matters 3) will apply itself especially to this, that it paint most vividly, as most verisimilar, the connection of its matter, more briefly with its principles, more richly with its weightiest consequences, not without a persuasion that is desirable, or else fertile in the tedium to be drawn from aversion, § 437. 4) If it also attempts to advance into lower things, and reason shines immediately before it, it will nonetheless move every stone to set forth its own supplements, inseparably joined with this, for what is to be cognised with complete certainty, § 439.

> § 573. Studium veritatis in aestheticodogmaticis, [p. 372] 5) ea lubentissime suis exponet, quae cogitaturus etiam certo nouit logice vera, §. 571. per harmoniam facultatum cognoscitiuarum inferiorum et superiorum, nunc exhibenda aesthetice vera; si hoc non conceditur praeferet logice sibi probabilia, sibi logice improbabilibus, §. 485. ob eandem harmoniam. Haec aut iudicabit suis praecipuis spectatoribus iam etiam fore verisimilia, et in iisdem securus acquiescit; aut suspicabitur, ea parum habitura apud hos verisimilitudinis. In vltimo casu aut habet occasionem ad dandam suis verisimilitudinem argumentis venuste probantibus, nec tunc latum vnguem auellitur a vero, quod ipsi videtur, et suos potius ad suam sententiam attrahere laborat, quam vt cum iis contraria sentiat, aut conciliare sibi probabilibus, suis quae sint sine dubio satis improbabilia, verisimilitudinem locus et tempus non permittunt.

§ 573. The pursuit of truth in aesthetico-dogmatic matters [p. 372] 5) will most gladly set out to its own people those things which he who is about to think also knows with certainty to be logically true, § 571, through the harmony of the lower and higher cognitive faculties, now to be exhibited as aesthetically true; if this is not granted, it will prefer what is logically probable to it over what is logically improbable to it, § 485, on account of the same harmony. These it will either judge will now also be verisimilar to its principal spectators, and rests secure in them; or it will suspect that they will have little verisimilitude with these. In the latter case either it has an occasion for giving its thoughts verisimilitude by charmingly proving arguments, and then it is not torn a finger’s breadth from the true, as it seems to itself, and labours rather to draw its own people to its own opinion than to think contrary things with them; or place and time do not permit reconciling verisimilitude to what is probable to it, but doubtless improbable enough to its own people.

> § 574. Si pulcre cogitaturus incidat in dogma sibi probabile, quod nec esse suis verisimile, nec a se iam tale reddi iisdem posse perspicit §. 573. amicus veritatis aut nec hoc, nec oppositum, spectatoribus verisimile, ponet, si licet ab vtroque abstrahere, aut, si ponendum est aesthetica necessitate alterutrum, multa cum grauitate perpendit, an spectatoribus [p. 373] suis praecipue attendendis verisimile, sit forsan error, communis quidem, oppido tamen innocens, an periculosior, et cuius fautores rei falsitatis moralis vel per indirectum agi possint ex merito. §. 470, 467. In priori casu vtetur opinione suorum, sicuti philosophi mathematicique fictionibus suis heuristicis, in posteriori latissime potius falsum errans cogitasse videri volet, §. 471. quam vt conscientiam vel famam suam exponat futuro falsitatis moralis opprobrio, §. 464.

§ 574. If he who is about to think beautifully falls upon a dogma probable to himself, which he perceives neither to be verisimilar to his own people, nor able now to be made such to them by himself, § 573, the friend of truth will either posit neither this nor its opposite as verisimilar to the spectators, if it is permitted to abstract from both, or, if one or the other must be posited by aesthetic necessity, weighs with much gravity whether what is verisimilar to the spectators [p. 373] especially to be attended to by him is perhaps an error, common indeed, yet quite innocent, or a more dangerous one, whose supporters could deservedly be charged, even indirectly, with moral falsity, § 470, 467. In the former case he will use the opinion of his own people, as philosophers and mathematicians use their heuristic fictions; in the latter he will rather wish to seem to have thought something false, erring most broadly, § 471, than expose his conscience or his reputation to the future reproach of moral falsity, § 464.

> § 575. Studium veritatis in aestheticodogmaticis 6) non solius illustrationis gratia, sed etiam ob §. 572, 569. multum in exemplis suae materiae versabitur, §. 526. in iisque singularia praeferet vniuersalibus, ideas notionibus, strictissime vera heterocosmicis et fabulosis, §. 472. aut ad haec quando venusta vocauerit necessitas, ea non dissimulabit esse fabulas, §. 565. aut fictiones aesthetice heuristicas, §. 574.

§ 575. The pursuit of truth in aesthetico-dogmatic matters 6) not for the sake of illustration alone, but also on account of § 572, 569, will be much occupied with examples of its matter, § 526, and in them will prefer singulars to universals, ideas to notions, the most strictly true to heterocosmic and fabulous things, § 472, or, when a charming necessity has called it to these, will not dissemble that they are fables, § 565, or aesthetically heuristic fictions, § 574.

> § 576. GENVS COGITANDI AESTHETICODOGMATICVM vel thema habet propius, quid agendum, vel omittendum sit, enuncians, vel minus. Hoc est THEORETICVM, illud PRACTICVM. Practicum denuo [p. 374] vel habet thema commendandum, PARAENETICVM, vel dissuadendum, ELENCTICVM. Quemadmodum Ciceronis et rhetorica et philosophica scripta sunt exempla generis cogitandi aestheticodogmatici, ita *officia* praesertim practici. Lucretius est exemplum cogitandi generis aestheticotheoretici. Saturae elenctici. In his Iuuenalis, quam omnino ficta promittat exempla, mauult *experiri,*

§ 576. The AESTHETICO-DOGMATIC MANNER OF THINKING either has a theme that more closely enunciates what is to be done or omitted, or not. The latter is the THEORETICAL, the former the PRACTICAL. The practical in turn [p. 374] either has a theme to be commended, the PARAENETIC, or one to be dissuaded, the ELENCTIC. Just as Cicero’s writings, both the rhetorical and the philosophical, are examples of the aesthetico-dogmatic manner of thinking, so the *Offices* are especially of the practical. Lucretius is an example of the aesthetico-theoretical manner of thinking. The satires, of the elenctic. In these Juvenal, rather than promise wholly fictitious examples, prefers *to try*

> *quid concedatur in illos, / Quorum Flaminia tegitur cinis atque Latina.*

*what is allowed against those / whose ashes the Flaminian and the Latin way cover.*

> § 577. Studium veritatis in aestheticodogmaticis cuiuscunque generis, §. 576. 7) si vel maxime complete certo cognoscenda tractet, tamen nunc non adscendet vltra VERISIMILITVDINEM aliquam, quam dicemus DOGMATICAM, qua dogma non quidem complete certum redditur, neque tamen vlla in eodem falsitas, repugnantia interna, vel contradictio cum complete certis, aut hoc saltim dogmate certioribus, nulla incohaerentia cum principiis, vnde deducendum foret, aut cum inde deriuandis consectariis totalis, e. c. nec intellectu, nec ratione, nec rationis analogo, quantae hae facultates in praecipuis obiectis personalibus supponendae sunt, appercipiatur, §. 483.

§ 577. The pursuit of truth in aesthetico-dogmatic matters of whatever kind, § 576, 7) even if it treats things to be cognised with the most complete certainty, will nevertheless now not ascend beyond a certain VERISIMILITUDE, which we shall call DOGMATIC, by which the dogma is not indeed rendered completely certain, yet no falsity in it, no internal repugnance or contradiction with completely certain things, or at least with things more certain than this dogma, no incoherence with the principles from which it would have to be deduced, or with the consequences to be derived from it, total, etc., is apperceived, whether by the intellect, by reason or by the analogue of reason, as great as these faculties are to be supposed in the principal personal objects, § 483.

> [p. 375] § 578. Nam definitiones statim, quando non exasciantur ad logicae artis seueras regulas, aut in descriptiones iterum pulcras affabre resoluuntur, propositiones generales si enthymematice omissis iudiciis intuitiuis, ex quibus formatae sunt, tamen exhibentur, vt experientiae, non axiomata solum et postulata secundaria miscentur primariis, sed et theoremata multa et problemata indemonstrabilium instar sumuntur, aut probantur saltibus logice illegitimis, etiamsi pulcris, formis crypticis, de quibus conuincendus non sit complete certus, interim elegantibus et oratoriis, scholia si regnant, et plurimum absorbent loci: quid aliud ex tali meditatione, si vel maxime complete certum thema habeat, nunc prodibit, nisi dogmatica verisimilitudo? §. 577.

[p. 375] § 578. For when definitions are not straightway hewn to the severe rules of the logical art, or are again skilfully resolved into beautiful descriptions; when general propositions, with the intuitive judgements from which they were formed enthymematically omitted, are nevertheless exhibited as experiences; when not only secondary axioms and postulates are mixed with primary ones, but many theorems and problems too are assumed as though indemonstrable, or are proved by leaps logically illegitimate, though beautiful, by cryptic forms, of which the one to be convinced is not completely certain, yet elegant and oratorical; when scholia reign and absorb most of the space: what else will now come forth from such a meditation, even if it has a theme that is most completely certain, but dogmatic verisimilitude? § 577.

> § 579. Si locus permitteret, vberius ex historia philosophica posset ostendi confusionem huius dogmata [sic: dogmatici] cogitandi generis et accurate logici ac intellectualis §. 568. fontem esse, ex quo 1) philosophi et omnes paene reliqui eruditi tot per saecula soliditate et certitudine superati sint a mathematicis, quibus sua suis exponendo semper verum fuit intellectum et rationem praesertim instruere, non promittendo solum, sed et praestando. 2) Platonis, haec duo cogitandi genera semper [p. 376] combinantis, ne dicam confundentis, discipuli, in tantam lapsi sunt incertitudinem, exceptis Aristotelicis, quorum praeceptor acroamaticis suis scriptis ostendit, quantum intersit inter logice verum, et aesthetice verisimile, si philosophemur. 3) Aeternae dogmaticorum scepticorumque, et nunc his, nunc illis viciniorum, lites. §. 9.

§ 579. If space permitted, it could be shown more fully from the history of philosophy that the confusion of this dogmatic manner of thinking with the accurately logical and intellectual one, § 568, is the source from which 1) the philosophers and almost all the other learned have for so many centuries been surpassed in solidity and certainty by the mathematicians, for whom, in expounding their own matters to their own followers, it has always been the true course to instruct the intellect and especially reason, not only by promising, but also by performing. 2) The disciples of Plato, who always [p. 376] combined, not to say confounded, these two manners of thinking, have fallen into such great uncertainty, excepting the Aristotelians, whose teacher showed in his acroamatic writings how much difference there is between the logically true and the aesthetically verisimilar, if we are to philosophise. 3) The eternal disputes of the dogmatists and the sceptics, and of those who are nearer now to the one, now to the other. § 9.

> § 580. Studium veritatis aestheticum absolutum S. XXXIIII. se comparatiue exseret in summo suo gradu perfectionis etiam materialis maxime curiosum in genere cogitandi aesthetica historico, §. 466, cuius 1) genus maxime ordinarium est, res facti, singularia praeterita, describens, 2) non negligendum, aesthetico statum animi praesentem exprimens, 3) non ita crebro, saepius tamen, ac videtur, obseruandum futura praeuidens. Medium si dicas empiricum, tertium manticum cogitandi genus: GENVS COGITANDI AESTHETICOHISTORICVM erit vel STRICTIVS historicum, vel EMPIRICVM, vel MANTICVM.

§ 580. The absolute aesthetic pursuit of truth, S. XXXIIII, will comparatively display itself in the highest degree of its perfection, even material perfection, as most curious in the aesthetico-historical manner of thinking, § 466, of which 1) the most ordinary kind is that which describes matters of fact, past singulars; 2) a kind not to be neglected by the aesthetician is that which expresses the present state of the mind; 3) one to be observed not so frequently, yet more often than it seems, is that which foresees things to come. If you call the middle one the empirical, the third the mantic manner of thinking: THE AESTHETICO-HISTORICAL MANNER OF THINKING will be either the MORE STRICTLY historical, or the EMPIRICAL, or the MANTIC.

> § 581. Exempla primi sunt generis eleganter cogitandi, de quo §. 580. *clari scriptores, quibus veteris populi Romani prospera vel aduersa memorata sunt,* secundi tum epistolae non ita [p. 377] paucae, quas Cicero, et Plinius de rebus ad se pertinentibus tunc, quum eae fierent, perscripserunt, tum carmina inter amandum dolendumue scripta de amore vel tristitia.

§ 581. Examples of the first kind of thinking elegantly, of which § 580, are *the famous writers by whom the prosperous or adverse fortunes of the ancient Roman people have been recorded*; of the second, both the not so [p. 377] few letters that Cicero and Pliny wrote about matters concerning themselves at the time when these were happening, and the poems written in the midst of loving or grieving, about love or sadness.

> *Verba miser frustra nil proficientia perdo,* / *Ipsa graues spargunt ora loquentis aquae* / — — — — / *Scilicet occidimus, nec spes, nisi vana, salutis,* / *Dumque loquor, vultus obruit vnda meos.* / *Hei mihi, quam celeri micuerunt nubila flamma!* / *Quantus ab aetherio personat axe fragor!* e. c.

*Wretched, I waste in vain words that avail nothing,* / *The heavy waters themselves drench the mouth that speaks* / — — — — / *Surely we are perishing, nor is there hope of safety, save a vain one,* / *And while I speak, the wave overwhelms my face.* / *Ah me, how swiftly the clouds flashed with flame!* / *How great a crash resounds from the ethereal vault!* etc.

> § 582. Cogitandi genus aestheticomanticum nolim in solis vaticiniis veris fictisue quaeri, e. g. ecl. Virg. IIII. sed praestat illud intermixtum aliis obseruare, quoties in futura dirigendus ex praesentibus, vel praeteritis, vel omnino generalibus est, citra diuinationem etiam omnem extraordinariam, animus. e. g.

§ 582. I would not have the aesthetico-mantic manner of thinking sought only in true or fictitious prophecies, e.g. Virg. ecl. IIII, but it is better to observe it intermixed with others, whenever the mind has to be directed towards things to come from things present, or past, or wholly general, even without any extraordinary divination. e.g.

> *Forsan et haec olim meminisse iuuabit.* / *O passi grauiora! deus dabit his quoque finem.* Virg.

*Perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even these things.* / *O you who have suffered worse! God will give an end to these things too.* Virg.

> *Quo nos cunque feret melior fortuna parente,* / *Ibimus. O! socii comitesque* / — — — — / *O! fortes peioraque passi* / *Mecum saepe viri, nunc vino pellite curas,* / [p. 378] *Cras ingens iterabimus aequor.* Hor. I. od. 7.

*Wherever a fortune better than our parent shall bear us,* / *We shall go. O comrades and companions* / — — — — / *O brave men, who have often suffered worse things* / *With me, now drive away cares with wine,* / [p. 378] *Tomorrow we shall set out again upon the vast sea.* Hor. I. od. 7.

> § 583. Genus pulcre cogitandi strictius historicum, et in aestheticis tam empiricum, quam manticum, differunt 1) a logica et critica seueriori cura historici, saltim bene praeliminari, qua per memoriam et iudicium intellectuale, multumque rationis vsum suam sibi materiem ex magna traditionum, rumorum, famae, calumniarum, fictionum, fabularum e. c. farragine seligit, ante, quam eleganti, quae placuerunt, contexat iucundae narrationis tela, 2) a logica experimentatorum et obseruatorum veri nominis inter philosophos solicitudine, qua rem sensam iudiciis intuitiuis et experientiis stricte dictis ita sistunt intellectui, vt vitium subreptionis pro virili caueatur, et enthymematice omissae maiores, opiniones praeconceptae: 2) [sic: 3)] a logica et rationali prouidentia, qua politicus e. g. futurum suae reipublicae statum, quasi ex aliqua specula, metitur.

§ 583. The more strictly historical manner of thinking beautifully, and in aesthetic matters the empirical as well as the mantic, differ 1) from the more severe logical and critical care of the historian, at least a good preliminary one, by which through memory and intellectual judgement, and much use of reason, he selects his matter for himself out of the great farrago of traditions, rumours, report, calumnies, fictions, fables etc., before he weaves the things that have pleased him into the elegant web of a pleasant narration; 2) from the logical solicitude of the experimenters and observers, truly so called, among the philosophers, by which they set the thing perceived before the intellect by intuitive judgements and experiences strictly so called in such a way that the vice of subreption is guarded against as far as in them lies, as are enthymematically omitted major premisses and preconceived opinions; 3) from the logical and rational foresight by which a politician, e.g., measures the future state of his republic, as if from some watchtower.

> § 584. Studium hoc veri in aestheticohistoricis, quoniam maximam partem inferioribus animi facultatibus exercetur, §. 583. non fictionibus solum latius dictis, §. 505. indiget, sed [p. 379] in meditationibus etiam paululum extendendis interseret complete certo a se cognitis, vt strictissime vera, tum generalia minus certa, tum singularia, quae num vere sint huius vniuersi possibilia, complete conuictum non est. §. 507. Hinc neque hoc veri studium assurget vltra verisimilitudinem, §. 483. neque tamen qualemcunque sataget attingere, sed sicut in interspersis suis generalibus dogmaticam, §. 577. amplectetur, sic in ideis strictissime dictam, §. 530. ne strictius quidem dictas fictiones historicas omnes refugientem, §. 509. tamen et in his auersam ab omnibus, quae falsitatis moralis, leuis partium studii, credulitatisue iure possent accusari, et poeticarum omnium fictionum, et vtopiam et mundos, praeter hunc, optimos, quoties historica fide suas cogitationes obligat. §. 566.

§ 584. This pursuit of truth in aesthetico-historical matters, since it is for the most part exercised by the lower faculties of the mind, § 583, needs not only fictions in the broader sense, § 505, but [p. 379] in meditations that are to be somewhat extended it will also intersperse among the things known to itself as completely certain, as most strictly true, both generals that are less certain, and singulars of which it has not been completely convinced whether they are truly possibles of this universe. § 507. Hence this pursuit of truth will neither rise above verisimilitude, § 483, nor yet busy itself to attain just any verisimilitude whatever, but just as in its interspersed generals it will embrace the dogmatic verisimilitude, § 577, so in its ideas the one most strictly so called, § 530, not shunning all historical fictions even in the stricter sense, § 509, yet even in these averse to everything that could justly be accused of moral falsity, of slight partisanship, or of credulity, and to all poetic fictions, and to utopias and worlds best apart from this one, whenever it binds its thoughts by historical faith. § 566.

#### Sectio XXXVI. Studium Veri Poeticum. — Section XXXVI. The Poetic Pursuit of Truth

> § 585. Aestheticum veri studium absolutum, S. XXXIIII. in aliis iam indicatis rationibus potest moueri ad genus cogitandi poeticum, §. 566. quando 1) venustae plenitudini [p. 380] requisitorum non satis historia porrigit, et aperte mauult vir bonus hinc mentiri copiam pulcriorem excogitans, quam callide fidem historicam corrumpere. 2) Quando plus dignitatis, vel etiam maiestatis dabunt, ficta exempla heterocosmica, quam historica, semper aliquid humani passa, quod supprimere saepe permittit ne strictissime quidem dicta verisimilitudo, §. 584. 3) Quando moralis plus veritatis, characterum, loci, temporis maior vnitas sperari potest, et obseruabilior ac, vt ita dicam, contractior nexus, ex heterocosmicis, quam ex rebus in hoc vniuerso propter rationes superiores distractioribus, aut propter imbecillitatem humanam inconstantioribus. 4) Quando ob anticipationes suorum potiorum in spectatoribus sperare potest notius ipsis heterocosmicum fore, quam euentum huius mundi, sed in parte eiusdem his admodum incognita situm. Sunt in mundo fabularum milesiarum, aut fabellarum aesopicarum satis versati multi hospites in historicis. 5) Quando fictionibus faciliorem fidem sperat, quam strictissime veris. Hoc non ita raro posse sperari fidem inueniet apud eos, qui nouerint, quoties, quot hominibus opus sit dicere: *non putaram*, 6) quando veritas strictissime dicta praeuidetur alia omnia, quam eam habitura vitam, quae potissimum intenditur. §. 561.

§ 585. The absolute aesthetic pursuit of truth, S. XXXIIII, can be moved, for other reasons already indicated, to the poetic manner of thinking, § 566, when 1) history does not supply enough for the charming fullness [p. 380] of the requisites, and the good man openly prefers for this reason to lie, by devising a more beautiful abundance, rather than cunningly to corrupt historical faith. 2) When fictitious heterocosmic examples will give more dignity, or even majesty, than historical ones, which have always undergone something human, which not even the most strictly so-called verisimilitude often permits to be suppressed, § 584. 3) When more moral truth, a greater unity of characters, place and time, and a more observable and, so to say, more compact connexion can be hoped for from heterocosmic things than from things which in this universe are, because of higher reasons, more scattered, or, because of human weakness, more inconstant. 4) When, because of the anticipations of its principal elements in the spectators, it can hope that the heterocosmic will be better known to them than an event of this world, but one situated in a part of it quite unknown to them. There are many well versed in the world of Milesian tales or of Aesopic fables who are strangers in historical matters. 5) When it hopes for easier belief in fictions than in things most strictly true. That this can be hoped for not so rarely will be found by those who know how often, and for how many men, there is need to say: *I would not have thought it*; 6) when truth most strictly so called is foreseen to be going to have anything but the life which is chiefly intended. § 561.

> [p. 381] § 586. Quod si studium veri absolutum impulerit pulcre cogitaturum ad heterocosmica fingenda, §. 585. iam transmutatur in studium verisimilitudinis poeticae, §. 530. quae tantum abest, vt eadem sit cum verisimilitudine historica, et strictissime dicta, vt, si ad alterutram, vel dogmaticam, §. 577. vel strictissime dictam eam referre necessarium esset, εἰκός poetarum ad dogmaticam potius referrem, fauente satis Aristotele, qui *historicum* iubet, *quae facta sunt, poetam, qualia fieri debent, referre, et inde poesin meliorem et magis philosophicam laudat, quam historiam, quia magis vniuersalia dicat, historia autem singularia. Vniuersale enim esse, contingit talem talia dicere aut facere, secundum necessarium aut verisimile, singulare autem, quid Alcibiades fecerit, aut passus sit.*

[p. 381] § 586. But if the absolute pursuit of truth has impelled the one who is to think beautifully to feign heterocosmic things, § 585, it is now transmuted into the pursuit of poetic verisimilitude, § 530, which is so far from being the same as the historical and most strictly so-called verisimilitude that, if it were necessary to refer it to one or the other, either to the dogmatic, § 577, or to the most strictly so called, I should rather refer the εἰκός [the likely] of the poets to the dogmatic, with the sufficient support of Aristotle, who bids *the historian* report *what has happened, the poet what kind of things ought to happen, and hence praises poetry as better and more philosophical than history, because it speaks more of universals, history however of singulars. For to be universal is that it befalls such a man to say or do such things according to the necessary or the verisimilar; singular however is what Alcibiades did or suffered.*

> § 587. Falluntur hinc critici quidam minus instructi verisimilitudinem poeticam ad historicae leges examinantes, quando poetam i. e. nunc fingentem heterocosmica statim condemnant peccati in verisimilitudinem, quando tunc et ibi fingit aliquem occidi, quando et vbi vixisse eundem adhuc historice vel verisimile, vel omnino certum sit, nullis vlterius auditis rei exceptionibus. Falluntur auctores, qui vere nouum mundum creantes [p. 382] de materiis etiam grauioribus in solis tamen fictionibus historicis subsistunt, et tunc rem suam optime se gessisse putant, quando bonum aliquem hominem eo induxerunt, vt nihil fraudis subesse cogitationibus senserit, habens, quicquid illi fingunt, pro strictissime veris, et anecdotis forsitan auro quouis carioribus. Hoc artificium videtur habere falsitatis aliquid per indirectum etiam aestheticae. §. 464.

§ 587. Hence certain less well-instructed critics are deceived who examine poetic verisimilitude by the laws of historical verisimilitude, when they straightway condemn the poet, i.e. the one now feigning heterocosmic things, of a sin against verisimilitude, when he feigns that someone was killed at a time and in a place at which and where it is historically either verisimilar or wholly certain that the same man was still alive, without hearing any further exceptions in the matter. Authors are deceived who, truly creating a new world [p. 382] even about weightier matters, nevertheless stop short at merely historical fictions, and then think they have managed their business best when they have brought some good man to the point of perceiving no fraud beneath their thoughts, taking whatever they feign for things most strictly true, and for anecdotes perhaps dearer than any gold. This artifice seems to have in it something of falsity, by an indirect route, even of aesthetic falsity. § 464.

> § 588. Nec ponenda praesertim est verisimilitudo poëtica in probabilitate, vel logica et disciplinari, vel historica et strictissime dicta illius hypotheseos, sub qua venustae cognitionis mediae obiecta, per fictionem poeticam fieri forte potuissent etiam in hoc vniuerso, quaeque noui mundi quasi basis et fundamentum est. §. 511. Nec est analogi rationis ordinario primas vniuersi caussas, elementa et stamina prima penitius examinare, dum haeret in effectis phaenomenis. Quando vero figmentum analogicum omnino talia illi ponit ob oculos, §. 516. quorum iam habet intra se quasdam anticipationes ex dudum sibi cognito mundo poetarum, §. 573. hypothesin qualemcunque, lemmatis instar, arripit, per eandem, velut notum aliquem pontem, in nouum tuum mundum *salire paratum habet, nec veretur*

§ 588. Nor, above all, is poetic verisimilitude to be placed in the probability, whether logical and disciplinary, or historical and most strictly so called, of that hypothesis under which the objects of a charming middle cognition might perhaps, through poetic fiction, have come to pass even in this universe, and which is, as it were, the basis and foundation of the new world. § 511. Nor is it the business of the analogue of reason ordinarily to examine more deeply the first causes, elements and primary threads of the universe, while it holds fast to the phenomena in their effects. But when an analogical figment sets before its eyes things, § 516, of which it already has within itself certain anticipations from the world of the poets long since known to it, § 573, it seizes upon any hypothesis whatever, after the fashion of a lemma, and by means of it, as by some familiar bridge, *it stands ready to leap* into your new world, *and does not fear*

> [p. 383] *Crura ponticuli, axulis stantis, irrediuiuus* / *Ne supinus eat, cauaque in palude recumbat.* Cat.

[p. 383] *The legs of the little bridge, standing on planks that cannot be renewed,* / *Lest it go over on its back and lie down in the hollow marsh.* Cat.

> § 589. Quum genus cogitandi poeticum §. 580. non sit, nisi venusta quaedam, saltim non inelegans, exceptio, §. 585. 25. omnis eiusdem verisimilitudo in eo consistit, vt vel rationis etiam analogo pateat, esse, quae salua totius pulcritudine potuit, minima, vel certe ne pateat eidem contrarium, ne quid citra necessitatem aestheticam, §. 491-503, 565. fictum vere dici posse videatur. Primam dicere VERISIMILITVDINEM liceat POETICAM POSITIVAM, NEGATIVAM alteram.

§ 589. Since the poetic manner of thinking, § 580, is nothing but a certain charming, or at least not inelegant, exception, § 585, 25, all its verisimilitude consists in this, that it be evident even to the analogue of reason that those things have been feigned which, saving the beauty of the whole, could be the fewest; or at least that the contrary be not evident to it, that nothing should seem able truly to be called feigned without aesthetic necessity, § 491–503, 565. Let it be permitted to call the first POSITIVE POETIC VERISIMILITUDE, the other NEGATIVE.

> § 590. Prima ergo quaestio foret in diiudicanda generis cogitationum poetici verisimilitudine, an omnino illud eligere fuerit aesthetice necessarium, an forsan etiam analogo rationis belle instructo pateat contrarium. Sic Quintilianus *historicis graecis* recte tunc obiicit *poeticam licentiam*, quoties poetice quantumcunque verisimilia suis immiscent, quoniam his per historias omnino locus non est, §. 584. Hanc verisimilitudinem, vt ita dicam, externam et respectiuam ad conditionem auctoris [p. 384] et dignitatem operis aut totius, cui immiscendum est poetice verisimile, et dispositiones praecipuorum, quibus placere velis, spectatorum, plerumque supponimus ex definitione restrictioris cogitandi generis, quod aliquis semel elegit, postulati instar, hypothetice deducendam.

§ 590. The first question, then, in judging the verisimilitude of the poetic manner of thought, would be whether it was aesthetically necessary to choose that manner at all, or whether perhaps the contrary is evident even to a well-instructed analogue of reason. Thus Quintilian rightly objects *poetic licence* to *the Greek historians* whenever they mix into their own writings things poetically verisimilar, however verisimilar they may be, since there is no place at all for these throughout histories, § 584. This verisimilitude, external, so to say, and relative to the condition of the author [p. 384] and the dignity of the work or of the whole into which the poetically verisimilar is to be mixed, and to the dispositions of the chief spectators whom you wish to please, we generally suppose is to be deduced hypothetically, after the fashion of a postulate, from the definition of the more restricted manner of thinking which someone has once chosen.

> § 591. Epopoeiam decent fabulae theologicae et heroicae, fictas fabellas genus cogitandi poeticum, et hinc peculiaris verisimilitudo. e. c. Haec patent axiomatice. Vnde postulata: Epopoeus, Aesopus e. c. esse qui velit, hanc quaerat verisimilitudinem. Vlterius ipsius meditationis diiudicatio vix adscendet aesthetica. An auctor bene, sapienter, et se suisque sperandis praesertim auditoribus conuenienter decreuerit epopoeus, Aesopus e. c. aliquis fieri verisimilitudinem et hinc pulcritudinem meditationis internam directo non tangit.

§ 591. Theological and heroic fables befit the epic, the poetic manner of thinking befits feigned fables, and hence a peculiar verisimilitude, etc. These things are evident axiomatically. Whence the postulates: whoever wishes to be an epic poet, an Aesop etc., let him seek this verisimilitude. Further than this, aesthetic judgement of the meditation itself will scarcely ascend. Whether an author has decided well, wisely, and in a manner suited to himself and to his own hearers, especially those he may hope for, to become an epic poet, an Aesop etc., does not directly touch the verisimilitude and hence the internal beauty of the meditation.

> § 592. Secunda quaestio erit: An nouus ille mundus, in quem poeta, siue prosaicus scriptor, siue metricus, siue pictor, siue sculptor, e. c. fuerit, nos introducturus est, sit ex ipsius intentionibus eleganter exsequendis mundus, post hunc, optimus? immo an thema possit in eodem vere perfectius [p. 385] elegantiusque sisti iucundo cuidam vigilantium somnio, ac in hoc illud mundo cogitari potuisset? an in his solis momentis ad finem venustum facientibus mundus nouus a nostro differat, an etiam frustra ponantur in eodem multa alia et diuersa? Ouidius optimum aliquem maximum poetarum mundum descripturus in suis metamorphoseon: tamen aliquam vult obseruare cum hoc vniuerso conspirantem chronologiam:

§ 592. The second question will be: whether that new world, into which the poet, whether a prose writer or a writer in verse, or a painter, or a sculptor, etc., is about to introduce us, is, from the standpoint of his own intentions to be elegantly carried out, the best world after this one? Nay, whether the theme could in it truly be set, more perfectly [p. 385] and more elegantly, in a certain pleasant dream of waking men, than it could have been thought in this world? whether the new world differs from ours only in those moments that make for the charming end, or whether many other and different things are also placed in it in vain? Ovid, about to describe in his Metamorphoses some best and greatest world of the poets, yet wishes to observe a certain chronology in agreement with this universe:

> *primaque ab origine mundi* / *Ad sua perpetuum deducere tempora carmen.*

*and from the first origin of the world* / *To bring down a continuous song to my own times.*

> § 593. Poetice ficturus, quantum vllus vnquam poeta mentiri potuit, orditur tamen ab istis historiis, quas non pauci dogmatice veras omnino, plerasque omnes verisimiles concedant, iisque primum non nisi fictiones interserit, quas historicarum limites transgredi vel nemo, vel certe potissimum attendendi eius lectores hariolari non poterant. En! tibi primum Chaos. v. 5-20.

§ 593. Though about to feign poetically as much as any poet ever could lie, he nevertheless begins from those histories which not a few would concede to be wholly true dogmatically, and almost all would concede to be verisimilar, and at first he inserts among them none but fictions which either no one, or at least the readers he had chiefly to attend to, could have guessed to transgress the limits of historical fictions. Behold! first you have Chaos. v. 5–20.

> *Hanc deus et melior litem natura diremit.* / Iamque separantur ignis, aqua, terra, aer, / *qui, quanto est pondere terrae* / *Pondus aquae leuius, tanto est onerosior igni.* 53.

*A god and a better nature settled this strife.* / And now fire, water, earth and air are separated, / *which, by as much as the weight of water* / *Is lighter than the weight of earth, by so much is heavier than fire.* 53.

> An ergo grauitatem aeris antlia demum [p. 386] inuenit? Interim omnia fiunt, vsque ad animalia-75.

Did the air-pump, then, only now discover the [p. 386] gravity of the air? Meanwhile all things come to be, down to the animals, 75.

> *Sanctius his animal, mentisque capacius altae,* / *Deerat adhuc, et quod dominari in caetera posset.* / *Natus homo est. Siue hunc diuino semine fecit* / *Ille opifex rerum, mundi melioris origo,* / *Siue recens tellus* / fuit, quam Prometheus / *Finxit in effigiem moderantum cuncta deorum.* / *Aurea prima sata est aetas, quae vindice nullo,* / *Sponte sua sine lege fidem rectumque colebat.* 90. / — — — — / *Protinus irrumpit venae peioris in aeuum,* / *Omne nefas, fugere Pudor Verumque, Fidesque,* / *In quorum subiere locum Fraudesque, Dolique* / *Insidiaeque et Vis et Amor sceleratus habendi.* 130. / — — — — / *In facinus iurasse putes. Dent ocius omnes,* / *Quas meruere pati, sic stat sententia, poenas,* 243. / — — — — / *Est tamen humani generis iactura dolori.* 246. / — — — — / *Rex superum trepidare vetat, sobolemque priori* / [p. 387] *Dissimilem populo promittit origine mira,* 252. / — — — — / *Iamque mare et tellus nullum discrimen habebant* / *Omnia pontus erant, deerant quoque littora ponto,* 292.

*An animal holier than these, and more capable of a lofty mind,* / *Was still lacking, and one that could have dominion over the rest.* / *Man was born. Whether that craftsman of things, the origin of a better world,* / *Made him from divine seed,* / *Or whether the fresh earth* / was that which Prometheus / *Fashioned into the likeness of the gods who govern all things.* / *First was sown the golden age, which, with no avenger,* / *Of its own accord, without law, kept faith and right.* 90. / — — — — / *Straightway there bursts into the age of worse vein* / *Every wickedness; Shame and Truth and Faith fled,* / *Into whose place came Frauds and Deceits* / *And Plots and Force and the wicked Love of possessing.* 130. / — — — — / *You would think they had sworn to crime. Let them all speedily pay* / *The penalties they have deserved to suffer; so stands the sentence,* 243. / — — — — / *Yet the loss of the human race is a grief to him.* 246. / — — — — / *The king of the gods forbids them to tremble, and promises an offspring* / [p. 387] *Unlike the former people, of wondrous origin,* 252. / — — — — / *And now sea and land had no distinction* / *All things were sea, and the sea too lacked shores,* 292.

> Iamque satis sibi strictissime veri verisimilisque historici propinasse vates videtur, vt imprudentes sensim ex hoc omnino vniuerso rapti, quasi per somnium, in eum mundum deferantur, vbi homines ex saxis, ex Daphne laurus, ex Ione iuuenca, ex iuuenca Io, et si qua sunt alia,

And now the bard seems to have given his readers enough to drink of the most strictly true and of the historically verisimilar, so that, unawares, gradually snatched away altogether out of this universe, as if through a dream, they are carried into that world where men come from stones, the laurel from Daphne, a heifer from Io, Io from a heifer, and whatever else there may be of

> *quae speciosa dehinc miracula promit.*

*the splendid miracles that he then brings forth.*

> § 595. Hae quaestiones §. 590. 592. non sunt solae, nec primariae, §. 585. 588. Sit necessarium heterocosmica ponere, sit eorum non maior, ac necessaria, differentia, ab hoc vniuerso. Iam tertium quaeritur: An ex omni mundo poetarum et eius regionibus vberioribus, dignioribus, verisimilioribus, notioribus, e. c. §. 22. nouam tuam potius desumseris fictionem, quam vt in ignotas fabularum ambages, sine necessitate aesthetica, tuos induxeris hospites? An hoc contrarium perfectioni possit etiam ab analogo rationis deprehendi? §. 513, 516. Habes iteratum Horatii praeceptum:

§ 595. These questions, § 590, 592, are not the only ones, nor the primary ones, § 585, 588. Let it be necessary to posit heterocosmic things; let their difference from this universe be no greater than is necessary. Now a third question is asked: whether you have rather taken your new fiction from the whole world of the poets and its richer, worthier, more verisimilar, better-known regions etc., § 22, than led your guests into unknown mazes of fables, without aesthetic necessity? Whether this, the contrary of perfection, can be detected even by the analogue of reason? § 513, 516. You have Horace’s precept repeated:

> [p. 388] *Ex noto fictum carmen sequar.*

[p. 388] *I shall follow a song feigned from what is known.*

> Fictionis poetica verisimilitudo praesertim postulat, vt mundo poetarum in iis, in quibus recedit ab hoc vniuerso, sit adeo similis et consentanea, ac illud pulcritudo totius permittit, quod cogitas, §. 484.

The verisimilitude of a poetic fiction demands above all that it be, with respect to the world of the poets, in those things in which it departs from this universe, as similar and consonant to it as the beauty of the whole which you are thinking permits, § 484.

> § 596. Hinc necessitas studii mythologici non illius graeci romanique tantum, sed omnium temporum et locorum, quorum fama, cabbala, traditiones dare poterunt regionem mundi poetici alicui cogitanti certorum in gratiam de certo themate praesertim commendabilem, §. 594. Nec obiicias dissensus veterum in ipso hoc mundo poetarum, si chaos eius primitiuum a deriuatiuo sensim illito mundo ac decore distinguas, tecumque cogites difficultatem, in qua non ita longe tempore inter se distantes poetae quondam versabantur notum sibi reddendi vix ante se natum locupletatumue mundum poeticum, quae nunc omnis paene disparuit. Probe perpendendum est argumentum Ouidii probans, quando iam in heterocosmica mergitur altius:

§ 596. Hence the necessity of the study of mythology, not only of that of the Greeks and Romans, but of all times and places, whose report, cabbala and traditions will be able to furnish a region of the poetic world especially commendable to someone thinking for the sake of certain people about a certain theme, § 594. Nor should you object the disagreements of the ancients in this very world of the poets, if you distinguish its primitive chaos from the derivative one gradually overlaid with adornment and grace, and consider with yourself the difficulty in which poets once found themselves, not so far distant from one another in time, of making known to themselves a poetic world scarcely born or enriched before them, a difficulty which has now almost wholly disappeared. Ovid’s argument is to be carefully weighed, proving, when he is already plunging deeper into heterocosmic things:

> *Quis hoc credat, nisi sit pro teste vetustas?* Met. I, 400.

*Who would believe this, unless antiquity stood as witness?* Met. I, 400.

> Cui consentit illud Virgilii de nauibus in nymphas mutatis:

With which agrees that saying of Virgil about the ships changed into nymphs:

> *Prisca fides facta, sed fama perennis.*

*The belief is ancient, but the fame is perennial.*

> [p. 389] § 597. Quartum quaeritur: An poetice fingens mundi poetici vtopiam tetigerit ingressusque sit, vltra §. 456, limites, et ita quidem, vt deprehendi possit in bidentali per ipsum analogon rationis, an omnino tristes eiusmodi campos vitris fractis merorumque somniorum interpretamentis auxerit? §. 574. Multo venustius princeps Gallorum epicus vates eremitam fatidicum, fanaticismi daemonem, Ludouicum sanctum ducem Henrici magni per caelos et inferos fingit, ac si deos maiorum minorumque gentium ex vtopicis graecorum vel romanorum intermundiis reuocasset.

[p. 389] § 597. The fourth question is asked: whether the one feigning poetically has touched upon and entered the utopia of the poetic world, beyond the limits of § 456, and that in such a way that he could be caught on the lightning-struck ground by the very analogue of reason, or whether he has altogether enlarged such dismal fields with broken glass and the interpretations of mere dreams? § 574. Far more charmingly does the prince of the French epic bards feign a prophetic hermit, the demon of fanaticism, and Saint Louis as the guide of Henry the Great through the heavens and the underworld, than if he had called back the gods of greater and lesser rank from the utopian intermundane spaces of the Greeks or Romans.

> § 598. Quinta sit quaestio: An poeta non ea coniunxerit, quae seorsim quidem sic se bene satis habere, qua possibilitatem aesthetice perspiciendam, possent, sint tamen in vnum conflata incompossibilia? Hoc tribus potissimum contingere posset rationibus, 1) si regiones mundi poetici per aeternas inimicitias seiunctae confunderentur, cuius casus exemplum est, §. 515. Mundus enim poetarum habet suas insulas et peninsulas, neque vatum

§ 598. Let the fifth question be: whether the poet has not joined together things which, taken separately, could indeed be in a good enough state, as far as their possibility is to be aesthetically perceived, but which, fused into one, are incompossible? This could happen chiefly for three reasons, 1) if regions of the poetic world severed by eternal enmities were confounded, an example of which case is in § 515. For the world of the poets has its islands and peninsulas, nor did a prudent god of the bards

> *Nequicquam deus abscidit* / *Prudens Oceano dissociabiles* / *Terras*

*In vain sever* / *By Ocean the unsociable* / *Lands*

> [p. 390] Quibus interiecta *vada* non bene *transiliuntur*, 2) si mundo poetarum affingitur aliquid, quod in se nihil implicat contradictionis aestheticae, sumtae tamen iam semel mundi poetici portioni sic repugnaret, vt fieret figmentum anomalon sine necessitate, §. 520.

[p. 390] between which lie *shallows* that are not well *leapt across*; 2) if something is fastened onto the world of the poets which in itself implies no aesthetic contradiction, but which would so conflict with a portion of the poetic world already once assumed that it would become an anomalous figment without necessity, § 520.

> § 599. 3) Si semel transgressis in heterocosmica nobis talia huius vniuersi phaenomena et ea strictissime vera denuo non opinantibus exponerentur, quibus, quoniam stare cum mundo ficto non possunt, velut expergefacti ex somnio vigilantium spontaneo cogeremur forsan subinuiti tunc, quando nondum tempus est, agnoscere ficta esse, et quidem strictius, omnia, quae, tanquam praesentia, praestigiis poetae lubenter cedentes ad aulea vsque volebamus intueri. Ob hoc vitium vitandum Aristoteles satis lepide poetam excusatione dignum iudicauit, *si facta pangat*, et strictissime vera scribat, quam tamen ipsi non concedit, nisi quando et in quantum sint verisimilia, quod hic interpretor in omni suo ambitu, vt habeant etiam verisimilitudinem poeticam, vt in nouo illo mundo, quem fingimus, aeque locum habeant, ac in hoc. Tunc enim, vt illius, non vt huius portiones spectatae spontaneum voluptatis caussa somnium temere non interrumpent.

§ 599. 3) If, once we had passed over into heterocosmic things, such phenomena of this universe, and these most strictly true, were set before us again when we did not expect it, by which, since they cannot stand together with the feigned world, we should be compelled, as if awakened from a spontaneous dream of waking men, perhaps somewhat against our will, and at a time when it is not yet time, to recognise as feigned, and that in the stricter sense, all the things which, as though present, we wished to gaze upon, gladly yielding to the poet’s illusions, right up to the curtain. To avoid this fault Aristotle rather wittily judged the poet worthy of excuse *if he composes things that have happened*, and writes things most strictly true, which however he does not concede to him, except when and in so far as they are verisimilar, which I here interpret in its full compass, that they have poetic verisimilitude too, so that they have a place in that new world which we feign just as much as in this one. For then, looked upon as portions of that world and not of this, they will not rashly interrupt the spontaneous dream dreamt for pleasure’s sake.

> [p. 391] § 600. Sextum quaeritur: An poeta mundum, praeter hunc, optimum suis finibus legens, §. 591, figmentum suum bene analogicum, §. 516, 595. conformauerit mundi poetici inter portiones insociabiles, §. 598. illi potissimum parti ac regioni, quae iisdem poetae finibus est optima? Habent omnes paene religiones aliquam suam partem in mundo poetarum. Quaeuis paene rerum publicarum historia, si surgere velis in prima ditionum tempora, fictionum et incertae satis famae

[p. 391] § 600. The sixth question is asked: whether the poet, choosing the world best after this one for his own ends, § 591, has conformed his well-analogical figment, § 516, 595, among the unsociable portions of the poetic world, § 598, above all to that part and region which is best for those same ends of the poet? Almost all religions have some part of their own in the world of the poets. Almost any history of a commonwealth, if you wish to go back to the first times of dominions,

> *caput inter nubila condit.*

*hides its head among the clouds*

> Hinc vtique peccaret in verisimilitudinem, etiam poeticam, qui Turcae e. g. mysteria veterum aegyptiorum affingeret, et Sinensibus Gothorum mythologias. Illi autem non peccarent, qui Christiani de Christiano Christianorum gratia nonnihil fingentes semper et vbique mundum superstitionum graecorum et romanorum habitant? Miltoni mundus est verisimilior.

of fictions and of rather uncertain report. Hence he would assuredly sin against verisimilitude, even poetic verisimilitude, who ascribed, e.g., to a Turk the mysteries of the ancient Egyptians, and to the Chinese the mythologies of the Goths. But would those not sin who, being Christians, feigning something about a Christian for the sake of Christians, always and everywhere inhabit the world of the superstitions of the Greeks and Romans? Milton’s world is more verisimilar.

> § 601. Septima sit quaestio: Si figmentum prorsus ignotum ausus aliquis est afferre, et octaua: si quis omnino figmentum anomalon formauerit, an vtrumque satis habeat internae verisimilitudinis, qua compensari possit, quicquid primo falsi simile talibus in fictionibus [p. 392] videbatur, vt vltima tandem fictio correctio potius haberi possit mundi poetici, quam turpis in eodem anomalia. §. 518, 520. Nona: An fabularum sententia, §. 526, de facto verisimilitudinem dogmaticam moralem latius dictam, §. 577. de iure, simul strictius dictam habeat? §. 433, 435. An satis ex fabulae euentu pateat, velitne sententiam auctor de facto tantum, an etiam de iure veram intelligi? §. 548.

§ 601. Let the seventh question be: if someone has dared to bring forward a wholly unknown figment, and the eighth: if someone has formed an altogether anomalous figment, whether each has enough internal verisimilitude to compensate for whatever at first seemed like falsity in such fictions, [p. 392] so that the last fiction may in the end be held rather a correction of the poetic world than a disgraceful anomaly in it. § 518, 520. The ninth: whether the maxim of fables, § 526, has in point of fact the dogmatic moral verisimilitude in the broader sense, § 577, and in point of right the one more strictly so called at the same time? § 433, 435. Whether it is sufficiently evident from the outcome of the fable whether the author wishes his maxim to be understood as true only in point of fact, or also in point of right? § 548.

> § 602. Phaedri l. II. f. 1. veram habet sententiam de iure, cuius exemplum est leo partem praedae praedoni denegatam innoxio viatori relinquens.

§ 602. Phaedrus, b. II. f. 1, has a maxim true in point of right, the example of which is the lion leaving to the innocent traveller the part of the prey denied to the robber.

> *Exemplum egregium prorsus et laudabile* / *Verum est auiditas diues, et pauper pudor.*

*An example altogether outstanding and praiseworthy;* / *But greed is rich, and modesty poor.*

> F. 2. sententiam de facto tantum intelligendam docet turpis viri caluities vxorii:

F. 2 teaches that the maxim is to be understood only in point of fact, by the baldness of a disgraceful uxorious man:

> *A foeminis vtcunque spoliari viros,* / *Ament, amentur, nempe exemplis discimus.*

*That men are in any case despoiled by women,* / *Whether they love or are loved, we learn, to be sure, from examples.*

> L. III. f. 5. vero quoniam maxime pronam hanc daret sententiam: prudens aliquando fert iniurias agendo gratias et incitando in potentiorem vindicem, quae, sane, vix fuisset strictius vera moraliter sententia: fabula quidem narratur, verior autem adscribitur sententia, licet nimis generalis:

But b. III. f. 5, since it would yield this maxim as the most obvious one: a prudent man sometimes bears injuries by giving thanks and by inciting against a more powerful avenger, which, to be sure, would scarcely have been a maxim true in the stricter moral sense: the fable is indeed narrated, but a truer maxim is ascribed to it, though too general:

> *Successus ad perniciem multos deuocat.*

*Success calls many down to their ruin.*

> [p. 393] § 603. Haec sententiae veritas moralis primarium est, quod in fabularum verisimilitudine sit attendendum, §. 600. cui iungi tamen secundariae possunt decima quaestio: An fabula, quae narrationis titulo strictius ornata non vltra fictiones historicas progredi debeat, incidat nihilominus in licentiam poeticam? An eadem leges fictionum historicarum affabre seruans possit in re grauiori eo vsque fallere, vt pro strictissime vero habeatur a multis cum notabili ipsorum detrimento? §. 527, 587. Exemplum fabulae, cui et veritas dogmatica, §. 601. desit, et vtrumque vitium inhaereat, quod iam indicauimus, esse potest Philostratus in sua de Apollonio Tyaneo fabula.

[p. 393] § 603. This moral truth of the maxim is the primary thing to which attention must be paid in the verisimilitude of fables, § 600; to which, however, secondary things can be joined, a tenth question: whether a fable which, adorned more strictly with the title of narration, ought not to proceed beyond historical fictions, nevertheless falls into poetic licence? Whether the same, skilfully observing the laws of historical fictions, can in a weightier matter deceive to such a point that it is taken for most strictly true by many, to their notable detriment? § 527, 587. An example of a fable which both lacks dogmatic truth, § 601, and in which both the faults inhere which we have already indicated, may be Philostratus in his fable about Apollonius of Tyana.

> § 604. Vndecima quaestio: An fabula, poetica etiam, §. 527, si opus fuisse videatur, non potuerit aeque bene veritatem sententiae dogmaticam exprimere strictius probabilis, ac strictius improbabilis? §. 532. Aequalis hic bonitas est aequalis totius pulcritudo, quam non semper obtinebunt, probabilitate historica gaudentes prae iis, in quibus verisimilior probabilitas, licet poetica tantum, fulget. §. 533. An fabula, etiam improbabilis belle et recte, nihil tamen improbabilium contineat, nisi quot et qualia requiruntur ad illustrandam sufficienter sententiam? §. 589. [p. 394] Haec videtur illa fuisse caussa, ob quam Longinus, non Iliadi, fabulae non minus poeticae, et ex meo sensu strictius etiam improbabili, sed Odysseae tamen, fabularum amorem vitio vertit, §. 311.

§ 604. The eleventh question: whether a fable, even a poetic one, § 527, if there seemed to be need of it, could not have expressed the dogmatic truth of the maxim just as well while more strictly probable as while more strictly improbable? § 532. Equal goodness here is equal beauty of the whole, which those enjoying historical probability will not always obtain in preference to those in which a more verisimilar probability, though only poetic, shines forth. § 533. Whether a fable, even one beautifully and rightly improbable, nevertheless contains no improbabilities except as many and such as are required for sufficiently illustrating the maxim? § 589. [p. 394] This seems to have been the reason why Longinus turned the love of fables into a fault not of the Iliad, a fable no less poetic and, in my sense, even more strictly improbable, but of the Odyssey, § 311.

> § 605. Duodecima quaestio non in eo consistet, potissimum, an fabula quaedam poetica, et fictio fabulosa, rectius rationalis sit, ac fictus aliquis apologus, atque pulcrius, praesertim hac aetate nostra, qua animalibus etiam praeter hominem aliis denuo nonnihil intellectus ac rationis veritate sic satis aesthetica tribuitur, an tandem rectius mere rationalis, quam mixta, §. 537. Haec potius sit: An fictis personis, iis etiam, quas alias bruta censemus, immo vegetabilia, suum tamen ἦθος verisimile tribuatur, quod aut ex analogia mundi poetici, aut ex insufficientibus historiae naturalis traditionibus, aut ex opinionibus eorum, quorum potissimum gratia scribimus, ipsis conueniat? §. 495.

§ 605. The twelfth question will not consist chiefly in this, whether some poetic fable and fabulous fiction is more rightly rational than some feigned apologue, and more beautifully so, especially in this age of ours, in which some measure of intellect and reason is once again, with truth aesthetic enough, attributed to animals other than man, or whether in the end the purely rational is more right than the mixed, § 537. Let it rather be this: whether to feigned persons, even to those which we otherwise reckon brutes, nay, vegetables, there is nevertheless attributed their own verisimilar ἦθος [character], which suits them either from the analogy of the poetic world, or from the insufficient traditions of natural history, or from the opinions of those for whose sake we chiefly write? § 495.

> § 606. In fabula Aeneidos rationali pius Aeneas ἦθος personae, quam ipsi semel imposuit poeta, sustinens ita primum prodit in scenam, L. I, 96.

§ 606. In the rational fable of the Aeneid, pious Aeneas, sustaining the ἦθος [character] of the person which the poet once imposed upon him, first comes on the scene thus, B. I, 96:

> *Extemplo Aeneae soluuntur frigore membra,* / [p. 395] *Ingemit et duplices tendens ad sidera palmas* / *Talia voce refert: O! terque quaterque beati,* / *Quos ante ora patrum, Troiae sub moenibus altis,* / *Contigit oppetere!*

*Straightway the limbs of Aeneas are loosened with cold,* / [p. 395] *He groans, and stretching both palms to the stars* / *Utters such words aloud: O three and four times blessed,* / *Whose lot it was to meet death before their fathers’ faces, beneath the high walls of Troy!*

> ita postremam scenam concludit, vt vel in hostem Turnum lenis esse inciperet, huius

and he so concludes the final scene that he was even beginning to be gentle towards his enemy Turnus, when

> *infelix humero quum apparuit alto* / *Balteus, et notis fulserunt cingula bullis* / *Pallantis pueri, victum quem vulnere Turnus* / *Strauerat, atque humeris inimicum insigne gerebat.* / *Ille oculis postquam saeui monumenta doloris* / *Exuuiasque hausit, furiis accensus et ira* / *Terribilis: Tune hinc spoliis indute meorum* / *Eripiare mihi? Pallas te hoc vulnere, Pallas* / *Immolat, ac poenam scelerato ex sanguine sumit.* / *Hoc dicens ferrum aduerso sub pectore condit* / *Feruidus: ast illi soluuntur frigore membra,* / *Vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub vmbras.*

*on his high shoulder appeared the ill-fated* / *Belt, and the sword-belt flashed with its familiar studs,* / *Of the boy Pallas, whom Turnus had laid low with a wound,* / *Conquered, and was bearing on his shoulders the hostile emblem.* / *He, after he had drunk in with his eyes the memorials of cruel grief* / *And the spoils, kindled with fury and terrible* / *In his wrath: Are you, clothed in the spoils of my own,* / *To be snatched from me here? Pallas with this wound, Pallas* / *Sacrifices you, and takes the penalty from your criminal blood.* / *So saying, he buries the steel in the breast that faces him,* / *Burning: but the other’s limbs are loosened with cold,* / *And his life with a groan flees indignant beneath the shades.*

> Gemitus et frigore soluta membra incipientis Aeneae, finientis in hoste sunt, pius autem in deos, patriam, suos Aeneas sibi constans semper, manet vnus et idem, §. 605.

The groan and the limbs loosened with cold belong to Aeneas as he begins, and, in his enemy, as he ends; but pious towards the gods, his country and his own, Aeneas, always consistent with himself, remains one and the same, § 605.

> [p. 396] § 607. Quaestio decima tertia: An in fabulis, quae vel huic simpliciter et per eminentiam connexae dici videantur, implicitis, §. 535. venustus ille nexus obseruatur, quo praeparantur in ipsa iam colligatione remotius, in transitu propius omnia catastrophae et solutioni ita, vt imprudentibus quidem, neque tamen non verisimilis, haec eueniat praesenti sic inserendo praeteritum, vt vel inopinatum maxime, natum tamen inde futurum appareat, eaque omnia seruent iucundam istam vnitatem, qua nihil cogitatorum deesse, postque factam solutionem nihil amplius desiderari posse videatur? §. 437, 439. Nec hic minor cura verisimilitudinis moralis, §. 604. et cuiusdam analogiae, in ipsis imponendis nominibus, §. 594.

[p. 396] § 607. The thirteenth question: whether in fables that are complex, which seem to be called connected with this one simply and by eminence, § 535, that charming connexion is observed by which all things are prepared for the catastrophe and the resolution, more remotely already in the very knotting, more closely in the transition, in such a way that this comes about, unforeseen indeed to the unwary, yet not without verisimilitude, by so grafting the past onto the present that the future, though most unexpected, nevertheless appears to be born from it, and all these things preserve that pleasant unity by which nothing of what is thought seems to be lacking, and after the resolution has been made nothing further seems able to be desired? § 437, 439. Nor is there here less care for moral verisimilitude, § 604, and for a certain analogy in the very imposing of names, § 594.

> *Quod si personis iisdem vti aliis non licet,* / *Qui magis licet currentes seruos scribere,* / *Bonas matronas facere, meretrices malas,* / *Parasitum edacem, gloriosum militem,* / *Puerum supponi, falli per seruum senem,* / *Amare, odisse, suspicari?* Ter. Eun. prol.

*But if it is not permitted to use the same persons as others,* / *How is it any more permitted to write running slaves,* / *To make good matrons, wicked courtesans,* / *A greedy parasite, a boastful soldier,* / *A child substituted, an old man deceived by his slave,* / *To love, to hate, to suspect?* Ter. Eun. prol.

> Immo vero, non licet solum, sed et oportet saepe numero, §. 433.

Nay rather, not only is it permitted, but it is also often necessary, § 433.

> § 608. Quaestio decima quarta: An sententia satis grandis est, vt eidem sine anthropomorphismo, qui vel analogo rationis talis esse [p. 397] videatur, crasso possint exempla diuina subsumi? an exempla diuinorum ita se gerant, vt ex iis per argumentum a minori ad maius, diuina pulcre per analogon rationis colligi possint? An in vtrisque casibus omnia vere se habeant, secundum exactum analogi rationis iudicium, θεοπρεπῶς. §. 435, 399. In Phaedri l. III. f. 17. primum licet quaerere, an aesopicis diuina fabulis miscere conueniat? Sed hoc mittamus. Deinde Mineruae admiranti *quare Diui sibi steriles arbores legerent,*

§ 608. The fourteenth question: whether the maxim is grand enough for divine examples to be subsumed under it without a gross anthropomorphism, such as would seem to be one even to the analogue of reason? [p. 397] whether the examples of divine things so conduct themselves that from them, by an argument from the lesser to the greater, divine things can be beautifully inferred by the analogue of reason? Whether in both cases everything is truly as it should be, according to the exact judgement of the analogue of reason, θεοπρεπῶς [in a manner befitting the gods]. § 435, 399. In Phaedrus, b. III. f. 17, one may first ask whether it is fitting to mix divine things into Aesopic fables? But let us leave that aside. Then, to Minerva wondering *why the gods chose for themselves barren trees,*

> *Olim quas vellent esse in tutela sua,* / *caussam dixit Iuppiter:* / *Honore fructum ne videamur vendere.*

*Which they once wished to be under their protection,* / *Jupiter gave the reason:* / *Lest we seem to sell the fruit for the honour.*

> Minerua oliuam propter fructum praefert, et corrigit sententiam suam, iamque sic sentit

Minerva prefers the olive on account of its fruit, and corrects her opinion, and now thus holds

> *Deorum genitor atque hominum sator:* / *Nisi vtile est, quod facimus, stulta est gloria.*

*The begetter of gods and sower of men:* / *Unless what we do is useful, the glory is foolish.*

> § 609. Sententia dicitur dictae fabulae:

§ 609. The maxim of the said fable is stated:

> *Nihil agere, quod non prosit, fabella admonet.*

*The little fable warns us to do nothing that is not useful.*

> Iam ergo quaeritur, an declaretur exemplo ficto aliter, quam supponendo, per ipsas Iouis curas posteriores stultam fuisse gloriam; dum

Now then it is asked whether this is declared by the feigned example otherwise than by supposing, through Jupiter’s own later concerns, that the glory had been foolish, while

> *Quercus Ioui* / *Et myrthus Veneri placuit, Phoebo laurea,* / *Pinus Cybellae, populus celsa Herculi*

*The oak pleased Jupiter* / *And the myrtle Venus, the laurel Phoebus,* / *The pine Cybele, the lofty poplar Hercules,*

> et inanem colorem fuisse, grandem illam caussam et aetiologiam, quam primo adduxerat, [p. 398] Iupiter, quae sane tanta est, vt eam multi interpretum ne assequuti quidem sint, et lectionem mutare nequicquam laborarint: ideo steriles nostras facimus, relinquendo mortalibus frugiferas, ne his pro diuino nobis praestando cultu fructum vendere videamur. Interim sunt tamen narratae arbores in tutela diuorum, qui memorantur, per mundum poeticum, ad hunc vsque diem. Quot simul obseruantur deesse verisimilitudines? §. 608. Verum vbi non detegas turpitudines eiusmodi, quam primum a vera religione recesseris?

and that there had been an empty colour in that grand reason and aetiology which [p. 398] Jupiter had first adduced, which is indeed so great that many of the interpreters have not even grasped it, and have laboured in vain to change the reading: therefore we make our trees barren, leaving the fruit-bearing ones to mortals, lest we seem to sell them fruit in return for the divine worship to be rendered to us. Meanwhile the trees that are told of are nevertheless under the protection of the gods who are mentioned, throughout the poetic world, down to this very day. How many verisimilitudes are observed to be lacking at once? § 608. But where would you not uncover disgraceful things of this kind, as soon as you have departed from true religion?

> § 610. Decimum quintum quaeritur, an praeter verisimilitudines sibi cum aliis communes fabulis, Milesia praesertim amoris, nunc caeci, nunc probe perspicacis, veritatem verisimilitudinemque, praecipue moralem, latius dictam, vbique seruarit, §. 433, 495? An sententias, quas illustratum it, laudabilium effata, et de facto tantum enunciantes aliquid, quod solet contingere illi, qui *amores*

§ 610. The fifteenth thing is asked, whether, beyond the verisimilitudes common to it with other fables, a Milesian tale, especially one of love, now blind, now thoroughly clear-sighted, has everywhere preserved truth and verisimilitude, especially moral, in the broader sense, § 433, 495? Whether, as to the maxims which it sets out to illustrate — sayings of praiseworthy persons, and such as pronounce only in point of fact something which is wont to befall him who

> *Aut metuat dulces, aut experiatur amaros,*

*Either fears sweet loves, or experiences bitter ones*

> satis vel implicite per decursum fictae narrationis et ipsum euentum, et characteres personarum, quae iisdem vtuntur, ceu principiis practicis, sufficienter discreuerit? §. 549.

— it has sufficiently distinguished them, at least implicitly, through the course of the feigned narration and the outcome itself, and the characters of the persons who use them as practical principles? § 549.

> § 611. Sententiae fabularum Milesiarum venustius [p. 399] practicae, §. 610. illae scilicet, quae finis vltimus et scopus sunt totius operis, redeunt ad duas has generales maxime formulas, vel illam Veneris:

§ 611. The maxims of Milesian tales that are more charmingly [p. 399] practical, § 610, those namely which are the final end and aim of the whole work, come back to these two most general formulas, either that of Venus:

> *Nunc amet, qui nunquam amauit, quique amauit, nunc amet!*

*Now let him love who has never loved, and let him who has loved, now love!*

> vel hanc de bene multis amoribus non minus veram, etiam aesthetice:

or this one about a good many loves, no less true, even aesthetically:

> Non amet, qui nondum amauit, quique amauit, non amet.

Let him not love who has not yet loved, and let him who has loved, not love.

> Hinc, prout paraeneticam, vel elencticam suam sibi sumsit auctor primariam sententiam, §. 576. verisimilitudinem moralem strictius etiam dictam, §. 435. obseruare sancte debet, ne quid commendet, bonis moribus repugnans, ne quid dissuadeat in exemplo docens, quod virtus ex §. 211, 214. considerata, vel omnino postulet vel certe non, nisi morosa, reprehendat, §. 467, 470.

Hence, according as the author has taken as his primary maxim a paraenetic or an elenctic one, § 576, he must scrupulously observe moral verisimilitude even in the stricter sense, § 435, so that he commends nothing repugnant to good morals, and dissuades from nothing by teaching through an example what virtue, considered according to § 211, 214, either altogether demands or at least does not censure, except when it is peevish, § 467, 470.

> § 612. Decima sexta claudat agmen quaestio: An fabula heroica, praeter verisimilitudinem sibi cum aliis fabulis communem, hanc sibi propriam seruat strenue, qua persona herois praecipui semper eadem sibi constet, et vna, ἄνεσιν quidem et aliquam remissionem aliquando passa, sublimis tamen vel in eo, vt sponte colligatur et eleuetur denuo pristinum et eximium in decus. S. XXI. XXVI. §. 433, 538. Aeneas Cartagine videbatur ipsi Ioui *exspectans,*

§ 612. Let the sixteenth question close the ranks: whether the heroic fable, beyond the verisimilitude common to it with other fables, strenuously preserves this one proper to itself, by which the person of the chief hero always remains consistent with himself and one, having indeed at some time undergone an ἄνεσις [relaxation] and some remission, yet sublime even in this, that of his own accord he collects himself and is raised again to his former and eminent glory. S. XXI, XXVI, § 433, 538. Aeneas at Carthage seemed to Jupiter himself to be *lingering,*

> [p. 400] Quem *nulla accendit* magnarum *gloria rerum,* / *Nec super ipse sua molitur laude laborem,*

[p. 400] Whom *no glory of great things kindles,* / *Nor does he himself undertake any labour for his own praise,*

> tamen haud ita multo post adeo soporem ipse denuo suis excusserat oculis, vt magnifice, neque tamen magniloquentiae crimen incurrens, hortari posset Ascanium l. XII. 435:

yet not so very long after he had himself again so shaken the slumber from his eyes that he could magnificently, yet without incurring the charge of grandiloquence, exhort Ascanius, b. XII. 435:

> *Disce, puer virtutem ex me verumque laborem* / *Fortunam ex aliis.* / — — — — / *Te pater Aeneas et auunculus excitet Hector.*

*Learn, boy, virtue from me, and true labour,* / *Fortune from others.* / — — — — / *Let your father Aeneas and your uncle Hector rouse you.*

> § 613. Veritatem aestheticam S. XXVII. probe distinguens a falsitate aesthetica, S. XXVIII. venustius exhibens in verisimilitudinibus, S. XXVIIII. per fictiones varias, S. XXX, et ipsas aliquando poeticas, S. XXXI. non sine fabulis: S. XXXII. quae narrat, fingit, immo fabulari censetur, vbi probationibus indigent, si belle probat, S. XXXIII, vti suum vbique veritatis studium, S. XXXIIII. quamcunque sequatur verisimilitudinis speciem, S. XXXV. tunc etiam, quando fit poeta, S. XXXVI. venuste prodit: erit ille,
