§ 613. Rightly distinguishing aesthetic truth, S. XXVII, from aesthetic falsity, S. XXVIII, exhibiting it more charmingly in verisimilitudes, S. XXVIIII, through various fictions, S. XXX, and these sometimes poetic, S. XXXI, not without fables, S. XXXII, which it narrates, feigns, nay, is deemed to tell as fables, where they need proofs, if it proves beautifully, S. XXXIII, following its own pursuit of truth everywhere, S. XXXIIII, whatever species of verisimilitude it may follow, S. XXXV, even then, when it becomes a poet, S. XXXVI, charmingly coming forth: he will be,

> *Iudice me, non sordidus auctor* / *Naturae verique,* §. 104. Hor.

*In my judgement, no mean author* / *Of nature and of truth,* § 104. Hor.

## Aestheticorum Pars Altera. — Aesthetics, Second Part.

> SCRIPSIT ALEXANDER GOTTLIEB BAVMGARTEN PROFESSOR PHILOSOPHIAE.

WRITTEN BY ALEXANDER GOTTLIEB BAUMGARTEN, PROFESSOR OF PHILOSOPHY.

> FRANCOFVRTI CIS VIADRVM,

Frankfurt on the Oder,

> IMPENSIS IOANNIS CHRISTIANI KLEYB, MDCCLVIII.

at the expense of Johann Christian Kleyb, 1758.

### Praefatio. — Preface

> Fidem, quam edens partem aestheticorum primam praefando dederam, liberaturus non ita multo post hanc publici iuris factam horis subcesiuis accedebam ad telam, quam exorsus fueram, quamque praemissa tunc synopsis breuiter indicat, curatius pertexendam. Praeeuntem scribendo non lentus sequebatur typographus, et cito satis eo vsque perueneramus, vt absolueretur, quod nunc legentibus offerendum est, quum me morbus in lectum deiiceret adeo grauis, adeo pertinax, vt saepe non mihi solum, et meis, sed ipsis etiam peritissimis medicis conclamatus viderer. Satis diu, reor, interruptum pependit opusculum, et penderet adhuc, si iudicarem aequum resistere bibliopolae, qui moram hucusque patienter tulit, et nunc, quae iam impressa habet, ulterius premere hoc minus persuaderi potest, quum nondum ea sit ratio meae valetudinis, quae vires libris eiusmodi scribendis idoneas magis, quam mortem, polliceatur. Non sum nescius odiosos auctores esse plerumque de rebus suis narrantes, quae populus curet scilicet. Rationes equidem tribus tantum verbis reddere volui, cur ne certitudinis quidem aestheticae prorsus exhausta materia, vitam venustae cognitionis dulcissimam pulcritudinem, methodum lucidam, et elegantem illam semioticam, quae pulcris in orationibns [sic: orationibus] eloquutio dici solet et actio, non tetigerim, nec ad partem practicam aestheticorum pedem proferendi spes sit, quam aliquando secundam dixi, quaeque iam informaueram singula dictatis acroaseos, quae meditationibus his propiorem occasionem suppeditauerat. Si quis tamen superes, amice lector, qui me curas, qui me nosti, qui me amas denique, disce fortunam ex aliis, ex me, qui iam octauum in annum per ambages aegritudinum circumerro, quae videantur inextricabiles, quam necessarium sit, maturius bene cogitandis optimis assuefieri. Quid enim agerem, vti nunc sum, pro virili hoc agere nescius, profecto, nescio. Dabam Traiecti cis Viadrum, a. d. II. Kal. April. MDCCLVIII.

Meaning to redeem the pledge which I had given in the preface when I published the first part of the Aesthetics, I was returning, not so very long after it had been made public, in my spare hours to the web which I had begun and which the synopsis then prefixed briefly indicates, so as to weave it through more carefully. The printer followed my writing without delay, and we had quickly enough got so far that what must now be offered to readers was finished, when an illness threw me on my bed, so grave and so stubborn that I often seemed given up for lost not only to myself and my own people but even to the most skilled physicians. Long enough, I think, has the little work hung interrupted, and it would hang still, if I thought it fair to resist the bookseller, who has patiently borne the delay so far and who now can the less be persuaded to hold back any longer what he already has in print, since the state of my health is not yet such as to promise strength fit for the writing of books of this kind rather than death. I am not unaware that authors who tell of their own affairs, as if the public cared about them, are generally tiresome. I only wished to give, in three words, the reasons why I have not touched even the not yet wholly exhausted matter of aesthetic certainty, the life of charming cognition, its sweetest beauty, lucid method, and that elegant semiotics which in beautiful speeches is usually called elocution and delivery, and why there is no hope of advancing a step into the practical part of the Aesthetics, which I once called the second, and which I had already drafted piece by piece in the dictations of my lecture course, which had furnished the nearer occasion for these meditations. Yet if any of you survive, friendly reader, who care for me, who know me, who, in short, love me, learn from others’ fortune, and from mine, who now for the eighth year wander through windings of sickness that seem inextricable, how necessary it is to grow accustomed in good time to thinking well about the best things. For what I should do, being as I now am, unable to do this with all my might, I truly do not know. Given at Frankfurt on the Oder, on the second day before the Kalends of April, 1758.

### Aestheticorum Generalium. — General Aesthetics.

### Caput I. Heuristica. — Chapter I. Heuristics

#### Sectio XXXVII. Lux Aesthetica. — Section XXXVII. Aesthetic Light

> § 614. Verioris in cogitando §. 18. pulcritudinis §. 17. elegantiarumque studiosus quarto loco §. 115, 177, 423. LVCEM, claritatem, et perspicuitatem cogitatorum omnium sectetur, M. §. 531. sed AESTHETICAM, quae vel analogo rationis ad discrimina rei percipienda sufficiat. §. 22. M. §. 531. Perspicuitatem, vt vnam ex primis virtutibus eloquentiae luculenter commendans Quintilianus VIII. 2. rectissime distinguit *perspicuitatem in verbis*, quae non est huius loci, §. 13. et *rerum perspicuitatem*, qua obiecta [p. 402] venustae meditationis sint *dilucida et negligenter quoque audientibus* attendentibus *aperta*.

§ 614. One who is studious of truer beauty in thinking, § 18, § 17, and of its elegances, will in the fourth place, § 115, 177, 423, pursue LIGHT, clarity and perspicuity in all that he thinks, M. § 531, but AESTHETIC light, such as suffices even for the analogue of reason to perceive the distinguishing features of a thing, § 22, M. § 531. Quintilian VIII. 2, luminously commending perspicuity as one of the first virtues of eloquence, most rightly distinguishes *perspicuity in words*, which is not of this place, § 13, from *perspicuity of things*, by which the objects [p. 402] of a charming meditation are *lucid and open even to those who listen* and attend *carelessly*.

> § 615. Heic si *negligenter* attendentem *audientemue* placeat et eum dicere, qui non intendat percipiendis rebus, quae tractantur, intellectus rationisque suae vires et neruos, vt ita dicam, rigidius: eo lubens in Quintiliani sententiam. Eam vero mentem optimo fuisse rhetori paene mihi persuaserim, quoniam caussam asserti subiungit, non semper esse *tam acrem iudicis* (spectatoris, lectoris, auditoris) *intensionem, vt obscuritatem apud se ipse discutiat, et tenebris orationis inferat quoddam intelligentiae suae lumen*. Sin eum modo *negligenter audientem* attendentemue vocare placeat, qui *multis cogitationibus auocatus*, et distractus omnino, vel animo volutans ab iis, quae tu cogites, diuersissima, vel ebrius oscitans et somno sit proximus, breuiter, qui nec analogon rationis aduertere tuis cogitationibus velit aut possit: huic etiamsi quaedam a te venustius cogitanda minus aperta sint, ea tamen pulcra luce propterea destitui nondum vniuersim concesserim.

§ 615. If here one is pleased to call him too a *careless* attender *or hearer* who does not strain too stiffly the powers and sinews, so to speak, of his understanding and reason in perceiving the things that are treated, I gladly go over to Quintilian’s opinion. And I could almost persuade myself that this was the best of rhetoricians’ meaning, since he adds as the reason for his assertion that *the attention of the judge* (spectator, reader, hearer) *is not always so keen that he himself dispels the obscurity for himself, and brings into the darkness of the speech some light of his own intelligence*. But if one is pleased to call a *careless hearer* or attender only him who, *called away by many thoughts* and wholly distracted, is either turning over in his mind things utterly different from what you are thinking, or is drunk, yawning, and next door to sleep; in short, him who neither will nor can turn even the analogue of reason to your thoughts: then, even if some things which you must think out with greater charm are less open to such a man, I would not yet concede universally that they are on that account destitute of beautiful light.

> § 616. *Tam clara*, quae meditamur ad elegantiae regulas, omnia esse debere, *vt in animum* audientis *oratio, vt sol in oculos, etiamsi in eam* [p. 403] *non intendatur, incurrat*, non sine ratione negauerim, §. 615. Sit caussarum patrono *curandum non, vt intelligere possit* iudex, *sed ne omnino possit non intelligere*. Non omnis venuste cogitaturus est patronus caussae, nec omnis, quem ille, ceu praecipuum suum obiectum personale, recte considerat, iudex est eiusmodi, quales esse solebant romanorum pedanei.

§ 616. That everything we meditate according to the rules of elegance ought to be *so clear that the speech bursts into the mind* of the hearer *as the sun into the eyes, even if he* [p. 403] *is not straining towards it*, I should deny, not without reason, § 615. Let it be *the care of an advocate in a cause, not that* the judge *may be able to understand, but that he may be wholly unable not to understand*. Not everyone who is to think charmingly is the advocate of a cause, nor is everyone whom he rightly regards as his chief personal object a judge of the kind that the Roman judges-delegate used to be.

> § 617. LVCEM et perspicuitatem AESTHETICAM ipsa veritas iubet distinguere in ABSOLVTAM, omni pulcre cogitando necessariam, §. 614. et COMPARATIVAM, eum absolutae gradum, qui non, nisi quibusdam venustius meditandis, affundendus est, cuius exemplum §. 616. vidimus. Claritatis intensio per distinctionem, adaequationem, profunditatem, intelligentiaeque veluti puritatem, M. §. 637. prorsus non est lux aesthetica, §. 614. hinc nec absoluta, nec comparatiua, sed logica. Hinc nec intenditur directo, tanquam finis primarius, a pulcre cogitaturo, §. 14. licet et prodesse non nunquam eidem inter venuste cogitandum possit, si eam de themate suam fecerit, §. 551. et per indirectum, quando partes thematis non ita paucae sensitiua in luce refulgent, obtineatur simul totius conceptus extensiue distinctus, M. §. 634. intellectui pulcro, M. §. 637.

§ 617. Truth itself bids us distinguish AESTHETIC LIGHT and perspicuity into ABSOLUTE, necessary to all beautiful thinking, § 614, and COMPARATIVE, that degree of the absolute which is to be poured over only certain things that are to be meditated with greater charm, of which we saw an example in § 616. The intensification of clarity through distinctness, adequacy, depth and, as it were, purity of intelligence, M. § 637, is not at all aesthetic light, § 614, and hence neither absolute nor comparative, but logical. Hence it is not aimed at directly, as a primary end, by one who is to think beautifully, § 14, although it may sometimes be of use to him in the course of charming thinking, if he has made it his own concerning the theme, § 551, and indirectly, when not so few parts of the theme shine out in sensate light, an extensively distinct concept of the whole, M. § 634, is at the same time obtained for the beautiful intellect, M. § 637.

> § 618. [p. 404] Omnis itaque lux aesthetica, quam in rebus intendas directo, perspicuitas rerum erit sensitiua, claritatis per multitudinem notarum extensio, §. 617. etiam absoluta, comparatiua vero viuidarum cogitationum et materiae nitor ac splendor. M. §. 531. *Neroni* Tacitus Ann. XIII. 3. *puerilibus statim annis coelanti, pingenti, cantus aut regimen equorum exercenti, et aliquando carmina pangenti*, (quae farrago variarum occupationum!) *viuidum animum* tribuit. *Spurinnae* Plinius ep. III. 1. inde putat *agile corpus* esse *et viuidum*, quod non solum, *quoad honestum fuit, obierat officia, gesserat magistratus, prouincias rexerat, multoque labore meruerat otium*, sed etiam *senex ambulabat mane millia passuum tria, nec minus animum, quam corpus, exercebat, mox vehiculum adscendebat*, e. c. Vbi mira denuo motuum variatio, quotidianaeque viuendi rationis vicissitudo.

§ 618. [p. 404] All aesthetic light, therefore, which you aim at directly in things, will be the sensate perspicuity of things, the extension of clarity through a multitude of marks, § 617, also the absolute; the comparative, however, will be the brilliance and splendour of vivid thoughts and of the matter, M. § 531. Tacitus, Ann. XIII. 3, ascribes *a vivid mind* to *Nero*, who *from his boyhood years at once was engraving, painting, practising song or the management of horses, and sometimes composing verses* (what a hodgepodge of various occupations!). Pliny, ep. III. 1, thinks that *Spurinna* has *an agile and vivid body* from this, that not only, *so long as it was honourable, had he discharged his offices, held magistracies, governed provinces, and earned his leisure by much labour*, but also *as an old man he walked three miles in the morning and exercised his mind no less than his body; presently he mounted his carriage*, etc. Where there is again a wonderful variation of motions and a changing of the daily manner of life.

> § 619. Hinc iure mihi meo videor eas demum cogitationes dicere posse viuidas, in quibus peculiaris quaedam varietas, et subita veluti notarum se mutuo prementium celeritas deprehenditur, ex quarum eminenti diffusione nitor et splendor ille meditationis exsurgat in parte, cuius totum esse tamen debet perspicuum et absolute clarum: Sic Quintilianus [p. 405] IIII. 1. licet ipsum exordium recte poscat *dilucidum*, §. 617. tamen *magis conciliatis animis et iam calentibus, certos locos* tantum admittit, *quorum naturalis vbertas licentias* aliquas *notari circumfuso nitore non patiatur*. Quemadmodum hic naturalem vbertatem nitoris quasi matrem veneratur: ita Cicero de claris or. 36. *Hyperidi, Aeschini*, e. c. *hanc copiam, succum illum et sanguinem incorruptum* tribuit, *in quo naturalis fuerit, non fucatus nitor*. §. 104, 115.

§ 619. Hence I seem to myself rightly entitled to call those thoughts at last vivid in which a certain peculiar variety is detected, and a sudden, as it were, rapidity of marks pressing one upon another, from whose eminent diffusion that brilliance and splendour of a meditation rises up in a part, the whole of which must nevertheless be perspicuous and absolutely clear: thus Quintilian, [p. 405] IIII. 1, although he rightly demands that the exordium itself be *lucid*, § 617, nevertheless admits only *certain passages, when minds are more conciliated and already warm, whose natural richness does not allow* some *licences to be noticed, for the brilliance poured round them*. As he here venerates natural richness as, so to say, the mother of brilliance, so Cicero, de claris or. 36, ascribes to *Hyperides, Aeschines*, etc., *this copiousness, that sap and uncorrupted blood, in which there was a natural brilliance, not a cosmetic one*, § 104, 115.

> § 620. Nitida viuiditas venustae meditationis ne confundatur cum eius ardore ac vita, §. 22. de qua deinceps curatius. Recte pulcreque coniunguntur, quoties fieri potest, vt cogitationes non splendeant solum, sed et ardeant. §. 142, 143. cf. Quint. VIII. 3. Natura tamen sua disiunctae sunt in cogitando veneres, per accuratam harum theoriam separatim expendendae. Deprehenditur etiam vna non raro sine altera. Hac ratione Cicero de legibus l. 6. *Antipatrum* narrat *inflasse paullo vehementius*, ac eius antecessores, et *habuisse illum vires agrestes quidem atque* horridas, (vi mouendi vitaque non destitutum) *sine nitore tamen et palaestra*. §. 619, 256.

§ 620. Let not the brilliant vividness of a charming meditation be confused with its ardour and life, § 22, of which more carefully hereafter. They are rightly and beautifully joined, as often as it can be done, so that thoughts not only shine but also burn, § 142, 143, cf. Quint. VIII. 3. Yet by their nature these graces in thinking are disjoined, and are to be weighed separately through an accurate theory of them. One is also not rarely found without the other. In this way Cicero, de legibus I. 6, relates that *Antipater blew somewhat more vehemently* than his predecessors, and that *he had powers rustic indeed and* rough (not destitute of the force of moving and of life), *yet without brilliance and polish*, § 619, 256.

> § 621. Idem Cicero de finibus IIII. 5. Catoni [p. 406] forsan non obiecturus Stoicam huius politicorum theoriam eum non tantundem mouere et ad bene merendum de republica compellere, ac se suam academicam, libere tamen Catoni obiicit Stoica *de politicis definire partirique squalidius*, dum *academicorum* de iisdem *niteat oratio*, quoniam *multa de republica scripserint, multa de legibus, multa non solum praecepta in artibus, sed etiam exempla in orationibus reliquerint bene dicendi*. Ex quo loco mihi nunc sufficit nitoris veram notionem eruere, Ciceronis autem obiectionem meam non facio, §. 251, 252. Nostrum iam ad finem conferamus tandem eundem de claris or. 238. vbi *valde nitentem et plane horridam orationem*, vt aduersa fronte pugnantes describit.

§ 621. The same Cicero, de finibus IIII. 5, though perhaps not about to object to Cato [p. 406] that this Stoic theory of politics does not move him and impel him to deserve well of the commonwealth as much as his own Academic one does himself, nevertheless freely objects to Cato that the Stoics *define and divide political matters rather squalidly*, while *the discourse of the Academics* on the same matters *shines*, since *they have written much about the commonwealth, much about laws, and have left behind many not only precepts in the arts, but also examples of speaking well in their speeches*. From this passage it suffices me now to draw out the true notion of brilliance; Cicero’s objection, however, I do not make my own, § 251, 252. For our purpose let us finally compare the same author, de claris or. 238, where he describes *a very brilliant and a plainly rough speech* as fighting front to front.

> § 622. Iam bis naturalem, non fucatum, requiri nitorem vidimus §. 619. Neque magis necessarium esse videatur monitum de quaquam ex primariis cogitationum elegantiis, ac de hoc venustae meditationis nitore, §. 22. Quoniam in nulla facilius a recta naturae imitatione deflectitur. *Atque etiam, qui specie capiuntur, vulsis, leuatisque, et inustas comas acu comantibus, et non suo colore nitidis, plus esse formae putant, quam possit tribuere incorrupta natura, vt pulcritudo corporis venire videatur ex malis moribus*. Quint. II. 5. Erit autem [p. 407] naturalis in cogitando nitor, 1) cui capiendo naturales animi dotes, non distortae cum violentia, non intensae vehementius sufficiant, vt profluens *secundum naturam* meditatio *nihil ex ingenio habere videatur*, §. 104.

§ 622. We have now twice seen that brilliance is required to be natural, not cosmetic, § 619. Nor would an admonition seem more necessary about any one of the primary elegances of thoughts than about this brilliance of charming meditation, § 22, since in none is it easier to deflect from the right imitation of nature. *And likewise those who are captivated by show think that there is more beauty in men who are plucked and smoothed, who curl their hair with the branding-iron and are glossy with a colour not their own, than uncorrupted nature can bestow, so that the beauty of the body seems to come from bad morals*, Quint. II. 5. Now brilliance in thinking will be [p. 407] natural, 1) when the natural endowments of the mind, not twisted with violence, not strained too vehemently, suffice to grasp it, so that a meditation flowing *according to nature* may *seem to have nothing of contrivance in it*, § 104.

> § 623. Naturalis in cogitando nitor erit 2) materiis, et rebus, de quibus cogites, sic aptus, accommodatus, et quasi proprius, vt ex iisdem earumque cogitatione necessario potius enasci, quam in eandem inferri illinique decoris caussa deprehendatur. Huius hinc amicus elegantiae, si qua *tractata* per internas ac innatas opes *posse nitescere desperat, relinquit* ea potius, quam vt peregrinis pigmentis cogat splendescere, 3) eorum, quorum potissimum caussa cogitas, naturali captui, horizonti, ingenio, genio, indoli, ipsis, vt ita dicam, oculis adeo proportionatus, vt ab his sine fatigatione possit imbibi, nec eos praestringens, lumine tamen satians, collustrans amabiliter, non vrens incommode. Tertium hoc naturalis nitoris requisitum non satis attendentes, eundem vbique negant deprehendi, quando cogitata e. g. legunt suae naturae, cogitandi sentiendique rationi, genio, principalibus studiis minus consentanea, quamuis largiri debeant eos se non esse, quos praesertim auctor vel docere, vel [p. 408] delectare secum decreuerat. §. 104. cf. Cic. de or. I. 81.

§ 623. Brilliance in thinking will be natural, 2) when it is so fitted, accommodated and, as it were, proper to the materials and the things of which you think, that it is found rather to spring necessarily from them and from the thinking of them than to be brought into them and smeared on for the sake of adornment. Hence a friend of elegance, if he *despairs that any things handled can shine* by their internal and inborn resources, *leaves* them rather than force them to glitter with foreign pigments; 3) when it is so proportioned to the natural capacity, horizon, wit, genius, disposition, the very eyes, so to speak, of those for whose sake above all you think, that it can be imbibed by them without fatigue, not dazzling them, yet sating them with light, illuminating them lovingly, not burning them uncomfortably. Those who do not sufficiently attend to this third requisite of natural brilliance deny that it is found anywhere, when, for instance, they read thoughts little in accord with their own nature, their way of thinking and feeling, their genius, their principal studies, although they ought to grant that they are not the ones whom above all the author had resolved either to teach or to [p. 408] delight. § 104, cf. Cic. de or. I. 81.

> § 624. *In picturis alios horrida, inculta, abdita et opaca, contra alios nitida, laeta, collustrata delectat. Quid est, quo praescriptum aliquod aut formulam exprimas, quum in suo quodque genere praestet, et genera plura sint? Hac ego religione non sum ab hoc conatu repulsus, existimauique in omnibus rebus esse aliquid optimum*, (pulcerrimum) *etiamsi lateret*, (multos) *idque ab eo posse, qui eius rei gnarus esset, indicari*. Cic. orator. 36. Si quos in aestheticis absoluta pulcritudinis luce destituta, §. 617. absolute horrida, inculta, abdita et opaca delectant, falluntur illi, nubemque pro Junone, per me licet, amplectantur. Verum in omni venustate generatim, sicut in pictura, modo sint omnia luce, quam absolutam diximus, conspicua, non omnia, sed quaedam tantum, comparatiue lucida

§ 624. *In paintings some are delighted by the rough, the unpolished, the retired and the dark; others, on the contrary, by the brilliant, the cheerful, the well-lit. What is there by which you could express any rule or formula, when each excels in its own kind, and the kinds are many? I have not been driven back from this attempt by such a scruple, and I have judged that in all things there is something best*, (most beautiful) *even if it lies hidden* (from many), *and that this can be pointed out by one who is expert in the matter*. Cic. orator. 36. If in aesthetic matters some are delighted by things destitute of the absolute light of beauty, § 617, absolutely rough, unpolished, retired and dark, they are deceived, and for all I care let them embrace a cloud in place of Juno. But in every charm in general, as in a painting, provided that all things are conspicuous in the light we have called absolute, not all, but only some are comparatively lucid,

> *Ore floridulo nitent*, / *Alba parthenice velut*, / *Luteumue papauer*, Cat.

*they shine with a flowery face*, / *as the white feverfew*, / *or the yellow poppy*, Cat.

> quaedam sunt vere, sunt belle perspicua, quanquam, cum nitidis illis et admodum collustratis vbi comparentur, appareant opaca, quaeque primo obtutu iudicentur horrida, §. 621. Eleganter, non omnia, sed

some are truly, are prettily perspicuous, although, when they are compared with those brilliant and thoroughly illuminated things, they appear dark, and at first glance would be judged rough, § 621. Elegantly, not all, but

> *plura nitent in carmine*. Hor.

*more things shine in the poem*. Hor.

> § 625. [p. 409] GENVS COGITANDI luce absoluta aesthetica non destitutum si dicamus SIMPLICITER DILVCIDVM et perspicuum (sensitiue) §. 617. sicuti comparatiua etiam luce fulgens NITIDVM et splendidum: praeeuntem sequimur Quintilianum VIII. 3. quando: *Emendate quidem*, ait, *et dilucide* §. 619. *dicentium tenue praemium est, magisque vitiis carere est, quam vt aliquam magnam virtutem adeptus esse videaris*. — — — — *Non assequutus esset Cicero docendo tantum iudicem, et vtiliter demum, ac latine perspicueque docendo*, quod eum assequutum esse *nitore fulgentium armorum*, §. 282. vidimus. *Sed hic ornatus*, (*licet enim repetere*, §. 622.) *virilis, fortis, ac sanctus sit, nec effoeminatam leuitatem, nec fuco eminentem colorem amet, sanguine et viribus niteat*. §. 619. *Hoc autem adeo verum est, vt, cum in hac maxima parte sint vicina virtutibus vitia*, §. 622. *etiam qui vitiis vtuntur, virtutis tamen his nomen imponant. Quare nemo ex corruptis dicat me inimicum esse culte dicentibus. Non nego hanc esse virtutem. Sed illis eam non tribuo.*

§ 625. [p. 409] If we call a MANNER OF THINKING not destitute of absolute aesthetic light SIMPLY LUCID and perspicuous (in the sensate way), § 617, just as one shining also with comparative light BRILLIANT and splendid, we follow Quintilian going before us, VIII. 3, when he says: *The reward of those who speak correctly and lucidly*, § 619, *is slight, and it is more a matter of being free from faults than of seeming to have attained some great virtue*. — — — — *Cicero would not have achieved, by merely instructing the judge, and by instructing him usefully in the end, and in good Latin and perspicuously*, what we saw, § 282, that he achieved *by the brilliance of flashing arms*. *But let this ornament* (*for one may repeat it*, § 622) *be manly, strong and chaste; let it love neither effeminate smoothness nor a colour made prominent by cosmetic; let it shine with blood and strength*, § 619. *And this is so true that, since in this most important part the vices lie close to the virtues*, § 622, *even those who use the vices nevertheless give them the name of virtue. Wherefore let none of the corrupt say that I am an enemy of those who speak with cultivation. I do not deny that this is a virtue; but I do not attribute it to them.*

> § 626. Naturalis splendoris simiam, fucum in exemplis ridet Horatius. A. P. 25.

§ 626. Horace laughs at the ape of natural splendour, cosmetic, in examples, A. P. 25.

> *Inceptis grauibus plerumque et magna professis*, / *Purpureus, late qui splendeat, vnus et alter* / [p. 410] *Assuitur pannus, quum lucus et ara Dianae*, / *Et properantis aquae per amoenos ambitus agros*, / *Aut flumen Rhenum, aut pluuius describitur arcus*. / *Sed nunc non erat his locus*.

*Often, to grave beginnings and great professions*, / *a purple patch or two is stitched on, to shine far and wide*, / [p. 410] *when the grove and altar of Diana*, / *and the windings of hurrying water through pleasant fields*, / *or the river Rhine, or the rainbow is described*. / *But this was not the place for these things*.

> Habes ciconiam in maleferiatos eiusmodi pictores, qui materiam sibi legunt satis bellam et de qua speres singulariter non pulcra solum, sed etiam nouitate praeclara, de qua promittat auctor ipse spe tua paene maiora, quando autem deuenitur ad rem, caecum imitatorum pecus nescit aliquid noui, quod rerum natura, de quibus agitur, pronissime suppeditaret, in plena luce sistere, nescit collustrare, quae praecipuum splendorem requirerent, sed, vnitate neglecta, detorquet attentionem in diuersam omnino, vel minus connexam rem aliam, ideo tantum illatam in male cohaerens opus, vt ea, iam vero in nitore picta ab ingeniis vere pulcris, nunc denuo pingatur, si diis placet, nitidius, vere per obscurum et asiaticum, nescio quem, apparatum. §. 325, 623.

Here you have the stork for ill-starred painters of this kind, who choose themselves a subject pretty enough, and from which you might hope for things not only singularly beautiful but also distinguished by novelty, concerning which the author himself promises things almost greater than your hope; but when it comes to the point, the blind herd of imitators does not know how to set in full light anything new which the nature of the things in question would most readily supply, does not know how to illuminate what would require special splendour, but, neglecting unity, twists the attention aside to some other thing wholly different, or less connected, brought into the ill-cohering work only so that this thing, already painted in brilliance by truly beautiful wits, may now be painted again, if the gods please, more brilliantly, in truth with some obscure and Asiatic apparatus, I know not what. § 325, 623.

> *Nota magis nulli domus est sua, quam mihi lucus* / *Martis, et Aeoliis vicinum rupibus antrum* / *Vulcani. Quid agant venti, quas torqueat vmbras* / *Aeacus, vnde alius furtiuae deuehat aurum* / [p. 411] *Pelliculae, quantas iaculetur Monychus ornos*, / *Frontonis platani, conuulsaque marmora clamant* / *Semper, et assiduo ruptae lectore columnae*. / *Exspectes eadem a summo minimoque poeta*. Iuu. I. 8.

*No one’s own house is better known to him than to me the grove* / *of Mars, and the cave of Vulcan near the Aeolian* / *rocks. What the winds are doing, what shades Aeacus* / *is tormenting, whence another is carrying off the gold of the stolen* / [p. 411] *fleece, how huge the ash-trees that Monychus hurls*, / *the plane-trees of Fronto and the convulsed marbles cry out* / *continually, and the columns broken by the unceasing reciter*. / *You may expect the same from the greatest and the least poet*. Juv. I. 8.

> § 627. Alii pictores ex minimis, de quibus Iuuenalis, decipiuntur audacibus quorundam magnorum ingeniorum dictis, quale ad §. 125. notauimus, quale Ciceronis est in prooemio paradoxorum: *Nihil est tam horridum*, §. 621. *tam incultum, quod non splendescat oratione et tanquam excolatur*. Nec enim sentiunt primarios eiusmodi viros, *fretos* suis viribus, si penitius asserta perspiciamus, *falsum constituisse* de venusti in cogitando hominis *officio, et non quid ars, sed quid ipsi* forte *possent, exposuisse*. Hinc pulcelli, de quibus loquimur, micrologi, §. 356. se plerumque putantes aliquid egregii, colligunt suum esse nunc illorum implere vaticinia et audere, nisi Minerua, Fortuna tamen iuuante, quae fieri posse Cicero quidam interdum dormitans effatus est. Quaerunt itaque materias, quas excogitare possunt natura sua minimum splendoris admissuras, easque, vel inuitis diis omnibus, tot peregrinis flosculis, tot ornamentis amiciunt, vt potissimis suorum spectatorum sistant quidem thema non dissimile [p. 412] plumis alienis apud Aesopum superbientis corniculae, semper tamen eo melius se cogitasse gaudeant in sinu, quo minus hi ipsi spectatores ex proposita sibi tabula naturalis voluptatis, si vel artis ignari forent, haurire se potuisse fateantur. §. 623, 119-121.

§ 627. Other painters from among the least, of whom Juvenal speaks, are deceived by the bold sayings of certain great wits, such as we noted at § 125, such as Cicero’s in the proem of the Paradoxes: *Nothing is so rough*, § 621, *so unpolished, that it may not shine with speech and be, as it were, cultivated*. For they do not perceive that leading men of this kind, *relying* on their own powers, if we look more deeply into what they assert, *have laid down something false* about the *duty* of a man who thinks charmingly, *and have expounded, not what the art, but what they themselves* perhaps *could do*. Hence the pretty little men of whom we speak, the micrologists, § 356, generally thinking themselves something remarkable, conclude that it is now their business to fulfil the prophecies of those men and to dare, with Minerva unwilling but Fortune helping, what a certain Cicero, sometimes nodding, has declared can be done. So they seek out materials which they can devise as by their nature admitting the least splendour, and clothe them, even against the will of all the gods, with so many foreign flowerets, so many ornaments, that they indeed present to the chief of their spectators a theme not unlike [p. 412] the jackdaw in Aesop strutting in borrowed plumes, yet always rejoice in their hearts that they have thought the better, the less these very spectators confess that they could have drawn natural pleasure from the picture set before them, even if they were ignorant of the art. § 623, 119–121.

> § 628. Neque solus Heliconis pygmaeus natura talis adscititium belle cogitandis fucum a splendore vere naturali vix ac ne vix quidem discernet: §. 359. mediocribus etiam ingeniis idem erit difficillimum, quando praua per adolescentiam contracta consuetudo naturam vere elegantem simulabit, §. 622. et temporum iniuriae, locorumque, quibus vixerint, barbaries intimam pulcerrimarum rerum naturam obtegens haerere semper in cortice coget, iisdemque satis deprauatum apud aequales iudicium solas fucatas veneres, vt ipsius naturae filias, venerari consueuerit, §. 622. 623. Interim felicius in aestheticis ingenium, S. II-VII. veluti Caesar apud Ciceronem de claris or. 261. *rationem adhibens*, §. 38. *consuetudinem vitiosam et corruptam pura et incorrupta consuetudine emendat*, quum ad dilucidam vbique cogitationum elegantiam §. 625. *adiungit ornamenta* quaedam singularia, *tum videtur tanquam tabulas bene pictas collocare in bono lumine ac splendidam quandam, minimeque veteratoriam, rationem* cogitandi *tenet*.

§ 628. Nor will only the pygmy of Helicon, such by nature, scarcely, and indeed not even scarcely, distinguish the cosmetic adventitiously added to things prettily thought from truly natural splendour, § 359: for mediocre wits too the same will be most difficult, when a bad habit contracted in adolescence counterfeits truly elegant nature, § 622, and the injuries of the times and the barbarism of the places in which they have lived, covering over the inmost nature of the most beautiful things, compel them always to stick in the bark, and a judgement sufficiently depraved among their contemporaries by the same fates has grown used to venerating only cosmetic graces as the daughters of nature herself, § 622, 623. Meanwhile a happier wit in aesthetic matters, S. II–VII, like Caesar in Cicero, de claris or. 261, *applying reason*, § 38, *corrects a vicious and corrupt usage by a pure and uncorrupted usage*, and when to a lucid elegance of thoughts everywhere, § 625, *he adds* certain singular *ornaments, then he seems to set well-painted pictures in a good light, and holds* a certain *splendid, and by no means crafty, manner* of thinking.

> § 629. [p. 413] Cogitationum nitor ac splendor quoniam est species. immo gradus quidam, perspicuitatis sensitiuae, genus cogitandi logicodogmaticum aeque bene caret eodem, ac aestheticodogmaticum intensioribus perspicuitatis intellectualis gradibus, §. 617, 567. Quo magis erit illud genus cogitandi formaliter philosophicum, scientificum, et rationi solidiori, puriori intellectui, peruium ac perspicuum, hoc minus nitoris habebit et perspicuitatis etiam analogo rationis pellucidae. §. 578. Quo plus genus cogitandi dogmaticum viuidi splendoris habet, hoc minus ad logica, hoc magis ad aesthetica referendum est. §. 568. Hinc contra quosdam recentiorum miscelliones librorum suorum philosophicorum genus cogitandi Cicero iudicat ipse aestheticodogmaticum, dum de fin. I. 6. *Qui habent*, inquit, *vt graeca anteponant iis*, (scriptis meis de philosophia) *quae et splendide dicta sint, neque sint conuersa de graecis?* Apertius adhuc mentem exponit in prooemio parad. vbi: *Degustabis*, ait, *genus hoc exercitationum mearum, quibus vti consueui, quum ea, quae in scholis dicuntur* θετικὰ, *ad nostrum hoc oratorium transfero dicendi genus*. §. 569.

§ 629. [p. 413] Since the brilliance and splendour of thoughts is a species, indeed a certain degree, of sensate perspicuity, the logico-dogmatic manner of thinking lacks it just as well as the aesthetico-dogmatic manner lacks the more intensive degrees of intellectual perspicuity, § 617, 567. The more formally philosophical and scientific that manner of thinking is, and the more pervious and perspicuous to a more solid reason and a purer intellect, the less brilliance will it have, and the less perspicuity even to a translucent analogue of reason, § 578. The more vivid splendour a dogmatic manner of thinking has, the less is it to be referred to logic, and the more to aesthetics, § 568. Hence, against certain hodgepodge-makers among the moderns, Cicero himself judges the manner of thinking of his own philosophical books to be aesthetico-dogmatic, when in de fin. I. 6 he says: *What reason have they to prefer Greek works to those* (my writings on philosophy) *which are both splendidly expressed and are not translated from the Greek?* He expounds his mind still more openly in the proem of the Paradoxes, where he says: *You will taste this kind of my exercises, which I have been accustomed to use, when I transfer the things which are called in the schools* θετικά [thetic, general questions] *to this our oratorical manner of speaking*. § 569.

> § 630. *Equidem* cum Cicerone off. I. 6. *existimo*, [p. 414] *Demosthenem, si illa, quae a Platone didicerat, tenuisset et pronunciare voluisset, ornate splendideque facere potuisse*. §. 567. Si vero fecisset ornate, si fecisset splendide, si se in philosophico disputandi genere praestitisset Demosthenem: tunc ex mea sententia non tam rationem et intellectum, qua potest fieri, cum evidentia instructurus, quam analogon rationis ingenti persuasionis lumine collustraturus fuisset. §. 629, 568.

§ 630. *For my part*, with Cicero, off. I. 6, *I judge* [p. 414] *that Demosthenes, if he had held to what he had learned from Plato and had wished to declaim it, could have done so ornately and splendidly*, § 567. But if he had done it ornately, if he had done it splendidly, if in the philosophical manner of disputation he had shown himself a Demosthenes, then in my opinion he would not so much have furnished reason and the intellect with evidence, so far as can be done, as have illuminated the analogue of reason with a vast light of persuasion. § 629, 568.

#### Sectio XXXVIII. Obscuritas Aesthetica. — Section XXXVIII. Aesthetic Obscurity

> § 631. Defectus et oppositum lucis ac claritatis quum sit *obscuritas*, lux autem et claritas vel sensitiua, vel intellectualis, S. XXXVII. rectissime iam veteres obscuritatem κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν ab obscuritate κατὰ νόησιν distinxerunt. Res et cogitatio, quae sensitiue percipienda non satis claritatis, extensiuae scilicet, aestheticaeque lucis habet, est obscura κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν. Hinc distinctiora, puriora, profundiora quaeuis per scientias, quoniam ea non assequitur analogon rationis, per hoc solum si quis velit considerare, non queretur ea solum obscura, sed etiam sentiet, vti sunt κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν.

§ 631. Since *obscurity* is the defect and opposite of light and clarity, while light and clarity are either sensate or intellectual, S. XXXVII, the ancients already most rightly distinguished obscurity κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν [according to sense] from obscurity κατὰ νόησιν [according to understanding]. A thing and a thought which, when to be perceived in a sensate way, does not have enough clarity, extensive clarity that is, and aesthetic light, is obscure κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν. Hence whatever is more distinct, purer, deeper by way of the sciences, since the analogue of reason does not attain it, if one wishes to consider it by this alone, one will not only complain that it is obscure, but will also feel it to be so, as it is, κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν.

> § 632. [p. 415] Res et cogitatio, quae per intellectum et rationem concipienda non tantum claritatis, intensiuae scilicet, distinctionis, puritatis, ac profunditatis habet, quantum ad distinguendum ex notis claris et rationibus probe perspectis, vel enucleatius pronunciandum, vel complete demonstrandum requiritur, est obscura κατὰ νόησιν. Hinc si quis bene multa non solum aesthetice dilucida, sed etiam pulcro nitore splendida, sicut eadem propinantur soli rationis analogo, distinctius tamen concipere, ratione rimari profundius laborauerit, ea saepe numero non queretur solum obscura, sed etiam sentiet, vti sunt κατὰ νόησιν.

§ 632. [p. 415] A thing and a thought which, when to be conceived through the intellect and reason, does not have as much clarity, intensive clarity that is, distinctness, purity and depth, as is required for distinguishing from clear marks and well-examined grounds, or for pronouncing in a more thoroughly analysed way, or for demonstrating completely, is obscure κατὰ νόησιν. Hence if anyone has laboured to conceive more distinctly, to search out more deeply with reason, a good many things which are not only aesthetically lucid but also splendid with beautiful brilliance, just as they are proffered to the analogue of reason alone, he will often not only complain that they are obscure, but will also feel it to be so, as they are, κατὰ νόησιν.

> § 633. Perspicuitatis ac lucis vti primaria laus est, ita turpe profecto huic laudabili claritati vere oppositae obscuritatis vituperium. §. 23. Haec etiam vel rerum et cogitationum, vel signorum, vocabulorum ac phrasium est obscuritas. De prima nunc nobis tantum agitur, §. 614. eiusque illa specie, quam olim dixerunt κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν. §. 631. Sint per meditationem venustam non ita pauca κατὰ νόησιν obscura, quorum accurata sit repertu difficilis definitio, genesis in fundo lateat, nexus parum euidenter a ratione perspiciatur; non curat hanc obscuritatem ad solas paene puras [p. 416] scientias relatam ingenium vere pulcrum, §. 632. modo detur effugere OBSCVRITATEM AESTHETICAM, defectum lucis aestheticae in suis (rebus ac cogitationibus) ad elegantiae leges examinandis. §. 632, 614.

§ 633. As the praise of perspicuity and light is a primary one, so, to be sure, the blame of the obscurity truly opposed to this praiseworthy clarity is disgraceful, § 23. This, too, is an obscurity either of things and thoughts, or of signs, words and phrases. We are now concerned only with the first, § 614, and with that species of it which they once called κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν, § 631. Let there be, in the course of a charming meditation, not so few things obscure κατὰ νόησιν, whose accurate definition is hard to find, whose genesis lies hidden at the bottom, whose connection is but little evidently perceived by reason; a truly beautiful wit does not trouble about this obscurity, which is referred almost to the pure sciences alone, [p. 416] § 632, provided that it be granted it to escape AESTHETIC OBSCURITY, the defect of aesthetic light in its own things (the things and thoughts) which are to be examined by the laws of elegance. § 632, 614.

> § 634. Obscuritas aesthetica vel erit defectus lucis in aestheticis absolutae, §. 617. quam CALIGINEM AESTHETICAM dicamus, et meram noctem, vel comparatiuae tantum, nitoris alicuius ac splendoris eximii, quae denuo vel nascetur per exceptionem non inelegantem, §. 25, defectus tantum apparens, VMBRA AESTHETICA, vel erit defectus vere talis et priuatio viuiditatis ad veram pulcritudinem requisitae, dabitque GENVS COGITANDI PLANE HORRIDVM cum aesthetica caligine. §. 621. Neque solam ipsam noctem horrebit vbique sedulo pulcre cogitaturus, sed etiam non minus, ac eos, quorum gratia fiat Aristarchus, horridulis quibusdam, dilucidis vtique, §. 625. sed non sine macula comparatiue

§ 634. Aesthetic obscurity will be either the defect of the light that is absolute in aesthetic matters, § 617, which let us call AESTHETIC DARKNESS, and sheer night; or of the comparative light only, of some brilliance and eminent splendour, which again will either arise through an exception that is not inelegant, § 25, an only apparent defect, AESTHETIC SHADE, or will be a defect truly such and a privation of the vividness required for true beauty, and will give a PLAINLY ROUGH MANNER OF THINKING, along with aesthetic darkness, § 621. Nor will he who is everywhere diligently to think beautifully shudder only at night itself, but also, no less than those for whose sake he becomes an Aristarchus, he will compel certain rather rough things, lucid indeed, § 625, but comparatively not without blemish

> *parum claris, lucem dare coget*,

*and too little clear, to give light*,

> vmbras autem pro formae commodis nunc sequetur, nunc fugiet, §. 614.

while shades he will now follow, now flee, according to the advantages of the form, § 614.

> § 635. Vmbrarum nomine complectimur omnia illa artificia, naturam imitantia, quibus quaedam [p. 417] inter venuste cogitandum non in tanta luce constituuntur, non tanta cum claritate extensiua dilatantur, ac fieri posset, ab ignaris venustae parsimoniae, §. 164. e. g. quando minus connexa themati velut e longinquo tantum ostenduntur, sensim magnitudine, sicut optice, decrescentia, quasi per nebulam. Sic enim per naturam rerum porticus aeque distantibus columnis ac aequalibus suffulta

§ 635. Under the name of shades we comprise all those artifices, imitating nature, by which certain things [p. 417] in the course of charming thinking are not set in so great a light, are not spread out with so great an extensive clarity, as could be done by those ignorant of charming parsimony, § 164; e.g. when things less connected with the theme are only shown as if from afar, gradually decreasing in magnitude, as in optics, as if through a mist. For thus by the nature of things a portico, supported on columns equally spaced and equal in size,

> *Longa*, tamen *parte ab summa si tota videtur*, / *Paullatim trahit angusti fastigia coni*, / *Tecta solo iungens, atque omnia dextera laeuis* / *Donec in obscurum coni contraxit acumen*, Lucr. IIII. 430.

*though long, if it is seen whole from its upper end*, / *gradually draws the tapering of a narrow cone*, / *joining the roof to the ground and all the right side to the left*, / *until it has contracted into the obscure point of the cone*, Lucr. IIII. 430.

> Sic per *obscurum coeptae lucis* paullatim panditur breuis meridies, quam inter et mediam noctem est media *post solis occasum obscura lux*.

Thus through *the obscurity of beginning light* the brief noon is gradually unfolded, and between it and midnight stands the intermediate *obscure light after the setting of the sun*.

> § 636. Turpem obscuritatem in pulcre cogitandis procreabit attentionis, quantam ab analogo rationis apud praecipuos tuos spectatores exspectare possis, nimia 1) intensio, quando simulas popularem aliquam cogitandi rationem, vere tamen ea concipis, eoque modo cum iisdem communicas, qui iam multum et eruditum intellectus et rationis vsum requirat probe capiendus, quae soli rationis [p. 418] horizonti relinquenda videantur. §. 121, 615, 622. 2) extensio et 3) protensio si tentetur, M. 628. dum satis ad venustos fines iam aperta atque dilucida vel 1) splendore tamen circumfunduntur adhuc nouo, praestringente oculos, §. 633. viuiditate notarumque plurimarum variatione animum distrahente a pulcra totius, thematis et primariarum eius partium, consideratione, §. 629. M. §. 638. vel 2) luxurianti diffusione §. 165. tamdiu illustrantur nouis semper ac nouis commentationibus, donec fatigatus mole rerum ac cogitationum animus fatiscat et silua quadam obruatur potius, quam recreetur. §. 623.

§ 636. A disgraceful obscurity in things to be thought beautifully will be begotten by the excessive 1) intension of such attention as you can expect from the analogue of reason among your chief spectators, when you counterfeit some popular manner of thinking, yet in truth you conceive things, and in that way communicate them to the same people, which, to be properly grasped, already require a great and learned use of the intellect and of reason, and which seem fit to be left to the horizon [p. 418] of reason alone, § 121, 615, 622; 2) if its extension and 3) its protension be attempted, M. 628, while things already sufficiently open and lucid for the ends of charm either 1) are nevertheless surrounded with yet new splendour, dazzling the eyes, § 633, with a vividness and a variation of very many marks that distracts the mind from the beautiful consideration of the whole, of the theme and of its primary parts, § 629, M. § 638, or 2) by a luxuriant diffusion, § 165, are illuminated with ever new and newer comments for so long that the mind, wearied by the mass of things and thoughts, grows faint and is rather buried under a kind of forest than refreshed, § 623.

> § 637. Secundam ac tertiam obscuritatis vitiosae genesin simul tangere videtur Cicero de Inu. II. 156. *Vniuscuiusque*, inquiens, *constitutionis exemplum supponere non grauaremur, nisi illud videremus, quemadmodum res obscurae dicendo fierent apertiores, sic res apertas obscuriores fieri oratione*. Quid enim? Exempla illa alias illustrantia, vel satis breuia fulgentissimis exornasset luminibus, et praestrinxissent hoc loco, vel pluribus diducta longo ordine exposuisset, et fatigassent hic spectatorum oculos. §. 636.

§ 637. Cicero seems to touch at once the second and third genesis of vicious obscurity, de Inu. II. 156, saying: *We should not have been reluctant to supply an example of each kind of issue, had we not seen that, just as obscure things become clearer by speaking, so clear things become obscurer by speech*. For what? Those examples, illuminating in other contexts, he would either have adorned, short enough as they were, with the most flashing lights, and in this place they would have dazzled; or he would have expounded them drawn out at length in a long series, and here they would have wearied the eyes of the spectators, § 636.

> § 638. Turpior nascetur obscuritas aesthetica, 4) [p. 419] si vel absolute et in se obscurum thema, chimaeram aliquam et merum nihil, quod videatur aliquid, eleganter aliquis explanandum sibi sumserit, vel certe rem relatiue non ad spectatorum solum, sed et ipsius auctoris captum adeo obscuram, vt eam nec sensibus ac imaginatione, nec intellectus vi consequatur ipse, quam tamen aliis pollicetur exponere. Huc *magna* pertinet, *neque ea naturalis*, §. 622, 623. *sed artificiosa* §. 110. *somniorum Antiphontis interpretatio. Eodemque modo et oraculorum et vaticinationum* bene multa mendacia, multaeque verorum etiam *explanationes, in quibus multa obscura sunt ac ambigua*. Cic. de diu. I. 116. cf. II. 115.

§ 638. A more disgraceful aesthetic obscurity will arise, 4) [p. 419] if someone has either undertaken to explain elegantly a theme absolutely and in itself obscure, some chimera and a mere nothing that seems to be something, or at any rate a thing relatively so obscure, not only to the grasp of the spectators but also to that of the author himself, that he himself attains it neither by the senses and the imagination nor by the force of the intellect, and yet promises to expound it to others. To this belongs that *great interpretation of dreams by Antiphon, and that not natural*, § 622, 623, *but artificial*, § 110. *And in the same way* a good many lies *of oracles and prophecies*, and many *explanations* even of true ones, *in which many things are obscure and ambiguous*. Cic. de diu. I. 116, cf. II. 115.

> § 639. Duplex eorum genus est, qui de bonis rebus et in se probe perspicuis earum omnino ignari, belle tamen, disserere frustra conantur. Primum est sincerius ac simplicius, eoque facilius detegendae turpitudinis, qui stolide sibi persuadent, rem bene geri, quoties de re, quam norunt cum ignarissimis, audacter incipiant, magnis hiatibus, signa sine mente, sed non sine flumine, profundere, obscurum per obscurius exponere, crepuscula collustrare tenebris, quas intelligere nemo alias possit, quoniam ipsi sua cogitantes non intellexerant. Alterum est magis subdolum et quasi veteratorium, quod in eadem [p. 420] rerum optimarum inscitia per eandem impudentiam de quibusuis venustam scilicet meditationem aggreditur, sed callido satis consilio suae mentis caliginem ita tegens, vt ignorantiae suae culpam in ipsam materiam et rem, de qua agitur, commode deuoluat, suisque spectatoribus, quorum aliquos aeque rerum ignaros inuenire non est difficile, largiatur non apud ipsos, sed in rebus cogitandis quaerendam esse caussam, cur illae nequeant intelligi. Sic enim dum fouet, et excusat suorum naeuos auctor eiusmodi ab his denuo non excusatus solum abibit, sed etiam saepe numero collaudatus, qui solus rerum tenebras viderit, quas alii, doctiores qui videri velint, soli meridiano comparantes mentiantur. §. 638.

§ 639. There are two kinds of those who try in vain to discourse, prettily nonetheless, about good things, perspicuous in themselves, of which they are wholly ignorant. The first is more sincere and simpler, and therefore its disgrace is more easily detected: those who stupidly persuade themselves that the business is well done whenever, concerning a thing which they know as well as the most ignorant, they boldly begin to pour out with great gapings signs without mind, though not without a stream of words, to expound the obscure by the obscurer, to illuminate twilight with darkness, which no one else can understand, since they themselves did not understand their own thoughts while thinking them. The other is more underhand and, as it were, practised in trickery, which in the same [p. 420] ignorance of the best things, with the same impudence, sets about a charming meditation, forsooth, on anything whatever, but with a sufficiently cunning design so covers the darkness of its own mind as conveniently to shift the blame for its ignorance on to the very matter and thing in question, and to grant its spectators, some of whom it is not difficult to find equally ignorant of the things, that the reason why those things cannot be understood is to be sought not in themselves but in the things to be thought. For thus, while an author of this kind cherishes and excuses the blemishes of his own people, he will depart from them not only excused in turn, but even often praised, as the only one who has seen the darkness of things, about which others, who wish to seem more learned, lie when they compare them to the noonday sun. § 638.

> § 640. Huius obscuritatis §. 636, 637. non vnum exemplum nobis offerunt Ciceronis libri de natura deorum, quorum l. III. 94. *Cotta dicendi finem facit: Haec fere*, inquiens, *dicere habui de natura deorum, non vt eam tollerem, sed vt intelligeretis, quam esset obscura, et quam difficiles explicatus haberet*. Quoniam enim per omnem eorum decursum euidentissimae religionis naturalis quaestiones, cum superstitionibus graecoromanis misere confunduntur, quarum plerasque Stoici sub tutelam philosophiae sinistris auibus receptum ibant, [p. 421] §. 636. quas omnes, sed cum veris verissimae religionis anticipationibus, in sinu certe, ridebant Epicurei: §. 637. Cotta academicus, dum illas impugnat, nunc obscuritatem porticus iure suo salse ridet, quoties hi somniorum interpretamenta crepabant, §. 638. nunc Epicureorum vanas ambages, et impudentem audaciam bene perstringit, quando hi diuinorum satis incurii, deorum tamen quasi carnem et quasi sanguinem, et intermundiorum otia multis exponebant, ne nihil omnino de diis dixisse viderentur, nunc autem et *vehementius inuectus etiam in illam rationem, quae de Prouidentia sanctissime et prouidentissime constituta est*, multa per se obscura callide fingit, quae sunt aperta cuiuis veriorem religionem agnoscenti. §. 639.

§ 640. Of this obscurity, § 636, 637, Cicero’s books on the nature of the gods offer us not one example only; in book III. 94 of them *Cotta makes an end of speaking*, saying: *This is roughly what I had to say on the nature of the gods, not in order to abolish it, but that you might understand how obscure it is, and how difficult the explanations it admits*. For since throughout their whole course the questions of a most evident natural religion are wretchedly confounded with Graeco-Roman superstitions, most of which the Stoics, under evil omens, were taking under the guardianship of philosophy, [p. 421] § 636, all of which, but together with the true anticipations of the truest religion, the Epicureans laughed at, at least in their sleeve, § 637: Cotta the Academic, while he assails them, now rightly and wittily laughs at the obscurity of the Porch, whenever these men were rattling off interpretations of dreams, § 638; now well censures the empty windings and impudent audacity of the Epicureans, when these, careless enough of divine things, nevertheless expounded at length the quasi-flesh and quasi-blood of the gods and the leisure of the intermundane spaces, lest they should seem to have said nothing at all about the gods; but now, *inveighing also more vehemently against that account which has been most holily and most providently established concerning Providence*, he cunningly feigns many things to be obscure in themselves which are open to anyone acknowledging the truer religion. § 639.

> § 641. Turpioris obscuritatis §. 638. notatae dabunt exempla, nunc alterutro, nunc vtroque morbo, de quo §. 639, laborantes veterum multi chemici, praesertim alchemistae, quibus arcana sunt omnia, praesertim philosophorum lapis, multi recentiorum etiam mystici, quoties vere diuinis non contenti noua sibi ac suis excogitant mysteria, omnis magiam simulans et nocturnum cum daemonibus commercium, si

§ 641. Examples of the more disgraceful obscurity noted in § 638 will be given, labouring now under one, now under both of the diseases spoken of in § 639, by many chemists of old, especially the alchemists, to whom all things are secrets, especially the philosophers’ stone, and by many mystics among the moderns too, whenever, not content with the truly divine, they devise new mysteries for themselves and their own, every one of them counterfeiting magic and a nocturnal commerce with demons, if

> *obscurum verborum ambage nouorum* / [p. 422] *Ter nouies carmen magico de murmurat ore*. Ou.

*obscure in the windings of strange words* / [p. 422] *she murmurs thrice nine times a spell from her magic mouth*. Ov.

> § 642. Primam obscuritatis caussam aestheticae §. 636. cauturus solicitus abstinebit a discernendis a se inuicem iis omnibus, quae singula quidem sunt dilucida, vel omnino nitida, §. 625. salua tamen pulcritudine totius, ad quod pertinent, confunduntur ac miscentur ab analogo rationis saepe numero. Sit in venusta quapiam pictura *Cnidius* aliquis *Gyges*, salua pulcritudine totius

§ 642. One who is anxious to guard against the first cause of aesthetic obscurity, § 636, will refrain from distinguishing from one another all those things which, though each one is lucid, or even brilliant, § 625, are nevertheless, without harm to the beauty of the whole to which they belong, often confounded and mingled by the analogue of reason. Let there be in some charming picture a *Cnidian Gyges*, without harm to the beauty of the whole,

> *Quem si puellarum insereres choro*, / *Mire sagaces falleret hospites* / *Discrimen obscurum, solutis* / *Crinibus ambiguoque vultu*: Hor. II. oda V. 21.

*whom, if you were to slip him into a chorus of girls*, / *the obscure difference would wonderfully deceive the shrewd guests*, / *with his flowing hair* / *and ambiguous face*: Hor. II, ode V. 21.

> Noli tunc proditorem agere, voluptatisque circulos turbare velle, superfluam potius distinguendi sagacitatem vmbris tege commodis. §. 634. M. 645.

Do not then play the betrayer and wish to disturb the circles of pleasure; rather cover a superfluous sagacity in distinguishing with convenient shades. § 634, M. 645.

> § 643. Secundam obscuritatis vel optima deturpantis viam §. 636. temere ingreditur I) de suis praecipuis spectatoribus melius praeclariusque sentiens, ac debebat, iisque penetrantius acumen et vberiorem attendendi perspiciendique vim tribuens, ac vere vel [p. 423] habent, vel exercent, adeoque, dum tantis ingeniis vix se putat satisfacturum ingenii sui modulo, quicquid est vbique nitoris, constipat et cogit, quantum potest, in vnum, et hac ratione

§ 643. The second way of obscurity, which disfigures even the best things, § 636, is rashly entered upon I) by one who thinks better and more highly of his chief spectators than he ought, and attributes to them a more penetrating acumen and a richer power of attending and perceiving than they truly either [p. 423] have or exercise, and so, while he thinks that he will scarcely satisfy such great wits with the small measure of his own wit, crowds and forces together, as far as he can, into one whatever brilliance there is anywhere, and in this way

> *plerumque modestus* / *Occupat obscuri speciem*.

*for the most part, being modest*, / *he takes on the appearance of the obscure*.

> § 644. Eandem in tenebras viam inibit II. de semet ipse, de sua suorumque cogitatorum auctoritate sentiens augustius, ac fas est, et hinc tacite postulans legi, velut aenigmata, relegi sua, quot verbis, tot ponderibus insignia, et haerentem in singulis picturae suae ductibus spectatorem subsistere, neque pedem vlterius, nec oculos proferre, nisi saepius volutatis animo, quae viderat, diuque perpensis, tandem assequutus sit, quid sibi velint. Ob hanc forte caussam *valde obscurus est Heraclitus, minime Democritus.* Apophthegmatibus ille suis σκοτεινός sibi nomen promeritus est, huius composita oratio et ornata, et artificio captum lectoris, §. 643. ac suam auctoritatem metientium, et expolitione distincta Ciceronis, immo lectorum hoc minus philosophicorum, calculum tulit. §. 251.

§ 644. The same road into darkness will be entered II. by one who thinks more loftily of himself, of the authority of himself and of his thoughts, than is right, and who hence tacitly demands that his works be read and, like riddles, re-read, remarkable for as many weights as they have words, and that the spectator, lingering on each stroke of his picture, halt and advance neither foot nor eyes any further until, having often turned over in his mind what he had seen and long weighed it, he has at last grasped what they mean. For this reason perhaps *Heraclitus is very obscure, Democritus not at all.* The former earned himself by his apophthegms the name σκοτεινός [the obscure]; the latter’s composed and ornate speech, by the artifice of those who measure the reader’s grasp, § 643, and their own authority, and by its distinct polish, has carried the vote of Cicero, nay, of readers less philosophical than he. § 251.

> § 645. Subobscurum hoc biuium §. 643, 644. [p. 424] cauebit aesthetica dynamica, §. 60. ita rationes virium et extendendae attentionis apud spectatores suos praecipuos subducens, vt in casu dubii, an hi belle cogitaturum satis assequuturi mentemque eius sint, vt ita dicam, exaequaturi, malit nimis apertus, quam opertus caligine videri, ita eiusdem auctoritatem apud eosdem dimensa, vt in casu dubii, an hi belle cogitantis lectionem decies repetituri sint, nec ne, malit prima lectione statim intelligi, quam vltima, §. 636. Praesertim hos sibi calculos recte commendatissimos habent caussarum *patroni*, à quibus *ius obscurum et ignotum* aliquando *patefaciendum* est *in iudicia atque illustrandum*, §. 615, 616. Negligat has rationes auctoris siue modestia, §. 643. siue fastus et arrogantia, §. 644. conueniet illi cum Horatio queri:

§ 645. This somewhat obscure fork in the road, § 643, 644, [p. 424] aesthetic dynamics, § 60, will beware of: so reckoning the powers of its principal spectators and the attention they can extend that, in a doubtful case whether these will sufficiently follow one who is to think beautifully and, so to speak, keep pace with his mind, it would rather appear too open than veiled in darkness; and so measuring his authority among the same that, in a doubtful case whether these will repeat ten times the reading of one who thinks beautifully or not, it would rather be understood at once on the first reading than on the last, § 636. Above all the *advocates* of causes have these reckonings rightly most commended to them, by whom a *right obscure and unknown* must sometimes be *laid open in the courts and illuminated*, § 615, 616. Should the author’s modesty, § 643, or his pride and arrogance, § 644, neglect these considerations, it will befit him to complain with Horace:

> *Breuis esse laboro, / Obscurus fio.*

*I labour to be brief, / I become obscure.*

> *Cauenda est, quae nimium omnia corripientes sequitur, obscuritas.* Quint. IIII. 2.

*The obscurity which follows upon those who cut everything too short must be avoided.* Quintilian IIII. 2.

> § 646. Neque tamen cum omni sua latitudine potuit obscuritatis notam omnem effugere Plato, ne fauentem quidem apud iudicem, Ciceronem, quaest. ac. IIII. 123. Tantae molis est rotunda breuitas, §. 166. optimum antidoton contra tertiam obscuritatis vitandae [p. 425] caussam, §. 636. Apud eundem Ciceronem de fin. II. 15. reprehenditur *Epicurus*, qui *nec nolit, si possit, plane et aperte loqui, nec de re obscura, vt physici,* §. 639. *aut artificiosa, vt mathematici, sed de illustri ac facili, etiam in vulgus peruulgata,* voluptate, *loquatur*, neque tamen possit intelligi. Si quid subest obiectionibus veri, quae satis suspectae sunt, dum vera voluptas putatur esse res facilis et in vulgus peruulgata: sane non aliud est Epicuri peccatum aestheticum, quam quod in diducendis suis acroasibus practicis per scripta a quibusuis legenda paullo verbosior, rotundaeque breuitatis negligentior fuit, vnde factum, vt pauci totam voluptatis theoriam ex eodem hauserint, attentione satis protensa, plurimi quandam eius partem, quasi totum, arripuerint, nunc hanc, nunc illam ex plurimis Epicuri scriptis cursim attendendo laciniam. §. 636.

§ 646. Yet not even with all his breadth could Plato escape every mark of obscurity, not even before a favourable judge, Cicero, quaest. ac. IIII. 123. Of such moment is rounded brevity, § 166, the best antidote against the third cause of obscurity to be avoided, [p. 425] § 636. In the same Cicero, de fin. II. 15, *Epicurus* is reproved, who *is not unwilling, if he can, to speak plainly and openly, nor speaks of an obscure matter, as the physicists,* § 639, *or of an artificial one, as the mathematicians, but of a thing illustrious and easy, and even commonly known to the vulgar,* pleasure, and yet cannot be understood. If there is something true in these objections, which are suspicious enough, since true pleasure is thought to be an easy thing and commonly known to the vulgar: assuredly Epicurus’ aesthetic sin is no other than that in drawing out his practical lectures through writings to be read by anyone he was a little too wordy and too negligent of rounded brevity, whence it came about that few drew the whole theory of pleasure from him with sufficiently sustained attention, while most seized on some part of it as though it were the whole, attending cursorily now to this, now to that scrap from the very many writings of Epicurus. § 636.

> § 647. Ad obturandum quartum turpioris obscuritatis fontem, §. 638. 1) ne quid aesthetice falsi, ne febriculosorum somnia, pulcris condecorare cogitationibus somnies, §. 456. Nec enim veri tantum amor, sed etiam perspicuitatis inde studium auocat, quoniam absolute obscuris eiusmodi vera semper deerit lux aesthetica. §. 614. 2) in ipsis fictionibus [p. 426] mundi poetici nolis vtopiam habitare, §. 514. per quam etiam peregrinanti via est,

§ 647. To stop up the fourth and fouler source of obscurity, § 638, 1) do not dream of adorning beautiful thoughts with anything aesthetically false, with the dreams of the feverish, § 456. For not only the love of truth but also the pursuit of perspicuity calls us away from this, since true aesthetic light will always be lacking to such absolutely obscure things, § 614. 2) In the very fictions [p. 426] of the poetic world do not wish to dwell in utopia, § 514, through which even for the wanderer the road is,

> *Quale per incertam lunam, sub luce maligna, / Est iter in siluis, vbi caelum condidit vmbra / Iuppiter, ac rebus nox abstulit atra colorem.* Virg.

*Such as, beneath an uncertain moon, under a grudging light, / Is a journey in the woods, when Jupiter has hidden the sky in shade / And black night has taken from things their colour.* Virg.

> § 648. 3) Ne de quoquam themate splendide prius, quam dilucide cogitare mens sit. §. 619, 625. 4) quae ne dilucide quidem exponere possis, ne speres vnquam naturali splendore collustrare, §. 622, 623. fucis autem commaculare nolis, §. 626, 627. 5) si quid tibi minus obscurum κατὰ νόησιν videatur, ne te iam eo ipso, dum illud venustatis ad regulas cogitaturus es, omnem obscuritatem aestheticam effugisse statuas §. 632, 633. 6) ne perspicuitatem singulorum tuorum conceptuum et totius a te ponendi confundens ex illa temere concludas ad hanc, apprime tamen necessariam, 7) caliginem ingenii tui ne satagas rebus et materiis imputare. §. 639.

§ 648. 3) Let it not be your mind to think splendidly of any theme before thinking of it lucidly, § 619, 625. 4) What you cannot even set forth lucidly, do not hope ever to illuminate with natural splendour, § 622, 623, and do not wish to besmear it with cosmetics, § 626, 627. 5) If something seems to you less obscure κατὰ νόησιν [according to the understanding], do not for that very reason, while you are about to think it by the rules of charm, conclude that you have escaped all aesthetic obscurity, § 632, 633. 6) Do not, confusing the perspicuity of your individual concepts with that of the whole you are to set forth, rashly infer from the former to the latter, which is nonetheless chiefly necessary. 7) Do not labour to impute the darkness of your own wit to the things and the materials. § 639.

> § 649. *Omnis cognitio multis est obstructa difficultatibus, eaque est et in ipsis rebus obscuritas* (obiectiua), *et in iudiciis nostris infirmitas,* (obscuritas subiectiua,) *vt non sine caussa et doctissimi et antiquissimi inuenire se posse, quod cuperent,* [p. 427] *diffisi sint.* Cic. quaest. ac. IIII. 7. Verum in ipsis rebus vbi latet absoluta obscuritas, vt sint in et per se inconceptibiles, illae non tangendae sunt, vltra limites, §. 647. Si qua materia talis esse videatur, vt in se clara et distincta nobis tamen per suam naturam esse ne dilucida quidem possit, multo minus splendescere: de ea non multum disputabo an ipsi rei, an potius infirmitati iudiciorum nostrorum adscribenda sit, qua circumuoluitur, caligo. Vnum hoc vrgeo, ne velut protestatione facto contraria rem ipsam multis dicamus obscuram, idque saepius, neque tamen eandem aptis potius vmbris circumdemus, quam explicare vel etiam illustrare vanas per ambages nequicquam conemur. §. 634, 635.

§ 649. *All cognition is obstructed by many difficulties, and there is both an obscurity in the things themselves* (objective), *and a weakness in our judgements,* (subjective obscurity,) *so that not without cause both the most learned and the most ancient, as to being able to find what they desired,* [p. 427] *have lost confidence.* Cic. quaest. ac. IIII. 7. But where absolute obscurity lies hidden in the things themselves, so that they are in and through themselves inconceivable, these are not to be touched, beyond the limits, § 647. If some material should seem to be such that, though clear and distinct in itself, it nonetheless by its nature cannot even be lucid for us, much less shine: about it I shall not much dispute whether the darkness in which it is enveloped is to be ascribed to the thing itself or rather to the weakness of our judgements. This one thing I urge: that we do not, as though by a protest contrary to the deed, tell many that the thing itself is obscure, and that repeatedly, and yet not rather surround it with fitting shades than vainly attempt to explain or even to illuminate it through empty circumlocutions. § 634, 635.

> § 650. Obscuritatem aestheticam generatim cauturus non curat ille quidem subtilitates κατ' αἴσθησιν superuacaneas, eas dispulsuris obscuritatem omnem κατὰ νόησιν intactas relinquit. §. 631, 632. neque trepidat confundere, quae salua pulcritudine totius vlterius in frustula dissecari non opus est. §. 642: vitat tamen confusum atque PERTVRBATVM COGITANDI GENVS, venustae distinctionis et analyseos nescium. Quam primum enim de toto certae materiae tot partes, tot varia videas animaduertenda per necessitatem [p. 428] aestheticam, quot in vnum confusa, simul in eundem spectatoris obtutum congesta, huius oculos praestringerent, et mole sua vim attendendi obruerent, §. 636, 637. *distincta* requiritur argumentorum *acies*, quae intellectui pulcro sistat totum partium successiuo splendore nitentium, §. 428, 618. cf. Quint. IIII. 2.

§ 650. He who would guard against aesthetic obscurity in general does not indeed trouble himself about superfluous subtleties κατ’ αἴσθησιν [according to sense]; he leaves them untouched for those who would dispel all obscurity κατὰ νόησιν [according to the understanding], § 631, 632; nor does he fear to confound things which, the beauty of the whole being preserved, need not be dissected further into fragments, § 642: yet he avoids the confused and PERTURBED MANNER OF THINKING, which knows nothing of charming distinction and analysis. For as soon as you see, concerning the whole of a certain material, so many parts, so many various things to be noticed by [p. 428] aesthetic necessity as, confounded into one and heaped together into the same glance of the spectator, would dazzle his eyes and overwhelm by their mass the power of attending, § 636, 637, a *distinct* array of arguments is required, which presents to the beautiful intellect the whole of the parts shining with successive splendour, § 428, 618; cf. Quintilian IIII. 2.

> § 651. Hinc longius si permittitur cogitationes protrahere, v. g. plures ad clepsydras, et singularis iure poscitur perspicuitas, vt a caussarum patronis, § 616, 645. rectius intellectus pulcer extensiuae distinctionis luce pascitur per contemplationem totius, dum partibus iam planissime dictis, iam nitore quodam ornatioribus recreatur analogon rationis, §. 617. quam si sequereris *Fusii* cuiusdam ac *Pomponii* meditandi rationem, quos Crassus apud Ciceronem de or. III. 50. *simulac agere coeperint, se* negat *intelligere, nisi admodum attenderit, ita confusam esse, ita perturbatam orationem, nihil vt sit primum, nihil secundum,* §. 650. *vt oratio, quae lumen adhibere rebus debeat, ea obscuritatem et tenebras afferat, atque vt quodammodo ipsi sibi in dicendo obstrepere videantur.*

§ 651. Hence, if it is permitted to draw out one’s thoughts at greater length, e.g. over several water-clocks, and a singular perspicuity is rightly demanded, as from the advocates of causes, § 616, 645, the beautiful intellect is more rightly fed by the light of extensive distinction through the contemplation of the whole, while the analogue of reason is refreshed by parts now stated most plainly, now more adorned with a certain brilliance, § 617, than if you were to follow the manner of meditating of a certain *Fusius* and *Pomponius*, of whom Crassus, in Cicero de or. III. 50, says that *as soon as they have begun to plead, he* does not *understand, unless he has attended most closely, so confused, so perturbed is their speech, that nothing is first, nothing second,* § 650, *so that the speech, which ought to bring light to things, brings obscurity and darkness, and that they seem in a manner to drown themselves out in speaking.*

> § 652. Quemadmodum autem lux aesthetica non [p. 429] est illa, qua potissimum genus cogitandi logicodogmaticum gaudeat atque collustretur: §. 629, 630. ita obscuritas, quam philosophis ac mathematicis scientifice commentantibus, veluti propriam ac naturalem, queruntur lectores vno rationis analogo percipere laborantes huic non scripta rationis effata, κατ' αἴσθησιν quidem est obscuritas, §. 631. neque tamen aesthetica, §. 633. Neque prius solidior philosophia mathematicorum vel assequetur vel tuebitur euidentiam, quam *obscuritates* eiusmodi *non culpae scribentium, sed inscientiae* vel inaduertentiae *non assequentium assignauerimus*, eadem cum veri conscientia animique tranquillitate, ac, non *Caecilius* Gellii XX. 1. *duodecim tabularum obscurissima*, sed mathematici tenebras illas, quarum plebs puluerem et radium reos agit.

§ 652. But just as aesthetic light is not [p. 429] that in which the logico-dogmatic manner of thinking chiefly rejoices and by which it is illuminated, § 629, 630: so the obscurity of which readers, labouring to perceive by the analogue of reason alone the pronouncements of reason not written for it, complain in philosophers and mathematicians writing scientifically, as though it were proper and natural to them, is indeed obscurity κατ’ αἴσθησιν [according to sense], § 631, yet not aesthetic, § 633. Nor will a more solid philosophy either attain or defend the evidence of the mathematicians before we assign *obscurities* of this kind *not to the fault of the writers, but to the ignorance* or inadvertence *of those who do not follow them*, with the same consciousness of truth and tranquillity of mind as, not *Caecilius* in Gellius XX. 1 those *most obscure* passages *of the twelve tables*, but the mathematician those shadows for which the common crowd arraigns the dust and the rod.

> § 653. Ipse Crassus apud Ciceronem, qui latissime profert oratoris, hinc et simul ingenii pulcri, pomoeria, quando se fingit contra eos disputare, qui oratorem ab omni doctrina rerumque maiorum scientia excludant, de or. I. 68. *Quoniam*, inquit, *philosophia in tres partes est distributa, in naturae obscuritatem,* §. 639. *in disserendi subtilitatem, in vitam atque mores: duo illa relinquamus, idque largiamur inertiae nostrae, tertium vero, quod semper oratoris fuit, nisi tenebimus, nihil oratori,* [p. 430] *in quo magnus esse possit, relinquemus.* Equidem nec illa duo priora sic relinquo, vt negem illorum solidam scientiam oratori, et omni felicius elegantiora cogitaturo singulariter vtilem, aliquibus autem omnino necessariam: nec tertium de moribus ac vita locum ita teneo, vt audeam vllis belle cogitaturis auctor esse nuda bene beateque viuendi praecepta, sicut intellectu comprehenduntur ac ratione demonstrantur, suis inserere, nisi plausum Antonii velint, §. 121. Neque tamen philosophus vbique meum putem de vita ac moribus ita cogitare, ne quid in meditationibus ad intellectus et rationis Cynosuram exactius directis obscuri superesse videatur ad earundem examen paene solum rationis analogon intensuris lectoribus, §. 652.

§ 653.
