III. 51. *de horridis rebus nitidum, de ieiunis plenum, de peruulgatis nouum.* Horridarum interim rerum verus ac naturalis color non est, nisi austerus, et fucum faceret florida rerum horridarum cogitatio, §. 688. Crassi nitet oratio, sed quantum nitere potest genus cogitandi aestheticodogmaticum, quod comparatum [p. 463] aestheticohistoricis, aut omnino poeticis, horridulum semper est ac austerum, §. 671, 566.

§ 695. The roughish manner of thinking does not exclude or shrink from aesthetic light and sensate perspicuity, indeed not even from all brilliance, but only from the greater, § 694, 693. It can be what Antonius says of Crassus’s rhetorical oration, Cic. Or. III. 51, *brilliant on rough matters, full on meagre ones, new on commonplace ones.* Meanwhile the true and natural colour of rough matters is nothing but austere, and a florid thought of rough matters would make a cosmetic, § 688. The oration of Crassus shines, but as much as the aesthetico-dogmatic manner of thinking can shine, which, compared [p. 463] with the aesthetico-historical manners, or with the poetic ones altogether, is always roughish and austere, § 671, 566.

> § 696. Austeram habes apud Virgilium Aen. IV. 247. descriptionem

§ 696. You have in Virgil, Aen. IV. 247, an austere description

> *Atlantis duri, caelum qui vertice fulcit,* / *Atlantis, cinctum assidue cui nubibus atris* / *Piniferum caput, et vento pulsatur et imbri,* / *Nix humeros infusa tegit, tum flumina mento* / *Praecipitant senis, et glacie riget horrida barba.*

*of hard Atlas, who props the sky on his crown,* / *of Atlas, whose pine-bearing head, girt without cease* / *by black clouds, is beaten by wind and rain;* / *snow poured over his shoulders covers them, then rivers plunge* / *from the old man’s chin, and his rough beard is stiff with ice.*

> Mox autem Aeneae floridam, §. 694. v. 261.

But soon a florid one of Aeneas, § 694, v. 261:

> *Atque illi stellatus iaspide fulua* / *Ensis erat, tyrioque ardebat murice laena* / *Demissa ex humeris, diues quae munera Dido* / *Fecerat, et tenui telas discreuerat auro.*

*And he had a sword starred with tawny jasper,* / *and a cloak let down from his shoulders blazed* / *with Tyrian purple, gifts which wealthy Dido* / *had made, and had picked out the weave with fine gold.*

> Vt hic colores iuxta se proxime positarum imaginum sese alterna vice excitant? In commissuris eorum ac transitu quam naturalis est ἁρμογή? §. 691.

How here the colours of images set next to each other set each other off in alternation! In their joinings and transition, how natural is the ἁρμογή [harmony of blending]! § 691.

> § 697. Austeram iungamus ex Ouidio descriptionem Boreae sibi coniugem rapientis, Met. VI. 702.

§ 697. Let us add from Ovid an austere description of Boreas carrying off his bride, Met. VI. 702.

> *Excussit pennas, quarum iactatibus omnis* / [p. 464] *Afflata est tellus, latumque perhorruit aequor,* / *Puluereamque trahens per summa cacumina pallam* / *Verrit humum, pauidamque metu, caligine tectus,* / *Orithyian amans furuis amplectitur alis.*

*He shook out his wings, by whose beating all* / [p. 464] *the earth was blown upon, and the broad sea shuddered,* / *and dragging his dusty mantle over the highest peaks* / *he sweeps the ground, and, covered in gloom, the lover* / *embraces with his dusky wings Orithyia, trembling with fear.*

> Floridam Aeneae descriptionem aliam v. §. 662. Vtrumque coloris genus quasi e longinquo, qua solet, breuitate Tacitus ostendit, quando narrat *Pharasmanem simul horridam suorum aciem, picta auro Medorum agmina, hinc viros, inde praedam, ostendere,* Ann. VI. 34.

For another florid description of Aeneas see § 662. Tacitus shows both kinds of colour as if from afar, with his usual brevity, when he relates that *Pharasmanes pointed at once to the rough battle-line of his own men and to the columns of the Medes painted with gold, here men, there booty,* Ann. VI. 34.

> § 698. Vtrumque colorum aestheticorum genus vel pingitur in rebus naturalibus, quatenus a moralibus distinguuntur, vel in moralibus deprehenditur. Horum verus ac naturalis color dabit tertiam ἤθους speciem, §. 195, 495. qua moratum cogitandi genus, §. 226. moribus characteribusque personarum, nationum, e. c. moralibus non dilucide solum exprimendis sufficiat, sed cuilibet etiam ex his eum locum, eum tonum, id lucis et vmbrae temperamentum, eum colorem tribuere nouerit, qui decet, §. 193. Ita primum apparenti cuiusdam virtutis personae conuenient austeri colores et genus cogitandi horridulum, omnis virtutis decor verus ac naturalis, [p. 465] at interior colores et genus cogitandi floridum admittit. Primum apparenti vitiorum quorundam laruae colores floridi laetumque cogitandi genus ac collustratum conueniunt; omnium vitiorum internae turpitudini colores austeri genusque cogitandi subobscurum, §. 676, 694.

§ 698. Each kind of aesthetic colours is either painted in natural things, inasmuch as they are distinguished from moral ones, or is found in moral things. The true and natural colour of the latter will give a third species of ἦθος [character], § 195, 495, by which the moral manner of thinking, § 226, may suffice not only for lucidly expressing the morals and characters of persons, nations, etc., in moral terms, but may also know how to assign to each of these that place, that tone, that tempering of light and shade, that colour which is fitting, § 193. Thus to the first appearance of the person of a certain virtue austere colours and the roughish manner of thinking will be suited; the true and natural adornment of every virtue, [p. 465] however, admits in its interior florid colours and the florid manner of thinking. To the first appearance of the mask of certain vices florid colours and a cheerful and well-lit manner of thinking are suited; to the internal ugliness of all vices austere colours and a somewhat obscure manner of thinking, § 676, 694.

> § 699. Videamus insigne exemplum in Horatii III. oda 24. vbi 1) luxuriam, vti primum apparet, genere cogitandi florido describens:

§ 699. Let us look at a notable example in Horace, III. ode 24, where 1) describing luxury, as it first appears, in the florid manner of thinking:

> *Intactis opulentior* / *Thesauris Arabum et diuitis Indiae* / *Caementis licet occupes* / *Tyrrhenum omne tuis et mare Apulicum:*

*Though richer than the untouched* / *treasures of the Arabs and of wealthy India* / *you occupy with your masonry* / *the whole Tyrrhenian and the Apulian sea:*

> statim subausterus verum huius vitii statum interiorem pingit:

at once, somewhat austere, he paints the true inner state of this vice:

> *Si figit adamantinos* / *Summis verticibus dira Necessitas* / *Clauos: non animum metu,* / *Non mortis laqueis expedias caput.*

*if dire Necessity drives her adamantine* / *nails into the topmost summits,* / *you will not free your soul from fear,* / *nor your head from the snares of death.*

> Pergit eadem austeritate morum magis innocentium externum habitum primo apparentem horridius describere, v. 8-28. redit adhuc horridulus ad interiorem luxuriae deformitatem sistendam ob oculos, v. 29-44.

He goes on with the same austerity to describe more roughly the outward habit, as it first appears, of more innocent morals, v. 8–28; still roughish, he returns to setting before our eyes the inner deformity of luxury, v. 29–44.

> § 700. Iam autem temperantiam suasurus ex vera [p. 466] huius virtutis natura, licet plerosque latente, diuitiis renunciare iubet, subito floridus:

§ 700. But now, about to urge temperance from the true [p. 466] nature of this virtue, though it is hidden from most, he bids us renounce riches, suddenly florid:

> *Vel nos in Capitolium,* / *Quo clamor vocat et turba fauentium,* / *Vel nos in mare proximum* / *Gemmas et lapides, aurum et inutile,* / *Summi materiem mali,* / *Mittamus.*

*Either to the Capitol,* / *where the shouting calls us and the crowd of applauders,* / *or into the nearest sea* / *let us send our gems and precious stones, and useless gold,* / *the material of the greatest evil.*

> Probe praeuidet, quam absonum hoc, quicquid erat consilii, debeat apparere potentiorum ciuium plurimis. Hinc sua se denuo virtute inuoluens illud probat austerus:

He foresees well how discordant this, whatever counsel it was, must appear to most of the more powerful citizens. Hence, wrapping himself again in his virtue, he proves, austere, that

> *Scelerum si bene poenitet,* / *Eradenda cupidinis* / *Praui sunt elementa, et tenerae nimis* / *Mentes asperioribus* / *Firmandae studiis.*

*if we truly repent of our crimes,* / *the elements of depraved desire* / *must be rooted out, and minds too tender* / *must be strengthened* / *by harsher studies.*

> Quoniam autem desperare videtur de consiliorum suorum fructu in seuera austeraque vitiorum intus et in cute male sanorum imagine conquiescit. §. 698.

But since he seems to despair of the fruit of his counsels, he rests in a severe and austere image of vices unsound within and under the skin. § 698.

> § 701. Coniungit Ouidius naturalium moraliumque colores in enarrandis quatuor orbis, quas fingit, aetatibus, Met. I. Aetatis aureae statum florido quam maxime cogitandi genere prosequutus moralem v. 90-100. §. 594. [p. 467] transit ad naturalem iisdem floribus conspergendum:

§ 701. Ovid joins the colours of natural and of moral things in recounting the four ages of the world which he feigns, Met. I. Having pursued the moral state of the golden age in the most florid manner of thinking, v. 90–100, § 594, [p. 467] he passes to the natural state, to be sprinkled with the same flowers:

> *Per se dabat omnia tellus.* / — — — — / *Ver erat aeternum, placidique tepentibus auris* / *Mulcebant Zephyri natos sine semine flores.* / — — — — / *Flumina iam lactis, iam flumina nectaris ibant,* / *Flauaque de viridi stillabant ilice mella.* v. 112.

*Of herself the earth gave all things.* / — — — — / *Spring was eternal, and with warm breezes the gentle* / *Zephyrs caressed the flowers born without seed.* / — — — — / *Now rivers of milk, now rivers of nectar flowed,* / *and yellow honey dripped from the green ilex.* v. 112.

> § 702. Iam tonum remittit in argentea aetate pingenda, v. 112-124. magis adhuc in aeneae breui commemoratione sensim cum aetatis illius hominibus

§ 702. He now lowers his tone in painting the silver age, v. 112–124, still more in the brief mention of the bronze age, gradually, together with the men of that age

> *ad horrida promtior arma,* v. 126.

*more prone to horrid arms,* v. 126.

> In ferrea autem aetate describenda vt totus inhorrescit? §. 594.

But in describing the iron age, how he bristles all over! § 594.

> *Viuitur ex rapto. Non hospes ab hospite tutus,* / *Non socer a genero. Fratrum quoque gratia rara est.* / *Imminet exitio vir coniugis, illa mariti.* / *Lurida terribiles miscent aconita nouercae.* / *Filius ante diem patrios inquirit in annos.* / *Victa iacet Pietas, et virgo caede madentes* / *Vltima caelestum terras Astraea reliquit.* / [p. 468] *Neue foret terris securior arduus aether,* / *Affectasse ferunt regnum caeleste Gigantas,* / *Altaque congestos struxisse ad sidera montes.* 153.

*Men live on plunder. Guest is not safe from host,* / *Nor father-in-law from son-in-law. Even among brothers goodwill is rare.* / *The husband threatens his wife with destruction, she her husband.* / *Dreadful stepmothers mix lurid aconites.* / *The son inquires before the day into his father’s years.* / *Piety lies vanquished, and the maiden Astraea, last* / *of the heavenly ones, has left the earth dripping with slaughter.* / [p. 468] *And lest the lofty aether be safer than the earth,* / *they say the Giants aspired to the heavenly kingdom,* / *and piled up mountains heaped to the stars.* 153.

> § 703. Pauci sunt, vel nemo, quem deceat, sicut

§ 703. Few there are, or none, whom it would befit, as

> *Omnis Aristippum decuit status, et color, et res,* Hor. ep. l. 17, 23.

*Every station, and colour, and circumstance befitted Aristippus,* Hor. ep. l. 17, 23.

> nisi Horatius in hoc etiam splendide mentitus est. Nihil magis principia negatae totalis similitudinis ac aequalitatis confirmat experientiae, quam characterum et personarum, morum et modorum agendi diuersitas. In quibus tamen ita exprimendis, vt distingui possint, naturam cuiusuis propriam ac suam imitari tanti est, vt, vel hoc vnum qui nesciat, eum poetae neget nomine dignum Horatius, quando Artis Poet. v. 86.

unless Horace in this too has lied splendidly. Nothing in experience confirms more the principles that deny total similarity and equality than the diversity of characters and persons, of morals and manners of acting. In expressing these, however, in such a way that they can be distinguished, it is of such moment to imitate the proper and own nature of each, that whoever is ignorant of this one thing alone, Horace denies him worthy of the name of poet, when, Art. Poet. v. 86,

> *Descriptas,* ait, *seruare vices, operumque colores* / *Cur ego, si nequeo ignoroque poeta salutor?* / *Cur nescire, pudens praue, quam discere, malo?* / *Versibus exponi tragicis res comica non vult.* / *Indignatur item priuatis ac prope socco* / *Dignis carminibus narrari caena Thyestae,* §. 690. / *Singula quaeque locum teneant sortita decentem.*

*To preserve the described turns,* he says, *and the colours of works,* / *why, if I cannot and know not how, am I hailed as poet?* / *Why do I, perversely modest, prefer not to know rather than to learn?* / *A comic subject will not be set forth in tragic verses.* / *Likewise the feast of Thyestes disdains to be narrated in private verses* / *and ones nearly worthy of the sock,* § 690. / *Let each single thing keep the fitting place allotted to it.*

> [p. 469] in naturalibus etiam et mechanicis, quod facilius, praesertim autem in moralibus, quod difficilius, §. 666, 691.

[p. 469] in natural and mechanical things too, which is easier, but especially in moral things, which is harder, § 666, 691.

#### Sectio XXXXII. Fucus Aestheticus. — Section XXXXII. Aesthetic Cosmetic

> § 704. Fuci aesthetici tum definitionem iam vidimus §. 688. tum quaedam genera, §. 626, 627. Sed eius a veris coloribus discernendi difficultas simul, ac necessitas separatam de eodem tractationem videtur requirere. §. 628, 625. Sicut autem veri colores sunt vel austeri, vel floridi: §. 693. ita et fucus erit vel nimis austerus, non horridulus, sed horridus, §. 634. vel nimis floridus et Iridis instar,

§ 704. Of aesthetic cosmetic we have already seen both the definition § 688 and certain kinds, § 626, 627. But the difficulty of distinguishing it from true colours, together with the necessity of doing so, seems to require a separate treatment of it. § 628, 625. Now just as true colours are either austere or florid: § 693, so cosmetic too will be either too austere, not roughish but rough, § 634, or too florid and like Iris,

> *Mille trahens varios aduerso sole colores.*

*Drawing a thousand varied colours against the sun.*

> Horridulum iam aliquid sonat illud Virgilii,

Something roughish already sounds in that line of Virgil,

> *Arma virumque cano.*

*Arms and the man I sing.*

> Austerius illud est circa medium totius carminis:

More austere is that near the middle of the whole poem:

> *Bella, horrida bella,* / *Et Tyberim multo spumantem sanguine cerno-*

*Wars, horrid wars,* / *And the Tiber foaming with much blood I behold—*

> Interim rem, de qua agebatur, secundum naturam exprimit verus color, et austeritatis [p. 470] gradus diuersus descriptas vices seruat, locumque decentem sortitus est. §. 703.

Meanwhile the true colour expresses according to nature the thing that was at issue, and the differing degree of austerity [p. 470] preserves the described turns and has obtained its fitting place. § 703.

> § 705. Huic horridulo colori compara fucum horridum Lucani:

§ 705. With this roughish colour compare the rough cosmetic of Lucan:

> *Bella per Emathios plus quam ciuilia campos,* / *Iusque datum sceleri canimus, populumque potentem,* / *In sua victrici conuersum viscera dextra,* / *Cognatasque acies, et rupto foedere regni* / *Certatum totis concussi viribus orbis* / *In commune nefas, infestisque obuia signis* / *Signa, pares aquilas, et pila minantia pilis.* / *Quis furor?* o! vates! *quae tanta licentia* ab ouo?

*Wars worse than civil across the Emathian plains,* / *and licence given to crime, we sing, and a mighty people* / *turned with victorious right hand against its own entrails,* / *and kindred battle-lines, and, the compact of rule broken,* / *the contest with all the forces of a shaken world* / *for common wickedness, and standards facing hostile standards,* / *matched eagles, and pila threatening pila.* / *What madness?* o! bard! *what licence so great* from the egg?

> Sic *incipiat scriptor* aliquis *cyclicus.* Color, non *suum decenter locum* nactus, iustoque saturatior, fucus est. §. 703, 688.

So let some *cyclic writer begin.* A colour that has not obtained *its place becomingly*, and is more saturated than is just, is cosmetic. § 703, 688.

> § 706. Silius Italicus iam auspicatur austerius Virgilio. §. 704.

§ 706. Silius Italicus already begins more austerely than Virgil. § 704.

> *Ordiar arma, quibus caelo se gloria tollit* / *Aeneadum, patiturque ferox oenotria iura* / *Carthago.*

*I shall begin with the arms by which the glory of the Aeneadae* / *raises itself to heaven, and fierce Carthage* / *suffers Oenotrian laws.*

> Initium, cui forte satur Horatius iam occlamet: Ohe! ampullas! Huic tamen satis [p. 471] naturalem colorem dixeris comparato cum principiis Claudiani de bello Gethico, quibus in ipso limine *furtiuae aurum pelliculae,* tritus ille fucus, §. 626. illitus est:

A beginning at which perhaps Horace, sated, would already cry out: Ho! bombast! Yet you would call its colour fairly [p. 471] natural compared with the opening of Claudian on the Gothic War, on which, at the very threshold, *the gold of a stolen fleece,* that worn-out cosmetic, § 626, has been smeared:

> *Intacti quum claustra freti coeuntibus aequor* / *Armatum scopulis audax irrumperet Argo* / *Oeteam [sic: Aeetam] Colchosque petens, propiore periclo,* / *Omnibus attonitis solus post numina Typhis* / *Incolumem tenui damno seruasse carinam* / *Fertur et ancipitem montis vitasse ruinam* / *Deceptoque vagae concursu rupis in altum* / *Victricem duxisse ratem.* e. c. vsque ad v. 35.

*When the bold Argo broke through the barriers of the untouched strait,* / *the sea armed with clashing rocks,* / *seeking Aeetes and the Colchians, with danger drawing near,* / *while all were thunderstruck, Tiphys alone, after the gods,* / *is said to have kept the ship unharmed with slight loss* / *and to have escaped the twofold ruin of the mountain,* / *and, the clash of the wandering rock eluded, to have led* / *the victorious vessel into the deep.* etc. up to v. 35.

> § 707. Horridus eiusmodi fucus, §. 704. non sola singularia potest deturpare, §. 708, 706 et genus cogitandi aestheticohistoricum, §. 566. pari ratione cauendus est aestheticodogmaticis, et vtriusque tum naturalia, quatenus moralibus opponuntur, exhibentibus, tum moralia, §. 698. Potest in eum delabi genus cogitandi aestheticodogmaticum theoreticum, potest et practicum, nunc paraeneticum, nunc elencticum, §. 576. In his versatus eo magis esse debet solicitus, ne descriptas migret vices, colorisque naturalis et fucorum limites, quoniam et omne iam dogmaticum meditandi genus habere videtur [p. 472] nonnihil horriduli, §. 695. et in moralium coloribus facilior lapsus est, dum duplex de iisdem, nunc exterius, et praecipitanter, nunc interius et penitius perspectis, solet iudicium ferri, §. 698. 703.

§ 707. A rough cosmetic of this kind, § 704, can not only disfigure singular things, § 708, 706 and the aesthetico-historical manner of thinking, § 566; for the same reason it is to be avoided by aesthetico-dogmatic thinkers, both those exhibiting natural things, insofar as they are opposed to moral ones, and those exhibiting moral things, § 698. The theoretical aesthetico-dogmatic manner of thinking can slip into it, and so can the practical, now the paraenetic, now the elenctic, § 576. One versed in these ought to be all the more careful not to transgress the described turns and the limits of natural colour and of cosmetics, since every dogmatic manner of meditating already seems to have [p. 472] something roughish about it, § 695, and in the colours of moral things the slip is easier, since a double judgement is usually passed on the same things, now viewed from outside and hastily, now from within and more deeply, § 698, 703.

> § 708. Fucum aestheticopracticum §. 707. non eum crassiorem nunc dissuadebimus, in quem inuehitur Iuuenalis, sat. 2. quando

§ 708. The aesthetico-practical cosmetic § 707 that we shall now dissuade from is not that cruder one against which Juvenal inveighs, sat. 2, when

> *Vltra Sauromatas fugere huic libet, et glacialem* / *Oceanum, quoties aliquid de moribus audent,* / *Qui Curios simulant, et Bacchanalia viuunt.* §. 362.

*Beyond the Sauromatae one would like to flee, and the icy* / *Ocean, whenever they dare something about morals,* / *who feign Curii and live Bacchanalia.* § 362.

> Subtilior hic culpandus in cogitationibus fucus etiam eorum est, quorum forte nec mala mens, nec malus animus est, licet verioris beatitudinis non satis conscius. Quaeratur e. g. de vero felicitatis colore, quem naturalem et non fucatum explanet aestheticodogmaticus. Sequuntur tunc sui sapientis archetypum, et inde deriuatas cogitandi loquendiue formulas, Stoici quae *dum mordicus tenent, neque sibi euelli ex ore* vel animo *volunt: horridiores euadunt, asperiores, duriores et oratione, et moribus,* et ipsa cogitandi ratione. Cic. de fin. IIII, 78. Hinc in eorum picturas boni, mali, virtutis, beatitudinis, felicitatis fucus inducitur nimis austerus. §. 704.

A subtler cosmetic is here to be blamed in the thoughts even of those who perhaps have neither a bad mind nor a bad heart, though not sufficiently conscious of truer blessedness. Let the question be, e.g., about the true colour of felicity, which the aesthetico-dogmatic thinker is to set forth natural and not painted. They then follow the archetype of their sage and the formulas of thinking or speaking derived from it, which the Stoics, *while they hold them with their teeth and will not let them be torn from their mouth* or mind, *come out rougher, harsher, harder both in speech and in morals,* and in the very manner of thinking. Cic. de fin. IIII, 78. Hence into their pictures of good, evil, virtue, blessedness, felicity a too austere cosmetic is introduced. § 704.

> § 709. [p. 473] Sub eadem hypothesi §. 708. sequetur Epicureus aliquis vnicam voluptatem, quam si formauerit animo, sicuti facilis est, et in vulgus peruulgata, neque totum caelestis nostrae Veneris systema, sed eius aliquam modo particulam, mente comprehenderit, §. 646. temere mollescet in eam leuitatem, vt mites forsan aliquos Felicitatis ductus satis feliciter imitetur, quos autem grauiores et austeros simul exprimere

§ 709. [p. 473] Under the same hypothesis § 708 some Epicurean will follow the single pleasure, which if he has formed in his mind, as it is easy and widely spread among the common people, and has not comprehended in his mind the whole system of our heavenly Venus but only some small particle of it, § 646, he will rashly soften into such lightness that he may perhaps imitate quite happily some gentle features of Felicity, but those graver and austere ones at the same time, which to express

> *iubet horrida Virtus,* / *Armatumque Fide pectus, Rectique cupido,* / *Audita asperitate,* Sil. XI. 205.

*horrid Virtue commands,* / *and a breast armed with Faith, and desire of the Right,* / *with hardship heard,* Sil. XI. 205.

> nolit laetioribus innectere, vel certe leuiculo penicillo per male locatum spuriae lucis nitorem obducet, et hinc ponere totum nesciet sine fuco nimis florido. §. 704. Peripateticorum in his theoriam denique sequutus a vero Felicitatis colore propius aberit. §. 688.

he will be unwilling to weave in with the gayer ones, or at any rate with a slight brush will overlay them through the ill-placed brilliance of a spurious light, and hence will not know how to compose the whole without too florid a cosmetic. § 704. Having finally followed the theory of the Peripatetics in these matters, he will come nearer to the true colour of Felicity. § 688.

> § 710. *Catholica, id est, (vt dicamus, quomodo possumus) vniuersalia, vel perpetualia.* (Quint. II. 14.) de moribus, virtutibus et vitiis, ex veritate coloris aesthetici satis exacta, §. 552. sibi familiaria reddere pulcre cogitaturus non tantum tenetur, si quando practica [p. 474] dogmatice tangere mens sit, §. 707. sed etiam ideo, quia moratum de singularibus, quoque tum strictissime veris, tum heterocosmicis, cogitandi genus illis catholicis et generalibus, veluti notionibus directricibus, vtitur in informandis singularium ideis §. 653, 547. Si quis Cynicorum ex disciplina virtutem ac mores generatim fucis vero austerioribus adsperserit, virtutem etiam singularem certae personae, quam narrabit, vel finget, eam circumscribet, quae

§ 710. *Catholic, that is (to say it as we can), universal or perpetual* (Quint. II. 14) things about morals, virtues and vices, sufficiently exact according to the truth of aesthetic colour, § 552, one who is to think beautifully is bound to make familiar to himself, not only if at any time he has a mind to touch upon practical matters [p. 474] dogmatically, § 707, but also because the moral manner of thinking about singulars, whether most strictly true or heterocosmic, uses those catholic and general things, as it were as directing notions, in forming the ideas of singulars § 653, 547. If anyone from the school of the Cynics has sprinkled virtue and morals in general with cosmetics that are in truth too austere, he will also draw the singular virtue of a definite person, whom he will narrate or feign, as one which

> *Sardois videatur amarior herbis,* / *Horridior rusco, proiecta vilior alga.* Virg. Ecl. VII.

*would seem bitterer than Sardinian herbs,* / *rougher than butcher’s-broom, cheaper than cast-up seaweed.* Virg. Ecl. VII.

> § 711. Si quis in Aristippi praecepta delapsus est, proptereaque virtutem et morum institutionem omnem fucis nimium floridis exprimit, §. 704. ex huius officina

§ 711. If anyone has slipped into the precepts of Aristippus, and therefore expresses virtue and the whole institution of morals with too florid cosmetics, § 704, from his workshop

> *Virtutis verae custos rigidusque satelles,*

*the guardian and rigid attendant of true virtue,*

> in concreto etiam, et indiuiduo singulari spectandus, §. 710. prodibit comtulus, venustulus, delicatulus, purpuram indutus, rosis coronatus, pastillos olens, vti *bibit Hymettia mella Falerno diluta,*

to be viewed even in the concrete and in a singular individual, § 710, will come forth neat, pretty, dainty, clad in purple, crowned with roses, smelling of pastilles, as he *drinks Hymettian honey diluted with Falernian,*

> *inter lances mensasque nitentes,* / *Dum stupet insanis acies fulgoribus, et quum* / *Acclinis falsis animus meliora recusat.* Hor. Serm. II. 2. 4.

*among the gleaming dishes and tables,* / *while the eye is dazed by the mad glitter, and when* / *the mind, inclined to false things, refuses the better.* Hor. Serm. II. 2. 4.

> § 712. [p. 475] Quemadmodum omnis quidem eruditio, tum practica, tum theoretica, verior ad veriores rebus ad eam pertinentibus, et singularibus, quae sub se continet, inducendos colores multum facit, §. 63-67; tamen nulla facilius fucum vitare dabit ingenio, quod natura mediocriter felix hanc solam imitabitur, quam corrupta praeconceptis opinionibus omnia falso colore tingentibus: § 707-711. Hic praesertim artis aestheticae tum verioris magnum adiumentum est ad veros in rebus colores quaerendos, fugiendos fucos, §. 68, 69. tum falsae praecepta plus nocent, quam si prorsus artem eiusmodi nescires, §. 73. quoniam dum ea sequeris, vt tibi videtur, omnino securus, deliberato consilio naturam deseris fucos et pigmenta captans, §. 688, 110. in quae forsan impetu mere naturali non incidisses, §. 52.

§ 712. [p. 475] Just as all learning indeed, both practical and theoretical, the truer it is, contributes much to inducing truer colours upon the things that pertain to it and the singulars which it contains under itself, § 63–67; yet none will more easily let a wit avoid cosmetic, a wit which, moderately happy by nature, will imitate nature alone, than one corrupted by preconceived opinions that tinge everything with false colour: § 707–711. Here especially the aesthetic art, when truer, is a great aid for seeking the true colours in things and shunning cosmetics, § 68, 69; but when false, its precepts do more harm than if you knew nothing at all of such an art, § 73, since while you follow them, as it seems to you, altogether secure, you desert nature with deliberate design, snatching at cosmetics and pigments, § 688, 110, into which perhaps by a merely natural impulse you would not have fallen, § 52.

> § 713. In deceptricibus artium aestheticarum, e. g. rhetoricarum, poeticarum, regulis non tanto cum periculo a veris coloribus ad fucos auocabunt omnino falsae, et adeo falsae, etiam aesthetice, vt ne pulcellam quidem aliquam veri speciem habeant, qua se tueantur: quam illae, quae tum magnis auctoritatibus defenduntur, tum in aliquibus locis exercentur commode, peccant autem in [p. 476] quantitate, quod logici dicunt, et catholicae cogitantur, quae tamen particulariter tantum verae sunt. §. 73. Hinc aestheticis tantopere distinguendae paucae venustatum *leges imnutabili [sic: immutabili] necessitate constrictae,* a consiliis aliquando bonis, *quae, velut si aliter fas non sit, quidam, tanquam iussi, sequuntur,* non raro praepostere. Nam *mutantur pleraque* praeceptorum *caussis, temporibus, necessitate, occasione. Nulla rogationibus plebisue scitis sancta sunt. Decet, vt in picturis atque statuis videmus, variari habitus, vultus, status. Raro reperitur genus praeceptorum catholicorum, vt non labefactari parte aliqua et subrui possit.* Quint. II. 14.

§ 713. Among the deceptive rules of the aesthetic arts, e.g. of rhetoric and poetics, those that are wholly false, and so false, even aesthetically, that they have not even some pretty semblance of truth to defend themselves with, will not call one away from true colours to cosmetics with so great a danger as those which are both defended by great authorities and in some places conveniently practised, but sin in [p. 476] quantity, as the logicians say, and are thought as catholic, though they are true only particularly. § 73. Hence aestheticians must so greatly distinguish the few *laws* of charms *bound by immutable necessity* from counsels sometimes good, *which, as if it were not lawful otherwise, certain people follow as though commanded,* not seldom preposterously. For *most* precepts *are changed by causes, times, necessity, occasion. None are sanctioned by bills or plebiscites. It is fitting, as we see in pictures and statues, that dress, countenance, posture be varied. Rarely is a kind of catholic precept found that cannot be weakened in some part and undermined.* Quint. II. 14.

> § 714. Quos regulae nimis laxae nondum satis a vero rerum colore deflectunt in fucos, horum multos eo contorquet caeca imitatio. Sentiunt amari probarique, licet *horridulas, Catonis* alicuius *orationes.* Cic. de Or. 152. et ecce! quoties placere volunt, vt subito horrescant! §. 704.

§ 714. Those whom rules too lax do not yet sufficiently deflect from the true colour of things into cosmetics, many of these blind imitation twists thither. They perceive that the *orations* of some *Cato,* though *roughish,* are loved and approved. Cic. de Or. 152. And lo! whenever they wish to please, how suddenly they bristle! § 704.

> *Quid? si quis vultu toruo ferus, et pede nudo,* / *Exiguaeque togae simulet textore Catonem,* / *Virtutemne repraesentet moresque Catonis?* / *Decipit exemplar vitiis imitabile.* Hor. I. ep. 19. 12.

*What? if someone, fierce with grim countenance and bare foot,* / *should counterfeit Cato by the weave of a scanty toga,* / *would he represent the virtue and the morals of Cato?* / *An example imitable in its vices deceives.* Hor. I. ep. 19. 12.

> Sentiunt alii delectari non paucos floribus [p. 477] poetarum et Curtii. Hinc tunc demum se disertos putant, quando quibuscunque datis occasionibus efflorescendo lasciuiunt. §. 254.

Others perceive that not a few are delighted by the flowers [p. 477] of the poets and of Curtius. Hence they think themselves eloquent only then, when on whatever occasions are given they run riot in flowering. § 254.

> *O! imitatores, seruum pecus! vt mihi saepe* / *Bilem, saepe iocum vestri mouere tumultus!*

*O imitators, servile herd! how often have your tumults* / *moved my bile, how often my laughter!*

> § 715. Laudabantur olim Atticorum venusta ingenia. *Quorum genera plura sunt, hi,* caeci imitatores. §. 714. *vnum modo, quale sit, suspicabantur. Putabant enim, qui horride inculteque dicat, modo id eleganter enucleateque faciat, eum solum attice dicere. Errabant, quod solum,* §. 713. *quod attice, non fallebantur.* §. 694. Cic. or. 28. Interim, quantus eorum cunque fuerit error, non tamen potuit, quin iisdem aliquando fucos nimis horridos pro veris rerum floridarum coloribus commendaret. §. 704, 248, 260. Nunc laudantur ex graecis et romanis auctores suo iure classici, iam austeris, iam floridis vsi commodissime coloribus. In quorum imitatione quoniam inprimis *considerandum est, ne quid perturbate, ne quid contorte* cogitetur, Cic. de Inu. l. 29. caeci imitatores, qui simile quantulumcumque suis deprehendisse per scripta classica satagunt, qui possent aliter, quam colores confundere, sicuti iura coqui, contortisque bellissimis ex Ciceronis alicuius aut omnino Demosthenis cogitandi rationibus ad alienissima fucum facere? §. 688.

§ 715. The charming wits of the Attics were once praised. *Of these there are several kinds; these,* the blind imitators, § 714, *suspected only one, of what sort it was. For they thought that one who speaks in a rough and unpolished manner, provided he does it elegantly and clearly, he alone speaks Attically. They erred in the “alone,”* § 713; *in the “Attically” they were not deceived.* § 694. Cic. or. 28. Meanwhile, however great their error was, it could not but sometimes commend to them cosmetics too rough in place of the true colours of florid things. § 704, 248, 260. Now authors from among the Greeks and Romans are praised as classical by their own right, who have used now austere, now florid colours most fittingly. Since in imitating them it is above all *to be considered that nothing be thought confusedly, nothing distortedly,* Cic. de Inu. l. 29, how could the blind imitators, who strive to have caught in the classical writings some likeness, however slight, to their own, do otherwise than confound colours, as cooks do sauces, and, twisting the most beautiful manners of thinking of some Cicero or even Demosthenes to the most alien things, make a cosmetic of them? § 688.

> § 716. [p. 478] Colores floridi *maxime sensus nostros impellunt voluptate, et specie prima acerrime commouent.* Saepe tamen *ab iisdem celerrime fastidio quodam et satietate abalienamur.* §. 693. *Quanto colorum pulcritudine et varietate floridiora sunt in picturis nouis pleraque, quam in veteribus? Quae tamen, etiamsi primo adspectu nos ceperunt, diutius non delectant, quum iidem nos in antiquis tabulis illo ipso horrido obsoletoque teneamur. Quanto molliores sunt et delicatiores in cantu flexiones et falsae voculae, quam certae et seuerae? quibus tamen non modo austeri, sed si saepius fiunt, multitudo ipsa reclamat.* Cic. de or. III. 98. cf. 99-103. et habebis praeclarum in fucos nimis floridos antidoton. §. 704.

§ 716. [p. 478] Florid colours *most strongly impel our senses with pleasure, and at first sight move them most keenly.* Often, however, *we are very quickly estranged from them by a certain disgust and satiety.* § 693. *How much more florid in beauty and variety of colours are most things in new pictures than in old ones? Which, however, though they captivated us at first sight, do not delight for long, while we ourselves are held in ancient panels by that very roughness and antiquity. How much softer and more delicate in singing are the flexions and falsetto notes than firm and severe ones? against which, however, not only the austere, but, if they occur too often, the multitude itself cries out.* Cic. de or. III. 98. cf. 99–103, and you will have an excellent antidote against too florid cosmetics. § 704.

> § 717. Interim pluribus fucus minis [sic: nimis] floridus est suspectus, quam nimis austerus. Minium his, cinnabaris, indicum et purpurissum, facilius fuci iudicantur, quam fucati etiam

§ 717. Meanwhile to more people the too florid cosmetic is suspect, rather than the too austere. For them red lead, cinnabar, indigo and purple are more readily judged cosmetics than those painted even

> *peruncti faecibus ora.*

*with their faces smeared with lees.*

> *Austeram accusationem* qui parat, si vel omnes humanitatis terminos transiliat, veritatem odium parientem se pingere, non fucum, sibi videbitur, *austeram curationem* propinare, non nigrae loliginis succum et meram aeruginem. Austeritatem vt nimis tristem [p. 479] effugiat, vel remouendo floridorum mentionem iniicit Ouidius, Trist. l. 1.

He who prepares an *austere accusation,* even if he should leap over all the bounds of humanity, will seem to himself to be painting the truth that begets hatred, not cosmetic, to be offering an *austere cure,* not the juice of the black cuttlefish and sheer verdigris. That he may escape austerity as too gloomy, [p. 479] Ovid, Trist. l. 1, throws in a mention of florid things even while removing them.

> *Nec te purpureo velent vaccinia fuco,* / *Non est conueniens luctibus ille color.* / *Nec titulus minio, neque cedro charta notetur,* / *Candida nec nigra cornua fronte geras.* / *Felices ornent haec instrumenta libellos,* / *Fortunae memorem te decet esse meae.*

*Nor let bilberries veil you with purple cosmetic,* / *that colour is not suited to mourning.* / *Nor let your title be marked with red lead, nor your paper with cedar,* / *nor bear white horns on a black front.* / *Let these instruments adorn fortunate little books;* / *it befits you to be mindful of my fortune.*

> § 718. Pari artificio Apelles excelluit, *quod vnum imitari nemo potuit. Absoluta opera atramento illinebat ita tenui, vt id ipsum repercussu claritates colorum excitaret, custodiretque a puluere et sordibus, ad manum intuenti demum appareret. Sed et tum ratione magna, ne colorum claritas oculorum aciem offenderet, veluti per lapidem specularem intuentibus e longinquo, et eadem res nimis floridis coloribus austeritatem occulte daret.* Plin. hist. nat. XXXV. 10. Tantae molis est poetae fucum nimis austerum et tristem, pictori nimis floridum solicite vitare. §. 717. Vereor tamen, ne festiuum illud, quod aiunt, apud Ouidium Trist. l. III. 10. habeat aliquid fucosi lenocinii:

§ 718. Apelles excelled by a like artifice, *which alone no one could imitate. He covered his finished works with a black varnish so thin that this very thing by its reflection called forth the brightness of the colours, and guarded them from dust and dirt, and appeared only to one looking at it close at hand. But also then with great reason, that the brightness of the colours should not offend the sharpness of the eyes, as for those looking from afar through a pane of specular stone, and that the same thing should covertly give austerity to too florid colours.* Plin. hist. nat. XXXV. 10. So great a labour it is for the poet carefully to avoid too austere and gloomy a cosmetic, for the painter one too florid. § 717. I fear, however, lest that witty saying, as they call it, in Ovid Trist. l. III. 10, has something of a cosmetic enticement:

> *Clauda quod alterno subsidunt carmina versu,* / *Vel pedis hoc ratio, vel via longa facit.* / — — — — / [p. 480] *Adspicis exsangui chartam pallere colore?*

*That the lame verses sink in alternate lines,* / *either the plan of the metre or the long journey does it.* / — — — — / [p. 480] *Do you see the paper pale with a bloodless colour?*

> Immo vero, quia non erubescunt epistolae.

Nay rather, because letters do not blush.

> § 717. [sic: 719] Vitiosum et corruptum cogitandi genus, quod huc vsque fucum appellauimus, §. 688. Quintilianus dicit *casuris, si leuiter excutiantur, flosculis nitens, euanescens ac moriens,* vt reliqua vitiosa cogitandi genera, *comparatione meliorum, quemadmodum lana tincta fuco citra purpuras placet, ac, si contuleris etiam lacernae, conspectu melioris obruitur. Si vero iudicium his corruptis acrius adhibeas, vt fucinis sulphura, iam illud, quod fefellerat, exuat mentitum colorem, et quadam vix enarrabili foeditate pallescat. Luceat igitur haec citra solem, et vt quaedam exigua animalia igniculi videntur in tenebris.* XII, 10. Si protraxeris fucatam eiusmodi Venerem ex angulis et vmbra in solem et maioris theatri celebritatem, *nec illi*

§ 719. The vicious and corrupt manner of thinking, which we have up to this point called cosmetic, § 688, Quintilian says *shines with little flowers that will fall if they are lightly shaken, vanishing and dying,* like the other vicious manners of thinking, *by comparison with better ones, just as wool dyed with a cosmetic pleases apart from purples, and, if you compare it even with a cloak, is overwhelmed by the sight of the better. But if you apply a keener judgement to these corrupt things, as sulphur to the dyed, then that which had deceived sheds its lying colour and grows pale with a certain scarcely describable foulness. So let these shine apart from the sun, as certain tiny animals seem to be little fires in the dark.* XII, 10. If you drag a painted Venus of this kind out of the corners and the shade into the sun and the throng of a larger theatre, *neither does*

> *iam manet humida creta, colorque* / *Stercore fucatus crocodili.* Hor. ep. od. XII.

*the moist chalk now stay on her, nor the colour* / *painted with crocodile dung.* Hor. ep. od. XII.

> § 720. Pulcre cogitandis *insidere quidam venustatis, non fuco illitus, sed sanguine diffusus debet color,* i. e. per ipsam materiae, cogitantis et obiectorum in personalibus praecipuorum naturam determinata lucis aestheticae modificatio. §. 688, 622, 623. Cic. de or. [p. 481] III. 199. *Ipsa formae dignitas coloris bonitate tuenda est.* §. 188. Cic. off. l. 1. 30. Hic autem *est quidam sine vllo fuco veritatis color.* §. 423. Cic. de cl. orator. 162. cuius *lineamentis flos pigmentorum recentium desit* potius, quam adsit nimius. 298. §. 691. Neque tamen desit naturam sequens variatio, §. 689. quia naturalis color vltra terminos a natura constitutos protractus et vno tenore continuatus tandem non nisi fucus est. Hinc intelligo Quintilianum, qui *Cassio Seuero* tribuit *ingenii plurimum, acerbitatem miram, summam vrbanitatem,* tamen in eodem non *grauitatem* solum, sed etiam *colorem orationis* desiderat, quoniam *stomacho et amaris salibus plus, quam consilio, dederit.* X. 1.

§ 720. Upon beautiful thoughts *there ought to sit a certain colour of charm, not smeared on with cosmetic but diffused with blood,* i.e. a modification of aesthetic light determined by the very nature of the matter, of the thinker, and of the principal objects in personal matters. § 688, 622, 623. Cic. de or. [p. 481] III. 199. *The very dignity of form is to be guarded by goodness of colour.* § 188. Cic. off. l. 1. 30. But here *there is a certain colour of truth without any cosmetic.* § 423. Cic. de cl. orator. 162, in whose *lineaments the flower of fresh pigments* should rather *be lacking* than be present in excess. 298. § 691. Yet let not the variation that follows nature be lacking, § 689, since a natural colour drawn beyond the bounds set by nature and continued in one unbroken tenor is in the end nothing but cosmetic. Hence I understand Quintilian, who attributes to *Cassius Severus very much wit, a wonderful acerbity, the highest urbanity,* yet misses in the same man not only *gravity* but also *colour of speech,* since *he gave more to his spleen and his bitter wit than to good counsel.* X. 1.

> § 721. Veniamus ad aliquas colorum oppositique coloribus fuci species, exempli gratia. I. A Cicerone desideratur *in externis oratoribus vrbanitate quadam colorata oratio.* Quaesitusque: *Quis est ille tandem vrbanitatis color? Nescio,* inquit, *tantum esse quendam scio. Id tu, Brute, intelliges, quum in Galliam veneris. In vocibus nostrorum oratorum recinit quoddam et resonat vrbanius. Nec hoc in oratoribus modo apparet, sed etiam in caeteris.* de cl. orat. 170. An hic est color idem illud, nescio quid, quod nunc Galli suis solis quidam tribuunt, externis denegant? Fucum illius similem ostendit Catulli *Suffenus,*

§ 721. Let us come to some kinds of colours and of the cosmetic opposed to colours, by way of example. I. Cicero misses *in foreign orators a speech coloured with a certain urbanity.* And when asked: *What then is that colour of urbanity? I do not know,* he says, *I only know that there is one. You, Brutus, will understand it when you come into Gaul. In the voices of our orators something rings and resounds more urbanely. Nor does this appear only in orators, but also in the rest.* de cl. orat. 170. Is this colour the same as that ‘I know not what’ which now certain Gauls attribute to their own alone, and deny to foreigners? A cosmetic resembling it is shown by Catullus’s *Suffenus,*

> [p. 482] *Homo venustus, et dicax, et vrbanus,* / *qui modo scurra,* / *Aut si quid hac re tritius, videbatur.*

[p. 482] *A charming man, and witty, and urbane,* / *who only just now a buffoon,* / *or if there is anything more polished than that, seemed.*

> Idem miram fucorum et apertae foeditatis miscelam exhibet, in poematibus quando

The same man exhibits a wonderful mixture of cosmetics and open foulness, when in his poems

> *bellus ille et vrbanus* / *Suffenus, vnus caprimulgus ac fossor* / *Rursus videtur. Tantum abhorret ac mutat.*

*that pretty and urbane* / *Suffenus seems a mere goatherd or ditch-digger* / *once more. So much does he differ and change.*

> § 722. II. Coniungam, vti coniunctum in Rutilii dicendi genere fuisse apud Ciceronem est de cl. or. 113. colorem tristem et seuerum, acrem atque vehementem. Primus est color luctibus conueniens, non ita reliqui, nisi quibusdam tragicis. Est tamen verus quidam *seueritatis* color, *non modo non inuidiosus, sed etiam popularis. Seueritatem* enim lego apud Ciceronem Fam. VIIII. ep. 14. non *veritatem animaduersionis tum bonis omnibus, tum infimo cuique gratissimam.* Est verus quidam color ex pudore relucentis acrimoniae, cuius *totum genus excellet* e. g. *in caussis, in quibus potest inflammari animus iudicis acri et vehementi quadam incitatione.* Cic. Or. II. 183. Quanquam *dubium non est, quin exordium dicendi vehemens et pugnax non saepe esse debeat.* 317.: Cicero tamen, operum colores qui satis norat, *vehementer se agere fatetur, iracunde, negat.* Philipp. VIII. 16.

§ 722. II. I shall join together, as it is said in Cicero to have been joined in Rutilius’s manner of speaking, de cl. or. 113, the gloomy and severe colour, the keen and vehement. The first is a colour suited to mourning, not so the rest, except to certain tragic matters. There is however a certain true colour of *severity, not only not invidious, but even popular.* For I read in Cicero Fam. VIIII. ep. 14 *severity,* not ‘truth’, *of chastisement, most welcome both to all good men and to each of the lowest.* There is a certain true colour of a keenness that shines out from modesty, *the whole kind* of which *will excel,* e.g. *in causes in which the mind of the judge can be inflamed by a certain keen and vehement incitement.* Cic. Or. II. 183. Although *there is no doubt that the exordium of a speech should not often be vehement and pugnacious.* 317: Cicero, however, who knew well enough the colours of his works, *confesses that he acts vehemently, denies that he acts angrily.* Philipp. VIII. 16.

> § 723. [p. 483] Hos colores mentiuntur fuci e. g. eorum *qui fronte graui et tristi supercilio vtilitatibus fisci contumaciter adsunt, quos nunquam principibus defuisse* putat Plinius Pan. 41. et omnis non iocis tantum ac hilaritati, sed etiam humanitati contraria seueritas in cogitando iudicandoque. Acerbam eiusmodi seueritatem amet vna

§ 723. [p. 483] These colours are counterfeited by the cosmetics e.g. of those *who with grave brow and gloomy frown stubbornly attend to the interests of the treasury, who* Pliny thinks *have never been wanting to princes,* Pan. 41, and by every severity in thinking and judging contrary not only to jests and hilarity but even to humanity. Such bitter severity let alone be loved by

> *Eumenidum intento turba seuera foro.* Prop. IIII. 11.

*the severe throng of the Eumenides in the strained court.* Prop. IIII. 11.

> Veram et fucatam acrimoniam pingit vna Cicero, mores pulcre cogitaturi formans de Or. I. 182. quando: *Haec,* ait, *adiuuant in oratore: lenitas vocis, vultus, pudoris significatio, verborum comitas. Si quid persequare acrius,* (hic habes verum colorem, §. 722.) *vt inuitus et coactus facere videare. — — — — Ea omnia, quae proborum, demissorum, non acrium, non pertinacium, non litigiosorum, non acerborum sunt,* (habes fucum pertinacis et acerbi litigiatoris) *valde beneuolentiam conciliant.* Quemadmodum *vehemens* proprie et recte Macrobio VI. 8. *nimio impetu ac vi mentis instructum* significat, M. §. 699: ita *genus* cogitandi *vehemens et atrox* fucum potius, quam verum ac laudabilem colorem, prae se feret, nisi admisceatur eidem *genus lenitatis atque mansuetudinis.* Cic. de or. II. 200.

True and painted keenness Cicero paints together, forming the morals of one who is to think beautifully, de Or. I. 182, when: *These things,* he says, *help in an orator: gentleness of voice, of countenance, the signifying of modesty, courtesy of words. If you pursue anything more keenly,* (here you have the true colour, § 722) *that you may seem to do it unwillingly and under compulsion. — — — — All those things which belong to the honest, the humble, the not keen, not obstinate, not litigious, not bitter,* (you have the cosmetic of the obstinate and bitter litigant) *greatly conciliate goodwill.* Just as *vehement,* properly and rightly for Macrobius VI. 8, signifies *furnished with excessive impetus and force of mind,* M. § 699: so the *vehement and atrocious manner* of thinking will display a cosmetic rather than a true and praiseworthy colour, unless there be mingled with it *a manner of gentleness and mildness.* Cic. de or. II. 200.

> § 724. Hinc *mollienda est in plerisque alio colore* [p. 484] *asperitas orationis.* Quint. XI. 1. Vnde colligas et asperum cogitandi genus colorem esse, et genus illud lenitatis atque mansuetudinis, §. 723. quo gnarus aliquis *animorum tractandorum artifex assequatur, vt aliquid eorum quoque caussa videatur facere, contra quos* armatus est. Iungamus luctibus conuenienti colori, §. 722. *necessarium periclitanti solicitudinis colorem,* eumque, quem *sola habet poenitentia, si nulla contingit* iis, qui peccauerant, *excusatio.* l. c.

§ 724. Hence *there must be softened in most cases by another colour* [p. 484] *the harshness of speech.* Quint. XI. 1. From which you may gather both that the harsh manner of thinking is a colour, and that manner of gentleness and mildness, § 723, by which some knowing *artificer in handling minds attains that he may seem to do something for the sake of those too against whom* he is armed. Let us join to the colour suited to mourning, § 722, *the colour of solicitude necessary to one in peril,* and that which *penitence alone has, if no excuse falls to* those who had sinned. l. c.

> *Adspice, quot submittat humus formosa colores!* Prop.

*Behold how many colours the beauteous earth sends up!* Prop.

> At caue, ne in fucum degenerent vel nimium *trucis atque violenti,* vel effaeminati, cogitandi generis, ne in foedam desperantium trepidationem, aut vilem ac humilem ante factorum exsecrationem ac palinodian.

But beware lest they degenerate into the cosmetic of a manner of thinking either too *savage and violent,* or effeminate, into the foul trepidation of the despairing, or a base and abject execration and palinode of past deeds.

> § 725. III. Est SVBMISSVM COGITANDI GENVS, animi viribus ac impetui parcentis propter reuerentiam. Quod quamdiu tantum sibi temperat ab affectanda vbertate, dignitate, exacto veri studio, nitore, ac ornatu, argumentationibus et contentione vehementioribus, quantum vel debita cogitanti, si qua debetur ipsi, reuerentia, vel ea, quam ipse debeat nunc rebus ac personis, de quibus aut contra quas meditatur, nunc futuris suae meditationis spectatoribus praecipuis, κατ’ [p. 485] ἤθη, §. 698, postulauerit: verum et naturalem colorem seruat, §. 622, 623. Neque negliget moratum hoc, §. 226, 227. et aequabile, §. 267. et strictius etiam temperatum cogitandi genus, §. 270. regulam illam apud Ciceronem, Off. I. 90: *Recte videntur praecipere, qui monent, vt, quanto superiores simus, tanto nos submissius geramus.*

§ 725. III. There is the SUBMISSIVE MANNER OF THINKING, of a mind sparing its powers and impetus out of reverence. So long as this restrains itself from affecting richness, dignity, exact pursuit of truth, brilliance and ornament, more vehement argumentations and contention, only so far as either the reverence due to the thinker, if any is due to him, or that which he himself owes now to the things and persons about which or against which he meditates, now to the principal future spectators of his meditation, κατ’ [p. 485] ἤθη [according to their characters], § 698, shall have demanded: it preserves the true and natural colour, § 622, 623. Nor will this moral, § 226, 227, even-tenored, § 267, and even more strictly temperate manner of thinking, § 270, neglect that rule in Cicero, Off. I. 90: *They seem rightly to teach who admonish that the higher we are, the more submissively we should bear ourselves.*

> § 726. Quam primum autem submissum cogitandi genus eo deprimitur, vt vel obliuiscatur pulcre cogitaturus suae dignitatis, vel falsam et superstitiosam reuerentiam, nescio quibus, nunc rebus, nunc personis exhibens rependoue simulans eadem retrahi se patiatur ab illa copia, dignitate, professione veritatis, ornatu, reprehensione, contentione tandem et impetu animi, quae prae se ferre decenter eleganterque potuisset: tunc idem *humile, submissum, molle, effaeminatum, fractum atque abiectum* cogitandi genus, vti βάθος, §. 217. ita fucus est. §. 688, 725.

§ 726. But as soon as the submissive manner of thinking is depressed to the point that one who is to think beautifully either forgets his own dignity, or, exhibiting or creepingly feigning a false and superstitious reverence towards I know not what things or persons, allows himself to be drawn back by them from that copiousness, dignity, profession of truth, ornament, refutation, and finally contention and impetus of mind, which he could have displayed becomingly and elegantly: then this same *humble, submissive, soft, effeminate, broken and abject* manner of thinking, like βάθος [bathos], § 217, is a cosmetic. § 688, 725.

> § 727. Hinc Quintilianus, XI. 1. in vitiis numerat *summissum* cogitandi *genus concitatis in caussis,* i. e. quas salua decori verioris reuerentia tamen omni animi impetu diligentiaeque neruis, omni cum copia, dignitate, ornatu ac ardore agi non oporteat solum, sed [p. 486] etiam necesse sit. Ibidem in aliis huc admodum facientibus exemplum adfert *Socratis,* cuius *ad absolutionem profuturum fuisset, si conciliasset oratione submissa,* §. 726. iudicum animos sibi, qui tamen, quoniam *id eum minime decuisset, sic egerit, vt, qui poenam suam honoribus summis esset aestimaturus.* Hic addit: *Quando ab hominibus sui temporis parum intelligebatur, posterorum se iudiciis reseruauit, breui detrimento iam vltimae senectutis aeuum omnium saeculorum consequutus.*

§ 727. Hence Quintilian, XI. 1, counts among the vices *the submissive manner* of thinking *in agitated causes,* i.e. those which, saving the reverence of truer decorum, it is nevertheless not only fitting but [p. 486] even necessary to plead with all impetus of mind and all the sinews of diligence, with all copiousness, dignity, ornament and ardour. In the same place, among other things very pertinent here, he brings the example of *Socrates,* for whom *it would have been profitable towards his acquittal if* with a submissive speech, § 726, *he had conciliated* the minds of the judges to himself, who however, since *that would least have befitted him, so acted as one who was going to value his penalty at the highest honours.* Here he adds: *Since he was little understood by the men of his time, he reserved himself for the judgements of posterity, and by the brief loss of a now extreme old age obtained the age of all centuries.*

> § 728. Pergit Quintilianus l. c. Scipionem *Africanum* commemorare, qui *patria cedere, quam cum Tribuno plebis, humillimo homine, de innocentia contendere, maluit.* Tanti putauit heros genus cogitandi male submissum cauere, §. 726. Fontes eius, auctore Quintiliano, sunt, *humiliora illa vitia, submissa adulatio, vilis pudor, in omni negotio neglecta auctoritas, quae fere accidunt his, qui nimium blandi esse volunt.* Adeo grauis submissi cogitandi generis aduersarius, quando fucus est, quaerit tamen: *Quis vero nesciat, quin nonnunquam submittenda sit et contrahenda oratio, ne iudex eam vel intelligere, vel capere non possit?* §. 725. Idem in *Cicerone* laudat, qui ne *in caussa Cluentii* quidem, etsi *mater* huius *palam caput filii impugnabat, oblitus est reuerentiae, quae parentibus debetur,* iubetque *in re minore ac minus* [p. 487] *infesta orationem* adhuc *leniorem et submissiorem.*

§ 728. Quintilian goes on, l. c., to mention Scipio *Africanus,* who *preferred to withdraw from his country rather than contend about his innocence with a Tribune of the plebs, a most lowly man.* So highly did the hero value guarding against the badly submissive manner of thinking, § 726. Its sources, according to Quintilian, are *those lowlier vices, submissive flattery, base shame, authority neglected in every business, which generally befall those who wish to be too agreeable.* So grave an adversary of the submissive manner of thinking, when it is a cosmetic, asks nevertheless: *Who indeed does not know that sometimes the speech must be lowered and contracted, lest the judge be unable either to understand or to grasp it?* § 725. The same man praises *Cicero,* who not even *in the cause of Cluentius,* although his *mother openly attacked the life of her son, forgot the reverence which is owed to parents,* and he bids *in a lesser and less* [p. 487] *hostile matter a speech* still *gentler and more submissive.*

> § 729. IIII. Est ERECTVM ET AVDAX COGITANDI GENVS animi vim ac impetum intendentis propter dignitatem, quo elate cogitatur et dicitur, licet non semper sublimiter, §. 287. In hoc cauendus est fucus arrogantiae. V. Est ludicrum et iocosum, in quo vitetur *affectata scurrilitas, praesertim in parum modestis ac pudicis,* et generatim, *ne nimium ridiculus esse velis.* VI. Est graue, in quo ne qua senilis auctoritas immatura deprehendatur. VII. Est dulce, cuius *decoctam* auersatur *dulcedinem* Cicero. Sed satis de his. §. 692.

§ 729. IIII. There is the ERECT AND BOLD MANNER OF THINKING, of a mind straining its force and impetus for the sake of dignity, in which one thinks and speaks loftily, though not always sublimely, § 287. In this the cosmetic of arrogance is to be guarded against. V. There is the playful and jocose, in which *affected scurrility* is to be avoided, *especially in things not very modest and chaste,* and in general, *that you should not wish to be too ridiculous.* VI. There is the grave, in which care is to be taken that no immature senile authority be detected. VII. There is the sweet, whose *decocted sweetness* Cicero turns away from. But enough of these. § 692.

#### Sectio XXXXIII. Argumenta Illustrantia. — Section XXXXIII. Illustrating Arguments

> § 730. ARGVMENTA, quorum (vel vnica, vel potior, vel nunc maxime consideranda,) vis est, lucem datae perceptioni affundere, sunt DECLARANTIA (explicantia). Dabunt itaque perspicuitatem vel intellectualem, RESOLVENTIA (analytica) quale est *definitio,* [p. 488] *propriam cuiusuis rei vim declarans,* Cic. de Or. I. 190. vel sensitiuam, § 614, 618. nunc absolutam certe, §. 617, 625, nunc omnino nitorem aliquem exhibent, et a potiori dicuntur ILLVSTRANTIA (pingentia). Cicero, Fam. V. ep. 13. *saepius dicendum, et non significandum modo,* quod fieri potest obscurius, *sed etiam declarandum* iudicat, quod optat Lucceium clare perspicere.

§ 730. ARGUMENTS whose force (whether sole, or chief, or now especially to be considered) is to pour light upon a given perception are DECLARATIVE (explicating). They will therefore give perspicuity either intellectual, RESOLVING (analytic), such as *definition,* [p. 488] *declaring the proper force of any thing,* Cic. de Or. I. 190, or sensate, § 614, 618, now certainly absolute, § 617, 625, now altogether exhibiting some brilliance, and from their predominant feature they are called ILLUSTRATING (painting). Cicero, Fam. V. ep. 13, judges that *one must more often say, and not only signify,* which can be done more obscurely, *but also declare,* what he wishes Lucceius to see clearly.

> § 731. Iustissima vitandi fuci cautio, S. XXXXII. suadebit in argumentis et figuris pingentibus ac illustrantibus §. 730, 26, praesertim ea tantum ornamenta sectari, quae praeter illustrationem simul vbertati, dignitati, verisimilitudini, reliquisque cogitandorum gratiis, vel singulis seruiant, vel saltim aliquibus, §. 142. quae vero tantum pinxerint, praetereaque nihil ad totius pulcritudinem conferre videantur, parca manu adspergere, vel ambitiosa recidere, §. 164.

§ 731. The most just caution of avoiding cosmetic, S. XXXXII, will persuade one, in painting and illustrating arguments and figures § 730, 26, to pursue especially only those ornaments which, besides illustration, serve at the same time richness, dignity, verisimilitude and the remaining graces of things to be thought, either all of them or at least some, § 142; but those which have only painted and besides seem to contribute nothing to the beauty of the whole, to sprinkle with a sparing hand, or to cut back as ambitious, § 164.

> § 732. Perceptiones praegnantes, M. §. 517. et complexae, M. §. 530. et ipsae, caetera si fuerint paria, magis splendent, quam minus complexae, et totius, quam ingrediuntur, meditationis possunt argumenta fieri illustrantia, §. 730. Hinc minus praegnantibus, minus complexis pulcre praeferuntur, praesertim quando ipsae [p. 489] adhaerentes perceptiones tamen aliquid simul probant, vel mouent, §. 731. Hinc magnum epithetorum bene lectorum artificium. Exemplis abundant pulcra omnia. Virgilii sumamus eclogam in primis eius poematibus primam. Ibi non dicit: Amaryllida *cantas,* sed:

§ 732. Pregnant perceptions, M. § 517, and complex ones, M. § 530, both shine more themselves, other things being equal, than less complex ones, and can become illustrating arguments of the whole meditation into which they enter, § 730. Hence they are beautifully preferred to the less pregnant, the less complex, especially when the [p. 489] adhering perceptions themselves at the same time also prove something, or move, § 731. Hence the great artifice of well-chosen epithets. All beautiful things abound in examples. Let us take Virgil’s first eclogue, the first among his poems. There he does not say: you *sing* Amaryllis, but:

> *Formosam resonare doces Amaryllida siluas,* v. 5.

*You teach the woods to resound with beauteous Amaryllis,* v. 5.

> non dicit:

he does not say:

> *Haec* vrbs multum *alias inter caput extulit vrbes,* sed *tantum,*

*This* city has much *lifted its head among other cities,* but *as much,*

> *Quantum lenta solent inter viburna cupressi.*

*As the cypresses are wont among the pliant wayfaring-trees.*

> Non dicit libertatem sibi venisse *seni,* sed:

He does not say that freedom came to him *as an old man,* but:

> *Candidior postquam tondenti barba cadebat.*

*After my beard fell whiter to the barber.*

> Non scribit: Nunquam illius obliuiscemur, sed:

He does not write: We shall never forget him, but:

> *Ante leues pascentur in aethere cerui,* / *Et freta destituent nudos in littore pisces:* / *Ante pererratis amborum finibus exsul* / *Aut Ararim Parthus bibet, aut Germania Tygrim,* / *Quam nostro illius labatur pectore vultus.*

*Sooner shall light stags graze in the air,* / *and the seas leave the fish bare on the shore:* / *sooner, the bounds of both wandered over, as an exile* / *shall the Parthian drink the Arar, or Germany the Tigris,* / *than his countenance slip from our breast.*

> Tandem non ait: iam vesper adest, sed:

Finally he does not say: now evening is here, but:

> *Iam summa procul villarum culmina fumant* / *Maioresque cadunt altis de montibus vmbrae.*

*Now the high rooftops of the farms smoke afar* / *and greater shadows fall from the lofty mountains.*

> § 733. Quoniam HYPOTYPOSIS, viuida alicuius [p. 490] descriptio, non illustrat solum, §. 618, sed etiam probat, §. 550, 551. inter meliora pingentium argumenta merito refertur, §. 731. DIATYPOSIS est hypotyposis ardentior. Hinc diatyposis est in argumentis illustrantium optimis, §. 731, cuius species est CHARACTERISMVS, diatyposis moratior. §. 226. Exempla dabit Lucianus, et Theophrastus, et huius imitator in Gallis princeps.

§ 733. Since HYPOTYPOSIS, the vivid description of something, [p. 490] not only illustrates, § 618, but also proves, § 550, 551, it is deservedly counted among the better of the painting arguments, § 731. DIATYPOSIS is a more ardent hypotyposis. Hence diatyposis belongs among the best of the illustrating arguments, § 731, and its species is CHARACTERISMUS, a diatyposis more concerned with character. § 226. Examples will be given by Lucian, and Theophrastus, and his chief imitator among the French.

> § 734. Vna perceptionum connexarum et coniunctarum, s. sociarum alteram potest declarare, imo etiam illustrare, §. 730, si simul cum hac attendatur viuide, M. §. 516, i. e. comparetur. M. §. 626. Hinc substitutio illius pro hac pulcre cogitanda, vel coniunctio illius cum hac, non sine viuiditate, dabit ARGVMENTVM illustrans A COMPARATIS, quod aliqui dicunt A MEDITATIONE, §. 730, nos dicamus figuram, §. 26, COMPARATIONEM et collationem LATIVS, quae complectitur assimilationem, sed in multa etiam alia argumentorum genera diffunditur, quam quae petantur a simili. e. g.

§ 734. One of two connected and conjoined, i.e. associated, perceptions can declare the other, indeed even illustrate it, § 730, if at the same time it is vividly attended to together with it, M. § 516, i.e. compared with it. M. § 626. Hence the substitution of the former for the latter in thinking beautifully, or the conjunction of the former with the latter, not without vividness, will yield the illustrating ARGUMENT FROM THINGS COMPARED, which some call the argument FROM MEDITATION, § 730; let us call it the figure, § 26, of COMPARISON and collation IN THE WIDER SENSE, which embraces assimilation, but spreads out also into many other kinds of arguments than those which are sought from the similar. E.g.

> *Tantaene animis caelestibus irae?* Aen. I. 15. et Carthaginis statim sequens illustratio 1) ab aetate 2) ab incolis 3) a situ 4) a diuitiis 5) a studiis belli 6) a fauore Iunonis, v. 16-22. Hinc odium in Aeneam, [p. 491] comparatis caussis aliis, v. 23-36. Tandem meditationis epiphonema:

*Can there be such anger in celestial minds?* Aen. I. 15. and the illustration of Carthage that immediately follows: 1) from its age 2) from its inhabitants 3) from its site 4) from its riches 5) from its pursuits of war 6) from the favour of Juno, v. 16-22. Hence the hatred against Aeneas, [p. 491] with other causes compared, v. 23-36. Finally the epiphonema of the meditation:

> *Tantae molis erat Romanam condere gentem.*

*So great a labour it was to found the Roman race.*

> § 735. Sicut in argumentis augentibus augmentum, §. 330, in probantibus aetiologiam, §. 545. figuram vidimus ita principem, vt reliquas ad augendum probandumue pertinentes sinu suo comprehendere videantur singulas: ita comparationem latius dictam in figuris illustrantibus generalem habeamus et principem, §. 734, sine qua ne hypotyposis quidem esse potest, §. 733. et ad quam, veluti fontem, reliquae tandem altius consideratae concurrunt. Nam quoniam ex vno simili, aequali, congruente, generatim, notabilius eodem, cognosci, hinc et viuidius cognosci, illustrarique potest, §. 730. alterum simile, aequale, congruens, et notabilius idem: M. §. 70, 572. comparatio latius dicta sub se comprehendet argumentum illustrans 1) a simili, aequali, congruente, notabilius eodem, quod figura dicitur a potiori ASSIMILATIO, §. 734. si similia, aequalia, congruentia, notabilius eadem coniungantur. Potest et eorundem vnum cogitando substitui pro altero.

§ 735. Just as among the augmenting arguments we saw augmentation, § 330, and among the proving ones aetiology, § 545, to be the principal figure, so that all the others pertaining to augmenting or proving seem each to be comprehended in its bosom: so let us hold comparison in the wider sense to be the general and principal figure among the illustrating ones, § 734, without which not even hypotyposis can exist, § 733, and to which, as to a fountain, the rest, when at last considered more deeply, run together. For since from one thing that is similar, equal, congruent, or in general notably the same, the other similar, equal, congruent and notably same thing can be cognised, hence also more vividly cognised and illustrated, § 730; M. § 70, 572; comparison in the wider sense will comprehend under itself the illustrating argument 1) from the similar, equal, congruent, notably same, which figure is called, from its chief part, ASSIMILATION, § 734, if similar, equal, congruent, notably same things are conjoined. One of these can also, in thinking, be substituted for the other.

> § 736. Assimilatio quo similiora, quo minus inaequalia, quo magis congruentia, et proportionata, [p. 492] secundum analogi rationis trutinam, inter se comparabit, hoc erit illa pulcrior, §. 735. Praedicata assimilatis l. comparatis communia TERTIVM COMPARATIONIS dicuntur. In diiudicando tertio comparationis quantitatis etiam est quaedam dimensio, §. 314, 315. Argumentum illustrans a simili non potest a sanae mentis homine ideo proferri, vt vnum in comparatis habeatur pro totaliter eodem cum altero, M. §. 269. hinc inter haec detecta quadam differentia perperam omne simile claudicare dicitur. Si in cogitatione A velis illustrare C, hinc assumas B simile τῷ A, in quo idem C belle possis et nitide contemplari, A SVBIECTVM ASSIMILATIONIS per B, TERMINVM ASSIMILATIONIS, simile non claudicans, illustratur, qua tertium comparationis C, etiamsi B possit habere D praedicatum quoddam, quod non est in A. Si vero C illud ipsum tertium comparationis constitutum, cuius gratia omnis peragitur assimilatio, longe se tamen aliter habeat, vel qualitate, vel quantitate, vel vtraque, secundum ipsam analogi rationis trutinam, in B, quam in A, tunc laborare pulcritudinem assimilationis non negauerim, §. 315.

§ 736. The more similar, the less unequal, the more congruent and proportioned the things that an assimilation compares with one another, [p. 492] according to the balance of the analogue of reason, the more beautiful it will be, § 735. The predicates common to the things assimilated, or compared, are called the TERTIUM COMPARATIONIS. In judging the tertium comparationis there is also a certain measuring of quantity, § 314, 315. An illustrating argument from the similar cannot be put forward by a man of sound mind with the intention that one of the compared things be held to be totally the same as the other, M. § 269; hence, when some difference has been detected between them, it is wrongly said that every simile limps. If in thinking of A you wish to illustrate C, and hence take up B, similar τῷ [to] A, in which you can contemplate the same C beautifully and clearly, then A, the SUBJECT OF THE ASSIMILATION, is illustrated through B, the TERM OF THE ASSIMILATION, a simile that does not limp, as regards the tertium comparationis C, even if B could have some predicate D which is not in A. But if that C itself, constituted as the tertium comparationis for whose sake the whole assimilation is carried out, nonetheless stands far otherwise, whether in quality, or in quantity, or in both, according to the very balance of the analogue of reason, in B than in A, then I should not deny that the beauty of the assimilation suffers, § 315.

> § 737. Assimilatorum in tertiis comparationis detecta quantitatis differentia saltim excusationi locum dabit, §. 736, qualis est:

§ 737. A difference of quantity detected in the tertia comparationis of things assimilated will at least give occasion for an excuse, § 736, such as:

> [p. 493] *si magna licet componere paruis,*

[p. 493] *if it is permitted to compare great things with small,*

> et Ouidii Trist. I. 5. pietatem vxoris suae comparantis cum pietate Liuiae matronali:

and that of Ovid, Trist. I. 5, comparing the piety of his wife with the matronly piety of Livia:

> *Grandia si paruis assimilare licet.*

*If it is permitted to liken grand things to small.*

> Assimilationis exemplum dabit Ciceronis Hortensius: *Vt ii, qui combibi purpuram volunt, sufficiunt prius lanam medicamentis quibusdam: sic litteris talibusque doctrinis ante excoli animus et ad sapientiam concipiendam imbui et praeparari debet.* Idem pro Roscio: *Vt ignis,* inquit, *in aquam coniectus continuo restinguitur et refrigeratur: sic referuens falsum crimen, in purissimam et castissimam vitam collatum, statim concidit et exstinguitur.* Item: *Vt non frugem, neque arborem in omni agro reperire possis: sic non omne facinus in omni vita nascitur.*

An example of assimilation will be given by Cicero’s Hortensius: *As those who wish to take up the purple dye first steep the wool in certain preparations: so by letters and by such teachings the mind must first be cultivated and be imbued and prepared for receiving wisdom.* The same, for Roscius: *As fire,* he says, *thrown into water is at once quenched and cooled: so a seething false charge, cast upon a most pure and most chaste life, immediately collapses and is extinguished.* Likewise: *As you cannot find crop or tree in every field: so not every crime arises in every life.*

> § 738. Regulam, quae iubet argumentis tantum illustrantibus praeferre simul aliam vtilitatem exhibentia, §. 731. sic illustrat assimilando Quintilianus VIII. 3: *An ego fundum cultiorem putem, in quo mihi quis ostenderit lilia et violas et amoenos fontes scaturientes, quam vbi plena messis aut graues fructu vites erunt? Sterilem platanum, et tonsas myrtos, quam maritam vlmum, et vberes oleas, praeoptauerim? Habeant illa diuites, licet, quid essent, si aliud nihil haberent? — — — — Et ego in ordinem et certa* [p. 494] *interualla meas arbores redigam. Quid enim, quaeso, illo quincunce speciosius? quid, in quamcumque partem spectaueris, rectius? Sed protenus in id quoque prodest, vt terrae succum aequaliter trahant. Oleae cacumina in altum exsurgentia ferro coercebo, in orbem formosius fundet, et protenus fructum ramis pluribus feret. Decentior equus, cui adstricta ilia, si idem velocior. Pulcer adspectu si athleta est, cuius lacertos exercitatio expressit, idem est certamini paratior. Nunquam vera species ab vtilitate diuiditur.*

§ 738. The rule which bids us prefer, to arguments that merely illustrate, those which at the same time exhibit some other usefulness, § 731, Quintilian VIII. 3 illustrates thus by assimilation: *Should I think that estate the better cultivated in which someone showed me lilies and violets and pleasant gushing springs, rather than one where there will be a full harvest or vines heavy with fruit? Should I prefer the barren plane-tree and clipped myrtles to the wedded elm and the fruitful olives? Let the rich have those things, by all means; what would they be, if they had nothing else? — — — — And I too shall bring my trees into order and fixed* [p. 494] *intervals. What, I ask, is more handsome than that quincunx? what straighter, in whatever direction you look? But straightaway it is also useful for this, that they draw the sap of the earth equally. The tops of the olive that rise too high I shall check with the knife; it will spread more beautifully into a circle, and will straightaway bear fruit on more branches. The horse whose flanks are tight is more comely, and the same is faster. Handsome to look upon is the athlete whose arms exercise has brought out, and the same is readier for the contest. True beauty is never divided from usefulness.*

> § 739. Assimilationis hoc §. 735. *in genere id est praecipue custodiendum ne id, quod similitudinis gratia adsciuimus, aut obscurum sit, aut ignotum. Debet enim, quod illustrandae alterius rei gratia assumitur, ipsum esse clarius, eo, quod illuminat. Quare poetis quidem permittamus sane huiusmodi exempla:*

§ 739. For assimilation, § 735, *in general this is chiefly to be guarded against, that what we have adopted for the sake of the similitude be neither obscure nor unknown. For what is taken up for the sake of illustrating another thing ought itself to be clearer than that which it illuminates. Wherefore let us by all means allow poets examples of this kind:*

> *Qualis vbi hibernam Lyciam Xanthique fluenta / Deserit, aut Delon maternam inuisit Apollo.*

*As when Apollo leaves wintry Lycia and the streams of Xanthus, / or visits his mother’s Delos.*

> *Non idem decebit oratorem, vt occultis aperta demonstret.* Quint. l. c. Efferamus legem generalius: Terminus comparationis et illustrationis omnis, hinc et assimilationis, spectatoribus nostris, quos praecipue debemus attendere, sit notior ac viuidior subiecto comparationis, illustrationis, et hinc etiam [p. 495] assimilationis, §. 736. Hinc poeta, qualis Virgilius, lectores suos potissimum attendendos per mundum graecae mythologiae poeticum versatissimos qui potuit supponere, recte potest assimilationem instituere, quam habet Quintilianus, sicut et illam Didus in templum venientis, Aen. I. 502:

*The same will not befit the orator, that he should demonstrate the open by the hidden.* Quint. l. c. Let us state the law more generally: The term of every comparison and illustration, hence also of assimilation, should be, for our spectators, to whom we must chiefly attend, better known and more vivid than the subject of the comparison, illustration, and hence also [p. 495] assimilation, § 736. Hence a poet such as Virgil, who could suppose his readers, those chiefly to be attended to, thoroughly versed in the poetic world of Greek mythology, can rightly set up the assimilation that Quintilian cites, as also that of Dido coming into the temple, Aen. I. 502:
