given by Jove,

> *qui foedere certo* / *Et premere et laxas sciret dare iussus habenas,* 67.

*who by a fixed covenant* / *should know, as bidden, both to tighten and to give the loose reins,* 67.

> § 779. Comparatio possessoris et possessi dat illustrationem γ) possessoris a re possessa:

§ 779. The comparison of possessor and possessed gives the illustration γ) of the possessor from the thing possessed:

> *Non illi imperium pelagi, saeuumque tridentem* / *Sed mihi sorte datum. Tenet ille immania saxa,* / *Vestras, Eure, domos. Illa se iactet in aula* / *Aeolus, et clauso ventorum carcere regnet.* 145.

*Not to him the rule of the sea and the fierce trident,* / *but to me was it given by lot. He holds the monstrous rocks,* / *your homes, Eurus. In that hall let Aeolus* / *vaunt himself, and reign in the closed prison of the winds.* 145.

> δ) ducis, principis, imperantis, dei a subditis et personis, in illius potestate constitutis. §. 778. Horatius ad Augustum:

δ) of the leader, prince, commander, god from his subjects and the persons set in his power, § 778. Horace to Augustus:

> *Praesenti tibi maturos largimur honores,* / *Jurandasque tuum per numen ponimus aras,* / *Nil oriturum alias, nil ortum tale fatentes.* / *Sed tuus hoc populus sapiens et iustus in vno,* / *Te nostris ducibus, te Graiis anteferendo,* / *Caetera nequaquam simili ratione modoque* / *Aestumat.* ep. II. 1. 20.

*To you, present among us, we bestow timely honours,* / *and set up altars to swear by your divinity,* / *confessing that nothing like it will arise elsewhere, nothing has arisen.* / *But this people of yours, wise and just in this one thing,* / *in preferring you to our leaders, you to the Greeks,* / *estimates the rest in nowise by a similar reasoning* / *and manner.* ep. II. 1. 20.

[p. 530]

#### Sectio XXXXVII. Tropi. — Section XXXXVII. Tropes

> § 780. TROPVM hic non attendo tantum, quatenus *est verbi vel sermonis a propria significatione in aliam cum virtute mutatio*, Quint. VIII. 6. multo minus, quem necessitas et linguae paupertas necessarium facit, quoties significandum est, cuius non est in data lingua proprium vocabulum, minime, quem ignorantia proprietatis in loquendo procudit: sed omnem elegantem perceptionis vnius pro altera substitutionem, siue vocabulis translatis significetur, quod notissimum, siue sonis sibi inuicem substitutis a musico, siue coloribus a pictore, siue per aliud quodcunque signorum genus eleganter te pro vno aliud cogitasse exprimas.

§ 780. By a TROPE I here do not attend only to what, insofar as it *is a change of a word or an expression from its proper signification to another with excellence*, Quint. VIII. 6, much less to the one which necessity and the poverty of a language make necessary, whenever something must be signified for which there is no proper word in the given language, least of all to the one which ignorance of propriety forges in speaking: but to every elegant substitution of one perception for another, whether it be signified by transferred words, which is the best known, or by sounds substituted for one another by the musician, or by colours by the painter, or through any other kind of signs whatever you elegantly express that you have thought one thing in place of another.

> § 781. Venustam intueamur troporum genesin, et pulueris exigui iactu componi potest *inexplicabilis*, quam Fabius praefatur l. c. nisi *grammaticorum inter ipsos, philosophorum* certe *pugna circa tropum, quae sint genera, quae species, qui numerus, quis cuique subiiciatur?* An sit figura e. c. In certo pulcrae tuae meditationis [p. 531] loco viuiditas postulet comparationem aliquam, §. 734. quam tamen ibidem diductam, amplam et copiosam, explicite cogitantis 1) subiectum 2) terminum comparationis, §. 736, non admittat rotunda breuitas, §. 166: habebis locum excipiendi, §. 24. Exceptio, qua sic satisfiat viuiditati, ne quid inde detrimenti capiat rotunda breuitas, erit possibilium minima, §. 24, sane non inelegans, §. 25. Quod si iam omittas, nec explicite cogites, nec peculiari termino significes, subiectum comparationis, sed eidem substituas, eiusdemque loco solum explicite cogites, solum significes terminum comparationis, auditori spectatoriue relinquens, vt inde tacitus ille secum euoluat subiectum comparationis, ita satisfecisti viuiditati comparationem poscenti, ne quid inde detrimenti ceperit rotunda breuitas, quoniam seriem explicite cogitatorum ne vno quidem auxisti signo vel verbulo. Vnde nascitur substitutio termini comparationis pro subiecto eiusdem non inelegans, tropus, §. 780.

§ 781. Let us look at the charming genesis of tropes, and with the throw of a little dust can be settled that *inexplicable* fight, as Fabius calls it in his preface l. c., if not *of the grammarians among themselves*, at least *of the philosophers, about the trope, what its genera are, what its species, what their number, which is subordinate to which?* Whether it is a figure, etc. In a certain place of your beautiful meditation [p. 531] let vividness demand some comparison, § 734, which, however, drawn out, ample and copious, explicitly thinking 1) the subject 2) the term of the comparison, § 736, rounded brevity does not admit in that same place, § 166: you will have occasion for an exception, § 24. The exception by which vividness is thus satisfied, so that rounded brevity suffers no detriment thereby, will be the least of those possible, § 24, surely not inelegant, § 25. But if you now omit the subject of the comparison, and neither think it explicitly nor signify it by a special term, but substitute for it, and in its place explicitly think only, and signify only, the term of the comparison, leaving it to the hearer or spectator silently to unfold for himself from it the subject of the comparison, then you have satisfied the vividness that demanded a comparison, without rounded brevity having suffered any detriment thereby, since you have not increased the series of things explicitly thought by even one sign or little word. Hence is born the not inelegant substitution of the term of a comparison for its subject, a trope, § 780.

> § 782. Quae sunt ergo troporum genera? quae species? Eaedem, quae comparationis latius dictae. §. 734-779. Qui numerus? innumerabilis. Quis cuique subiicitur? Qui non est METAPHORA, contracta assimilatio, [p. 532] §. 735-741, nec SYNECDOCHE, contracta comparatio maioris et minoris, S. XXXXIIII. nec IRONIA, contracta antithesis, S. XXXXV. erit ille sane METONYMIA, contracta comparatio strictius dicta, S. XXXXVI. quemadmodum eruditus, qui nec theologus, nec iureconsultus, nec medicus nominatur, eo ipso philosophicum in ordinem amandatur per academias.

§ 782. What, then, are the genera of tropes? what the species? The same as those of comparison in the wider sense, § 734–779. What is their number? innumerable. Which is subordinate to which? The one which is not METAPHOR, a contracted assimilation, [p. 532] § 735–741, nor SYNECDOCHE, a contracted comparison of the greater and the lesser, S. XXXXIIII, nor IRONY, a contracted antithesis, S. XXXXV, will surely be METONYMY, a contracted comparison in the stricter sense, S. XXXXVI, just as the learned man who is called neither theologian, nor jurist, nor physician is by that very fact consigned by the academies to the philosophical order.

> § 783. An figurae tropi sunt, an tropi figurae? *Plerique has tropos esse existimauerunt — — — — Vsus est idem. Nam et vim rebus adiiciunt, M. §. 515, et gratiam praestant, §. 780, 26. Nec desunt, qui tropis figurae nomen imponant, quorum est C. Artorius Proculus. Quin adeo similitudo manifesta, vt eam discernere non sit in promtu — — — — Haec scio, quam multiplicem habeant, quamque scrupulosam disputationem. — — — — Haec de quibus loquimur, siue tropi, siue figurae dicentur, idem efficient. — — — — Illud tamen notandum, coire frequenter in easdem sententias, et tropon, et figuram. Tam enim translatis, quam propriis figuratur oratio. Est autem non mediocris inter auctores dissensio, et quae vis nominis eius, et quot genera, et quam multae sint species.* Quint. VIIII. 1.

§ 783. Are figures tropes, or tropes figures? *Most have thought these to be tropes — — — — The use is the same. For they both add force to things, M. § 515, and afford grace, § 780, 26. Nor are there lacking those who impose the name of figure on tropes, among whom is C. Artorius Proculus. Indeed the likeness is so manifest that it is not easy to discern it — — — — I know how manifold and how scrupulous a dispute these things have. — — — — These things of which we speak, whether they are called tropes or figures, will produce the same effect. — — — — This, however, is to be noted, that trope and figure frequently coincide in the same thoughts. For speech is figured as much by transferred as by proper words. There is, moreover, no slight disagreement among authors both as to what the force of its name is, and how many its genera, and how numerous its species.* Quint. VIIII. 1.

> *Grammatici certant, et adhuc sub iudice lis est.* Hor.

*Grammarians contend, and the case is still before the judge.* Hor.

> [p. 533] § 784. Philosopho nodus in scirpo quaeri videatur. §. 781. Non omnes figurae tropi sunt, §. 26, 780. Rectius autem bonus ille Proculus, si tropon ex notione Quintiliani paullisper extensa sumas, §. 780, nec eo necessarias quascunque, multo minus insicetas ignorantium linguam, quam loquuntur, translationes referas. Omnis tropus, quem definiui, est FIGVRA, sed CRYPTICA, cuius genuina forma non statim apparet, quoniam est figura contracta per substitutionem §. 782.

[p. 533] § 784. To a philosopher it may seem that a knot is being sought in a bulrush, § 781. Not all figures are tropes, § 26, 780. But that good Proculus would be more in the right, if you take the trope according to Quintilian’s notion somewhat extended, § 780, and do not refer to it any necessary transferences whatsoever, much less the tasteless ones of those ignorant of the language they speak. Every trope, as I have defined it, is a FIGURE, but a CRYPTIC one, whose genuine form does not appear at once, since it is a figure contracted through substitution § 782.

> § 785. Logici scholasticorum docent PROPOSITIONEM EXPONIBILEM, ex affirmanti et negante cryptice compositam, quales exclusiuae, exceptiuae, restrictiuae, e. c. Nisi vererer latinis incommodus esse auribus, tropos figuras dicerem exponibiles. Quemadmodum enim barbaram propositionibus denominationem dedit schola, quoniam expositione indigent, vt appareat genuina vtriusque partis forma, ex quibus coaluerunt; sic tropus, vt grammaticis etiam, qui non sunt philosephi [sic: philosophi], figura appareat, expositione indiget. Si ex termino comparationis, qui solus in tropo cogitatur explicite, significatus proprius, eruas omissum subiectum comparationis, significatum improprium, [p. 534] et hoc, neglecto breuitatis amore, explicite manifestoque penes terminum comparationis cogites, et vtrumque te cogitare peculiaribus cuiuis terminis et signis declares, TROPVS EXPONITVR.

§ 785. The logicians of the schoolmen teach the EXPONIBLE PROPOSITION, cryptically composed of an affirmative and a negative, such as the exclusive, the exceptive, the restrictive, etc. Did I not fear being troublesome to Latin ears, I should call tropes exponible figures. For just as the school gave propositions that barbarous denomination because they need exposition, in order that the genuine form of each of the two parts out of which they have coalesced may appear; so the trope, in order that it may appear as a figure even to grammarians, who are not philosophers, needs exposition. If from the term of comparison, which alone is thought explicitly in the trope, the proper signification, you draw out the omitted subject of comparison, the improper signification, [p. 534] and, neglecting the love of brevity, think this explicitly and manifestly alongside the term of comparison, and declare that you are thinking both by terms and signs peculiar to each, THE TROPE IS EXPOUNDED.

> § 786. Metaphoram exponens habebis manifestam assimilationem, §. 735. Synecdochen exponens videbis comparationem maioris et minoris. Est ergo vel ADSCENDENS SYNECDOCHE, vel DESCENDENS, §. 742. Expone ironiam: habebis antithesin, §. 763. Metonymia denique resoluetur in aliquam comparationem strictius dictam. §. 773, 782. Quicquid itaque de figuris commemoratis huc vsque dictum est. §. 730-779. illud vt de tropis, earum crypsesi, repetamus, non est necesse.

§ 786. Expounding a metaphor you will have a manifest assimilation, § 735. Expounding a synecdoche you will see a comparison of greater and lesser. It is therefore either an ASCENDING SYNECDOCHE, or a DESCENDING one, § 742. Expound an irony: you will have an antithesis, § 763. Metonymy, finally, will be resolved into some comparison more strictly so called. § 773, 782. Whatever, therefore, has been said thus far about the figures mentioned, § 730–779, it is not necessary that we repeat it concerning tropes, the cryptic form of those figures.

> § 787. *In totum metaphora breuior est similitudine,* (assimilatione manifesta et explicita, §. 735.) §. 781, 782. *quod illa comparatur* (explicite) *rei, quam volumus exprimere* (subiecto comparationis) *haec pro ipsa re dicitur. Comparatio est,* (et quidem manifesta assimilatio) *fecisse quid hominem, vt leonem. Translatio est, quum dico de homine leo est.* (et quidem metaphora) Quint. VIII. 6. Sed est etiam audacior metaphora, quam comparatio, hinc ausi [p. 535] hominem cum leone comparare, saporis eruditi homines non audent temere leonem eundem dicere, §. 313. Non tango species metaphorae, quoniam *iam non pueris praecipimus, vt, accepto genere, species intelligere non possint.* ib. Caueantur 1) quarum *frequens vsus et obscurat, et taedio complet,* §. 731. 2) *humiles, sordidae, deformes,* §. 736, 762. 3) *nimio maiores aut, quod saepius accidit, minores,* §. 737, vnde tumor vel βάθος. 4) *dissimiles,* quarum ipsum comparationis tertium notabiliter differt in termino et subiecto assimilationis, §. 736. 5) *durae, i. e. a longinqua similitudine ductae,* §. 741. *Metaphora,* sicut omnis tropus, §. 781. *si in alienum locum venit, debet plus valere,* §. 26, *eo, quod expellit.* Quint. ib.

§ 787. *On the whole metaphor is shorter than simile,* (manifest and explicit assimilation, § 735.) § 781, 782. *in that the latter is compared* (explicitly) *with the thing we wish to express* (the subject of comparison) *whereas the former is said in place of the thing itself. It is a comparison,* (and indeed a manifest assimilation) *that a man did something like a lion. It is a transference, when I say of a man, he is a lion.* (and indeed a metaphor) Quintilian VIII. 6. But metaphor is also bolder than comparison; hence men of learned taste who have ventured [p. 535] to compare a man with a lion do not venture rashly to call the same man a lion, § 313. I do not touch on the species of metaphor, since *we are no longer instructing boys, so that, once the genus has been received, they could not understand the species.* ib. Let these be avoided: 1) those whose *frequent use both obscures and fills with tedium,* § 731. 2) *the low, the sordid, the ugly,* § 736, 762. 3) *those far too great or, what happens more often, too small,* § 737, whence turgidity or βάθος [bathos]. 4) *the dissimilar,* in which the very third term of the comparison differs notably in the term and in the subject of assimilation, § 736. 5) *the harsh, i.e. drawn from a far-fetched likeness,* § 741. *A metaphor,* like every trope, § 781. *if it comes into another’s place, ought to be worth more,* § 26, *than that which it drives out.* Quintilian ib.

> § 788. Expositionis §. 786. et diiudicationis §. 787. ad exercitium haec exempla sunto:

§ 788. For practice in the exposition of § 786 and the adjudication of § 787 let these be the examples:

> *Homo homini deus est, si suum officium sciat.* Caecil.

*Man is a god to man, if he knows his duty.* Caecil.

> *Egomet credidi / Homini docto mandare, id lapidi mando maximo.* Plaut.

*I myself believed / I was entrusting it to a learned man; I am entrusting it to the greatest of stones.* Plaut.

> *Te quia rugae / Turpant, et capitis niues.* Hor.

*Since wrinkles / disfigure you, and the snows upon your head.* Hor.

> *Aut porcus Vmber, aut obesus Etruscus. / [p. 536] Nec vllius natantis impetum trabis. / Nequisse praeterire, sine palmulis / Opus foret volare, sine linteo. / Ille, post phaselus, antea fuit / Comata silua. Nam Cytherio in iugo / Loquente saepe sibilum edidit coma.* Cat.

*Either an Umbrian pig, or a fat Etruscan. / [p. 536] Nor that any swimming timber’s rush / could have outstripped her, whether with oars / she had to fly, or with canvas. / She, afterwards a pinnace, before was / a leafy wood. For on the Cytherian ridge / she often gave forth a whistling with speaking hair.* Cat.

> § 789. Synecdoche adscendens §. 786, erit elegans substitutio 1) totius pro parte, §. 780, 743. Plautus *vlmorum Acheronta* per iocum dicit seruum vlmeis saepe virgis vapulantem.

§ 789. Ascending synecdoche, § 786, will be an elegant substitution 1) of the whole for the part, § 780, 743. Plautus in jest calls a slave often flogged with elm rods *an Acheron of elms*.

> *Seruiet aeternum, qui paruo nesciet vti.* Hor.

*He will be a slave for eternity who will not know how to use little.* Hor.

> Vel ipsa scilicet aeuiternitas pars tantum aeternitatis est. Virgilius aliquando *elephantum* pro ebore, dente elephanti, ponit. §. 753. 2) superioris pro inferiori, §. 744. Huc εὐφημισμοί, quibus ad mortem pertinentia circumscribebant huius non lubenter memores; *si quid illi grauius acciderit, etc.* pro consolatione lugentium,

Even eviternity itself, of course, is only a part of eternity. Virgil sometimes puts *elephant* for ivory, the elephant’s tooth. § 753. 2) of the superior for the inferior, § 744. Hither belong the εὐφημισμοί [euphemisms], with which those not gladly mindful of death would circumscribe the things that pertain to it; *if anything graver should befall him, etc.* for the consolation of mourners,

> *Paullum quidlibet alloquutionis / Moestius lacrumis Simonideis.* Cat.

*A little something of consolation / sadder than the tears of Simonides.* Cat.

> quibus Venerea solebant obumbrare.

with which they used to veil the things of Venus.

> *Tibi vltro supplicatum aduenio ob stultitiam meam.* Plaut.

*I come to you of my own accord to make supplication on account of my folly.* Plaut.

> (stuprum illatum filiae)

(the violation done to his daughter)

> [p. 537] § 790. Synecdoche descendens, §. 786. est venusta substitutio 1) partis pro toto: §. 746.

[p. 537] § 790. Descending synecdoche, § 786, is a charming substitution 1) of the part for the whole: § 746.

> *Plotius et Varius Sinuessae, Virgiliusque / Occurrunt, animae, quales neque candidiores / Terra tulit, neque queis me sit deuinctior alter.* Hor. I. sat. V.

*Plotius and Varius, and Virgil, at Sinuessa / come to meet us, souls such that earth has borne / none more candid, nor is there another to whom I am more attached.* Hor. I. sat. V.

> *Sic forsan tener ausus est Catullus / Magno mittere passerem Maroni.* Mart. IIII. ep. 14.

*Thus perhaps the tender Catullus dared / to send the sparrow to great Maro.* Mart. IIII. ep. 14.

> (poema de passere pro toto libro, quo continetur.) 2) inferioris pro superiori perceptione, §. 749.

(the poem about the sparrow for the whole book in which it is contained.) 2) of the inferior for the superior perception, § 749.

> *Nullo fata loco possis excludere, quum mors / Venerit, in medio Tibure Sardinia est.* Mart. 60.

*You could shut out the fates from no place; when death / has come, in the midst of Tibur there is Sardinia.* Mart. 60.

> Illud pro saluberrimo, haec pro loco, qui pestilens habebatur, est posita.

The former is put for the most healthful place, the latter for a place which was held to be pestilential.

> § 791. Ironicam Ciceronis illusionem habet *C. Verres, praetor vrbanus, homo sanctus et diligens,* et illud in Clodium: *Integritas tua te purgauit, mihi crede, pudor eripuit, vita ante acta seruauit.* Nec irrisione caret, vti Fabius recte notat, initium orationis pro Ligario: *Nouum crimen, C. Caesar, et ante hunc diem inauditum.*

§ 791. Cicero’s ironic mockery is in *C. Verres, urban praetor, a holy and diligent man,* and in that against Clodius: *Your integrity has cleared you, believe me, your modesty has rescued you, your past life has saved you.* Nor is it without mockery, as Fabius rightly notes, the beginning of the speech for Ligarius: *A new crime, C. Caesar, and unheard of before this day.*

> [p. 538] *Insere nunc, Meliboee, pyros, pone ordine vites! / — — — — / Scilicet is superis labor est, ea cura quietos / Exagitat!* Virg.

[p. 538] *Now graft your pears, Meliboeus, set your vines in rows! / — — — — / No doubt this is a toil for the gods above, this care disturbs / their rest!* Virg.

> § 792. Metonymia erit venusta substitutio, §. 782. 1) efficientis caussae pro effectu:

§ 792. Metonymy will be a charming substitution, § 782. 1) of the efficient cause for the effect:

> *Rarae sine Mentore mensae.* Juu. VIII.

*Tables rare without a Mentor.* Juv. VIII.

> ⁠2) effectus pro caussa:

⁠2) of the effect for the cause:

> *Pallentes habitant morbi, tristisque senectus.* Virg.

*There dwell pale diseases, and sad old age.* Virg.

> *Donec virenti canities abest.* Hor. l. 9.

*So long as grey hair is far from you in your green years.* Hor. l. 9.

> Senectutis effectus est canities. 3) medii pro fine:

Grey hair is an effect of old age. 3) of the means for the end:

> *Phyllida mitte mihi, meus est natalis, Jola!* Virg.

*Send me Phyllis, it is my birthday, Iollas!* Virg.

> ⁠4) finis pro medio. §. 774.

⁠4) of the end for the means. § 774.

> *Meritos aris mactauit honores.* Virg.

*He slew the due honours upon the altars.* Virg.

> § 793. 5) Signi pro signato:

§ 793. 5) of the sign for the thing signified:

> *Dum pueris omnis pater et matercula pallet,* Hor.

*While for the boys every father and little mother turns pale,* Hor.

> Pallor signum timoris est. 6) Signati pro signo. §. 775.

Pallor is a sign of fear. 6) of the thing signified for the sign. § 775.

> *Nunc te marmoreum pro tempore fecimus, at tunc, / [p. 539] Quum foetura gregem suppleuerit, aureus esto.* Virg.

*Now we have made you of marble for the time being, but then, / [p. 539] when the offspring have filled up the flock, be of gold.* Virg.

> ⁠7) Phaenomenorum in corpore pro simultaneis eorum in anima contingere solitis, §. 776.

⁠7) of phenomena in the body for those that are wont to occur simultaneously with them in the soul, § 776.

> *O! te, Bollane, cerebri / Felicem! / O! ego laeuus, / Qui purgor bilem sub verni temporis horam!* Hor.

*O! you, Bolanus, happy / in your brain! / O! unlucky I, / who purge my bile about the hour of the spring season!* Hor.

> ⁠8) affectionum animae pro correspondente cum iisdem corporis statu:

⁠8) of the affections of the soul for the state of the body corresponding to them:

> *Si mihi nan [sic: non] animo fixum immotumque sederet, / Ne cui me vinclo vellem sociare iugali, / Postquam primus amor deceptam morte fefellit, / — — — — / Huic vni forsan potui succumbere culpae.* Aen. IV. 19.

*If it did not sit fixed and immovable in my soul / to wish to join myself to no one in the bond of wedlock, / after my first love deceived me, cheated by death, / — — — — / to this one fault perhaps I could have succumbed.* Aen. IV. 19.

> § 794. 9) Loci vel aetatis, temporis, horae, continentis pro re vel persona isto loco, vel tempore contenta. §. 777.

§ 794. 9) of the place or the age, the time, the hour, the container, for the thing or person contained in that place or time. § 777.

> *Quinque adeo magnae, positis incudibus, vrbes / Tela nouant, Atina potens, Tiburque superbum, / Ardea, Crustumerique et turrigerae Antennae.* Aen. VII. 630.

*Five great cities, indeed, with anvils set up, / forge new weapons, mighty Atina and proud Tibur, / Ardea, and Crustumeri, and tower-bearing Antemnae.* Aen. VII. 630.

> *Adspice venturo laetentur vt omnia saeclo!* Ecl. IIII. 52.

*Behold how all things rejoice in the age to come!* Ecl. IIII. 52.

> [p. 540] 10) Contenti in tempore locoue pro tempore et loco:

[p. 540] 10) of what is contained in a time or place for the time and place:

> *Nunc etiam pecudes vmbras et frigora captant, / Nunc virides etiam occultant spineta lacertos, / Thestylis et rapido fessis messoribus aestu / Allia serpillumque herbas contundit olentes.* Ecl. II. 10.

*Now even the cattle seek the shades and the cool, / now even the thickets hide the green lizards, / and Thestylis, for the reapers wearied by the fierce heat, / pounds garlic and wild thyme, fragrant herbs.* Ecl. II. 10.

> *Te campo quaesiuimus in minore / Te in circo, te in omnibus libellis.* Cat.

*We sought you in the lesser Campus, / you in the Circus, you in all the little books.* Cat.

> (pro tabernis librariis.)

(for the bookshops.)

> § 795. 11) Dei, domini, ducis, imperantis pro re possessa vel persona, quae in eius est potestate: *Sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus.*

§ 795. 11) of the god, the master, the leader, the ruler for the thing possessed or the person who is in his power: *Without Ceres and Bacchus Venus grows cold.*

> *Jam proximus ardet / Vcalegon.* Virg.

*Now next door burns / Ucalegon.* Virg.

> *Vbi is homo est? / Jam deuorandum censes, si conspexeris? / Dum datur, dum calet, deuorari decet.* Plaut.

*Where is that man? / Do you think he should be devoured now, if you have caught sight of him? / While it is given, while it is hot, it is fitting that it be devoured.* Plaut.

> Confer, §. 141. sis, Catulli locum citatum. 12) rei, vel personae, quae alicui, tanquam possessori, vel imperanti, competunt, pro hoc homine, possessore vel imperante. §. 778.

Compare, if you please, § 141, the passage of Catullus cited. 12) of the thing, or person, which belongs to someone, as to a possessor or ruler, for this man, the possessor or ruler. § 778.

> *Cedant arma togae.* Cic.

*Let arms yield to the toga.* Cic.

> *Flerunt Rhodopeiae arces. / Altaque Pangaea, et Rhesi Mauortia tellus,* Georg. IV. 461.

*The Rhodopeian heights wept, / and lofty Pangaea, and the Mavortian land of Rhesus,* Georg. IV. 461.

> [p. 541] *Ille seu Parthos Latio imminentes / Egerit iusto domitos triumpho,* Hor. I. od. 12.

[p. 541] *He, whether the Parthians threatening Latium / he shall have driven subdued in a just triumph,* Hor. I. od. 12.

> § 796. Quam metalepsin antecedentis pro consequente dicunt, et consequentis pro antecedente, quamque suo iure ac merito comitatur metalepsis concomitantium, quando simultaneorum vnum ponitur pro altero: est ea metonymia, §. 782, 773, quoniam substituit perceptiones sibi mutuo socias, quarum vel vtraque dato tempore fuerant sensationes, vel altera imaginatio, altera sensatio, vel altera sensatio, altera praeuisio, M. §. 576. Sic antecedens ponitur pro consequente in euphemismo Catulli de pomo Atalantae,

§ 796. What they call the metalepsis of the antecedent for the consequent, and of the consequent for the antecedent, and which by its own right and desert the metalepsis of concomitants accompanies, when one of simultaneous things is put for the other: this is metonymy, § 782, 773, since it substitutes perceptions mutually associated with one another, of which either both were sensations at a given time, or the one an imagination, the other a sensation, or the one a sensation, the other a foresight, M. § 576. Thus the antecedent is put for the consequent in Catullus’s euphemism about Atalanta’s apple,

> *Quod zonam soluit diu ligatam,* 2.

*Which loosed the girdle long tied,* 2.

> et apud Virgilium, quando Silenum antiquissima cantantem narrat: Ecl. VI.

and in Virgil, when he tells of Silenus singing of the most ancient things: Ecl. VI.

> *Tum Phaetontiadas musco circumdat amarae / Corticis, atque solo proceras erigit alnos.*

*Then he surrounds the daughters of Phaethon with the moss of bitter / bark, and raises them from the ground as tall alders.*

> Consequens pro antecedente:

The consequent for the antecedent:

> *Caeduntur tumidae, medico ridente, mariscae.* Juu. II. 13.

*Swollen figs are cut away, the doctor laughing.* Juv. II. 13.

> vnum concomitantium pro altero:

one of the concomitants for the other:

> *Vos lanam trahitis, calathisque peracta refertis / Vellera, vos tenui praegnantem stamine fusum / Penelope melius, leuius torquetis Arachne.* 55

*You card the wool, and carry back in baskets the finished / fleeces, you twist the spindle pregnant with its slender thread / better than Penelope, more deftly than Arachne.* 55

> [p. 542] § 797. ANTONOMASIA, qua pro idea, conceptu singularium et indiuiduorum, et famosiori vel vsitatiori, eiusdem signo, quod in oratione solet esse nomen, nunc proprium dici solitum, substituitur conceptus alius, vel plures conceptus in periphrasin et circumscriptionem combinati, nunc cum priore reciproci, nunc latiores eodem, aut vice versa; est synecdoche, nunc adscendens speciei, vel generis pro indiuiduo, §. 789, nunc descendens, indiuidui pro specie vel genere, §. 790, 786. nunc tandem descriptio propria, quae scilicet describendo non sit latior, manifesta potius est figura, §. 550, 733. quam tropus. §. 780. *Magnanimus Anchisiades* apud Virgilium V. est antonomasia adscendens. Patronymicum enim, etiamsi vnicus sit tantum filius, aut vnica filia, tamen horum indiuiduis latius patet in regno possibilium heterocosmice, quia plures esse potuissent filii filiaeue, immo in hoc etiam mundo, quoniam non solis filiis filiabusue conuenit, sed posteris etiam

[p. 542] § 797. ANTONOMASIA, by which for the idea, the concept of singular and individual things, and for the more famous or more usual sign of the same, which in speech is wont to be a name, now usually called proper, there is substituted another concept, or several concepts combined into a periphrasis and circumscription, now reciprocal with the former, now wider than it, or vice versa; is a synecdoche, now ascending, of the species or genus for the individual, § 789, now descending, of the individual for the species or genus, § 790, 786, now, finally, a proper description, one, namely, which does not become wider by describing, is rather a manifest figure, § 550, 733, than a trope. § 780. *The great-souled son of Anchises* in Virgil V. is an ascending antonomasia. For the patronymic, even if there be only a single son or a single daughter, nevertheless extends more widely than these individuals in the realm of possibles, heterocosmically, because there could have been several sons or daughters; indeed even in this world, since it fits not only sons or daughters, but also their descendants

> *Natorum natis, et qui nascentur ab illis,*

*The children of their children, and those who shall be born from them,*

> Antonomasia descendens est apud Plautum:

A descending antonomasia is in Plautus:

> *I hac mecum, vt videas simul / Tuam Alcumenam pellicem, Juno mea.*

*Come this way with me, that you may see at the same time / your Alcumena, the concubine, my Juno.*

> *Debetur magnus patinae subitusque Prometheus,* Juu. 4.

*A great and sudden Prometheus is owed to the dish,* Juv. 4.

> [p. 543] (pro figulo.)

[p. 543] (for the potter.)

> *Nec surdum, nec Tiresiam quemquam esse deorum.* 14.

*That none of the gods is deaf, nor a Tiresias.* 14.

> § 798. Haec antonomasia descendens praecipue placuit multis venustatum amatoribus, §. 797, 755. Clodium in sorores etiam ardentem Cicero *Romanum Jouem* dicit, §. 756, 754. *Quae autem hic insidiae sunt? aut quis nobis Hannibal nauigat?* Petr.

§ 798. This descending antonomasia has especially pleased many lovers of charms, § 797, 755. Clodius, burning even for his sisters, Cicero calls *the Roman Jupiter*, § 756, 754. *But what ambushes are here? or what Hannibal sails against us?* Petr.

> *Consulit ictericae lento de funere matris, / Ante tamen de te, Tanaquil tua.* Juu. 2.

*She consults about the slow funeral of her jaundiced mother, / but first about you, your Tanaquil.* Juv. 2.

> Hac ratione totam periodi platonicae fabulam explicari debere reor, et locum Virgilii:

In this way I think the whole fable of the Platonic period ought to be explained, and the passage of Virgil:

> *Alter erit tum Tiphys, et altera, quae vehat, Argo, / Dilectos heroas, erunt etiam altera bella, / Atque iterum ad Troiam magnus mittetur Achilles.* ecl. 4.

*Then there shall be another Tiphys, and another Argo, to carry / chosen heroes; there shall be other wars too, / and again a great Achilles shall be sent to Troy.* ecl. 4.

> § 799. Antonomasian, quae figura potius, quam tropus sit, habes in circumscriptione Socratis ipsi tamen propria: §. 797.

§ 799. An antonomasia which is a figure rather than a trope you have in the circumscription of Socrates, yet proper to him alone: § 797.

> *Aethereusque Platon, et qui fabricauerat illum, / Damnatusque suas melius damnauit Athenas.* Man.

*And ethereal Plato, and he who had fashioned him, / and who, condemned, better condemned his own Athens.* Man.

> [p. 544] *barbatum hoc crede magistrum / Dicere, sorbitio tollit quem dira cicutae.* Pers.

[p. 544] *believe that this bearded master / says it, whom the dire draught of hemlock carries off.* Pers.

> Ad antonomasian adscendentem refero sermonis illam communicationem, qua pulcre cogitaturus fauorabilia, sibi soli forsan conuenientia, suis simul spectatoribus auditoribusue simul tribuit, et odiosa, his forte solis propria, sibi tamen simul adscribit, in persona, quam vocant pluralis numeri primam, ponit enim speciem praesentium pro certis indiuiduis.

To ascending antonomasia I refer that communication of speech by which one who is to think beautifully attributes favourable things, perhaps fitting himself alone, at the same time to his spectators or hearers, and odious things, perhaps proper to these alone, he nevertheless ascribes to himself at the same time, in the person which they call the first of the plural number; for he puts the species of those present for certain individuals.

> § 800. Εὐφημισμοί, quaeque κατὰ λιτότητα belle cogitantur cum aliqua extenuatione, §. 329. non tam tropi sunt peculiares, quam casus aliqui, quorum obuentu moratum cogitandi genus, §. 227. ad aliquam potius figurarum e. g. periphrasin, vel tropum ex allatis quemcunque suaserit confugere, quam rem nude et explicite, qualis cogitanti primum in mentem forte venerit, minus eleganter vel concipere, vel efferre, §. 789, 796. Sic extenuat synecdoche partis pro toto, nisi loqui velis de rebus ad te pertinentibus, instar gloriosi militis, extenuat laudabilis illius, quod tibi tuisue velles adscribere, negare potius oppositum, quam illud ipsum affirmare.

§ 800. Εὐφημισμοί [euphemisms], and whatever things are thought prettily κατὰ λιτότητα [by litotes] with some extenuation, § 329, are not so much peculiar tropes as certain cases, at whose occurrence the moral manner of thinking, § 227, will have advised one to take refuge rather in some one of the figures, e.g. periphrasis, or in any trope whatever of those adduced, than to conceive or express less elegantly the thing nakedly and explicitly, such as it may first have come into the thinker’s mind, § 789, 796. Thus the synecdoche of the part for the whole extenuates, unless you wish to speak of things pertaining to yourself, after the fashion of the braggart soldier; it extenuates something praiseworthy, which you would wish to ascribe to yourself or your own, to deny the opposite rather than to affirm that very thing.

> *Nec sum adeo informis, nuper me in littore vidi.*

*Nor am I so ill-formed; lately I saw myself on the shore.*

> *Si quid mihi humanitus acciderit,* est synecdoche [p. 545] adscendens §. 789. *vixisse* est metalepsis antecedentis pro consequente, §. 796. vti et illa loquendi formula, quae viuere iubentur et valere, quae missa facimus, quibus nuncium mittimus, in posterum aspernaturi.

*If anything should befall me after the manner of men,* is an ascending synecdoche [p. 545] § 789. *to have lived* is a metalepsis of the antecedent for the consequent, § 796, as is also that formula of speaking by which the things we dismiss, to which we send notice, about to spurn them henceforth, are bidden to live and fare well.

> *Omnia vel medium fiant mare. Viuite, siluae!*

*Let all things become even the midst of the sea. Live, you woods!*

> § 801. Tropus, vti humana omnia, gradus etiam admittit, et maius ac minus, dum potest crescere 1) extensiue, continuando tropum dati generis per plures cogitationes explicite pingendas aut significandas, et haec cuiuscunque tropi continuatio dabit ALLEGORIAN, 2) intensiue, quando non vnicum solum et immediatum subiectum comparationis omittitur et occultatur, substituto per tropum termino comparationis, sed ille ponitur comparationis terminus, ex quo debeas, exponendo tropum, eruere primo certum aliquod subiectum comparationis, quod dein, quam primum erutum ac inuentum est, subito transit in nouum et tacitum etiam terminum relationis, nunc demum expositione repetita pandentem subiectum illud comparationis, quod primario nunc cogitandum, et extra tropum explicite ponendum proprieque significandum fuisset. Haec troporum intensio, tropus, vt ita dicam, interne duplicatus, vel omnino multiplicatus, METALEPSIS est, si metalepsin, [p. 546] de qua §. 796, metonymian potius, vti est, denominemus.

§ 801. A trope, like all things human, admits also of degrees, and of more and less, since it can grow 1) extensively, by continuing a trope of a given kind through several thoughts to be explicitly depicted or signified, and this continuation of any trope whatever will yield ALLEGORY, 2) intensively, when not only the single and immediate subject of comparison is omitted and hidden, the term of comparison being substituted through the trope, but that term of comparison is put from which you must, in expounding the trope, first draw out some definite subject of comparison, which then, as soon as it has been drawn out and found, suddenly passes over into a new and likewise tacit term of relation, which only now, by a repeated exposition, discloses that subject of comparison which was primarily to be thought now, and which outside the trope would have had to be explicitly set down and properly signified. This intensification of tropes, a trope, so to speak, internally doubled, or even multiplied, is METALEPSIS, if we name the metalepsis [p. 546] of which § 796 treats rather a metonymy, as it is.

> § 802. Allegorian latius non omni solum troporum generi tribuimus, ironiae etiam, §. 801. vniformiter decurrenti, qualis esset congeries metaphorarum, quarum et inter terminos comparationis est nexus quidam arctior analogo rationis obseruandus, congeries metonymiarum eiusmodi, e. c. sed etiam crama quoddam et miscelam troporum diuersi generis serie continua sese excipientium, ita, vt allegorumena sint, quibuscunque subest sensus mysticus. Jam clarum est, quanta hic pateat ianua in caliginem aestheticam, quanta sit opus cura, ne longius petitum videatur obscuritatis potius, quam illustrationis, argumentum, §. 634, 741. Hinc vmbram qui malunt, quam noctem, ALLEGORIIS PVRIS, quarum subiecta comparationis omittuntur omnia, saepe praeferunt MIXTAS, quibus saltim aliquando, clauium instar, subiecta comparationis, explicite etiam cogitata, interseruntur. §. 736.

§ 802. Allegory in the wider sense we attribute not only to every kind of trope, to irony too, § 801, running uniformly on, such as would be a heap of metaphors between whose terms of comparison there is also a certain closer nexus to be observed by the analogue of reason, a heap of metonymies of this kind, etc., but also to a certain blend and mixture of tropes of different kinds succeeding one another in a continuous series, so that allegorical utterances are whatever has a mystical sense underlying it. Now it is clear how great a door stands open here into aesthetic darkness, how great a care is needed, lest the argument seem far-fetched, an argument of obscurity rather than of illustration, § 634, 741. Hence those who prefer shade to night often prefer to PURE ALLEGORIES, in which all the subjects of comparison are omitted, MIXED ones, in which at least now and then the subjects of comparison, explicitly thought as well, are inserted like keys. § 736.

> § 803. Allegoria pura Ciceronis est, pro Quinctio: *Ita fit, vt ego, qui tela depellere, et vulneribus mederi debeam, tum id facere cogar, quum etiam telum aduersarius nullum iecerit: [p. 547] illis autem id tempus impugnandi detur, quum et vitandi istorum impetus potestas ademta nobis erit, et, si qua in re, quod parati sunt facere, venenatum aliquod telum iecerint, medicinae faciendae locus non erit.* Mistam habet pro Milone: *Equidem caeteras tempestates et procellas in illis duntaxat fluctibus concionum semper putaui Miloni esse subeundas.* Huc fabulae, §. 526. apologi, §. 537. et AENIGMATA, complexus praedicatorum non bene conuenientium, et vix in vna sede, vno subiecto, morantium, quorum subiectum, clauis, vel reticetur, vel occulitur. Justus lucis et vmbrae dispensator Virgilius, imitatus oracula, §. 671, non abhorruit ab allegoria descendentis antonomasiae, §. 798, 801:

§ 803. A pure allegory of Cicero’s is, for Quinctius: *So it comes about that I, who ought to ward off the weapons and heal the wounds, am compelled to do this at a time when the adversary has not yet thrown any weapon: [p. 547] but to them that time for attacking is granted when the power of avoiding their assault will have been taken from us, and when, if in any matter, as they are prepared to do, they have hurled some poisoned weapon, there will be no room for applying a remedy.* A mixed one he has for Milo: *For my part I always thought that the other storms and tempests, in those billows of the assemblies at least, were to be undergone by Milo.* Hither belong fables, § 526, apologues, § 537, and RIDDLES, a complex of predicates not well agreeing, and scarcely dwelling in one seat, one subject, whose subject, the key, is either passed over in silence or hidden. Virgil, a just dispenser of light and shade, imitating oracles, § 671, did not shrink from the allegory of a descending antonomasia, § 798, 801:

> *Non Simois tibi, nec Xanthus, nec Dorica castra / Defuerint. Alius Latio iam partus Achilles / Natus et ipse dea.*

*Neither a Simois, nor a Xanthus, nor a Doric camp / shall be wanting to you. Already another Achilles has been brought forth in Latium, / himself too born of a goddess.*

> § 804. Quem protendit tropum allegoria, nisi serio caueas, in turpem obscuritatem, intendit metalepsis, §. 801. Sed videamus bonas. In primo §. 789. exemplo habes synecdochen duplicatam 1) adscendentem totius pro parte, vlmorum pro virgis, et 2) descendentem inferioris pro superiori vlmearum virgarum pro quibusuis ligneis. In *passere Catulli* est, §. 790. 1) metonymia signati [p. 548] pro signo, vel contenti pro continente, et deinde 2) synecdoche partis pro toto. In illo: *Integritas tua te purgauit,* §. 791. est metaphora et ironia complicatae. In primo §. 794. exemplo est metalepsis primo metonymiam continentis pro contento, et dein synecdochen totius pro parte sistens, nisi omnes earum vrbium ciues fabros ferrarios, instar Cyclopum, iudicaueris. Quando pro: nunc meridies est, dicitur: *Nunc pecudes frigora captant,* habes metalepsin metonymiae, qua 1) contentum, phaenomenon rusticum, pro continente tempore et 2) contentum frigus pro continente aura ventoue dicitur, nisi malis vltimum tropum synecdochen partis pro toto, dicere, quo pertinet tropus abstracti pro concreto. §. 794. *Joue frigido.*

§ 804. The trope which allegory stretches out, unless you seriously take care, into ugly obscurity, metalepsis intensifies, § 801. But let us look at good ones. In the first example of § 789 you have a doubled synecdoche 1) ascending, of the whole for the part, of elms for rods, and 2) descending, of the inferior for the superior, of elm rods for any wooden ones whatever. In the *sparrow of Catullus* there is, § 790. 1) a metonymy of the thing signified [p. 548] for the sign, or of the content for the container, and then 2) a synecdoche of the part for the whole. In that: *Your integrity has cleared you,* § 791, metaphor and irony are intertwined. In the first example of § 794 there is a metalepsis presenting first a metonymy of the container for the content, and then a synecdoche of the whole for the part, unless you judge all the citizens of those cities to be blacksmiths, like Cyclopes. When for: it is now midday, one says: *Now the cattle seek the cool,* you have a metalepsis of metonymy, by which 1) the content, a rustic phenomenon, is said for the containing time and 2) the contained cool for the containing air or wind, unless you prefer to call the last trope a synecdoche of the part for the whole, to which the trope of the abstract for the concrete belongs. § 794. *With Jupiter cold.*

> § 805. Durat adhuc allegoria, §. 801. metonymiae contentorum phaenomenorum rusticorum pro continente tempore, §. 794. et tamen accedit per metalepsin antonomasia descendens, quando *Thestylis* pro quauis muliere rustica ponitur, §. 798. Quum *homo, dum calet, deuorandus* censetur, §. 795. metonymiae possessoris pro re, quam habet, per metalepsin additur altera, qua phaenomena corporis in anima simultaneis solent substitui, Jupiter §. 141. pro vento est metalepsis ex metonymia dei pro re, cui praeest, et [p. 549] ex synecdoche generis superioris pro inferiori, concrescens. Praesit enim aeri iam Jupiter, non Juno, non tamen aerem generatim, sed aerem vehementius commotum indicare poeta voluit. Pari ratione *pes* in hoc Catulli loco dictus est per metalepsin metaphoram et synecdochen partis pro toto comprehendentem.

§ 805. The allegory still lasts, § 801, of the metonymy of the contained rustic phenomena for the containing time, § 794, and yet there is added through metalepsis a descending antonomasia, when *Thestylis* is put for any country woman whatever, § 798. When *the man, while he is hot,* is judged *fit to be devoured,* § 795, to the metonymy of the possessor for the thing he has there is added through metalepsis another, by which the phenomena of the body are wont to be substituted for the simultaneous ones in the soul; Jupiter § 141, for the wind is a metalepsis growing together out of a metonymy of the god for the thing over which he presides, and [p. 549] out of a synecdoche of the superior genus for the inferior. For granted that Jupiter, not Juno, now presides over the air, yet the poet wished to indicate not air in general, but air more violently stirred. In the same way *foot* in this passage of Catullus is said through a metalepsis comprising a metaphor and a synecdoche of the part for the whole.

> § 806. Ad metalepsin referri poterunt pleraeque syllepses, vti vocant casus, in quibus vnum signum duos significatus, vtrumque primarium, sustinere videatur. §. 801.

§ 806. To metalepsis may be referred most syllepses, as they call the cases in which one sign seems to sustain two significations, each of them primary. § 801.

> *Nerine Galatea, thymo mihi dulcior Hyblae.* ecl. 7.

*Nereid Galatea, sweeter to me than the thyme of Hybla.* ecl. 7.

> Hic in: *dulcior* syllepsin deprehendunt, quae concrescens ex metaphora et synecdoche speciei pro genere metalepsis est. Si tropum durum et longius petitum CATACHRESIN et abusionem dicamus, fallor, an eius, quid tropus sit, non satis meminimus? §. 780. Est dura, est longius petita perceptionis pro perceptione, signi improprii pro proprio, vocabuli translati in locum proprii substitutio, sed eo ipso, quia dura, quia longius est petita, quamquam excusari non nunquam ipsa necessitate potest, tamen tropus nunquam est, saepe tropis opposita cogitationum deformatio. De tropis etiam valent obseruata de figuris, §. 339. quoniam sunt figurae crypticae, §. 783.

Here in: *sweeter* they detect a syllepsis, which, growing together out of metaphor and synecdoche of the species for the genus, is a metalepsis. If we call a harsh and far-fetched trope CATACHRESIS and abuse, am I mistaken, or have we not sufficiently remembered what a trope is? § 780. It is a harsh, it is a far-fetched substitution of perception for perception, of an improper sign for a proper one, of a transferred word in the place of the proper one; but for that very reason, because it is harsh, because it is far-fetched, although it can sometimes be excused by necessity itself, nevertheless it is never a trope, but often a deformation of thoughts opposed to tropes. Of tropes too hold the observations made about figures, § 339, since they are cryptic figures, § 783.

> [p. 550] § 807. Potest etiam hyperbole, si lateat in substitutione perceptionis minoris pro maiore, vel maioris pro minore, tropus esse, §. 339, 780. Neque tamen omnis hyperbole tropus est, neque peculiare troporum genus constituit, ad synecdochen, comparationem maioris et minoris, totius et partis, crypticam, §. 742, 782. referenda. Multo minus omnem emphasin possum tropum dicere, M. §. 517. minime peculiarem troporum classem fingere. Sane tropus omnis, sed etiam omnis figura, bene locata, pulcre significata, suam habet comitem emphasin §. 26, 783.

[p. 550] § 807. Hyperbole too, if it lies hidden in the substitution of a lesser perception for a greater, or of a greater for a lesser, can be a trope, § 339, 780. Yet neither is every hyperbole a trope, nor does it constitute a peculiar kind of tropes, being to be referred to synecdoche, the cryptic comparison of greater and lesser, of whole and part, § 742, 782. Much less can I call every emphasis a trope, M. § 517, least of all invent a peculiar class of tropes. Indeed every trope, but also every figure, well placed, beautifully signified, has emphasis as its companion § 26, 783.

#### Sectio XXXXVIII. Thaumaturgia Aesthetica. — Section XXXXVIII. Aesthetic Wonder-Working

> § 808. Lux nouitatis perceptiones illustrat egregie, M. § 549, 550. Nouitatis intuitus, ADMIRATIO curiositatem excitat, M. §. 688. curiositas attentionem, M. §. 625, 529. attentio ad rem viuide sibi pingendam nouam lucem affert. M. §. 628, 531. Pulcre hinc cogitanda, quando illustranda sunt, §. 730. bene sistuntur admirationem nouitate, clarius cognoscendi studium admiratione, [p. 551] tandem attentionem studio clarius rem cognoscendi conciliantia. Conciliatio nouitatis, per hanc admirationis, per hanc curiositatis, per hanc attentionis AESTHETICA, breuitatis caussa, dicatur a nobis THAVMATVRGIA.

§ 808. The light of novelty illustrates perceptions excellently, M. § 549, 550. The intuition of novelty, WONDER, excites curiosity, M. § 688, curiosity attention, M. § 625, 529, attention brings new light to the thing to be vividly depicted to oneself. M. § 628, 531. Hence things to be thought beautifully, when they are to be illustrated, § 730, are well presented when they win wonder by novelty, the desire of knowing more clearly by wonder, [p. 551] and finally attention by the desire of knowing the thing more clearly. The AESTHETIC winning of novelty, through this of wonder, through this of curiosity, through this of attention, let it, for brevity’s sake, be called by us WONDER-WORKING.

> § 809. Crassus apud Ciceronem de or. l. 137, quando statim a limine suae dissertationis excusatione dignum iudicat, se noua non dicturum, hoc ipso tacite concedit, quam scripsimus, regulam, §. 808. *Quum audieris,* inquiens, *non tam arbitror te haec admiraturum, quam existimaturum tum, cum ea audire cupiebas, caussam, cur cuperes, non fuisse. Nihil enim dicam reconditum, nihil exspectatione vestra dignum, nihil aut inauditum vobis, aut cuiquam nouum.* Pastores ipsi laudauere, quando

§ 809. Crassus in Cicero de or. l. 137, when right at the threshold of his discourse he judges it worthy of an excuse that he will say nothing new, tacitly concedes by that very fact the rule which we have written, § 808. *When you have heard,* he says, *I think you will not so much wonder at these things as judge that, when you desired to hear them, there was no reason why you should desire it. For I shall say nothing recondite, nothing worthy of your expectation, nothing either unheard of by you or new to anyone.* The shepherds themselves gave praise, when

> *Pollio et ipse facit noua carmina.* Ecl. 3. 86.

*Pollio too himself makes new songs.* Ecl. 3. 86.

> *Nouitates si spem afferunt, vt tanquam in herbis non fallacibus fructus appareat,* §. 731. *non sunt illae repudiandae.* Cic. de am. 70. Quid aliud Quintilianus, quando dissuadet non multum ab initio orationis *omnem in reliquum nouitatis gratiam praecerpere?* IV. 5. Assentitur Horatius l. c. §. 294. Nouas res boni ciues, nouos homines contemnant, qui *nil, nisi Cecropidae:* nos recte nouam pulcre cogitandi [p. 552] materiem, et gratam in ipsis cogitationum elegantiis nouitatem amabimus, §. 808.

*If novelties bring hope, so that, as in herbs that do not deceive, fruit appears,* § 731. *they are not to be rejected.* Cic. de am. 70. What else does Quintilian do, when he dissuades from *plucking beforehand, not far from the beginning of a speech, all the grace of novelty for the remainder?* IV. 5. Horace agrees l. c. § 294. Let good citizens despise new things, new men, those who are *nothing, unless sons of Cecrops:* we shall rightly love new matter for thinking beautifully [p. 552] and a pleasing novelty in the very elegances of thoughts, § 808.

> § 810. *Qui libenter audiunt, et magis attendunt, et facilius credunt, plerumque ipsa delectatione capiuntur, nonnunquam admiratione auferuntur. — — — — Recte Cicero his ipsis ad Brutum verbis quadam in epistola scribit: Nam eloquentiam, quae admirationem non habet, nullam iudico. Aristoteles quoque eandem petendam maxime putat.* Quint. VIII. 3. Sed quae potest esse, nisi nouitatis, admiratio? §. 808. Obiecerit forsan aliquis: *esse praestantem illam et diuinam sapientiam: nil admirari.* Cic. Tusc. III. 30.

§ 810. *Those who hear gladly, and attend more, and believe more easily, are for the most part captivated by the delight itself, sometimes carried away by wonder. — — — — Rightly does Cicero write in these very words to Brutus in a certain letter: For I judge the eloquence which has no wonder to be no eloquence at all. Aristotle too thinks that it is this above all which is to be sought.* Quintilian VIII. 3. But what wonder can there be, except that of novelty? § 808. Someone will perhaps object: *that that excellent and divine wisdom is: to wonder at nothing.* Cic. Tusc. III. 30.

> *Nil admirari, prope res est vna, Numici, / Solaque quae possit facere ac seruare beatum.* Hor. l. ep. 6.

*To wonder at nothing is almost the one thing, Numicius, / and the only one that can make and keep a man happy.* Hor. l. ep. 6.

> Vnde colligas admirationis studium ad fucos potius, §. 688. et mendacia vere non splendida, §. 625. relegandum esse, quam naturali accensendum ornatui. §. 622, 623.

Whence you might gather that the pursuit of wonder is to be banished rather to cosmetics, § 688, and to lies truly not splendid, § 625, than to be reckoned among natural ornament. § 622, 623.

> § 811. Verum salua res est. Qui fuit veterum siue mos, siue morbus, etiam tunc, quum distinctissime rationem instruere docendo debuissent philosophi, captare tropis paradoxa, [p. 553] et apophthegmatibus in ipsa saepius aenigmata, praecipitare liberum spiritum, §. 803. aut hic etiam iubentes *nil admirari* per hyperbolen volunt a vehementiori tantum quotidianarum curarum, ignoranti ac stupida, admiratione reuocare, aut metonymia consequentis pro antecedente, §. 796. rerum humanarum obliti, caecitatisque mortalibus ineuitabilis diuinam sapientiam ab omni ignorantia, matre admirationis, cecinerunt immunem; aut tandem fallacem potius, et fucatam, quam veram et homini naturalem professi sunt sapientiam, cui summi numinis in admiratione sapientissima transigetur, si sapit, aeternitas.

§ 811. But the case is safe. Those for whom it was, whether the custom or the disease of the ancients, even then, when as philosophers they ought by teaching to have instructed reason most distinctly, to hunt after paradoxes with tropes, [p. 553] and with apophthegms often to plunge the free spirit into riddles themselves, § 803, either here too, bidding us *to wonder at nothing,* wish through hyperbole only to call us back from the too vehement, ignorant and stupid wonder of everyday cares, or by a metonymy of the consequent for the antecedent, § 796, forgetful of human affairs and of the blindness unavoidable for mortals, have sung divine wisdom as immune from all ignorance, the mother of wonder; or, finally, have professed a wisdom fallacious rather and painted, than true and natural to man, for whom, if he is wise, eternity will be passed in the most wise wonder at the supreme deity.

> § 812. Licet itaque non fucatae, sed Gratiis litanti, sapientiae, neque *rudes* tantum *et agrestes,* sed hominum, *animos admiratione mulcere,* §. 808. Ne tamen nouitatis studio nimium abripiamur, hae cautelae sunto. 1) Nouitatem obiecti et materiae cum nouitate rerum et cogitationum ne temere confundas, §. 18. Haec in primis quaeritur, non illa, §. 808. De nouis noua meditari non nego facilius, neque gratiam nouitati materiarum denego, nec lucem. Interim de antiquissimis non solum, sed etiam de dudum cognitis, animo tamen voluere potest

§ 812. It is therefore permitted to a wisdom not painted, but sacrificing to the Graces, *to soothe with wonder the minds* not only of *the rude and rustic,* but of men, § 808. Yet lest we be carried away too much by the pursuit of novelty, let these be the cautions. 1) Do not rashly confuse the novelty of the object and matter with the novelty of the things and thoughts, § 18. The latter is sought in the first place, not the former, § 808. I do not deny that it is easier to meditate new things about new things, nor do I deny grace to the novelty of matters, nor light. Meanwhile, not only on the most ancient things, but also on things long known, he can nevertheless turn over in his mind

> *carmina non prius / [p. 554] Audita Musarum sacerdos*

*songs not before / [p. 554] heard, a priest of the Muses*

> *non vsitata nec tenui latus penna per aetherem,* potest de recentissimis negotiis, dum calent, *indoctus in triuiis*

*borne through the ether on no common or slender wing,* he can, about the most recent affairs, while they are hot, *unlearned at the crossroads*

> *Stridenti miserum stipula disperdere carmen.*

*spoil a wretched song on a screeching straw.*

> § 813. 2) Neque materias, neque cogitationes captare velis absolute nouas, nondum vnquam cogitata, quibus non abripiaris solum a strictissime veris, §. 441. sed etiam fictionibus poeticis prorsus ignotis, §. 518. certissime tandem deseraris in turpem vtopiam, §. 514, 469. verisimilitudine destitutam omni, §. 483. meram caliginem, §. 638. M. 889. Memento Phaetontis, quem absolutae nouitatis et admirationis studiosum, licet relatiua iam

§ 813. 2) Nor should you wish to hunt after matters, or thoughts, absolutely new, never yet thought, by which you would not only be carried away from the most strictly true, § 441, but also, by poetic fictions wholly unknown, § 518, would at last most certainly be stranded in an ugly utopia, § 514, 469, destitute of all verisimilitude, § 483, sheer darkness, § 638. M. 889. Remember Phaethon, whom, eager for absolute novelty and wonder, though already relatively

> *rerum nouitate pauentem,*

*fearful at the novelty of things,*

> pater admonet, venustorum ingeniorum communis pater, §. 82:

his father admonishes, the common father of charming wits, § 82:

> *Sors tua mortalis, non est mortale, quod optas. / Plus etiam, quam quod superis contingere fas sit, / Nescius affectas. / Nate, caue, dum resque sinit, tua corrige vota,* §. 812. / — — — — / *Denique quicquid habet diues circumspice mundus,* §. 513. / [p. 555] *Eque tot ac tantis caeli, terraeque, marisque,* §. 509. / *Posce bonis aliquid. Nullam patiere repulsam. / Deprecor hoc vnum, quod vero nomine poena, / Non honor est.* §. 810. *Poenam, Phaeton, pro munere poscis,* §. 808.

*Your lot is mortal; what you ask is not mortal. / Even more than what it is right should fall to the gods above, / unknowing, you aspire to. / Son, take care, while the matter still allows, correct your wishes,* § 812. / — — — — / *Finally, look around at whatever the rich world holds,* § 513. / [p. 555] *and from so many and so great goods of sky, and earth, and sea,* § 509. / *ask for something. You will suffer no refusal. / This one thing I deprecate, which by its true name is a penalty, / not an honour.* § 810. *A penalty, Phaethon, you ask for instead of a gift,* § 808.

> § 814. 3) In relatiue nouis primario tuo obiecto personali, quae tibi nouitas sufficiat, §. 813. ne satis tibi denuo sit, partim materiam eligendam, partim significanda de eadem fuisse huc vsque, partialiter saltim, incognita, maxima sit in hoc cura, num ea sint hactenus incognita, quae a te nota reddita nunc demum lucem et gratiam nouitatis per te sint acceptura, et admirationem motura, quando vix antea subobscure percepta nunc intueamur. §. 808. Inuentor non est incognitorum venditor, sed olim incognita nota reddens. Neque venustum cognoscendi studium mouebit, multo minus explebit, aut admirationem merebitur vltra plebem sapientium, multus in incognitis, quorum ipse suam tantum prodit ignorantiam, nouam ipsis potius inducens caliginem, quam vt ea nouam in lucem nouerit protrahere, §. 627. Vix quisquam incognita crepando, quae nesciat tandem illustrare, spectatorem, vt

§ 814. 3) In things relatively new for your primary personal object, where that novelty suffices you, § 813, let it not again be enough for you that the material to be chosen in part, and in part the things to be signified concerning it, have hitherto been, at least partially, unknown; let your greatest care here be whether those things are hitherto unknown which, made known by you, will now at last receive through you the light and grace of novelty and will stir wonder, when we now intuit what before was scarcely and dimly perceived, § 808. The discoverer is not a vendor of unknown things, but one who makes known what was formerly unknown. Nor will the man who is much occupied with unknown things, of which he merely betrays his own ignorance, inducing a fresh darkness upon them rather than knowing how to draw them forth into new light, § 627, move the charming desire to know, much less satisfy it, or earn wonder beyond the common herd of the wise. Scarcely anyone, by rattling off unknown things which in the end he does not know how to illuminate, will delude the spectator, like

> *coruum, deludet, hiantem,*

*the gaping crow,*

> [p. 556] impune, quin occinatur miserabili thaumaturgo:

[p. 556] with impunity, without its being sung back at the wretched wonder-worker:

> *Num furis, an prudens ludis me obscura canendo?* Hor. II. S. 5, 58.

*Are you raving, or do you knowingly mock me by singing darkly?* Hor. II. S. 5, 58.

> § 815. 4) Ne relatiue nouorum ea tibi legas cogitanda, quae cognitu vel indigna vere sunt, vel saltim primariis tuis spectatoribus videantur attentionem suam adeo non mereri, prudens vt praeuidere possis dotium tuarum aestumator opis tuae non fore, curiositatem tuorum in haec dirigere. §. 808. Sint spectatores tibi, qui videantur etiam primarii, male feriati minutiarum amatores, quorum aures vili venustae cogitationis lenocinio lubentissime titillarentur, quales §. 184. tanguntur, primaria tamen lex dignitatis aesthetica, quam absoluta iam poscit et inuoluit magnitudo, §. 185, 178. turpiter cederet inferiori curiositatem obseruandi regulae, §. 808, quae subordinatur demum legi lucis aestheticae. §. 614. nec id quidem necessario, §. 617, 625. Maius erit, et, quo rarius, hoc eo ipso recentius, curiosius, admirabilius et attentione dignum, si possis spectatorem alia omnia, et leuissima quaeuis exspectantem initiare maioribus deuiamque mentem sensim in grauiorum nobiliorumque contemplationem allicere, ducere, defigere. Tentat artificium Horatius I. od. 27.

§ 815. 4) Among things relatively new, do not choose to think those which either are truly unworthy of being known, or at least seem to your primary spectators so far from meriting their attention that you, a prudent appraiser of your own gifts, can foresee that it will not be within your power to direct the curiosity of your people towards them, § 808. Should you have spectators, who seem even primary ones, idle lovers of trifles whose ears would be most gladly tickled by the cheap allurement of charming thought, such as are touched upon in § 184, the primary aesthetic law of dignity, which absolute magnitude already demands and involves, § 185, 178, would nevertheless yield shamefully to the inferior rule of observing curiosity, § 808, which is in the end subordinated to the law of aesthetic light, § 614, and not even that necessarily, § 617, 625. It will be greater, and, the rarer it is, by that very fact the more recent, the more curious, the more admirable and worthy of attention, if you can initiate into greater things the spectator who expects anything else and any trifles whatever, and gradually entice, lead and fix his wandering mind in the contemplation of graver and nobler things. Horace attempts the artifice in I. od. 27.

> [p. 557] *Natis in vsum laetitiae scyphis / Pugnare Thracum est. Tollite barbarum / Morem* — — — — / *ah! miser, / Quanta laboras in Charybdi, / Digne puer meliore flamma!*

[p. 557] *To fight with cups made for the use of gladness / is a Thracian thing. Away with the barbarous / custom* — — — — / *ah! wretch, / in what a Charybdis you labour, / youth worthy of a better flame!*

> § 816. In absolute dignis, etiamsi spectatores habeas in primariis etiam, qui satis amarent, vel in grauiorum tractatione relatiuae te dignitatis minus anxium obseruatorem, vel iisdem omnino praeferri leuicula, comparatiue saltim, §. 197-201: ne nimium des placentiae, quoniam relatiua demum, non absoluta catholica, *dignitas* est *admirabilis* illa §. 187, quam sectari iubent, §. 808-810. An in solis piorum sedibus contingeret, quod narrat Horatius II. od. 13?

§ 816. In things absolutely worthy, even if you have, among your primary spectators too, some who would rather like you, in the treatment of graver matters, to be a less anxious observer of relative dignity, or even that trifles be preferred outright to them, at least comparatively, § 197–201: do not grant too much to the desire to please, since it is only relative, not absolute and universal, *dignity* that is the *admirable* one of § 187, which § 808–810 bid us pursue. Would it happen only in the seats of the pious, what Horace relates in II. od. 13?

> *Aeoliis fidibus querentem / Sappho puellis de popularibus, / Et te sonantem plenius aureo, / Alcaee, plectro dura nauis, / Dura fugae mala, dura belli, / Vtrumque sacro digna silentio / Mirantur vmbrae dicere. Sed magis / Pugnas et exactos tyrannos / Densum humeris bibit aure vulgus.*

*Sappho, complaining on Aeolian strings / of the girls of her own people, / and you, Alcaeus, sounding more fully with golden / plectrum the hardships of the ship, / the cruel ills of flight, the ills of war, / the shades marvel at both as they say things worthy / of sacred silence. But the crowd, / packed shoulder to shoulder, drinks in with its ear rather / battles and tyrants driven out.*

> § 817. [p. 558] Verum a) possunt quaedam, attentione mortalium dignissima, tamen aliquibus, qui forte tui sint spectatores primarii, certis in locis, temporibus, et occasionibus, minus opportuna, minus tempestiua vere esse, quibus nunc aduertant animum, pro grauitate rei, b) possunt aliis, quorum caussa potissimum cogitas talia videri, per errorem, largior, sed per errorem tamen, datis tuis viribus, dato tempore, non vincibilem. In vtroque casu proferres tuis inaudita forsitan, immerito forsan incognita, neque tamen admirationem moueres, sed taedium. Noua dare cogitares, sed gratia nouitatis excideres, §. 815. Quo grauiora sunt, quae cogitare parabas, hoc maiori opus erit solicitudine, ne iis ea, qui fruge inuenta, quicquid egeris, glandibus vesci malunt, contemtim proculcanda temere proiicias.

§ 817. [p. 558] But a) some things, most worthy of the attention of mortals, can nevertheless truly be, for certain people who may happen to be your primary spectators, in certain places, times and occasions, less opportune, less timely, for them to turn their mind to now, in proportion to the gravity of the matter; b) they can seem such to others, for whose sake above all you think, through an error, I grant, but an error nonetheless not to be overcome, given your powers and given the time. In either case you would offer your people things perhaps unheard of, perhaps undeservedly unknown, and yet you would move not wonder but tedium. You would intend to give new things, but you would fall short of the grace of novelty, § 815. The graver the things you were preparing to think, the greater the care that will be needed lest you rashly cast them, to be trampled underfoot with contempt, before those who, when grain has been found, prefer, whatever you do, to feed on acorns.

> § 818. 5) Ne eo in gradu inaudita quaeras, vt non sapientum solum fidem transcendant, §. 424, non solum logica, et aesthetica, quam requirunt, §. 431-439, nunc generali, §. 440, nunc strictissima, nunc heterocosmica, §. 441. verisimilitudine destituta tuis obiectis personalibus praecipuis videri debeant, §. 483, sed etiam dynamometria praeuidere possis aesthetica, [p. 559] §. 60. non fore tuarum virium, dato tempore, datis capitibus, seu spectatoribus, ea reddere vel aesthetice, quantum necesse sit, verisimilia, §. 555. Alias, noua quidem profari videberis, sed nuces cassas, vitra fracta, somniorum interpretamenta, portenta Thessala, fabulas aniles, absurda, recens aliquis nugiuendulus, neque curiositatem tuis concilians, nec admirationem, nisi quam irrisio comitem habet, et quae nunc sane non quaerebatur, §. 808-810. Pone spectatores tuos praecipuos, qualis erat Iuuenalis, pone tibi neque vires, neque tempus esse legis hebraeae maximam illis ob oculos ponendi verisimilitudinem, ne quid nunc certius dicam: pone te tamen iisdem exponere,

§ 818. 5) Do not seek things unheard of to such a degree that they not only transcend the belief of the wise, § 424, and not only must seem to your chief personal objects to be destitute of the verisimilitude, both logical and aesthetic, which they require, § 431–439, now general, § 440, now the strictest, now heterocosmic, § 441, § 483, but also that you can foresee by aesthetic dynamometry, [p. 559] § 60, that it will not be within your powers, given the time, given the heads, that is, the spectators, to render them even aesthetically verisimilar, so far as is necessary, § 555. Otherwise you will seem indeed to utter new things, but empty nuts, broken glass, interpretations of dreams, Thessalian portents, old wives' tales, absurdities, some new-fangled pedlar of trifles, winning for your people neither curiosity nor wonder, except that which has derision for its companion, and which surely was not what was sought now, § 808–810. Suppose your chief spectators to be such as Juvenal was; suppose that you have neither the power nor the time to set before their eyes the fullest verisimilitude of the Hebrew law, to say nothing now more certain: suppose nevertheless that you expound to them

> *Tradidit arcano quodcunque volumine Moses.* XIV. 102.

*whatever Moses handed down in his secret volume.* XIV. 102.

> loqueris illis noua, inaudita multa romanis legibus, sed *metuentem sabbata, nil praeter nubes et caeli numen adorantem, cui suilla ac humana caro nil distet, cui septima quaeque lux ignaua sit, praeputia ponentem,* ea, quam optaras, nec curiositate prosequentur, nec admiratione.

You speak to them new things, many unheard of in Roman laws; but the man *who fears the sabbaths, who worships nothing but the clouds and the divinity of the sky, for whom the flesh of swine and the flesh of men differ not at all, for whom every seventh day is idle, who lays aside the foreskin* — these things they will pursue with neither the curiosity nor the wonder you had hoped for.

> § 819. 6) Ne facile cogitanda venustius speres spectatorum gratia, quibus tractandorum et totum et partes, immo vero partium etiam partes [p. 560] forsitan, ita noua sint, vt non nisi longe petitis aliquantulum illustranda possis praeuidere, §. 741. Saltim enim dura videbitur spectatoribus tractatio, §. 787. nisi omnino non satis protensionis et simul intensionis in attendendo secum ferentes de te capiendo desperent, et sic omnis simul et curiositas concidat, et admiratio lucem et gratiam pulcris meditationibus circumfundens, §. 808. Belle cogitans nec omnem paraenesin a Paradiso,

§ 819. 6) Do not readily hope to think things more charmingly for the sake of spectators for whom both the whole and the parts of the things to be treated, nay even the parts of the parts [p. 560] perhaps, are so new that you can foresee they can be illuminated only a little, and only by far-fetched means, § 741. For at least the treatment will seem hard to the spectators, § 787, if they do not altogether despair of grasping you, not bringing with them enough extension and at the same time intension in attending, so that all curiosity collapses at once, and with it the wonder that pours light and grace around beautiful meditations, § 808. He who thinks finely neither begins every exhortation from Paradise,

> *Nec gemino bellum Troianum orditur ab ouo,*

*Nor the Trojan war from the twin egg,*

> sed vt possit

but, so that he may

> *in medias res / Non secus, ac notas, auditorem rapere,*

*carry the hearer into the midst of things / no otherwise than if they were known,*

> res eligit, quarum, totum vbi nouum fuerit, sint tamen partium apud auditores anticipationes quaedam, quarum partes si nouae creantur, totius tamen iam adsit praeconcepta quaedam animis imago, §. 484.

he chooses matters of which, when the whole is new, there are nevertheless certain anticipations of the parts among the hearers, and when the parts are created new, there is nevertheless already present in their minds a certain preconceived image of the whole, § 484.

> § 820. MATERIAS ABSOLVTE EXHAVSTAS, de quibus nemo mortalium cuiquam aliquid venuste noui propinare possit amplius, alias ad horizontem aestheticum pertinentes, §. 119. vix reor vllas esse, RESPECTIVE autem exhaustae videri possint, de quibus datum ingenium datis obiectis personalium primariis vix aliquid venuste noui possit exponere. Hinc dissuaserim, si tecum est materiarum optio [p. 561] 7) ne temere thema tibi constituas, quod respectu tui tuorumque spectatorum ipsi tibi iusto te pede metienti possit exhaustum videri. Quoniam illud nihilominus aggressus aut pulcrum nouitatis studium desperabundus abiicies contra §. 808. trita quaeuis et dicta sexcenties repetere satagens, aut illius tenax in magno periculo versaberis noui quidem, sed non naturalis, §. 622, 623. non coloris, sed fuci §. 688. rebus tuis inducendi. §. 706, 324.

§ 820. MATERIALS ABSOLUTELY EXHAUSTED, about which no mortal could any longer offer anyone anything charmingly new, though they otherwise belong to the aesthetic horizon, § 119, I think there are scarcely any; but RESPECTIVELY exhausted may seem those about which a given wit can scarcely expound anything charmingly new to the primary ones among its given personal objects. Hence I should advise, if the choice of materials is yours, [p. 561] 7) that you do not rashly set yourself a theme which, with respect to you and your spectators, may seem exhausted to you yourself, measuring yourself by your own just foot. For having undertaken it nonetheless, either, despairing, you will throw away the beautiful desire for novelty, against § 808, striving to repeat any commonplaces and things said six hundred times over, or, holding fast to it, you will be in great danger of laying upon your matters a colour that is new indeed, but not natural, § 622, 623, not a colour but a cosmetic, § 688, § 706, 324.

> § 821. 8) Ne tantum nouitatis et inopinati tuam in meditationem congeras, vt ipsa nouarum rerum et cogitationum frequentia, ac constipatione tollatur omnis ille iucundus eleganter cogitatorum color, quo subito potius fusa, naturalique facilitate fluentia videantur nunc demum, quo ponuntur, tempore, quam multo cum sudore iam ante excussa per artem et longos labores ingenio, velut Minerua Iouis capiti. Tunc enim nimia nouitate suspecta redditur nouitas, et acute dictum vnum vel alterum si placuit, vt nouum, decem vno halitu effusa vetera credimus et praeparata. §. 788. *Pleraque gratiora sunt, si inuenta subito, nec domo allata, sed inter dicendum ex ipsa re nata videantur. Vnde illa non iniucunda schemata: paene excidit mihi, et: fugerat me, et: recte* [p. 562] *admones.* Quint. IIII. 5. Hinc diiudica morem verba honoris coram loquentium et gratiarum actiones pro praesenti beneficio tamen domi praeparatas afferentium non solum, sed etiam palam legentium, ne quis nesciat, se iam gratias egisse voti nondum compotes.

§ 821. 8) Do not heap up so much of novelty and of the unexpected into your meditation that by the very frequency and crowding of new things and thoughts all that pleasant colour of elegantly thought things is taken away, whereby they seem rather to have been poured out suddenly, and to flow with a natural ease, now at last, at the time at which they are set down, than to have been struck out by the wit already beforehand with much sweat, through art and long labours, like Minerva from the head of Jupiter. For then novelty is rendered suspect by excess of novelty, and if one or another acute saying has pleased as new, we believe ten, poured out in one breath, to be old and prepared, § 788. *Most things are more pleasing if they seem to have been found on the sudden, not brought from home, but born from the matter itself in the course of speaking. Hence those not unpleasing figures: it almost escaped me, and: it had slipped my mind, and: you rightly* [p. 562] *remind me.* Quint. IIII. 5. Hence judge the custom of those who speak words of honour face to face, and who not only bring thanksgivings for a present benefit that have nonetheless been prepared at home, but even read them out openly, lest anyone fail to know that they have already given thanks before obtaining their wish.

> § 822. In primis autem amabilem suis nouitatem conciliaturus omni ope caueat, 9) ne facile noua omnia et inaudita se prolaturum spondeat, qualia promissa plerumque relinquenda sunt circumforaneae circulatorum eloquentiae. Quum enim propter εἰκός necessarium sit nota miscere incognitis, §. 819, periculosum est, non sine specie saltim arrogantiae totalem vtilium rerum ignorantiam, in qua huc vsque versati sint, non ita tecte suis exprobrare primariis spectatoribus, et simul offensos erigere in tot sui iudices criticosque seueriores, qui primo secum:

§ 822. But above all, he who would win for his people a lovable novelty should take care with all his might, 9) not readily to promise that he will bring forth things all new and unheard of, promises of the kind that should for the most part be left to the itinerant eloquence of mountebanks.
