Incidas in meditationibus aestheticis in propositionem demonstratiuam, quam indigere confirmationibus argumentorum probe praeuideas, habeas autem argumentationem necessariam in promtu, sed simul aliam aliquam probabilem tantum. Interim in illa praesagiat animus haesuros tuos, obiectum tuum personale primarium, in ipso probationis cardine, velut oblato quodam nodo Gordio, defuturam illi necessario tuo argumento relatiuam vel omni, vel magna ex parte, sensitiuam euidentiam, intellectualem autem horizontem tuorum, nunc certe, transcendere. [p. 595] Hanc autem, probabilem scilicet, alteram probationem planam sperare possis et perspicuam fore tuis et oppido euidentem vel ipsi rationis analogo. Hic praefer argumentationem probabilem necessariae. Incertum certo? certo veris credibilia? §. 837. Vtique. Verum non ideo, quia praeferendum incertum est, sed quia tuis est sensitiue certius intellectualiter certis, quae nunc certe, non intelligunt. Non ideo, quia credibile non est certo verum, sed quia tuis tamen hoc probabile est credibilius, ac illa certo vera, quorum ipsos, nunc certe, transcendit euidentia. §. 839.

§ 865. Suppose you light, in aesthetic meditations, upon a demonstrative proposition which you well foresee needs the confirmation of arguments, and you have a necessary argumentation ready to hand, but at the same time some other, merely probable one. Meanwhile, in the former, your mind forebodes that your people, your primary personal object, will stick at the very hinge of the proof, as if at some Gordian knot set before them, and that the sensate evidence relative to that necessary argument of yours will be wanting to it, either wholly or in great part, while the intellectual evidence transcends, now at least, the horizon of your people. [p. 595] But this other, the probable proof, you may hope will be plain and perspicuous to your people and thoroughly evident even to the analogue of reason itself. Here prefer the probable argumentation to the necessary. The uncertain to the certain? Credible things to the certainly true? § 837. Assuredly. But not because the uncertain is to be preferred, but because for your people it is more sensately certain than things intellectually certain, which, now at least, they do not understand. Not because the credible is not certainly true, but because for your people this probable thing is nonetheless more credible than those certainly true things, whose evidence, now at least, transcends them. § 839.

> § 866. *Probabile,* quando Cicero dicit, 46. *quod fieri solet,* §. 484. exhibet occasionem obseruandi quartam ἤθους speciem, §. 195, 495, 698. qua moratum cogitandi genus §. 226. 1) velut aliud agendo, tacite suos de probatis auctoris moribus intimius semper intimiusque persuadeat, §. 227. ita, vt illi suo sibi marte tandem personam cogitantis et characterem moralem, vt amabilem absolute, sic nunc simpliciter honestum, nunc nobilem, nunc omnino grandem, prouti materiis, obiectis et dynamometriae suae naturali proportionate se pingere voluerit, §. 462. euidenter deprehendisse videantur. §. 213

§ 866. *Probable,* when Cicero says, 46, *is what is wont to happen,* § 484, offers an occasion to observe the fourth species of ἤθους [character], § 195, 495, 698, by which the moral manner of thinking § 226 1) as if doing something else, tacitly persuades its people ever more and more intimately of the approved morals of the author, § 227, so that they seem to themselves to have evidently detected, by their own exertion at length, the person of the thinker and his moral character, as absolutely lovable, so now simply honourable, now noble, now altogether grand, according as he has wished to paint himself in proportion to his materials, his objects and his natural dynamometry, § 462. § 213

> [p. 596] § 867. Ἦθος persuasorium §. 866. 2) memor illorum, *qui nihil rectum, nisi quod ipsorum moribus conueniat, putabunt,* Corn. pr. quos noueris non esse paucissimos, si qua cum iisdem congruant, quae velit persuadere, ea more maiorum et institutis sacrosanctis ritibus, ipsis gentium consuetudinibus, diuturnoque moratiorum vsu commendando triumphabit; si qua persuadenda dissentire videantur ab iisdem, ea sibi non sumit tractanda, nisi sub hypothesi §. 846. 3) de morum optimorum verissima pulcritudine, de vera vitiorum turpitudine per naturales maxime colores vtrorumque laborat intime suos persuadere, §. 574. 4) in moribus strictissime veris scapham scapham non dicit solum, sed etiam confirmat, quando pulcre potest et vitiis pulcella, et foeda virtutibus larua detrahi, §. 580.

[p. 596] § 867. The persuasive ἦθος [character] § 866 2) mindful of those *who will think nothing right save what agrees with their own morals,* Corn. pr., whom you know to be not the fewest, if any things that it wishes to persuade agree with these, it will triumph by commending them through the custom of the ancestors and sacrosanct institutions and rites, through the very usages of nations, and through the long practice of the more moral; if any things to be persuaded seem to disagree with these, it does not take them up to be treated, except under the hypothesis of § 846; 3) it labours to persuade its people intimately of the truest beauty of the best morals, of the true baseness of vices, chiefly through the natural colours of both, § 574; 4) in morals most strictly true it not only calls a spade a spade, but also confirms it, when the pretty mask can be beautifully drawn off from vices, and the ugly one from virtues, § 580.

> § 868. Ἦθος persuasorium 5) mores et facta, de quibus dubitari potest, nunc in bonam, nunc in malam partem interpretatur, non sine probabilitate, saltim aesthetica, secundum regulas veritatis moralis, de qua §. 435, 467. secundum easdem 6) historice fingendis moribus et factis eam probabilitatem circumdabit, vt, licet, quomodo acta res sit, ignoremus, [p. 597] ius tamen iurandum credulitatis vix perhorresceremus persuasi non aliter agi potuisse, §. 509. 7) in ipsis fictionibus moralium poeticis obseruabit certitudinem ex analogia cum mundo poetico §. 511. 513. et earundem interna verisimilitudine resultantem, §. 589. vt spectator tuus persuadeatur, non quidem, quae facta sunt, tamen verissime narrari, qualia fieri debent, heterocosmica, §. 586. 8) vbique lucem et vmbram in nuda veritate moralium pingenda sic temperabit, §. 666. vt haec aliquando plena in luce refulgeat, §. 625. nunc subindicetur tantum pluribus ad cogitandum spectatori relictis, §. 654-662. nunc strictissime vera pateant analogo rationis et fidei historicae, §. 441. nunc in ipsis fabulis dominari veritatem, §. 556. viuide sentiens in admirationem simul splendidorum mendaciorum, §. 477. rapiatur spectator bene locata thaumaturgia, §. 808.

§ 868. The persuasive ἦθος [character] 5) interprets morals and deeds, of which one can doubt, now in a good, now in a bad sense, not without probability, at least aesthetic, according to the rules of moral truth, of which § 435, 467; according to the same 6) it will surround morals and deeds feigned historically with such probability that, although we may not know how the matter was done, [p. 597] we should yet scarcely shudder at an oath of credulity, persuaded that it could not have been done otherwise, § 509; 7) in the very poetic fictions of moral matters it will observe the certainty resulting from the analogy with the poetic world § 511, 513, and from their internal verisimilitude, § 589, so that your spectator is persuaded that, though not things which were done, yet things most truly narrated are such as ought to happen, heterocosmic things, § 586; 8) everywhere it will so temper light and shade in painting the naked truth of moral matters, § 666, that this sometimes shines out in full light, § 625, now is only hinted at, many things being left to the spectator to think over, § 654–662, now things most strictly true lie open to the analogue of reason and to historical faith, § 441, now the spectator, vividly feeling that truth rules in the very fables, § 556, is at the same time swept into admiration of splendid lies, § 477, by well-placed wonder-working, § 808.

> § 869. *Probabile* porro Ciceroni est, *quod est in opinione positum,* de inu. I. 46. Nos illud concessimus verisimile, §. 484. neque tamen eidem generatim probabilitatem tribuere possumus, ne aestheticam quidem semper. §. 485. Exempla Ciceronis sunt: *Impiis apud inferos poenas esse praeparatas, eos, qui* [p. 598] *philosophiae dent operam, non arbitrari deos esse.* Primum est adhuc plurimorum opinio, neque tamen probabilitatem vel aestheticam apud aliquos auditorum nanciscerer argumentis ex inferno petitis, apud eos scilicet, qui futura post hanc vitam omnia negare magnum aliquid perperam opinantur. Nec apud alios nunc in confirmando plus proficerem, Sisyphi lapidem et aquas Tantali fugientes minatus, quoniam has inferorum poenas non amplius in suis habent opinionibus. Secundum est opinio verissima, si de diis et exactius philosophantibus loquaris, sin atheismum imputes philosophis, multos nunc inuenies auditores, quibus eiusmodi criminationes non amplius imponant.

§ 869. *Probable,* further, is for Cicero *what is placed in opinion,* de inu. I. 46. We have conceded that to be verisimilar, § 484, yet we cannot generally attribute probability to it, not even aesthetic probability always. § 485. Cicero’s examples are: *That for the impious punishments are prepared in the underworld; that those who* [p. 598] *devote themselves to philosophy do not think that there are gods.* The first is still the opinion of very many, yet I should not obtain probability, even aesthetic, among some of my hearers by arguments sought from the underworld, among those, namely, who wrongly opine that it is something great to deny everything that is to come after this life. Nor among others should I now make more progress in confirming by threatening the stone of Sisyphus and the fleeing waters of Tantalus, since they no longer have these punishments of the underworld in their opinions. The second is a most true opinion, if you speak of the gods and of those who philosophise more exactly; but if you impute atheism to philosophers, you will now find many hearers upon whom accusations of this kind no longer impose.

> § 870. Assensus noster nobis incerto datus est OPINIO NOSTRA. Opiniones suas frustra persuadendis obtruderet aliquis confirmandi gratia, nisi sint eaedem simul opiniones eorum, quibus potissimum cogitat. Hinc ante omnia videndum in opinionum vsu, an sint opiniones obiecti tui personalis primarii, an forsan aliorum tantum. Opinamur vel non ponderatis ad assensum rationibus OPINIONE PRAEIVDICATA, vel opinione nunc logice, nunc saltim aesthetice [p. 599] probabili, vel nobis etiam dubiae, vel omnino improbabili opinioni assentimur, quoniam id vel licere, vel omnino moraliter necessarium putamus, vel ponimus verosimilem nobis, donec an probabilis sit, nec ne magis liqueat, vt ita dicam, interimistice et prouisionaliter. Ad quam classem quaedam opinio intra mentem tuorum pertineat quum vix et raro certus esse poteris, post id, an in opinione eorum positum sit, quod ad confirmandum afferri possit, potior cura tuum erit, an opinio tuorum ex animi tui sententia sit error, an minus, vt agere possis ex §. 574.

§ 870. Our assent given to something uncertain is OUR OPINION. Someone would in vain thrust his own opinions upon those to be persuaded for the sake of confirming, unless they are at the same time the opinions of those for whom he chiefly thinks. Hence before all it is to be seen, in the use of opinions, whether they are opinions of your primary personal object, or perhaps only of others. We opine either, without having weighed the reasons for assent, by PREJUDICED OPINION, or we assent to an opinion now logically, now at least aesthetically [p. 599] probable, or even one doubtful to us, or one altogether improbable, since we think that this is either permissible or altogether morally necessary, or we posit it as verisimilar for us, until it becomes clearer whether it is probable or not, so to speak, interimistically and provisionally. Since you can seldom and hardly be certain to which class a given opinion within the minds of your people belongs, after this, whether what can be adduced for confirming is placed in their opinion, it will be your greater care whether the opinion of your people is, in the judgement of your own mind, an error or not, so that you can act according to § 574.

> § 871. Si tandem Ciceroni *probabilia* dicuntur omnia, *quae habent* ad mores et opiniones *aliquam similitudinem, contraria, paria, quaeque cadant sub eandem rationem*, de inu. I. 46. vereor, ne verisimile et probabile, perspicuum et euidens, si sequaris, saepenumero confuderis. §. 852. In ipsis exquisitis ab eloquentissimo viro exemplis fallor, an parua satis vis ad persuadendum analogo rationis deprehendetur, splendidum et oculos primo obtutu praestringens ab euidenti si doctum est distinguere? Interim qui semper non dabunt, aliquando saltim probabilem confirmationem suggerent loculi, §. 132.

§ 871. If, finally, Cicero calls *probable* everything *that has* with respect to customs and opinions *some similarity, contraries, equals, and whatever falls under the same reasoning*, de inu. I. 46, I fear that, if you follow him, you will often enough confuse the verisimilar and the probable, the perspicuous and the evident. § 852. In the very examples chosen by that most eloquent man I am mistaken, or else a rather small power of persuading the analogue of reason will be detected, if it is the mark of the learned to distinguish what is splendid and dazzles the eyes at first glance from what is evident? Meanwhile those pigeon-holes, which will not always give one, will at least sometimes supply a probable confirmation, § 132.

> § 872. [p. 600] Pari sunt in pretio, qui sequuntur, 48. probabilium loci, *signum, credibile, iudicatum, comparabile. Signum* esse dicit, *quod quiddam significat* e. c. Hactenus quis neget? Quando vero de signis generatim addit, *indigere ea testimonii, et grauioris confirmationis*, de signis illud omnibus eo minus concesserim, quo minus, 1) omnia signa tantum probabilia sunt, quoniam ex aliquibus persuasio completa, e. g. ex putrefactione totius corporis certitudo mortis, 2) probabilia etiam, si vere sint, quae dicuntur, semper grauioris confirmationis indigent, §. 861, 865. Miseros medicorum filios, qui in sua prognosi probabili collatis signis morborum omnibus, tamen indigent vbique testimonii aut grauioris confirmationis!

§ 872. [p. 600] Of equal value are the loci of probables that follow, 48, *the sign, the credible, the adjudged, the comparable.* He says that a *sign* is *what signifies something*, etc. Thus far who would deny it? But when he adds of signs in general that *they need testimony and weightier confirmation*, I should concede that about all signs the less, the less 1) all signs are only probable, since from some there is complete persuasion, e.g. from the putrefaction of the whole body the certainty of death, 2) probables too, if what is said be true, always need weightier confirmation, § 861, 865. Wretched sons of the physicians, who in their probable prognosis, having collated all the signs of diseases, nevertheless everywhere need testimony or weightier confirmation!

> § 873. *Credibile* non tam *sine vllo teste auditoris opinione firmatur*, §. 869, 870. quam ob internam suam probabilitatem etiam tunc persuadet, quando testium etiam auctoritatem minus perspectam habeamus. *Iudicatum* est Ciceroni *res assensione, aut auctoritate, aut iudicio, alicuius aut aliquorum comprobata*, idque *vel religiosum, vel commune, vel approbatum. Comparabile* diuidit idem in *imaginem, collationem et exemplum.* §. 871.

§ 873. *The credible* is not so much *established without any witness by the opinion of the hearer*, § 869, 870, as it persuades, on account of its internal probability, even then, when we have even the authority of the witnesses less thoroughly examined. *The adjudged* is for Cicero *a matter approved by the assent, or the authority, or the judgement of someone or of some persons*, and that *either religious, or common, or approved. The comparable* the same author divides into *image, collation and example.* § 871.

> § 874. [p. 601] Haec §. 861-873. atque his similia postquam enarrauit Cicero, 49. ita concludit: *At fons quidem confirmationis, vt facultas tulit, apertus est, nec minus dilucide, quam rei natura ferebat, demonstratus est.* §. 639. Neque tamen ipse sibi satisfecisse videtur, quando statim addit: *In praesentia tantum modo numeros, et modos et partes argumentandi confuse et permiste dispersimus.* Dicamus enim, quod res est. Fontem confirmationis cuiuslibet non generalia quaedam aperient topica, sed natura thematis penitius cognita, confirmandorumque veritas, quam fieri potest, clarissime perspecta. Ipsa scientifica pulcre meditaturi conuictio, rigoroseque demonstrandi habitus multum ipsi proderit, si vim rationis temperare, vim argumenta splendide collustrandi nouerit excitare. Neque demonstrabit hos tam varios fontes rhetor vllus, vllus aestheticus, sed pulcra potius eruditio, §. 63. et experientia, quae in rebus facti signis existentiam maxime probabilibus exponendi suppeditabit vsum. Hausturis ex fontibus iam descriptis quaedam forte topica nonnumquam ansam aliquam dabunt, alias confirmationum aesthetice solidarum erunt arena pro fundamento. §. 839.

§ 874. [p. 601] After Cicero has recounted these things, § 861–873, and others like them, 49, he concludes thus: *But the fountain of confirmation has indeed been opened, so far as our ability allowed, and demonstrated no less lucidly than the nature of the matter bore.* § 639. Yet he does not seem to have satisfied himself, when he at once adds: *For the present we have only scattered, confusedly and in a mixed way, the numbers, modes and parts of arguing.* Let us say what the case is. The fountain of any confirmation whatever will be opened not by certain general topics, but by the nature of the theme more deeply known, and by the truth of the things to be confirmed, examined as clearly as can be done. The scientific conviction of the one who is to meditate beautifully, and the habit of demonstrating rigorously, will profit him much, if he knows how to temper the power of reason and to arouse the power of illuminating the arguments splendidly. Nor will any rhetorician, any aesthetician, demonstrate these so various fountains, but rather beautiful erudition, § 63, and experience, which will supply the practice of setting forth, in matters of fact, existence by the most probable signs. To those who are to draw from the fountains already described, certain topics will perhaps sometimes give some handle; otherwise they will be sand for a foundation of aesthetically solid confirmations. § 839.

> § 875. [p. 602] Post *inuentionem argumenti absolutionem argumentandi* praecipit Cicero, 50. eamque *vel inductione, vel ratiocinatione* fieri putat. Nunc semestres etiam logici norunt inductionem esse ratiocinationis speciem. Idem euinci potest, si sumamus ipsam Ciceronis de *ratiocinatione* descriptionem, 57. *Est oratio ex ipsa re probabile aliquod eliciens, quod expositum et per se cognitum sua se vi et ratione confirmat.* Sed longaeuus error est inductionem a ratiocinatione, tanquam opposito aliquo ac plane diuerso seiungendi, quoniam ratiocinatio et eius genus ad ordinarios syllogismos propius accedens paene ad haec vsque tempora confusum est. Nos nunc de forma pulcrarum argumentationum multi non erimus, quoniam est aptior in aesteticis [sic: aestheticis] locus de eadem exponendi.

§ 875. [p. 602] After *the invention of the argument* Cicero prescribes *the completion of the argumentation*, 50, and thinks it comes about *either by induction or by ratiocination*. Now even logicians of one semester know that induction is a species of ratiocination. The same can be proved, if we take Cicero’s own description of *ratiocination*, 57: *It is a discourse eliciting something probable from the matter itself, which, when set out and known in itself, confirms itself by its own force and reasoning.* But it is a long-lived error to separate induction from ratiocination, as though from something opposed and plainly different, since ratiocination and its genus, approaching more closely to ordinary syllogisms, have been confused almost up to these very times. We shall not now say much about the form of beautiful argumentations, since there is a fitter place in aesthetics for expounding it.

> § 876. Ad locum aesthetices de pulcris ratiocinationibus rite formandis ablegemus excutienda, quae Cicero habet de inductionibus n. 51-56. et tractationem de ratiocinationibus venustis tam simplicibus, quam concatenatis, qua patebit illas esse posse ac solere tripertitas, neque tamen semper vel tot constare partibus necessario: has vel trium tantum partium esse posse, solere tamen quatuor, [p. 603] vel quinque partibus absolui, quanquam plures etiam articulos non omnino reformident. Vnde diiudicari poterit controuersia, de qua Cicero l. c. 57-76. Nunc solum notemus eiusdem iudicium, quo *abhorrere* censet *ab vsu oratorio* (hinc multo magis a poëtico, generatim aesthetico) *multa et obscura* (κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν, §. 631.) *de quibus certum est artificium constitutum*, (logicum) *quibus* scilicet *rationibus tractentur argumentationes in philosophia.*

§ 876. To the place in aesthetics on the right forming of beautiful ratiocinations let us relegate for examination what Cicero has on inductions, n. 51–56, and the treatment of charming ratiocinations, both simple and concatenated, from which it will appear that the former can be, and usually are, tripartite, yet do not always necessarily consist of even so many parts: that the latter can be of only three parts, yet usually are completed in four [p. 603] or five parts, although they do not altogether shrink from even more members. Whence the controversy of which Cicero treats, l. c. 57–76, can be adjudicated. Now let us only note the judgement of the same author, by which he reckons that *there are abhorrent from oratorical use* (hence much more from poetic, in general from aesthetic use) *many and obscure things* (κατ᾽ αἴσθησιν [according to sensation], § 631) *about which a certain art has been constituted* (the logical one), namely *by what reasonings argumentations are handled in philosophy.*

> § 877. Praebet enim occasionem concessae §. 862. 863. libertati nunc adiungendi consilium expresse dissuasorium, in venustis confirmationibus ne adhibeas ratiocinationes, quarum forma secundum logices artificium legitima logicorum gnaris sine vlla crypsi, sine vllo saltu, sine vllis additamentis variationibusue retenta statim appareat, quosque formales logici dicunt. Logices imperitis formales eiusmodi syllogismos qualemcunque, maiorem tamen, certitudinem, ac alios, dare, nunquam expertus sum, nec a priori conuictus, si cum vere persuasoriis, vti fas est, comparentur. Periti logices aut operae pretium iudicabunt aliquam tuarum ratiocinationum etiam in formali rationis certitudine maiori contemplari, [p. 604] et tunc ipsi formam tuis logicam induere poterunt: aut certitudinem eiusmodi, nunc certe, non desiderant, hinc nec his proderis, vel placebis singulariter. Interim horizontem nunc tuum transcendens, §. 121. manca, §. 159. ἦθος aestheticum negligens, §. 193, 194. male tenuia, §. 232. sicca, exilia, arida, exsangvia, ieiuna, §. 246. studium veri male locatum, nunc tuo, verisimilitudinis aestheticae studio praeferens, §. 555, 561. probans non persuadens, §. 541. aesthetice obscura, §. 633, 636, cogitare, neque tamen aesthetice solidus iudicaberis. §. 840, 842.

§ 877. For it furnishes the occasion of now adding to the liberty conceded in § 862, 863 an expressly dissuasive counsel: that in charming confirmations you do not employ ratiocinations whose form, legitimate according to the art of logic, appears at once to those versed in logic, retained without any concealment, without any leap, without any additions or variations, and which the logicians call formal. That formal syllogisms of this kind give to those unskilled in logic some certainty, yet a greater one than others, I have never found by experience, nor am I convinced of it a priori, if they are compared, as is proper, with the truly persuasive ones. Those skilled in logic will either judge it worth the effort to contemplate some one of your ratiocinations also in the greater formal certainty of reason, [p. 604] and then they themselves will be able to clothe your ratiocinations in logical form: or they do not desire certainty of this kind, at least now; hence you will neither profit nor particularly please these. Meanwhile you will be judged to think things transcending your present horizon, § 121, maimed things, § 159, neglecting the aesthetic ἦθος [character], § 193, 194, badly thin things, § 232, dry, meagre, arid, bloodless, jejune things, § 246, preferring a badly placed zeal for truth to your present zeal for aesthetic verisimilitude, § 555, 561, proving but not persuading, § 541, aesthetically obscure things, § 633, 636, and yet not aesthetically solid. § 840, 842.

> § 878. Confirmaturus potius materiam suarum probationum curans, secundum S. XII. poterit hylen quandam et quasi siluam rationum aliquando detegere 1) coordinatarum plurium, quaeque singulae connectantur quidem satis belle cum confirmando, videantur tamen a se inuicem satis independentes, 2) subordinatarum inter se, sic, vt totae quidem et integrae series ad confirmandum vsque diductae non ita multae sint, ad harum autem singulas multae tanquam vlteriores probationes concurrant, et in bene longam plurium membrorum probantium concatenationem possint concrescere. Si [p. 605] breuitas quasdam relinquere iusserit, posteriores venustius, ac primo loco descriptae, recidentur. Numerus enim et quasi synathroismus quidam nouorum semper nouorumque argumentorum plus gratiae, plus viuiditatis habebit, ac vnius argumenti transscendens forte patientiam analogi rationis protensio. Haec intensiuam veri conscientiam, certitudinem rationis amabilem sagacitati, maiorem exhiberet, fateor, sed illa copiosius probare visa rationis analogo nunc quaerendam maiorem extensiuam veri conscientiam pollicetur, sensitiuam euidentiam, §. 847.

§ 878. The one who is to confirm, caring rather for the matter of his proofs, according to S. XII, will be able sometimes to uncover a certain hyle and as it were forest of reasons 1) of several coordinate ones, each of which is indeed connected prettily enough with what is to be confirmed, yet seem fairly independent of one another, 2) of ones subordinated among themselves, so that the whole and entire series, drawn out all the way to what is to be confirmed, are not so many, but to each of these many concur as further proofs, and can grow together into a good long concatenation of several proving members. If [p. 605] brevity bids some be left out, the later ones will be cut away more charmingly than those described in the first place. For the number and as it were a certain synathroismus of ever new and new arguments will have more grace, more vividness, than the stretching out of a single argument, perhaps transcending the patience of the analogue of reason. The latter would exhibit an intensive consciousness of the truth, a certainty of reason lovable to sagacity, a greater one, I confess; but the former, seen by the analogue of reason to prove more copiously, promises the greater extensive consciousness of truth now to be sought, sensate evidence, § 847.

> § 879. Neque tamen argumenta confirmaturus numeret solum, §. 878, sed etiam ponderet, §. 177. quantum ex quouis veritas et verisimilitudo confirmandi patere possit, iudicans, M. §. 697. vt digna relatu possit adhibere secundum iustam lucis et vmbrae dispensationem singula collocando, §. 666. reiectis omnino FRIVOLIS, quorum vis dilucide probandi vel nulla, vel infinite parua. §. 839, 191. Nec ea temere speres, saltim vt vmbras, grauiora comitari posse. §. 661. Quid enim? si vel vnius eiusmodi probationis ex vmbra protrahatur admirabilis imbecillitas, et euidenter ponatur ob oculos, [p. 606] quam ineptum sit ad persuadendum? Tunc sane vel optimis aliis meras contemtus et obliuionis tenebras poterit adspergere. §. 665. *Satius est, omni ante actae vitae se abstinere conuicio, quam leuibus, aut friuolis, aut manifesto falsis reum incessere, quia fides caeteris detrahitur, et qui nihil obiicit, omisisse credi potest maledicta, tanquam superuacua, qui vana congerit, confitetur vanum in anteactis argumentum, in quibus vinci, quam tacere, maluerit.* Quintilianus Inst. or. L. VII. c. 2. *de coniectura.*

§ 879. Yet let the one who is to confirm not only count his arguments, § 878, but also weigh them, § 177, judging how much the truth and verisimilitude of what is to be confirmed can be made manifest from each, M. § 697, so that he can employ those worth relating, placing each according to the just dispensation of light and shade, § 666, with the FRIVOLOUS ones altogether rejected, whose power of proving lucidly is either none or infinitely small. § 839, 191. Nor should you rashly hope that these can accompany the weightier ones, at least as shades. § 661. For what? if the admirable feebleness of even one proof of this kind be dragged out of the shade, and it be evidently set before the eyes [p. 606] how inept it is for persuading? Then indeed it will be able to sprinkle even the best of the others with the sheer darkness of contempt and oblivion. § 665. *It is better to refrain altogether from reproach of a life earlier lived than to assail the accused with trifling, or frivolous, or manifestly false charges, because credit is withdrawn from the rest; and he who objects nothing may be believed to have omitted abuse as superfluous, while he who heaps up empty charges confesses his argument on the earlier matters to be empty, in which he would rather be beaten than keep silent.* Quintilian, Inst. or. L. VII. c. 2, *on conjecture.*

> § 880. Confirmaturus si solam verisimilitudinem §. 483. illustrantibus §. 730. in argumentis eligendis acquieuerit; me quidem arbitro, satisfecit officio nunc suo, §. 839, 855. eam tamen verisimilitudinis speciem vel gradum, quem promiserat, vel res, vel obiectum ipsius personale praesertim attendendum rite postulauerit, illustrare quum per naturam ipsam iubeatur, §. 104. argumenta tantum heterogeneam a quaesita verisimilitudinem, vel eodem gradu minorem illustratura, vel omittet omnino, vel in vmbras saltim coniiciet, luci his vnice reseruatis, quae talem et tantam verisimilitudinem exhibent, qualis et quanta poscebatur. S. XXXV. Exempla legem [p. 607] generalem declarabunt, §. 730. determinatiores regulae.

§ 880. If the one who is to confirm has rested content, in choosing arguments, with those alone that illustrate verisimilitude, § 483, § 730; in my judgement at least he has satisfied his present duty, § 839, 855; yet since he is bidden by nature itself, § 104, to illustrate that species or degree of verisimilitude which he had promised, or which the matter, or his personal object especially to be attended to, has rightly demanded, he will either omit altogether, or at least cast into the shades, arguments that would only illustrate a verisimilitude heterogeneous from the one sought, or less in the same degree, reserving the light solely for those which exhibit such and so much verisimilitude as was demanded. S. XXXV. Examples will declare the general [p. 607] law, § 730, more determinate rules.

> § 887 [sic: 881]. Si de possibilitate naturali cuiusdam obiecti quaeritur, §. 432. aut de morali latius dicta, § 433. argumentis absolutam tantum confirmaturis, vel nullus, vel in vmbra tantum locus est. §. 431, 880. Si de veritate morali cuiusdam obiecti quaeritur, §. 435. argumentis possibilitatem eiusdem moralem latius dictam §. 433. tantum confirmaturis vel nullus, vel in vmbris vnice locus est. §. 880. Si quaeritur vnitas actionis, loci, temporis hypothetica, §. 439. argumentis vnitatem generalium absolutam confirmaturis nullus, nisi forsan in vmbris, locus est. §. 880. Si de veritate obiecti singulari, s. existentia quaeritur, argumentis veritatem generalium, sub quibus obiectum contineatur, vnice confirmaturis, aut nullus, aut vnicus in vmbris, locus est. §. 440, 880. Si quaeritur, an aliquid sit strictissime verum, argumentis quamcunque possibilitatem eiusdem tantum, vel veritatem heterocosmicam declaraturis, aut nullus, aut vmbra sola, locus est. §. 441. 880.

§ 881. If the question is of the natural possibility of some object, § 432, or of the moral one more broadly so called, § 433, for arguments that would confirm only the absolute one there is either no place, or a place only in the shade. § 431, 880. If the question is of the moral truth of some object, § 435, for arguments that would confirm only its moral possibility more broadly so called, § 433, there is either no place, or a place solely in the shades. § 880. If the hypothetical unity of action, place, time is sought, § 439, for arguments that would confirm the absolute unity of generalities there is no place, unless perhaps in the shades. § 880. If the question is of the singular truth of an object, i.e. its existence, for arguments that would confirm solely the truth of the generalities under which the object is contained there is either no place, or only one in the shades. § 440, 880. If it is asked whether something is true in the strictest sense, for arguments that would declare only any possibility whatever of it, or its heterocosmic truth, there is either no place, or only the shade. § 441, 880.

> § 882. Confirmaturus fictiones strictissime veras, §. 506. si meras strictius historicas §. 509. [p. 608] vel omnino poëticas, §. 511. ad persuadendum afferret, etiamsi vel nostro illae, vel poetarum mundo hae non viderentur contradicere, §. 513. nec vtopiam saperent, §. 514. analogicae §. 576. nec prorsus ignotae, §. 518. nec anomala figmenta, § 520. immo si fictis huiusmodi lucem potissimam affuderit, iure censebitur mendacium mendacio tegere, ne perpluat, §. 881.

§ 882. If the one who is to confirm fictions true in the strictest sense, § 506, should bring forward for persuasion merely historical ones in the stricter sense, § 509, [p. 608] or altogether poetic ones, § 511, even if the former did not seem to contradict our world, nor the latter the world of the poets, § 513, nor to savour of utopia, § 514, analogical ones, § 576, nor altogether unknown, § 518, nor anomalous figments, § 520, indeed if he has poured the chief light upon fictions of this kind, he will rightly be judged to be covering a lie with a lie, lest the rain come through, § 881.

> § 883. Si de verisimilitudine strictissime dicta dati obiecti quaeritur, §. 530. confirmaturus omittat fabulas, §. 526. historicas etiam, multo magis poëticas, §. 527. saltim ne multum in iis haereat, §. 881. nisi forsan aliquando in strictius probabilibus, §. 532. aut narrationibus eiusmodi, quae strictissime vera continere, fabulosis immixta, §. 526, 527. potest aesthetice saltim probabile reddere, §. 533. In vltimo casu confirmaturus prouocans ad ea, quae in narrationibus, quae fabulae dicuntur, strictissime vera esse satis ostendit, §. 485, 847. non habet, generatim caussam, cur haec argumenta vel taceat, vel obumbret, §. 880.

§ 883. If the question is of the verisimilitude, in the strictest sense, of a given object, § 530, let the one who is to confirm omit fables, § 526, historical ones too, and much more poetic ones, § 527, or at least not dwell much on them, § 881, unless perhaps sometimes in the case of things probable in the stricter sense, § 532, or of narrations of the kind which, mingled with fabulous matter, can at least render aesthetically probable that they contain things true in the strictest sense, § 526, 527, § 533. In the last case the one who is to confirm, appealing to those things which he sufficiently shows to be true in the strictest sense in the narrations that are called fables, § 485, 847, has in general no cause either to pass over these arguments in silence or to shade them, § 880.

> § 884. Aestheticodogmatica confirmaturus quum satisfaciat officio, nunc suo, licet non [p. 609] adscendat vltra verisimilitudinem dogmaticam, §. 577. dilucide propinandam, §. 839. non est generatim, cur abstineat a commemorandis, vel etiam in aliquo nitore sistendis argumentis persuasoriis logice forsan dubiis aut improbabilibus, probabilibus tamen aesthetice, vel ab ipso commode ad hanc probabilitatem euehendis, §. 486. Genus cogitandi strictius aesthetico-historicum studiosum veri ac solidi nec patietur sua confirmaturum vel intra possibilitatum quarumcunque rationes, §. 881. vel intra nitide pingendam aliquam poëticam verisimilitudinem subsistere, §. 880, nec ad rationales credibilitatis, auctoritatis testium, interpretationis locorum ambiguorum, diiudicationis contradictionum apparentium, geographiae, chronologiae, genealogiae, e. c. calculos et discussiones assurgere, §. 580, 583. Hinc historicorum, venustae simul soliditati, §. 839. ac logicae criticorum accurationi litare volentium, tot prodromi, notae, marginalia, appendices, e. c. §. 584, 847.

§ 884. Since the one who is to confirm aesthetico-dogmatic things satisfies his present duty, although he does not [p. 609] ascend beyond dogmatic verisimilitude, § 577, to be lucidly set before the reader, § 839, there is in general no reason for him to refrain from mentioning, or even from setting in some brilliance, persuasive arguments that are perhaps logically doubtful or improbable, yet aesthetically probable, or that can conveniently be raised by him to this probability, § 486. The aesthetico-historical manner of thinking in the stricter sense, zealous for the true and the solid, will suffer the one who is to confirm its matters neither to halt within the reasons of possibilities of whatever kind, § 881, nor within some poetic verisimilitude to be brilliantly painted, § 880, nor to rise to the rational calculations and discussions of credibility, of the authority of witnesses, of the interpretation of ambiguous passages, of the adjudication of apparent contradictions, of geography, chronology, genealogy, etc., § 580, 583. Hence the so many prodromes, notes, marginalia, appendices, etc. of historians wishing to sacrifice at once to charming solidity, § 839, and to the logical accuracy of the critics, § 584, 847.

> § 885. Confirmaturus habeat argumenta persuasionis satis multa: non sufficit inde friuola, nec quaesitam verisimilitudinem promittentia reiicere: cogitandorum explicite cuiuis satis etiam pro dignitate lucis, viuiditatis, [p. 610] et claritatis affundendum est extensiuae, §. 618. quo collustrentur ipsae res, quae ad persuadendum adhibentur, ea potissimum parte sui, latere, vel facie, quae NERVVM PROBANDI contineat, necessitatem positis his admittendi simul veritatem confirmandi, §. 855. 839. Hinc coordinatarum etiam rationum, § 878 nec ineptarum ob §. 879-884. si plures in hyle persuasurorum argumentorum adhuc supersint, quam vt quaeuis per breuitatem rotundam satis luci suae possit exponi: praestat aliquas earundem aesthetice firmiores in omni suo naturali nitore proferre, §. 625, 622. ne neglectis quidem veris coloribus, § 688. vel floridissimis, §. 693. ad non mediocrem vsque, si fieri potest, thaumaturgiam, §. 808. quam omnibus nimium cumulatis, singulis punctim et concisim, aut tamen iusto breuius, expositis obruere forsan et obtundere lectores e. c. primarios, non vere persuadere. §. 839. 634.

§ 885. Let the one who is to confirm have persuasive arguments enough in number: it does not suffice thereupon to reject the frivolous ones, and those not promising the verisimilitude sought: upon each of the things to be thought explicitly there must also be poured enough extensive light, vividness, [p. 610] and clarity, in proportion to its dignity, § 618, so that the very things which are employed for persuading be illuminated, especially in that part, side or face of themselves which contains the NERVE OF THE PROOF, the necessity, these being posited, of admitting at the same time the truth of what is to be confirmed, § 855, 839. Hence if, even of coordinate reasons, § 878, and ones not inept on account of § 879–884, there still remain more in the hyle of the arguments that are to persuade than that each can be set forth in a rounded brevity in a light sufficient for it: it is better to bring forward some of the same, the aesthetically firmer, in all their natural brilliance, § 625, 622, without neglecting even true colours, § 688, or the most florid ones, § 693, up to a not mediocre wonder-working, if it can be done, § 808, than, with all of them too much heaped up, each set out point by point and cut short, or at any rate more briefly than is right, perhaps to overwhelm and to blunt the readers, e.g. the primary ones, and not truly to persuade. § 839, 634.

#### Sectio LII. Reprehensio. — Section LII. Refutation

> § 886. Quanquam reprehensio nonnunquam tantum animo confirmandi thesin per indirectam probationem tentari potest: §. 854. [p. 611] nos tamen eam heic considerabimus in grauioribus illis casibus, vbi contrarium a nobis confirmando, huic oppositum, et theseos nostrae antithesis obiecto nostro primario posset aliquid veritatis in se continens videri, vel multum. §. 855. Dissentientes enim aesthetice refutare, vel reprehendere pulcre cogitaturis magis est necessarium, ac demonstratori logico refutare conclusionibus suis rigide demonstratis contradicentes, quia 1) est in opinione multorum, licet praeiudicata, positum, contra quae multa possint obiici (quomodocunque, quantulacunque,) certa non videri. §. 870.

§ 886. Although refutation can sometimes be attempted only with the intention of confirming a thesis by indirect proof, § 854, [p. 611] we shall nevertheless consider it here in those weightier cases where the contrary of what we are to confirm, opposed to it, and the antithesis of our thesis, could seem to our primary object to contain in itself something of truth, or much. § 855. For to refute or reprehend aesthetically those who dissent is more necessary for those who are to think beautifully than it is for the logical demonstrator to refute those who contradict his rigidly demonstrated conclusions, because 1) it is laid down in the opinion of many, though a prejudiced one, that things against which many objections (of whatever kind, however small) can be raised do not seem certain. § 870.

> § 887. 2) Vere etiam probabilitas omnis, tam logica, quam aesthetica, non tantum auctis rationibus pro tua sententia pugnantibus, sed etiam imminutis et dilutis rationibus, contra eandem quae fecissent, crescit et intenditur. §. 485. Hinc et probabilitatibus logicis magis necessarium est rationes dubitandi infirmare, vel intellectui falsitatem contra dicendorum exponere, quam demonstrationibus, quas completas et mathematicas dixeris. 3) Non adeo leui momento tuas in partes probabilitatis aestheticae pertrahetur trutina, ac logicae, nec adeo acutum cernimus sensitiue, ac intellectualiter, [p. 612] quae pars rationum superponderet. Hinc persuasioni aestheticae consulitur, non addendo solum pondera parti, quae subsidere, sed et demendo parti, quae debeat notabilius alleuari, quo haec videbitur falsis, hoc illa videbitur sensitiue veris similior. §. 483, 489.

§ 887. 2) Truly also every probability, as much the logical as the aesthetic, grows and is intensified not only by increasing the reasons fighting for your opinion, but also by diminishing and diluting the reasons that would have made against it. § 485. Hence for logical probabilities too it is more necessary to weaken the reasons for doubting, or to expose to the intellect the falsity of what is said against them, than it is for demonstrations that you would call complete and mathematical. 3) The balance of aesthetic probability is not drawn over to your side by so slight a weight as that of logical probability, nor do we discern so acutely by sense as by intellect [p. 612] which side of the reasons outweighs. Hence aesthetic persuasion is served not only by adding weights to the side that ought to sink, but also by taking them from the side that ought to rise more noticeably, by which the latter will seem more like the false, the former more like what is sensately true. § 483, 489.

> § 888. Vere Columella dixerit: *Reprehendisse peccantem non satis est, si non et recti viam doceas*, et recte iungat vtrumque belle cogitaturus, § 854, 855. tamen §. 886, 887. rationes nobis dedisse videmur, ex quibus ex parte possit intelligi, qui fiat, vt in sensitiuae cognitionis sphaera paedagogos facilius inuenias, quam patres; qui tentent, an

§ 888. Columella may truly have said: *To have reprehended the sinner is not enough, if you do not also teach the way of the right*, and the one who is to think prettily may rightly join both, § 854, 855; yet in § 886, 887 we seem to have given reasons from which it can in part be understood how it comes about that in the sphere of sensate cognition you more easily find pedagogues than fathers; those who try whether

> *ab exitio possint reprendere euntes,*

*they can catch back from ruin those going to it,*

> quam qui nondum in deuia lapsos directe ducant in amorem optimi, satyricos tandem facilius, quam paraeneticos. Optimum est, quod Cicero virtuti tribuit, si sensibus nostris Aristippi voluptas blandiatur, Qu. ac. I. 139. si similibus in casibus, vt practicis, ita etiam theoreticis, viri boni suada, *reuocat, vel potius reprehendit manu. Pecudum illos esse motus dicit. Hominem iungit deo.* §. 829, 838.

than those who directly lead those not yet fallen into byways into the love of the best; satirists, finally, more easily than exhorters. The best is what Cicero attributes to virtue, if the pleasure of Aristippus should flatter our senses, Qu. ac. I. 139, if in similar cases, practical as well as theoretical, the persuasion of a good man *calls back, or rather reprehends with the hand. It says those are the motions of cattle. It joins man to god.* § 829, 838.

> § 889. Reprehensioni fontes aperire hoc minus necessarium est, si vere Salustius ad Caesarem: [p. 613] *Ad reprehendenda aliena facta, aut dicta, ardet omnibus animus. Vix satis apertum os, aut lingua promta videtur, quae meditata pectore euoluat.* Vix tamen eandem definiuerat Cicero de inu. I. 61. *per quam argumentando aduersariorum confirmatio*, §. 886. 855. *diluitur aut infirmatur, aut alleuatur*, §. 887. 854. quum eundem huic fontem tribuit, quo vtitur confirmatio, 62. de quo §. 861-873. et praesertim §. 874. vbi dicta verissime simul omni reprehensionum fonti conueniunt. §. 65.

§ 889. To open the fountains for refutation is the less necessary, if Sallust to Caesar spoke truly: [p. 613] *For reprehending the deeds or sayings of others everyone’s spirit burns. Scarcely does a mouth seem open enough, or a tongue ready enough, to unroll what the breast has meditated.* Yet Cicero had scarcely defined it, de inu. I. 61, as that *by which, in arguing, the confirmation of one’s adversaries*, § 886, 855, *is diluted or weakened or lightened*, § 887, 854, when he assigns to it the same fountain which confirmation uses, 62, on which see § 861–873 and especially § 874, where what was said most truly suits at the same time every fountain of refutations. § 65.

> § 890. Sint interim haec reprehensuris consilia: 1) non argumentorum solum, et praemissarum, sed conclusionis etiam primario impugnandae pingatur falsitas. §. 839. Quod in ipsis logicis refutationibus est vtile: heic magis iudico necessarium, §. 887. quoniam multi sic comparati sumus, vt tacite nobiscum statuamus, etiamsi vel perperam, vel ex minus idoneis praemissis, hucusque probata sit quaedam conclusio; nondum tamen eandem iam ideo falsam esse, posse satis veram, et nobis adhuc ignota ratione vel iam probatam esse rite, vel a nobis doctiore probandam propediem. Huic non ita falsae multorum opinioni succus in dato reprehensionis exemplo subducitur, si non subsistamus [p. 614] in subruendis antitheseos argumentis, sed et ipsam hanc conclusionem ita declaremus esse falsam aesthetice S. XXVIII. vt obiectum nostrum primarium, non datis solum, sed et forsan inueniendis quibuscunque fulcris, tamen eandem sustineri posse desperet. §. 455.

§ 890. Meanwhile let these be counsels for those who are to refute: 1) let the falsity not only of the arguments and premisses, but also of the conclusion that is principally to be impugned, be painted. § 839. What is useful in logical refutations themselves, I judge here more necessary, § 887, since many of us are so constituted that we tacitly settle with ourselves that, even if some conclusion has hitherto been proved either wrongly or from less suitable premisses, it is nevertheless not yet on that account already false; that it can be true enough, and by a reason still unknown to us either already duly proved, or soon to be proved by someone more learned than we. The sap is drawn from this not-so-false opinion of many in a given example of refutation, if we do not halt [p. 614] at undermining the arguments of the antithesis, but also declare this conclusion itself to be aesthetically false, S. XXVIII, in such a way that our primary object despairs that it can be sustained by any props whatever, not only those given, but also perhaps those to be found. § 455.

> § 891. Huic consilio §. 890. satisfacit partim iam ipsa confirmatio, partim artificium nostrae directae probationi, et antitheseos praemissarum, vel formae probandi, vel vtrarumque subuersioni inugendi [sic: iungendi] ex ipsa sumta eadem conclusione et antithesi deducta, dilucide, vel etiam splendide deducta, magnam tamen analogo rationis falsitatem et incongruentiam eiusdem tandem et velut ex improuiso ob oculos ponentia, §. 853, 884. Cicero de Inu. I. 63. *omnis argumentatio reprehenditur, si aut ex iis, quae sumta sunt, non conceditur vnum, pluraue*, (negando praemissas) *aut his concessis complexio confici ex his negatur: aut si genus ipsum argumentationis vitiosum esse ostenditur* (negando formam vel certam, vel legitimam omnino) *aut si contra firmam argumentationem alia aeque firma, aut firmior, ponitur.*

§ 891. This counsel, § 890, is satisfied partly already by the confirmation itself, partly by the art of joining to our direct proof, and to the subversion of the antithesis’s premisses, or of its form of proving, or of both, things deduced from that same conclusion and antithesis taken as a premiss, lucidly, or even splendidly deduced, which yet at last and as if unexpectedly set before the eyes the great falsity and incongruity of the same for the analogue of reason, § 853, 884. Cicero de Inu. I. 63: *Every argumentation is refuted if either of those things that have been assumed one or more is not conceded* (by denying the premisses), *or, these being conceded, it is denied that the conclusion is made out from them: or if the very kind of argumentation is shown to be faulty* (by denying the form to be either certain or legitimate at all), *or if against a firm argumentation another equally firm, or firmer, is set.*

> § 892. [p. 615] In eadem reprehensione possunt plura membra disiunctionis a Cicerone positae post se inuicem tentari, §. 891. modo 2) armis aduersarii semper parentur contraria arma, quae plus verae lucis fundere videantur, vt nostrorum lumen maius obscuret illa. S. XXXX. Non aeque firma placent tantum, quantum firmiora, §. 891. Huc praeiudicia in reprehendendis latentia detegere, §. 870. eadem cum praemissis aliis falsis per instantias euidentiores infringere. S. L. comparationibus paralogismos reprehendendorum eludere, quorum euidentes praemissae tamen aperte falsam dent conclusionem, S. XXVIII. saltus illegitimos et supplendi impossibilitatem ob oculos ponere, e. c. quae logici docent, eleganter et ad analogi rationis modulos exsequi. §. 844.

§ 892. [p. 615] In the same refutation several members of the disjunction set down by Cicero can be attempted one after another, § 891, provided only 2) that against the adversary’s arms contrary arms are always prepared, which seem to pour forth more true light, so that the greater light of ours obscures theirs. S. XXXX. Equally firm ones please only as much as firmer ones, § 891. Hither belong: to uncover the prejudices lurking in what is to be refuted, § 870, to break them, together with other false premisses, by more evident instances, S. L, to elude by comparisons the paralogisms of what is to be refuted, whose evident premisses nevertheless give a plainly false conclusion, S. XXVIII, to set before the eyes illegitimate leaps and the impossibility of supplying what is missing, etc., what the logicians teach, to carry out elegantly and to the measures of the analogue of reason. § 844.

> § 893. In primis 3) vtiliter, ad hominem quae dicuntur argumenta, quem reprehendis, armis propriis aggrediendo adhibebuntur, quoniam hominem ipsi sibi contradicentem tanquam auctorem veritatis sequi, vix est, qui sibi persuadere possit, hinc labefactatur hoc modo certe praeiudicium auctoritatis, quod pro patronis antitheseos pugnare potuisset, tanquam aesthetice saltim solidis, [p. 616] §. 839. *Artificis est inuenire in actione aduersarii, quae in semet ipsa pugnent, aut pugnare videantur.* Quint. inst. V. 13. quod totum caput heic legi meretur. 4) In reprehendendo hoc magis sollicitus esto de genere cogitandi satis digno, §. 223. quo minus aestheticus cum logico suadere potest abstinentiam ab omnibus affectiones animi mouentibus, §. 22. quo difficilius est aliquando vehementer, neque tamen iracunde agere, §. 722-725.

§ 893. Especially 3) what are called arguments ad hominem will be usefully employed, by attacking the man you refute with his own arms, since there is scarcely anyone who can persuade himself to follow a man contradicting himself as an author of truth; hence in this way at least the prejudice of authority is shaken, which could have fought for the patrons of the antithesis, as at least aesthetically solid, [p. 616] § 839. *It is the part of the skilled man to find in the adversary’s pleading things that fight with themselves, or seem to fight.* Quint. inst. V. 13, the whole chapter of which deserves to be read here. 4) In refuting be the more solicitous about a manner of thinking sufficiently dignified, § 223, the less the aesthetician, with the logician, can urge abstinence from everything that moves the affects of the mind, § 22, and the more difficult it sometimes is to act vehemently and yet not angrily, § 722–725.

> § 894. Vltimum dignitatis consilium §. 182. heic etiam, tanquam ex ipsis eleganter cogitandi fontibus §. 866. fluens considerari velim, non tantum, quatenus idem virtus et pietas postulant, §. 183. Quod in obscoenis sibi permiserunt antiquorum non pauci, §. 184. in reprehendendo paene plures similem eidem licentiam sumserunt, vt adeo rationibus impugnare veterem, sed malum, morem eo magis necessarium videatur, quo pluribus eum, alioquin satis insignibus, exemplis hodierni imitatores eiusdem facile tueantur. Quomodo reprehendat apud Homerum heros heroa, quis nescit? Sed quanto iam in hoc Aeneis Virgilii moratior est? *In hoc ipso* (Demosthene) *diligenter examinante verborum omnium pondera reprehendit* [p. 617] *Aeschines quaedam et exagitat, illudensque dura, odiosa, intolerabilia esse dicit. Quin etiam quaerit ab ipso, quum quidem eum belluam appellet, vtrum illa verba, an portenta sint: vt Aeschini ne Demosthenes quidem videatur Attice dicere.* Cic. Or. 26. Ad reprehensionem hanc *belluae* cuius est erubescere? Demosthenis, an potius Aeschinis?

§ 894. The last counsel of dignity, § 182, I should wish to be considered here too as flowing from the very fountains of thinking elegantly, § 866, and not only insofar as virtue and piety demand the same, § 183. What not a few of the ancients permitted themselves in obscenities, § 184, almost more of them have taken a like licence in refuting, so that to impugn by reasons an old, but bad, custom seems the more necessary, the more examples, otherwise notable enough, today’s imitators of the same can easily shelter it by. How in Homer hero reprehends hero, who does not know? But how much more mannerly already is Virgil’s Aeneid in this? *In this very man* (Demosthenes), *who diligently examines the weight of all his words,* [p. 617] *Aeschines reprehends and harries certain things, and mocking them says they are harsh, odious, intolerable. Nay more, he asks him, since indeed he calls him a beast, whether those are words or monstrosities: so that to Aeschines not even Demosthenes seems to speak Attic.* Cic. Or. 26. At this refutation of the *beast*, whose part is it to blush? Demosthenes’s, or rather Aeschines’s?

> § 895. *Quanto rectius hic, qui nil molitur* inique Cassius contra Plancium et huius patronum, Ciceronem, cui tamen iam *grauiora atque magna* videntur, quod Ciceronis *discessum, quem saepe deflerat* Cassius, *nunc quasi reprehendere et subaccusare voluit, dicens non* Ciceroni *auxilium, sed* Ciceronem *auxilio defuisse?* Cic. pro Plancio 86. Quis nescit eundem discessum non *reprehendi*, sed etiam *exagitari* potuisse *duris, odiosis*, quaeque Ciceroni visa essent *intolerabilia*, verbis *illudendo* tam facta, quam non facta, nisi belle, §. 893. praetulisset accusator Plancii submissum dicendi genus in illius patronum? §. 725. Vtinam ipse Cicero in Pisonem, virum censorium, in ipsum Antonium, eleganti modestia vehementiam vbique temperasset. §722-724.

§ 895. *How much more rightly this man, who contrives nothing* wrongfully: Cassius against Plancius and his patron, Cicero, to whom nevertheless *weightier and great* things now seem to be at stake, because Cassius *wished now as it were to reprehend and covertly accuse* Cicero’s *departure, which he had often lamented, saying that not aid had failed* Cicero, *but* Cicero *had failed the aid*? Cic. pro Plancio 86. Who does not know that the same departure could have been not only *reprehended* but even *harried* with *harsh, odious* words and such as would have seemed *intolerable* to Cicero, *mocking* both what was done and what was not done, had not the accuser of Plancius prettily, § 893, preferred a subdued manner of speaking against Plancius’s patron? § 725. Would that Cicero himself, against Piso, a man of censorial rank, against Antony himself, had everywhere tempered his vehemence with elegant modesty. § 722–724.

> § 896. Non iambos Archilochi, non hendecasyllabos Catulli, non Nasonis Ibin, aut alia, caeteroquin venusta, sed ob neglectum bene [p. 618] moratum cogitandi genus turpiter reprehendentium

§ 896. Not the iambics of Archilochus, not the hendecasyllables of Catullus, not Naso’s Ibis, or other things, otherwise charming, but, on account of the neglected well-mannered [p. 618] manner of thinking of those who refute shamefully,

> *Tincta Lycambeo sanguine tela moror.* §. 893. 186.

*I delay the darts dyed in Lycambes’s blood.* § 893, 186.

> Si non itur, qua eundum est, nec eundum est grauitati aestheticae, qua itur §. 189. Nondum audeo praecipere generatim pulcre reprehensuris, vt abstineant omnino ab omnibus, quae personalia vel magis barbare personalitates dicunt, ab omnibus, quae singularem illum hominem, cui contradixeris, proxime tangunt, eiusque patriam, genus, ingenium, mores, vitam, adolescentiam, et si qua sunt alia, §. 752-757. fidenter tamen procul esse iubeo, si quis gratiis litare voluerit, vel in aduersariis ipsis rimari obiecta humillima et abiecta, §. 195. quoniam omnino non possunt exponi §. 224, 225. strictius morato cogitandi genere §. 227, vel absolute tantum tali. §. 228.

If one does not go where one must go, neither must aesthetic gravity go where one does go, § 189. I do not yet dare to prescribe in general to those who are to refute beautifully that they abstain altogether from everything that they call personal, or more barbarously personalities, from everything that most nearly touches that singular man whom you have contradicted, his fatherland, family, wit, character, life, youth, and whatever else there is, § 752–757; yet I confidently bid be far off, if anyone wishes to sacrifice to the graces, even the rummaging in the adversaries themselves for the lowest and most abject objects, § 195, since they cannot at all be set forth, § 224, 225, in a manner of thinking well-mannered in the stricter sense, § 227, or only absolutely such. § 228.

> § 897. Ne peccem ipse praestans, quod dissuadeo, non abiecta vel obtutu primo iuuat exempla proferre. Sufficiat vna Senecae apocolocyntosis in Claudium, qua Stoicus ille minus decantatam, forte tamen minus eluendam laudi virtutis suae maculam inussit, quam auaritia. Quis crederet? Philosophus, quantus Seneca videtur, exsul in Sardinia descenderat ad lacrumas et supplicationes [p. 619] in Polybium Claudii libertum profusas, in quibus sapientiae Claudii plus, quam satis est, adulatur, reuocatus ab eodem Claudio, non tam malo, quam simplici, multisque beneficiis cumulatus, quantum ab eodem aliquid proficisci poterat, quod eius nomine fiebat, eundem imperatorem suum post eius mortem ore Neronis laudat propter sapientiam adeo, vt risum mouerit audientibus, et idem sub tempus, vrgente nulla ratione politica, tamen tam acerbe ridet, veneno exstinctum, vt nec ab hoc sibi temperare ioco posset, quem nunquam sine indignatione legi: *Vltima vox eius haec inter homines audita est, quum maiorem sonitum emisisset illa parte, qua facilius loquebatur: Vae mi! puto, concacaui me.* Paene pudet haec scripsisse post Senecam.

§ 897. Lest I myself commit, by providing them, what I dissuade from, it is not pleasant to bring forward examples abject even at first glance. Let one suffice, Seneca’s apocolocyntosis against Claudius, by which that Stoic branded upon the praise of his virtue a stain less sung of, yet perhaps less to be washed out, than avarice. Who would believe it? A philosopher, as great as Seneca seems, in exile in Sardinia had descended to tears and supplications [p. 619] poured out to Polybius, Claudius’s freedman, in which he flatters the wisdom of Claudius more than is enough; recalled by the same Claudius, not so much a bad as a simple man, and heaped with many benefits, so far as anything could proceed from the same which was done in his name, he praises the same emperor, his own, after his death through the mouth of Nero for his wisdom, so that he moved the hearers to laughter, and at the same time, no political reason pressing, he nevertheless laughs so bitterly at the man killed by poison that he could not restrain himself even from this jest, which I have never read without indignation: *This was his last utterance heard among men, after he had emitted a greater sound from that part with which he spoke more easily: Oh dear! I think I have befouled myself.* It is almost shameful to have written these things after Seneca.

> § 898. Iniuriae verbales, quae vel simplicem honorem laedunt, turpissimae quidem in reprehensionibus sunt, quae maiestatem sublimium tueri debeant §. 317. turpiores in medio cogitandi genere, quod ciuilitatem et mores intensi iam honoris postulat, §. 278. neque tamen in ipso tenui cogitandi genere carent turpitudine, §. 262. Prius impetitus eiusmodi luto si fueris, nec a retorsionibus abstinere debeas aggressori, debes tibi, debes spectatoribus, et ipsi magnanimitati aestheticae. [p. 620] §. 189, 275. S. XXIIII-XXVI. Ad hunc lapidem Lydium argumentum ab inuidia, consequentiarum synathroismos, immeritas vel immodicas irrisiones examinemus, memores nationis et saeculi, §. 867. quorum huic ferenda quae videantur, illi tamen ἦθος omnino iam laedere iudicabuntur. §. 213, 212.

§ 898. Verbal injuries, which wound even simple honour, are indeed most shameful in refutations which ought to guard the majesty of sublime things, § 317; more shameful in the middle manner of thinking, which already demands civility and the manners of intensified honour, § 278; nor yet are they free of shamefulness in the thin manner of thinking itself, § 262. If you have first been assailed with mud of this kind, and ought not to abstain from retorts against the aggressor, you owe it to yourself, you owe it to the spectators, and to aesthetic magnanimity itself, [p. 620] § 189, 275, S. XXIIII–XXVI, to examine on this Lydian stone the argument from envy, the synathroismi of consequences, undeserved or immoderate mockeries, mindful of the nation and the age, § 867, of which what seem bearable to the one will nevertheless be judged by the other already to wound the ἦθος [character] altogether. § 213, 212.

> § 899. Et bonis moribus facilius obedies, et inanem operam insumere saepius supersedebis, si tibi dictum putes 5) neutiquam reprehendenda tibi esse omnia, quae contra tuas sententias, vel dicta sint, vel dici possint, sed ea tantum, quae suspicaris obiecto tuo personali primario verisimilia, nisi reprehendas, quaeque speraueris post reprensionem tuam ab eodem in aesthetice falsis habenda, §. 887. Par ratio responsionum ad reprehensiones aliorum in nos nostraque directarum, §. 886, 898. Quemadmodum *illud stultissime praecipitur, quod defendi non possit, silentio dissimulandum, siquidem est id, de quo iudex pronunciaturus est:* ita alii, *diligentia lapsi, verbis etiam, vel sententiolis omnibus respondendum putant*, quae contradici posse autumant, *quod est et infinitum et superuacuum* §. 171. *Sit, cui respondeas.* Caue *vitium nimium soliciti, et circa omnia momenta luctantis.* Quint. inst. V. XIII. Quot scriptis galeatus ille prologus [p. 621] aptari potuisset minus eleganter, quem belle praemisit Cicero l. I. de finibus bonorum et malorum?

§ 899. You will both more easily obey good morals, and more often spare yourself the expending of vain labour, if you think it said to you 5) that by no means are all things to be refuted by you that either have been said or can be said against your opinions, but only those which you suspect to be verisimilar to your primary personal object unless you refute them, and which you may hope, after your refutation, will be held by the same among aesthetically false things, § 887. The same reckoning holds for answers to the refutations of others directed against us and ours, § 886, 898. Just as *that is most foolishly prescribed, that what cannot be defended should be dissembled by silence, if indeed it is that on which the judge is to pronounce:* so others, *lapsing through diligence, think that answer must be made even to all the words or little sentences* that they suppose can be contradicted, *which is both endless and superfluous*, § 171. *Let there be something you answer.* Beware *the vice of one too anxious, and wrestling with every moment.* Quint. inst. V. XIII. To how many writings could that helmeted prologue [p. 621] have been fitted less elegantly, which Cicero prettily set before l. I. de finibus bonorum et malorum?

#### Sectio LIII. Argumenta Persuasoria. — Section LIII. Persuasive Arguments

> § 900. ARGVMENTA, quorum (vel vnica, vel potior, vel nunc maxime consideranda) vis est sensitiuam datae perceptioni certitudinem conciliare, sunt PERSVASORIA §. 829. Ergo omnia argumenta, omnes figurae viuide probantes, S. XXXIII. verisimilitudinemque pulcram illustrantes, Sect. XXXIII. [sic: XXXXIII.] erunt persuasoriae, §. 26. Habes ansam intendendi tuorum argumentorum efficaciam eleganter, §. 142. si probantia potissimum illustres, et pingentia veritati consecres aestheticae, quoniam tunc illa non probabunt solum, haec non splendorem solum afferent, sed vtraque simul persuadebunt. §. 143. Sic pleonasmus apparens, cuius otiose positum ad dandam alterius hypothesin et determinationem, vel omnino medium terminum, negotiosum est, confirmabit, §. 145, 855. e. g. *Hisce meis oculis vidi.* Contra id:

§ 900. ARGUMENTS whose power (whether the only one, or the chief one, or the one now most to be considered) is to procure sensate certainty for a given perception are PERSUASIVE, § 829. Therefore all arguments, all figures that prove vividly, S. XXXIII, and that illustrate beautiful verisimilitude, Sect. XXXIII, will be persuasive, § 26. You have a handle for elegantly intensifying the efficacy of your arguments, § 142, if you illustrate especially those that prove, and consecrate those that paint to aesthetic truth, since then the former will not only prove, the latter will not only bring splendour, but both together will persuade. § 143. Thus an apparent pleonasm, whose idly placed element is busy in giving the hypothesis and determination of another, or in general the middle term, will confirm, § 145, 855, e.g. *With these my own eyes I saw it.* Against that:

> *Vidimus? an qui amant ipsi sibi somnia fingunt?*

*Have we seen? or do those who love fashion dreams for themselves?*

> § 901. [p. 622] Pari artificio, quae videantur synonomiae, vel exergasiae, coniungi possunt, tanquam aequipollentes, quarum tamen acutior lector vel auditor, vnam videat rationem, in elegantibus, sufficientem alterius, §. 900, 146. Confirmaturus, §. 878-885. satisfacturus et reprehendens §. 899. memor, probantia quaedam vel refellentia in vmbras coniecturus, venuste nonnunquam recurret ad praeteritionem. §. 148. Nec poenitet huc INTERROGATIONEM retulisse, §. 332. seu crypticam declarationem nos optare, vt aliquis conscientiam suam de veritate alicuius rei dicat, vel cogitet. Prudens enim si caueris modo, ne interroges, vbi personale tuum obiectum primarium vel haesurum, vel omnino dissensurum, praeuideri poterat, sine vlteriori addita persuasione: vna apta interrogatione multum obtinebis, vt auditor e. c. ipse sibi tradat, et in mentem denuo reuocet, quicquid rationum de re, quam asseris, iam nouerat, et simul tibi concilietur non raro, quem suae iam scientiae non parum confidere non inuitus animaduertit, §. 840. aliquando sensibilius moueatur, quem inuites intra se descendere sensus animi scrutaturum intimos, et ea certa sibi iam dudum deprehendere, quae nunc bona vel mala dicuntur. §. 142.

§ 901. [p. 622] By a like artifice, things that would seem synonymies or exergasiae can be joined as equipollent, of which, nevertheless, the more acute reader or hearer would see one to be the reason, sufficient in elegant matters, of the other, § 900, 146. The one who is to confirm, § 878–885, who is to satisfy and refute, mindful of § 899, being about to cast certain proving or refuting things into the shades, will sometimes charmingly have recourse to preterition. § 148. Nor am I sorry to have referred hither INTERROGATION, § 332, or the cryptic declaration that we wish someone to state, or to think, his own consciousness about the truth of some matter. For if only you prudently take care not to interrogate where it could be foreseen that your primary personal object would either hesitate or altogether dissent, without further persuasion added: by one apt interrogation you will obtain much, so that the hearer, e.g., himself hands over to himself and recalls to mind afresh whatever reasons he already knew about the matter you assert, and at the same time not rarely is won over to you, when he notices, not unwillingly, that you place no small confidence in his own knowledge, § 840; sometimes he is moved more sensibly, when you invite him to descend into himself to search the innermost senses of his mind, and to find already long since certain for himself those things which are now called good or bad. § 142.

> § 902. [p. 623] Repetitio, cum multis suis speciebus heic etiam repetatur, vel ob id ipsum, quod non solum persuadet, §. 333. sed tamen magnam persuadendi vim habet, non inepta quaeuis, et tautologica, sed aetiologiarum praecipuarum in rotundam aliquam breuitatem contractarum. §. 545. Omnis enim aetiologia viuide cogitata quum sit argumentum persuasorium, §. 839. illarum eam, sine qua non posse videatur absolui persuasio posse, dicamus cum veteribus RATIONEM per eminentiam, et aetiologiarum rationumue potissimam, FIRMAMENTVM, cf. Cicero de Inu. I. 18, 19. Rationem et firmamentum vel iisdem, vel paullulum inflexis cogitandi modis breuiter, sed iterato cogitandam sistere, vel hoc habet efficaciae ad persuadendum, vt firmius haereat animis obiecti tui personalis, cui potissimum argumento confidis. §. 342-345. Non sine persuadendi lenocinio *peruigilium Veneris* toties repetit:

§ 902. [p. 623] Repetition, with its many species, is here also to be repeated, even for this very reason, that it not only persuades, § 333, but has indeed a great power of persuading, not any inept and tautological repetition, but that of the principal aetiologies contracted into some rounded brevity. § 545. For since every aetiology vividly thought is a persuasive argument, § 839, let us call that one of them without which persuasion would seem unable to be completed, with the ancients, the REASON by eminence, and the chief of the aetiologies or reasons, the FIRMAMENT, cf. Cicero de Inu. I. 18, 19. To set the reason and the firmament before the mind for thinking briefly, but repeatedly, either in the same or in slightly inflected modes of thinking, has this efficacy for persuading, that the argument in which you place most confidence sticks more firmly in the mind of your personal object. § 342–345. Not without the allurement of persuasion the *Pervigilium Veneris* so often repeats:

> *Nunc amet, qui nunquam amauit. Quique amauit, nunc amet.*

*Now let him love who never loved. And he who has loved, now let him love.*

> § 903. In his argumentis commendetur probationum climax et ea gradatio, §. 334. qua totum certissima sua parte certius esse redditum, non aurificis statera, sed quadam populari trutina examinatum videatur, §. 250, [p. 624] 879. Cauturus vel vmbram anticlimacis in probando, ne facile persuadearis eorum consiliis, qui debilius argumentum fortioribus interserere suadent, quod praemittere non audeas. §. 879. An vnquam venustus a certioribus in incertiora decursus, nisi forsan in iocis pyrrhonicis? In hyperbolis confirmantium e. g. *sole meridiano clarius est*, et reprehendentium e. g. *contra solem loquutos* praeferantur crypticae, quae sic limites certitudinis improbabilitatisque assignandae transgrediantur, vt id ipsum factum esse vix ac ne vix quidem appareat. §. 339.

§ 903. In these arguments let the climax of proofs be commended, and that gradation, § 334, by which the whole seems to have been rendered more certain than its most certain part, examined not by the goldsmith’s balance but by a certain popular scale, § 250, [p. 624] 879. Being on guard against even the shade of an anticlimax in proving, do not be easily persuaded by the counsels of those who urge interposing among stronger arguments a weaker one, which you would not dare to put first. § 879. Is a running-down from the more certain to the less certain ever charming, unless perhaps in Pyrrhonian jests? In the hyperboles of those who confirm, e.g. *it is clearer than the noonday sun*, and of those who refute, e.g. *those who have spoken against the sun*, let cryptic ones be preferred, which so transgress the limits of the certainty and improbability to be assigned that this very thing scarcely, or not even scarcely, appears to have been done. § 339.

> § 904. Non nego Quintiliani regulam §. 903. *Fiduciam orator* (pulcre persuasurus omnis) *prae se ferat, semperque ita dicat* (significanda cogitet) *tanquam de casu optime cogitet* (de persuadendis suis obiectis personalibus probe persuasus). Inst. V. 13. Moneo tantum, ne nimiae certitudinis ostentator de fide periclitetur. Hinc agnosco casus, in quibus belle ad confirmandum reprehendendumue possit adhiberi DVBITATIO, narratio vel simulatio status animi, cui rationes pro quadam sententia pugnantes et contra eandem connumeranti censentur aequales, praesertim si venuste transeas ab hac ad bellam euidentiae parrhesian. §. 349. S. L.

§ 904. I do not deny Quintilian’s rule, § 903: *Let the orator* (everyone who is to persuade beautifully) *display confidence, and always speak* (think what is to be signified) *as though he thought best of his case* (thoroughly persuaded concerning the personal objects he is to persuade). Inst. V. 13. I only warn that the ostentatious displayer of excessive certainty is in danger as to his credit. Hence I recognise cases in which DOUBT can prettily be employed for confirming or refuting, the narration or simulation of a state of mind for which, counting up the reasons fighting for a certain opinion and against it, they are reckoned equal, especially if you charmingly pass from this to a pretty parrhesia of evidence. § 349. S. L.
